questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Ranjit Singh01-39’s Sikh State — Why Did It Hold While He Lived and Collapse After His Death?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"Ranjit Singh01-39 built a powerful Sikh State that held together for almost forty years. Yet within a decade of his death, it was lost to the EIC. Examine the reasons."
Demand of the question: Show what held the Sikh State together under Ranjit Singh01-39 + show why those binding factors broke after his death.
Suggested intro (~25 words): "Ranjit Singh01-39 united the Misls into one strong Sikh State. The State held by his personal command. When he died in 1839, those personal threads snapped."
Guiding themes:

1. Misl unification + personal authority — Ranjit Singh01-39 brought the 12 Misls under one rule by 1801. Authority rested on his person, not on institutions. (see 'How did Ranjit Singh01-39 unify the Misls and build a powerful Sikh State?')

2. 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC — stopped Sikh State expansion south of the Sutlej. Bought time but locked the State into a fixed boundary. (see 'What were the terms of the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC?')

3. Expansion + modernised army — post-1809 Ranjit Singh01-39 pushed west and north; built a European-trained army with French and Italian officers. (see 'How far did Ranjit Singh01-39 expand the Sikh State after 1809?' and 'What kind of State did Ranjit Singh01-39 build — and what made it hold together?')

4. Post-1839 collapse — weak successors, court factionalism, palace intrigues; the EIC won the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-46) and the Second (1848-49); Punjab annexed 1849. (See Ch 14 — 'What were the terms of the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC?' Sikh State annexation)
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): "Ranjit Singh01-39 built a State that ran on his person. With no institutions to outlast him, the State could not survive his death."
revise: How did Ranjit Singh01-39 unify the Misls and build a powerful Sikh State?
What were the terms of the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC?
How far did Ranjit Singh01-39 expand the Sikh State after 1809?
What kind of State did Ranjit Singh01-39 build — and what made it hold together?
What were the terms of the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC?

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Tipu Sultan's modern embassies
questions.stem: Prelims 2001 — Who among the following Indian rulers established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines?
explanation: Answer: (d)

Why (d) is correct: Tipu82-99 set up modern embassies in France, Turkey, & Egypt — alongside other administrative innovations such as a new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. You will find this in 'What made Tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?' (inside the ⚠ Alert block). The chapter's 'What made Tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?' section also covers Tipu82-99's iron-cased rocket artillery (later studied by William Congreve), his government-owned trading company (30 trading centres including Muscat, Oman), his sanad request to the Khalifa, and his French alliance — Tree of Liberty + Jacobin Club membership — which alarmed the British and became one of the reasons for the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War of 1799.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Haider Ali61-82 built the modern Mysore army on a French model (with Risalas) and fought the EIC in the early Anglo-Mysore Wars, but he did not set up modern embassies in foreign countries.
2. (b) Mir Qasim was a Nawab of Bengal who fought the EIC at the Battle of Buxar (1764) — covered elsewhere in your notes — and did not establish foreign embassies.
3. (c) Shah Alam II60-06 was the Mughal Emperor whose authority was reduced after Buxar; foreign embassies were not part of his programme.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: With reference to Akbar56-05's co-option of the Rajputs, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Around the 16th century, Rajputana had no single central power — there were roughly twenty major Rajput clans.
2. Akbar56-05 co-opted the more powerful Rajput chiefs, who then helped him subdue the smaller ones.
3. The chosen Rajput chiefs were brought into the Mughal system as Mansabdars; their home territories were recognised as Vatan Jagirs.
4. Rajputs made up roughly 15% of all Mansabdars — the Hindu bloc within the Mansabdari system.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. All four facts are taken from the record: 16th-c Rajputana with ~20 clans + Akbar56-05's selective co-option + the Mansabdar/Vatan-Jagir framework + the 15% Hindu bloc.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the 1680 Rajput revolt under Aurangzeb58-07?

options.text: The revolt was led by all twenty major Rajput clans together against Mughal taxation.

Aurangzeb58-07 interfered in Marwar's succession; Marwar and Mewar both revolted, but other Rajput chiefs refused to join — fearing Mewar's dominance would replace Mughal dominance — & the rebellion collapsed.
The revolt succeeded and established an independent Rajput federation under Sawai Jai Singh99-43.
The revolt was triggered by the Subsidiary Alliance imposed by the EIC.

explanation: is correct. The record carries the answer: Aurangzeb58-07's 1680 interference in Marwar's succession + Marwar+Mewar revolt + other chiefs refusing to join (fear of Mewar dominance) + rebellion collapsing. (a), (c), (d) are factually wrong.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: With reference to Marthanda Varma29-58 & the Battle of Colachel 1741, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Marthanda Varma29-58 built a strong, centralised State by subjugating local chiefs across the region.
2. He built a European-style military with modern weapons and trained soldiers.
3. At the Battle of Colachel (1741), Marthanda Varma29-58's army crushed the Dutch East India Company.
4. The defeat permanently ended Dutch political and military ambitions in Kerala.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. All four facts are taken from the record: Marthanda Varma29-58 (1729–58) + European-style military + 1741 Battle of Colachel + the permanent end of Dutch political-military ambitions in Kerala.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the State monopoly Travancore established on the Malabar coast?

options.text: The monopoly was on Dutch spice imports only and was abolished after the 1741 victory.

Travancore established a State monopoly over Malabar-coast trade; revenues were reinvested into the military, irrigation works, & transport infrastructure — a classic example of a small State using trade income to build State capacity.
The monopoly was a joint venture between Travancore and the EIC under the 1805 Subsidiary Alliance.
The monopoly was on Portuguese pepper exports only.

explanation: is correct. The record ◆ Takeaway carries the answer: Travancore's State monopoly over Malabar trade + revenues reinvested into military / irrigation / transport + the State-capacity-from-trade thesis. (a), (c), (d) are factually wrong.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: With reference to the 1805 Subsidiary Alliance & 1809 Velu Thampi revolt, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In 1805, a mutiny broke out among the Nair troops over non-payment of salaries.
2. Travancore sought British help and was compelled to sign a Subsidiary Alliance (1805).
3. Velu Thampi Dalawa was the Prime Minister of Travancore.
4. In 1809, Velu Thampi rallied the Nair troops and issued the Kundara Proclamation calling on the people to rise against British control; the revolt was suppressed and Velu Thampi took his own life.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. All four facts are taken from the record: 1805 Nair mutiny + Subsidiary Alliance 1805 + Velu Thampi Dalawa as PM + the 1809 Kundara Proclamation revolt + the suicide.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the 1565 Battle of Talikota?

options.text: A battle between the Marathas and Tipu82-99 leading to the annexation of Mysore.

Also called Rakkasa-Tangadi; a coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeated the Vijayanagar forces; 1565 marks the operational end of Vijayanagar as a major power, even though the dynasty lingered until 1646.
A naval battle between Travancore and the Dutch East India Company.
The battle in which Haider Ali61-82 overthrew NanjRaj.

explanation: is correct. The record carries the answer: Battle of Talikota / Rakkasa-Tangadi 1565 + Deccan Sultanates coalition + operational end of Vijayanagar in 1565 + dynasty lingered until 1646. (a), (c), (d) are factually wrong.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: With reference to Haider Ali61-82's takeover of Mysore in 1761, consider the following statements:
items: 1. By 1761, the Wodeyars had been reduced to figureheads by a powerful and corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj.
2. Haider Ali61-82 began as a junior military officer; the Wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts.
3. In 1761, he overthrew NanjRaj and seized effective power — while keeping the Wodeyar as a nominal head of State.
4. He took French assistance for military training, technology transfer, & organisational reform — restructuring the army into Risalas (regiments).
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. All four facts are taken from the record: 1761 NanjRaj reduces Wodeyars to figureheads + Haider Ali61-82 begins as junior officer + 1761 overthrow of NanjRaj + Wodeyar as nominal head + French assistance + Risala restructuring.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the subjugation of Poligars and Deshmukhs under Haider Ali61-82?

options.text: Poligars were Mughal-appointed governors of Mysore districts; Deshmukhs were senior military commanders.

Poligars were local chieftains and landlords who controlled land, temples, & their own armed men — the real rulers of the countryside since the Vijayanagar era; Deshmukhs were revenue collectors who functioned like primary zamindars; both were systematically subjugated over roughly twenty years to dismantle non-State power.
Poligars were French-trained infantry units; Deshmukhs were Khalisa-land tax collectors.
Poligars and Deshmukhs were the same office under different names in different parts of Mysore.

explanation: is correct. The record carries the answer: Poligars = local chieftains + temples + armed men + countryside-rulers since Vijayanagar; Deshmukhs = revenue collectors functioning like primary zamindars; 20-year subjugation; non-State power systematically dismantled. (a), (c), (d) are factually wrong.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: With reference to Military Fiscalism in Mysore, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Khalisa land (revenue went directly to the State treasury) was expanded.
2. Jagirdari land (revenue assigned to nobles or commanders) was shrunk.
3. Deshmukhs were removed as intermediaries; State officials collected taxes directly and received salaries.
4. Detailed field surveys assessed land fairly — soil fertility, crop type, irrigation access, past production trends — preventing over-assessment.
5. Sericulture (silk cultivation) was introduced; cash crops were promoted; old irrigation canals were repaired and new ones built.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. All five components of Military Fiscalism are taken from the record: Khalisa expansion + Jagirdari shrinkage + Deshmukh removal as intermediaries + field surveys preventing over-assessment + sericulture + cash crops + irrigation investments.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Prelims 2001 — replicated for practice. Who among the following Indian rulers established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines?
explanation: Tipu82-99. The record carries the answer (Prelims 2001 verbatim): Tipu82-99 set up modern embassies in France, Turkey, & Egypt + the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar + new coinage. (a), (b), (c) are factually wrong distractors.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to Tipu82-99's military and administrative innovations, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Tipu82-99 built a modern navy and established a government-owned trading company modelled on the EIC, with thirty trading centres including Muscat, Oman.
2. He developed iron-cased rocket artillery — later studied by the British; William Congreve's rockets drew directly from Tipu82-99's designs.
3. He set up modern embassies in France, Turkey, & Egypt — alongside a new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar.
4. He sent a request to the Khalifa for a sanad — an official order recognising him as a ruler independent of Mughal authority.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. All four facts are taken from the record: modern navy + 30-centre government trading company (incl. Muscat) + iron-cased rockets (Congreve linkage) + embassies in France/Turkey/Egypt + Mauludi Calendar + Khalifa sanad request.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: With reference to Tipu82-99's French alliance and ideological positioning, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the 1790s, Tipu82-99 sent an ambassador to France seeking military technology and a formal alliance against the British.
2. In 1798, Napoleon attacked Egypt and the Middle East — partly to disrupt British trade in the Arabian Sea.
3. Tipu82-99 planted a Tree of Liberty in Mysore as a symbolic gesture of friendship with revolutionary France.
4. Tipu82-99 became a member of the Jacobin Club — the radical political organisation at the heart of the French Revolution.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. All four facts are taken from the record: 1790s France ambassador + 1798 Napoleon Egypt + Tree of Liberty in Mysore + Jacobin Club membership.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the end of Mysore's power?

options.text: Mysore was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1856.

The Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) ended with the death of Tipu82-99 at Seringapatam, & Mysore's power was broken — the ambition (dominate South India + control international trade) was real, but the capacity, ultimately, was not enough.
Mysore was annexed via Subsidiary Alliance in 1805 alongside Travancore.
Mysore voluntarily merged with the Maratha Confederacy after the Third Battle of Panipat 1761.

explanation: is correct. The record carries the answer: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War 1799 + Tipu82-99's death at Seringapatam + Mysore's power broken + the ambition-vs-capacity thesis (Vijayanagar 2.0 ambition; Military Fiscalism couldn't replenish faster than warfare drained). (a), (c), (d) are factually wrong.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Why did the Already Autonomous States survive longer than the Successor States?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"The Already Autonomous States (Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore) lasted longer in the 18th century than the Mughal Successor States (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad). Examine the reasons."

Demand of the question: Show why the three Already Autonomous States survived longer + compare with how Successor States collapsed earlier. The verb "examine" means lay out the reasons clearly using regional evidence.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Already Autonomous States survived longer than the Successor States because each carried a pre-Mughal identity, a defensible geography, and a strategic resource base of its own.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Pre-Mughal identity — Rajputs had centuries-old clan identity (see 'Akbar56-05 and Rajputs' and 'Rajputs vs Aurangzeb58-07 and Marathas'); Travancore was never under the Mughals (see 'Travancore:'; Mysore inherited Vijayanagar legacy (see 'How did Mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century India?'.
2. Defensible geography — Rajputana desert + Travancore Western Ghats + Mysore plateau limited Mughal/Maratha reach.

3. Resource base — Travancore Malabar trade monopoly (see 'Travancore:'; Mysore Military Fiscalism (see 'How did Mysore fund this military machine?'; Rajputs in trade-route control (Marwar Delhi-Agra-Ahmedabad).

4. State capacity — Marthanda Varma29-58 + Haider Ali61-82 built modern European-style armies (see 'Travancore:' and 'How did Mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century India?'); Rajputs preserved Mansabdari but on their own terms after 1707 (see 'Rajputs vs Aurangzeb58-07 and Marathas'.

5. Slower EIC takeover — EIC used Subordinate Alliance (Subsidiary Alliance) rather than direct annexation, buying time (see 'Rajputs vs Aurangzeb58-07 and Marathas' and 'Travancore vs Mysore & EIC'); Mysore lasted till Fourth Anglo-Mysore War 1799; Travancore till SA 1805 + Velu Thampi revolt 1809.
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): Pre-existing identity + geography + a strategic resource base gave the Already Autonomous States the slack the Successor States never had.
revise: How did Mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century India?
How did Mysore fund this military machine?

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Compare Mysore (Haider Ali + Tipu) and Travancore (Marthanda Varma) approaches to building State capacity in the 18th century.
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"Both Mysore and Travancore built strong State capacity in the 18th century, yet by different routes. Compare the two approaches."
Demand of the question: Compare — cover similarities + differences — across military, fiscal, and institutional dimensions. Conclude with the contrast in outcome.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Mysore (Haider Ali61-82 + Tipu82-99) and Travancore (Marthanda Varma29-58) both built strong 18th-century States — but Mysore through Military Fiscalism, Travancore through trade monopoly.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Military reorganisation — Mysore French-assisted Risalas + iron-cased rocket artillery + modern navy (see 'How did Mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century India?' and 'What made Tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?'); Travancore European-style army that crushed the Dutch at the Battle of Colachel (1741) (see 'Travancore:'.

2. Revenue base — Mysore Military Fiscalism: Khalisa expansion + Jagirdari shrinkage + field surveys + sericulture + irrigation (see 'How did Mysore fund this military machine?'; Travancore State monopoly on Malabar coast trade reinvested in military + irrigation + transport (see 'Travancore:'.

3. Institutional reach — Mysore Haider Ali61-82 subjugated Poligars + Deshmukhs (see 'How did Mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century India?'; Travancore Marthanda Varma29-58 subjugated local chiefs to centralise the State (see 'Travancore:'.

4. International strategy — Mysore Tipu82-99 sent embassies to France/Turkey/Egypt + alliance with revolutionary France (see 'What made Tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?'; Travancore Marthanda Varma29-58 ended Dutch ambitions at Colachel 1741 (see 'Travancore:'.

5. Outcome contrast — Mysore wars drained State faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish (see 'What made Tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?'; fell at Fourth Anglo-Mysore War 1799. Travancore signed Subsidiary Alliance 1805 + Velu Thampi revolt 1809 (see 'Travancore vs Mysore & EIC'.
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): Mysore chose military fiscalism; Travancore chose trade monopoly. Both built strong States; both ultimately lost to the EIC by different routes.
revise: How did Mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century India?
How did Mysore fund this military machine?
What made Tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Hughly piracy in the Bay of Bengal
questions.stem: Prelims 1995 — Hughly was used as a base for piracy in the Bay of Bengal by
explanation: Answer: (a)

Why (a) is correct: The Portuguese had been misusing their trade privileges from their Bengal base — engaging in piracy & the slave trade. This is why Shahjahan27-58 ordered his Bengal governor Qasim Khan to take direct action in 1631–32, defeating the Portuguese and ejecting them from Hugli. You will find this in 'Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe (1615-19)'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (b) The French had no Bengal piracy base — their factories at Chandernagore (1690s) were trading posts, not pirate dens.
2. (c) The Danish base was at Tranquebar (Tamil Nadu) and Serampore (Bengal, from 1755) — both lawful trading posts.
3. (d) The British EIC's Bengal entry came after 1651 (Hugli factory under Shah Shuja's nishan) — well after the Portuguese piracy had been suppressed by Shahjahan27-58.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: European-entry statements
questions.stem: Prelims 2003 — With reference to the entry of European powers into India, which one of the following statements is not correct?

options.text: The English opened their first factory in South India at Masulipatnam
In Eastern India, the English Company opened its first factory in Orissa in 1633
Under the leadership of Dupleix, the French occupied Madras in 1746

explanation: Answer: (a)

Why (a) is the not-correct option: Albuquerque captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510, not 1499. Vasco Da Gama arrived at Calicut in 1498 — he traded and departed without establishing any settlement. You will find this in '2nd Governor Afonso de Albuquerque09-15 (1509–1515)'.
Why the other options are correct (and so not the answer):
1. (b) The English first South-India factory was at Masulipatnam (1611) — a real fact in 'What Made the Dutch VOC Historically Unique?' (cross-referenced).
2. (c) The English first Eastern-India factory was at Balasore and Hariharpur in Orissa in 1633 — a real fact.
3. (d) Dupleix42-54 did capture Madras in 1746 (1st Carnatic War, with La Bourdonnais35-46) — a real fact.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.title: Modern Kochi
questions.stem: Prelims 2005 — Which one of the following is a correct statement?

options.text: Modern Kochi was a Dutch colony till India's independence
The Dutch defeated the Portuguese and built Fort Williams in the modern Kochi
Modern Kochi was first a Dutch Colony before the Portuguese took over
Modern Kochi never became a part of the British Colony

explanation: Answer: (b)

Why (b) is correct: The Dutch captured Cochin from the Portuguese in 1663 & held it as their key base in South India (Summary Table T2 row). You will find this in 'What Made the Dutch VOC Historically Unique?'.
Why the other options are wrong:

1. (a) Modern Kochi was NOT a Dutch colony till India's independence — Cochin came under British rule from 1795 till 1947.2. (c) The order is reversed — Portuguese came first (1500), Dutch took it from them (1663).
3. (d) Cochin was part of the British Colony after 1795 till 1947.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.title: 1613 EIC factory permission
questions.stem: Prelims 2006 — In the year 1613, where was the English East India Company given permission to set up a factory (trading post)?
explanation: Answer: (d)

Why (d) is correct: Jahangir05-27 issued a Royal Farman in 1613, the imperial decree that gave the EIC the legal right to set up a permanent factory at Surat, following the Battle of Swally (1612). You will find this in 'How EIC Broke Portuguese Dominance and Establish Itself in India?'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Bangalore had no EIC factory in 1613 — it became part of British India only after the Anglo-Mysore Wars (1799 onwards).
2. (b) Madras was acquired from Hindu Nayakas in 1639, not 1613.
3. (c) Masulipatnam had a temporary EIC factory in 1611 — but the 1613 imperial farman was specifically for Surat.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.title: First British fort
questions.stem: Prelims 2007 — Which one of the following was the first fort constructed by the British in India?
explanation: Answer: (b)

Why (b) is correct: Fort St. George (Madras) was built between 1639 & 1644 — the first fort built by the EIC in India and the anchor of the first permanent settlement. You will find this in 'Madras Presidency (from 1652/1653)'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Fort William at Calcutta was built between 1696–1700 — much later than Fort St. George.
2. (c) Fort Saint David at Cuddalore was acquired in 1690 (purchased from Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram89-00) — also later, and not built but purchased.
3. (d) Fort St. Angelo (Kannur Fort) was built by the Portuguese in 1505, not the British.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.title: Last Europeans to come
questions.stem: Prelims 2007 — Who among the following Europeans, were the last to come to pre-independence India as traders?
explanation: Answer: (c)

Why (c) is correct: The French East India Company was founded in 1664 & set up its first Indian factory at Surat in 1668 — the latest among the four. You will find this in 'The French in India — and the Story of Pondicherry'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Dutch first factory in India: Masulipatnam, 1605 ('What Made the Dutch VOC Historically Unique?'.
2. (b) English EIC first factory in India: Masulipatnam, 1611 ('How EIC Broke Portuguese Dominance and Establish Itself in India?'.
3. (d) Portuguese first arrived in India: Vasco Da Gama at Calicut, 1498 ('the Portuguese in India').
The full chronology is: Portuguese 1498 → Dutch 1605 → English 1611 → Danish 1620 → French 1664/1668.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.title: Pondicherry occupation sequence
questions.stem:
Prelims 2010 — With reference to Pondicherry, consider:
(1) The first European power to occupy Pondicherry were the Portuguese.
(2) The second European power to occupy Pondicherry were the French.
(3) The English never occupied Pondicherry.
explanation: Answer: (a)

Why (a) is correct: Statement 1 is correct — the Portuguese were the first to occupy Pondicherry (16th century). The full layered sequence is: Portuguese (16th c.) → Danes (briefly 1624) → French (1674) → Dutch (briefly 1693) → English (1761/1793/1814) → India (1954). You will find this in 'The French in India — and the Story of Pondicherry' (inside the ⚠ Alert block).
Why the other statements are wrong:
1. Statement 2 is wrong — the second occupiers were the Danes (briefly in 1624), not the French. The French came fourth, in 1674.
2. Statement 3 is wrong — the English captured Pondicherry multiple times (1761, 1793, 1814) — they restored it to the French each time via subsequent treaties.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.title: English introductions to India
questions.stem:
Prelims 2012 — Which of the following were introduced into India by the English?
(1) Land-revenue assessment by soil and crop.
(2) Mobile cannons in warfare.
(3) Tobacco and red chillies.
explanation: Answer: (d)
Why (d) is correct: None of the three were introduced by the English. You will find the cross-reference in 'Why Did the Portuguese Decline?' (Portuguese contributions).
Why each statement is wrong:
1. Statement 1 — Land-revenue assessment by soil and crop was already prevalent in medieval India (Sher Shah Suri, Akbar's Todar Mal system) long before the British.
2. Statement 2 — Mobile cannons in warfare were introduced by Babur26-30 at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 — not by the English.
3. Statement 3 — Tobacco and red chillies were introduced by the PortugueseSec. 4.8 (Why Did the Portuguese Decline?)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.title: 1st quarter of 17C English factories
questions.stem:
Prelims 2015 — In the first quarter of seventeenth century, in which of the following was/were the factory/factories of the English East India Company located?
(1) Broach (2) Chicacole (3) Trichinopoly
explanation: Answer: (a)

Why (a) is correct: Among the three, only Broach (Bharuch) had an EIC factory in the first quarter of the 17th century. EIC factories during 1616–19 (Roe-era expansion) were at Agra, Ahmedabad, & Broach (Bharuch) — all within the Mughal Empire. You will find this in 'Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe (1615-19)'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. Chicacole (today's Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh) had no EIC factory in this period — it was outside Mughal direct control and EIC trading there came much later.
2. Trichinopoly (Tamil Nadu) was deep in the Carnatic — the EIC's South India trade in the early 17th century was centred on Masulipatnam, not Trichinopoly.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.10
questions.title: Bengal export staples
questions.stem: Prelims 2018 — The staple commodities of export by the English East India Company from Bengal in the middle of the 18th century were

options.text: raw cotton, oil seeds and opium
copper, silver, gold, spices and tea

explanation: Answer: (d)

explanation: Answer: (c)

Both Charters were issued by Parliament; both reduced EIC privileges.
The 1657 Charter granted territorial sovereignty in Bengal; the 1661 Charter restricted trading rights to Surat alone.

explanation: — 1657 Cromwell Charter = permanent joint-stock company; 1661 Charles II60-85 Charter = quasi-State power (forts, troops, war/peace, civil/criminal jurisdiction; minting added 1676).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_23
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the EIC's First Voyage (1601–1603)?

options.text: The fleet sailed to Surat and established the first English factory in India.

The fleet sailed not to India but to Indonesia (Java and Sumatra) — consistent with the EIC's original priority of the spice trade — & established the very first EIC factory there; on the way, the fleet looted a Portuguese ship in the Strait of Malacca (cargo of textiles and spices); historians have noted that the EIC's first major profit came not from trade but from outright piracy, & shareholders received substantial dividends when the fleet returned in 1603.
The fleet was sent by Cromwell51-60 directly to capture Goa from the Portuguese.
The fleet sailed to Bengal and founded Calcutta in 1603.

explanation: — First Voyage 1601–03 sailed to Indonesia (Java/Sumatra) — not India; established the very first EIC factory there; on the way, fleet looted a Portuguese ship in Strait of Malacca; first major EIC profit came from outright piracy, not trade; substantial dividends paid on return in 1603.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_24
questions.stem: With reference to the Danish East India Company and Danish settlements in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Danish East India Company was established in 1616 by a Charter from King Christian IV88-48 of Denmark-Norway, granting a 12-year monopoly.
2. Tranquebar (Tharangambadi) in Tamil Nadu — with its first fort, Fort Dansborg — served as the official administrative headquarters of Danish India from 1620 until the Danes left in 1845.
3. Serampore (Srirampur / Frederiksnagore) in Bengal was acquired in 1755 via a parwana from Nawab Alivardi Khan40-56 & grew into the most commercially successful Danish trading post in India.
4. The Danish company eventually sold all its Indian mainland settlements to the British EIC by 1845.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. — All four verbatim from chapter source.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_25
questions.stem: With reference to the Serampore Mission Press (1799–1800), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Serampore Mission Press was established by the Danes in 1799–1800.
2. It was associated with Baptist missionaries, including William Carey.
3. It translated the Bible into Indian vernacular languages, ran schools, & made an immense contribution to early printing and education in Bengal.
4. Unlike the Portuguese missionary work in Goa (which involved forced conversions through the Goa Inquisition), the Danish missionary work was not based on forced conversions.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. — Serampore Mission Press 1799–1800 by the Danes + Baptist missionaries (William Carey) + Bible vernacular translations + schools + immense contribution to early printing and education in Bengal + missionary work was not based on forced conversions (contrast with Goa Inquisition).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_26
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the Battle of Swally (1612) & the Royal Farman of 1613?

options.text: The Battle of Swally was fought between the EIC under Captain William Hawkins and the Dutch in the Bay of Bengal.

The Battle of Swally (also called Battle of Suvali) saw Captain Thomas Best lead a small EIC armed trading fleet to a decisive victory over the Portuguese; impressed by English naval capability, Jahangir05-27 issued a Royal Farman in 1613 — the imperial decree that gave the EIC the legal right to set up a permanent factory at Surat.
The 1613 Farman was issued by Akbar and granted the EIC trading rights in Goa.
The Battle of Swally was fought between the Portuguese and the Marathas, with the EIC playing no role.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: The Battle of Swally (also called Battle of Suvali) in 1612 saw Captain Thomas Best lead a small EIC armed trading fleet to a decisive victory over the Portuguese. Impressed by English naval capability, Jahangir05-27 issued a Royal Farman in 1613 — the imperial decree that gave the EIC the legal right to set up a permanent factory at Surat. This was the foundational legal-political moment of EIC presence in Mughal India.

(a) ✗ — Hawkins came earlier (1609) and the Battle of Swally was against the Portuguese, not the Dutch; the location was Surat (Arabian Sea), not Bay of Bengal. (c) ✗ — the Royal Farman 1613 was for a Surat factory, not Hugli. (d) ✗ — Madras / Fort St. George came much later (1639).
*Memory hook: Thomas Best beat the Portuguese at Swally 1612 → Jahangir gave the Farman 1613 → Surat factory permanent.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_27
questions.stem: With reference to Captain William Hawkins (1608) versus Captain Thomas Best (1612) at the Mughal court, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Captain William Hawkins arrived at the Mughal court in 1608 — earlier than Thomas Best — but his mission failed to secure permanent trading rights for the EIC.
2. Captain Thomas Best's victory at the Battle of Swally (1612) — defeating the Portuguese — convinced Jahangir05-27 of EIC naval capability.
3. Jahangir05-27 issued the Royal Farman of 1613 to the EIC after Best's victory, granting permanent factory rights at Surat.
4. The 1613 Farman was issued before the Battle of Swally took place.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3 only. Statement (4) is the trap — the 1613 Farman came AFTER the Battle of Swally, not before.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_28
questions.stem: With reference to Sir Thomas Roe's mission to Jahangir05-27's court (1615–19), consider the following statements:
items: 1. King James I03-25 sent Thomas Roe as his formal ambassador to Jahangir05-27's court; Roe arrived at Surat in 1615 & stayed until 1619.
2. Roe's account — The Embassy of Thomas Roe to the Court of the Great Mogul — remains one of the most important primary sources for the Mughal Empire of this period.

3. Jahangir05-27 refused to sign a formal treaty between equals — the Mughal Emperor saw no reason to treat a trading company as a sovereign equal — but Roe extracted a Royal Farman in 1618 giving the EIC the right to establish factories throughout the Mughal Empire and liberal trading rights.

4. The EIC rapidly expanded its factory network during 1616–1619, establishing new factories at Agra, Ahmedabad, & Broach (Bharuch), & the newly constituted Surat Presidency (1618) became the EIC's first administrative Presidency in India.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: All four statements verified verbatim from Chapter 'Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe (1615-19)'. (1) King James I03-25 sent Roe as formal ambassador to Jahangir05-27’s court; Roe arrived at Surat in 1615 and stayed till 1619. (2) Roe’s account — "The Embassy of Thomas Roe to the Court of the Great Mogul" — is a key primary source for Mughal history of this period. (3) Jahangir refused to sign a formal treaty between equals; the Mughal Emperor saw no need to treat a trading company as a sovereign. (4) Roe successfully negotiated trade concessions for the EIC — the result was the Royal Farman of 1618 confirming factory rights.
*Memory hook: Roe 1615–19 — no formal treaty, but factory rights via the 1618 Farman.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_29
questions.stem: With reference to the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The treaty was signed at Whitehall in London and sealed by the marriage of Charles II60-85 of England and Princess Catherine of Braganza of Portugal.
2. Portugal paid a dowry of 500,000 pounds in cash; England received Bombay and Tangier (in Morocco).
3. The two countries agreed on trade and military cooperation, with England agreeing to protect Portugal's remaining possessions.
4. In 1668, the British Crown transferred Bombay to the EIC at an annual rent of 10 pounds.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: All four statements verified verbatim from Chapter 'Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661- Dowry Diplomacy'. (1) Treaty signed at Whitehall, London, sealed by the marriage of Charles II60-85 of England and Princess Catherine of Braganza of Portugal. (2) Portugal paid a dowry of £500,000 cash; England received Bombay + Tangier (Morocco). (3) Trade and military cooperation agreed; England agreed to protect Portugal’s remaining possessions. (4) In 1668 the British Crown transferred Bombay to the EIC at a nominal annual rent of £10 — launching the Bombay Presidency.
*Memory hook: Catherine of Braganza’s dowry = Bombay; transferred to EIC in 1668 for £10/year.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_30
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the Amboyna Massacre (1623) & the Treaty of Breda (1667)?

options.text: The Amboyna Massacre was a battle between the British and the Mughals in Bengal; the Treaty of Breda 1667 ended this conflict.

The Amboyna Massacre (1623) saw the Dutch kill English traders in the Indonesian spice islands — a brutal episode that ended English ambitions in Indonesia; the Anglo-Dutch rivalry then settled into a practical geographical compromise formalised in the Treaty of Breda (1667), under which the British agreed to leave Indonesia to the Dutch and the Dutch agreed to leave the English alone in India, with both maintaining minor presences in each other's primary domains.
The Treaty of Breda 1667 was signed between France and Britain over the Carnatic.
The Amboyna Massacre was an incident in Bengal between the EIC and the Marathas.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: The Amboyna Massacre (1623) saw the Dutch kill English traders in the Indonesian spice islands — a brutal episode that ended English ambitions in Indonesia. The Anglo-Dutch rivalry then settled into a practical geographical compromise formalised in the Treaty of Breda (1667), under which the British took Indian sub-continent dominance and the Dutch kept Indonesia.

(a) ✗ — The Amboyna Massacre was not Mughal-British; it was Dutch-English in the spice islands of Indonesia. (c) ✗ — Breda 1667 was an Anglo-Dutch settlement, not a French-Dutch one. (d) ✗ — the Treaty did not divide the East Indies; it formalised a regional swap (Indonesia to Dutch, India to British).
*Memory hook: Amboyna 1623 → Dutch keep Indonesia; Britain takes the subcontinent. Breda 1667 made it official.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_31
questions.stem: With reference to the Dutch power in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Dutch captured Cochin from the Portuguese in 1663 & held it as their key base in South India.
2. In 1741, at the Battle of Colachel, the Travancore King Marthanda Varma29-58 decisively defeated the Dutch — ending their political power in Kerala.
3. In 1759, at the Battle of Bedara (also called Battle of Chinsura), the British EIC defeated the Dutch in Bengal — crushing their remaining ambitions in India.
4. By 1658, the Dutch had also removed the Portuguese from Ceylon (today's Sri Lanka).
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: All four statements verified verbatim from Chapter 'How Did the Dutch Rise, Dominate — and Then Fall in Asia?'. (1) Dutch captured Cochin from the Portuguese in 1663 + held it as their key South India base. (2) At the Battle of Colachel (1741) Marthanda Varma29-58 of Travancore decisively defeated the Dutch, ending their political power in Kerala. (3) At the Battle of Bedara (also Chinsura) 1759 the EIC defeated the Dutch in Bengal — crushing their remaining Indian ambitions. (4) By 1658 the Dutch had removed the Portuguese from Ceylon.
*Memory hook: Colachel 1741 (Travancore) + Bedara 1759 (EIC) — two battles, two ends to Dutch India.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_32
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes how Britain took over Dutch overseas colonies in 1795?

options.text: Britain personally invaded the Netherlands in 1795 & expelled the Dutch from Cochin.

Once the Netherlands came under French control during the French Revolutionary Wars, the Dutch became effectively allied with France (Britain's primary adversary); Britain therefore declared all Dutch overseas colonies enemy territory and took them over — by 1795, the British had occupied the remaining Dutch settlements in South Asia: Cochin (Kerala coast), Chinsura (Bengal), Pulicat and Tuticorin (Coromandel Coast), & coastal Ceylon including Trincomalee and Colombo.
The Dutch left South Asia voluntarily in 1795 after a peaceful agreement with the EIC.
Britain and the Dutch jointly administered Cochin from 1795.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: Once the Netherlands came under French control during the French Revolutionary Wars, the Dutch became effectively allied with France — Britain’s primary adversary. Britain therefore declared all Dutch overseas colonies enemy territory and took them over. By 1795 the British had occupied the remaining Dutch settlements in South Asia: Cochin, Pulicat, Negapatnam, Chinsura, and Ceylon.

(a) ✗ — Britain did not invade the Netherlands; the takeover happened in the colonies as a knock-on of the French Revolutionary Wars. (c) ✗ — there was no formal British-Dutch agreement to share India in 1795. (d) ✗ — the takeover was not via the Treaty of Paris (1763) — that treaty concerned the Seven Years’ War, not the French Revolutionary Wars.
*Memory hook: 1795 — Netherlands fell to France, so Britain took Dutch colonies overseas as enemy territory.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_33
questions.stem: With reference to the distinction between a Crown Colony and EIC-administered territory in Ceylon's case, consider the following statements:

questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_34
questions.stem: With reference to the French presence in India and Pondicherry — early establishments, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Compagnie des Indes Orientales (French East India Company) was founded in 1664 by Jean-Baptiste Colbert under King Louis XIV43-15.
2. The French set up factories at Surat (1668) & Masulipatnam (1669); the Surat factory was on a farman given by Aurangzeb58-07, & Masulipatnam was on a farman from the Sultan of Golconda.

3. The French obtained permission to set up a township at Chandernagore in 1673 from Shaista Khan64-88, the Mughal Governor of Bengal — but due to financial crunch, settlement was only established in 1690–92.
4. Pondicherry was acquired in 1674 from the Sultan of Bijapur, Sikandar Adil Shah72-86.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: All four statements verified verbatim from Chapter 'The French in India — and the Story of Pondicherry'. (1) Compagnie des Indes Orientales founded 1664 by Jean-Baptiste Colbert under King Louis XIV43-15. (2) French factories at Surat (1668) on Aurangzeb58-07’s farman + Masulipatnam (1669) on a farman from the Sultan of Golconda. (3) Permission for Chandernagore in 1673 from Shaista Khan (Subahdar of Bengal). (4) Pondicherry purchased in 1674 from the Sultan of Bijapur Sikandar Adil Shah72-86.
*Memory hook: Compagnie 1664 + Surat 1668 + Masulipatnam 1669 + Chandernagore 1673 + Pondicherry 1674 — the French build-out across India.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_35
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes François Martin01-06 & the founding of French power in India?

options.text: François Martin01-06 was a Portuguese governor who briefly captured Pondicherry in 1693 before the French re-took it.

François Martin01-06 — Governor-General 1701–1706 — is regarded as the real founder of French power in India; he centralised French administration by making Pondicherry the capital in 1701 & built Fort Louis to defend the new city.
François Martin01-06 was a Mughal noble who granted Pondicherry to the French in 1674.
François Martin01-06 was the French naval officer who recaptured Madras for the British in 1746.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: François Martin01-06 — Governor-General 1701–1706 — is regarded as the real founder of French power in India. He centralised French administration by making Pondicherry the capital in 1701 and built Fort Louis to defend the new city.

(a) ✗ — Martin was French, not Portuguese; the Dutch (not he) briefly captured Pondicherry in 1693. (c) ✗ — he was a French East India Company official, not a Mughal noble. (d) ✗ — he centralised at Pondicherry, not at Chandernagore.
*Memory hook: François Martin 1701 — Pondicherry capital + Fort Louis built — the real founder of French India.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_36

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_37
questions.stem: With reference to the sequence of European occupation of Pondicherry, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The French were the first European power to occupy Pondicherry.

4. The British captured Pondicherry again in later conflicts (such as in 1793) before finally returning it to France.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_39
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes how EIC Presidencies became Provinces of British India?

options.text: The Presidencies were directly converted into independent princely states post-1858.

A Presidency was a regional headquarters of EIC trade — given Presidency status when a settlement had grown large enough with significant warehouses, offices, residential buildings, & a fort; over time, as the EIC annexed surrounding territories, these towns grew into cities and the Presidencies expanded into Provinces of British India (the part of India governed directly by the British), named after the major forts built within them.
Presidencies were Mughal-administered districts handed over to the EIC after the Battle of Buxar.
The 1717 Farman of Farrukhsiyar13-19 directly converted Presidencies into Provinces.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: A Presidency was a regional headquarters of EIC trade, given Presidency status when a settlement had grown large enough to need significant warehouses, offices, residential buildings, and a fort. Over time, as the EIC annexed surrounding territories through wars (Plassey 1757 onwards) and Subsidiary Alliances, these towns grew into cities and the Presidencies expanded into Provinces of British India — the three being Madras, Bombay, and Bengal (Calcutta).

(a) ✗ — The Presidencies were not converted into princely states; they became British Indian Provinces. (c) ✗ — the Presidencies were not Mughal-granted; they were EIC settlements. (d) ✗ — the EIC did not abolish the Presidency system in 1858; on the contrary, Crown rule inherited and consolidated it.
*Memory hook: Trading post → Presidency → Province — three stages of EIC territorial growth.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_41
questions.stem: With reference to the Madras Presidency (from 1652/1653), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The EIC's first factory in India was a temporary one at Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) in the Northern Sarkars in 1611.

2. In 1639, the EIC — led by Francis Day — purchased land at the village of Madraspatanam from Hindu Nayakas (provincial governors of the Vijayanagara Empire) & built Fort St. George between 1639 & 1644 — the first fort built by the EIC in India.

3. The Madras Presidency was formally established as the Presidency of Fort St. George in 1652 under orders of the Court of Directors in London; due to the time required for the order to travel by ship, the decision was actually implemented in India in 1653.
4. In 1690, the EIC purchased a fort at Cuddalore (south of Madras) from Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram89-00 & named it Fort Saint David.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. — All four verbatim from chapter source: Masulipatnam 1611 first temporary + Francis Day 1639 land purchase from Hindu Nayakas + Fort St. George 1639–1644 (first EIC fort in India) + Madras Presidency 1652/1653 (London → India implementation gap) + Cuddalore Fort Saint David 1690.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_42
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the establishment of the Bombay Presidency (1687)?

options.text: Bombay Presidency was set up in 1687 immediately after Bombay was captured from the Marathas at the Battle of Salbai.

From 1613 to 1687, Surat was the EIC's main trade centre on the west coast; the shift to Bombay happened due to the growing power of the Marathas in Gujarat which made Surat increasingly risky; Bombay — a cluster of seven islands — offered a more defensible location; King Charles II60-85 received Bombay in 1661 as part of the Portuguese marriage dowry and transferred it to the EIC in 1668 at rent of 10 pounds per annum; the Bombay Presidency was established in 1687, replacing Surat as the EIC's western headquarters; Bombay Castle (also known as Casa Da Orta) was originally built by the Portuguese.
The Bombay Presidency was set up in 1687 after Aurangzeb58-07 transferred Bombay to the EIC via a Farman.
Bombay Presidency was established immediately after the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661 — i.e., on the day Catherine of Braganza arrived in London.

explanation: — 1613–1687 Surat as EIC main west-coast trade centre + Maratha threat in Gujarat made Surat risky + Bombay 7 islands defensible + 1661 Anglo-Portuguese dowry to Charles II60-85 + 1668 Crown-to-EIC at £10/annum + Bombay Presidency 1687 + Bombay Castle (Casa Da Orta) originally Portuguese.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_43
questions.stem: With reference to the Calcutta Presidency (from 1699/1700), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The EIC's Bengal presence began with a factory at Hugli in 1651 — permitted by a nishan (a decree issued by a prince) from Shah Shuja, the Mughal governor of Bengal and son of Shahjahan27-58.
2. In 1690, the EIC founded a settlement at the village of Sutanuti — the Calcutta establishment.
3. The Calcutta Presidency was formally established in 1699/1700 as the Presidency of Fort William with its own Governor.
4. Through the 18th century, the EIC developed Calcutta Port aggressively; Calcutta eventually accounted for 60% of all EIC trade from India.

explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. — Hugli 1651 (nishan from Shah Shuja) + 1690 Sutanuti settlement + Calcutta Presidency 1699/1700 (Presidency of Fort William) + 60% of all EIC India trade through Calcutta by 18th century.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_44
questions.stem: With reference to Cuddalore and Fort Saint David, consider the following statements:

4. Fort Saint David was the first fort built by the EIC anywhere in India, predating Fort St. George.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3 only. — Statements (1)–(3) verbatim from chapter source: 1690 Cuddalore from Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram89-00 + Cuddalore Fort layered history (Dutch 1608 + Portuguese pressure halt + Hindu merchant completion) + Shivaji74-80 conquest of nearby Jinji 1677. Statement (4) is the trap — Fort Saint David was NOT the first EIC fort; that distinction belongs to Fort St. George at Madras (1639–1644).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_45
questions.stem: With reference to Fort William and later developments at Calcutta, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Fort William at Calcutta was built between 1696 & 1700 — much later than Fort St. George at Madras (1639–1644).
2. Fort William was named after King William III89-02.
3. In 1698, the EIC obtained the zamindari of Kolikata, Sutanuti and Govindapur from the Sabarna Roy Chowdhury family for 1,300 rupees.
4. In 1800, Fort William College was established by Wellesley98-05 for training EIC civil servants.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Why did the Portuguese rise so quickly in India after 1498 and then decline by the early 17th century?
body: 150 words · 10 marks

"The Portuguese were the first European power to establish themselves in India after 1498, yet by the early 17th century they had been displaced by the Dutch and the English. Examine the reasons for both the rise and the decline."
Demand of the question: Explain BOTH the rise (factors that enabled Portuguese dominance) AND the decline (factors that ended it). Use chronology to anchor your answer.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Portuguese rise after 1498 rested on State-backed trade, naval power, and the Cartaz system; their decline by 1600s was driven by religious intolerance, overstretch, and rivals’ better commercial models.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):
'the Portuguese in India'
'the Portuguese in India'
'the Portuguese in India'
'the Portuguese in India'

5. Rival commercial models — Dutch VOC (joint-stock + private capital + share trading) and English EIC (Royal Charter monopoly) outcompeted the Crown-monopoly model from the early 1600s (see 'How Did the Dutch and English Break the Portuguese-Spanish Monopoly?' and 'What Made the Dutch VOC Historically Unique?' + 'English EIC and the Royal Charter of 1600'.
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): The same State-monopoly model that built Portuguese dominance — capital concentrated in the Crown — left no slack when rivals brought capital + competition.
