questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: What made the Dutch VOC historically unique, and how did the English EIC’s charter evolution shape its rise in India?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"The Dutch VOC (1602) and the English EIC (1600) were both joint-stock companies. Examine the unique features of the VOC, and how the EIC’s evolving charters shaped its rise to dominance in India."
Demand of the question: Cover BOTH (a) VOC’s unique features and (b) EIC charter evolution as institutional engines of rise. Compare where the question invites comparison.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The VOC was the first true joint-stock corporation with tradable shares; the EIC began as a Crown-monopoly trader, then its charters expanded its powers to fight rivals + tax India.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. VOC firsts — first multinational corporation, first tradable shares (Amsterdam Stock Exchange 1602), sovereign powers (declare war, sign treaties, mint coin) granted by the States-General (see 'What Made the Dutch VOC Historically Unique?'.
'Charters until 1793 and evolution of EIC's Legal Character'
'Charters until 1793 and evolution of EIC's Legal Character'
'Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661- Dowry Diplomacy'
'Charters until 1793 and evolution of EIC's Legal Character'

Suggested conclusion (~20 words): The VOC pioneered the joint-stock corporation; the EIC evolved its charters into a State-like instrument that absorbed Bombay, won Plassey, and eventually became British India.
'Charters until 1793 and evolution of EIC's Legal Character'

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Battle of Wandiwash
questions.stem: Prelims 1995 — Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

options.text: Battle of Buxar — Mir Jafar vs. Clive
Battle of Wandiwash — French vs. East India Company
Battle of Chilianwala — Dalhousie vs Marathas
Battle of Kharda — Nizam vs. East India Company

explanation: Answer: (b)

Why (b) is correct: The Battle of Wandiwash was fought in 1760 between the French and the East India Company. It was the decisive battle of the 3rd Carnatic War. The British, led by Eyre Coote, defeated the French, led by Count de Lally. You will find this in 'Why Did France Lose 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63)?'.
Why the other options are wrong:

1. (a) Battle of Buxar (1764) was fought between Mir Qasim — not Mir Jafar — & the EIC. Mir Jafar was the EIC's man at Plassey (1757); by Buxar he had been replaced by Mir Qasim, who then fought the EIC.
2. (c) Battle of Chilianwala (1849) was fought between Dalhousie48-56's EIC army and the Sikhs — not the Marathas. It was part of the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War.
3. (d) Battle of Kharda (1795) was fought between the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Marathas — not the East India Company.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: Dupleix as the first European to take part in Indian princely quarrels
questions.stem: Prelims 1996 — Who among the following were the first European to initiate the policy of taking part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories?
explanation: Answer: (b)

Why (b) is correct: Dupleix42-54 invented the model of empire building in India. His blueprint was simple: put your chosen candidate on the throne, station your army at his expense, take territory as payment for the army, and sit in the royal court as the real power behind the throne. He first used this model in the 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — backing Muzaffar Jung50-51 in Hyderabad and Chanda Sahib49-52 in Carnatic. You will find this in 'The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?' (Phase 1 — French Victory (1749–51). The Subsidiary Alliance framework — often credited to Wellesley98-05 after 1798 — was operationally pioneered by Dupleix42-54 in Hyderabad in 1751. The EIC was the refiner, not the inventor.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Robert Clive57-67 came later. He used and refined Dupleix42-54's model in Bengal (Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764) — but he did not invent it.

2. (c) Afonso de Albuquerque was a 16th-century Portuguese conqueror who took Goa in 1510. He belonged to a much earlier era of direct conquest — not the "back-a-claimant" model Dupleix42-54 invented.
3. (d) Warren Hastings was a later EIC Governor-General (1772–85). Like Clive57-67, he was a refiner of the Dupleix42-54 model — not the originator.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: With reference to the two kinds of wars the EIC fought in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The EIC fought wars to protect or expand trade, and wars for territory.

2. Wars for territory happened when the Governor or Governor-General was personally ambitious — Robert Clive57-67, Wellesley98-05, Francis Hastings13-23, and Dalhousie48-56 are listed as the major empire builders.
3. The EIC Army itself had a structural interest in war — overhyping border threats created pressure for expansion, which created new borders, which created new threats.
4. By 1857, the EIC controlled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4. — All four facts taken verbatim from chapter source: trade-vs-territory wars + GG empire-builders list (Clive57-67/Wellesley98-05/Hastings13-23/Dalhousie48-56) + structural army interest in war + 63%/78% territory/population by 1857.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: With reference to the Wars for Trade, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Anglo-Mughal War of 1686–90 — also called Child's War — was named after Josiah Child, who was Governor of Bombay and "General" of all EIC forces in India, and John Child, who was Chairman of the Court of Directors of EIC in London.
2. In February 1690, Aurangzeb58-07 pardoned the EIC in return for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation, despite the EIC having been the aggressor that seized Hugli and attacked Mughal ships in the Arabian Sea.

3. The 1691 "Farman" — granting the EIC duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum — was technically a Parwana issued by the Subahdar of Bengal under Aurangzeb58-07's approval, not an Imperial Farman.
4. Aurangzeb58-07 chose not to abolish the EIC because its trade brought forex/gold into India, which he needed for his own constant warfare.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 2, 3 and 4 only. Statement (1) is the trap — roles SWAPPED. Josiah Child was Chairman of the Court of Directors of EIC in London; John Child was Governor of Bombay & "General" of all EIC forces in India. The statement reverses the two — same surname, easy swap under exam pressure. Statements (2), (3), (4) are correct — verbatim from: EIC seized Hugli + attacked Mughal ships in Arabian Sea, Feb 1690 pardon for Rs 1.5 lakh; 1691 Farman technically a Parwana issued by Subahdar of Bengal under Aurangzeb58-07's approval, Rs 3,000 per annum for duty-free trade in Bengal; Aurangzeb58-07's economic-utility motive — forex/gold for war.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: With reference to the reasons for the Carnatic Wars, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Carnatic Wars (1746–63) were fundamentally an extension of the Anglo-French rivalry in Europe brought to Indian soil.
2. The two European companies in southern India — French EIC at Pondicherry and English EIC at Madras — found themselves on opposing sides whenever London and Paris went to war.
3. The Carnatic region was politically fragmented, with weak Mughal authority and rival claimants to the Nawabship of Carnatic — making it open ground for European interference.
4. All three Carnatic Wars were fought entirely on Indian soil with no European war as the trigger.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3 only. Statement (4) is the trap — all three Carnatic Wars were extensions of European wars: 1st Carnatic War = War of the Austrian Succession (1740–48); 3rd Carnatic War = Seven Years' War (1756–63). Only the 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) was fought primarily on Indian terms (the succession disputes), but even that was framed by the Anglo-French rivalry.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the Battle of Adyar / St Thome (1746)?

options.text: Fought between the EIC and the Nawab of Bengal, ending EIC trade in Surat.

Fought on the north bank of the River Adyar; a French force of roughly 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers completely destroyed the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry; the French victory rested on superior artillery, tactical discipline (infantry squares), and regular cash salaries — the first time it was proven that a small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery could crush a vastly larger traditional Indian army.
Fought between Robert Clive57-67 and Dupleix42-54 directly — Clive57-67 won.
Fought between the British navy and a French fleet — naval battle, not a land battle.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: At the Battle of Adyar / St Thome (1746), a small French force of ~700 French-trained Indian sepoys and ~300 French soldiers completely destroyed the Nawab of Carnatic’s 10,000-strong traditional cavalry. The French victory rested on three things — superior artillery, tactical discipline (infantry squares), and regular cash salaries. This was the first proof in India that a small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery could crush a vastly larger traditional Indian army.

(a) ✗ — The battle was fought between the French and the Nawab of Carnatic, not Bengal, and it concerned southern India, not Surat. (c) ✗ — Clive57-67 and Dupleix42-54 never fought each other directly; Clive came into the picture only from the 2nd Carnatic War (Phase 2). (d) ✗ — Adyar / St Thome was a land battle on the north bank of the River Adyar, not a naval engagement.
*Memory hook: 300 + 700 destroyed 10,000 — the first time European-trained infantry beat a traditional Indian cavalry on Indian soil.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748)?

options.text: The Treaty divided the Carnatic between the French and the British and recognised Dupleix42-54 as the supreme authority in southern India.

The Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) ended the War of the Austrian Succession in Europe and, by extension, the 1st Carnatic War in India; under its terms, Madras (which the French had captured in 1746) was restored to the British in exchange for Louisbourg in North America — making it a global swap that prized Atlantic territory over Indian holdings.
The Treaty was signed at Pondicherry between Dupleix42-54 and the EIC, with no European involvement.
The Treaty handed the Northern Sarkars to the French permanently and ended British presence in Madras.

explanation: (Consequence — Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748)

Why (b) is correct: The Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) ended the War of the Austrian Succession in Europe and, by extension, the 1st Carnatic War in India. Under its terms, Madras (which the French had captured in 1746) was restored to the British in exchange for Louisbourg in North America — a global swap in which European powers prized Atlantic territory over Indian holdings.

(a) ✗ — The treaty did not divide the Carnatic; Dupleix42-54 was not recognised as supreme authority. (c) ✗ — the treaty was a European-level agreement signed at Aix-La-Chapelle, not a local one at Pondicherry. (d) ✗ — the Northern Sarkars were not part of this treaty; the British kept Madras after the swap.
*Memory hook: Madras swapped for Louisbourg — the Atlantic mattered more to Europe than India in 1748.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: With reference to the succession disputes that triggered the 2nd Carnatic War, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Hyderabad, after Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 died in 1748, his son Nasir Jung48-50 and his grandson Muzaffar Jung50-51 claimed the throne; the British backed Nasir Jung48-50 and the French backed Muzaffar Jung50-51.
2. In Carnatic, Md Ali Wallajah52-95 (the incumbent Nawab Anwaruddin's son) was backed by the British, while the rival claimant Chanda Sahib49-52 was backed by the French.
3. The same two European powers — British and French — backed opposing sides in both succession disputes.
4. Both succession disputes were settled peacefully through Mughal imperial mediation, without military intervention.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3 only. Statement (4) is the trap — both succession disputes triggered the 2nd Carnatic War, a major military intervention. Mughal mediation did not happen; the Mughal Emperor was already weak by 1748.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes Phase 1 of the 2nd Carnatic War (1749–51)?

options.text: The British under Robert Clive57-67 captured Pondicherry from the French and installed Md Ali Wallajah52-95 as Nawab of Carnatic.

Phase 1 saw French ascendancy: at the Battle of Ambur (1749), Anwaruddin was killed and Chanda Sahib49-52 was made Nawab of Carnatic; in Hyderabad, Nasir Jung48-50 was killed in December 1750 and Muzaffar Jung50-51 was made Nizam — but Muzaffar Jung50-51 was also killed in February 1751, after which the French installed Salabat Jung51-62 as Nizam (a French puppet); during this phase, Dupleix42-54 invented the Subsidiary Alliance blueprint — back a claimant, station your army at his expense, take territory as payment for the army, and sit in court as the real power.
The British signed the Treaty of Pondicherry in Phase 1 itself, ending the war early.
Phase 1 was a military stalemate with no decisive battles.

explanation: (Phase 1 — French Victory (1749–51)

Why (b) is correct: Phase 1 of the 2nd Carnatic War (1749–51) saw French ascendancy. At the Battle of Ambur (1749) Anwaruddin (Nawab of Carnatic) was killed and Chanda Sahib49-52 was installed as Nawab. In Hyderabad, Nasir Jung48-50 was killed in December 1750 and Muzaffar Jung50-51 was made Nizam; Muzaffar Jung was killed in February 1751, after which the French installed Salabat Jung51-62 as Nizam — a French puppet. During this phase, Dupleix42-54 invented the Subsidiary Alliance blueprint: back a claimant, station your army at his expense, take territory as payment for the army, and sit in court as the real power.

(a) ✗ — Clive57-67 captured Arcot in Phase 2 (not Pondicherry, not in Phase 1); Md Ali Wallajah52-95 was installed in Phase 2. (c) ✗ — the Treaty of Pondicherry was signed in 1754, after Phase 2. (d) ✗ — Phase 1 had decisive French victories at Ambur and in Hyderabad, not a stalemate.
*Memory hook: Phase 1 = Dupleix’s blueprint invented; Phase 2 = Clive copies it.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to Phase 2 of the 2nd Carnatic War (1751–52), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Robert Clive57-67 launched the Siege of Arcot in 1751 — a diversionary attack on the Carnatic capital — to relieve British pressure on Trichinopoly.
2. Clive57-67's small force of around 200 British soldiers and 300 Indian sepoys held Arcot for 53 days against a much larger Franco-Carnatic army.
3. By 1752, Chanda Sahib49-52 was defeated and killed; Md Ali Wallajah52-95 was made Nawab of Carnatic with British backing.
4. Phase 2 ended French ascendancy in Carnatic and proved that the EIC could match the French at the empire-building game.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why (c) All four is correct: Statement 1 ✓ — Clive57-67 launched the Siege of Arcot in 1751 as a diversionary attack on the Carnatic capital to relieve British pressure on Trichinopoly. Statement 2 ✓ — Clive’s small force of ~200 British soldiers + 300 Indian sepoys held Arcot for 53 days against a much larger Franco-Carnatic army. Statement 3 ✓ — by 1752 Chanda Sahib49-52 was defeated and killed; Md Ali Wallajah52-95 was made Nawab of Carnatic with British backing. Statement 4 ✓ — Phase 2 ended French ascendancy in Carnatic and proved that the EIC could match the French at the empire-building game.
(a)(b)(d) all undercount; all four statements are correct, so (c) is the only valid answer.
*Memory hook: 200 British + 300 sepoys held Arcot for 53 days — Clive’s first big move on the empire-building game.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754)?

options.text: The Treaty made the British Nawab of Carnatic and gave the French permanent control of Hyderabad.

The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) ended the 2nd Carnatic War; under its terms both sides agreed not to interfere in the internal politics of Indian states, and Dupleix42-54 was recalled to France — France saw him as the architect of an unprofitable adventure that had cost the Crown without delivering returns; the Treaty was a French diplomatic loss because it rolled back Dupleix42-54's gains and ended his blueprint at the State level.
The Treaty divided the Carnatic into French and British spheres permanently.
The Treaty was signed at Madras, not Pondicherry, and was negotiated by Robert Clive57-67.

explanation: (Treaty of Pondicherry (1754)

Why (b) is correct: The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) ended the 2nd Carnatic War. Under its terms both sides agreed not to interfere in the internal politics of Indian states, and Dupleix42-54 was recalled to France. Paris saw Dupleix as the architect of an unprofitable adventure that had cost the Crown without delivering returns. The treaty was a French diplomatic loss because it rolled back Dupleix’s gains and ended his blueprint at the State level — even as the EIC quietly kept copying it.

(a) ✗ — The treaty installed nobody; it just rolled back both sides’ gains. (c) ✗ — there was no permanent French/British division of Carnatic. (d) ✗ — the treaty was signed at Pondicherry, not Madras; Dupleix42-54 negotiated for the French side, not Clive57-67.
*Memory hook: France recalled Dupleix — abandoned his blueprint; EIC kept using it.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: With reference to the Battle of Wandiwash (1760), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Wandiwash 1760 was the most decisive battle of the 3rd Carnatic War.
2. The British were led by Eyre Coote (of British State, not EIC); the French were led by Count de Lally (of French State, not French EIC).
3. After Wandiwash, the French lost everywhere — including Pondicherry itself, their headquarters since 1701 with Fort Louis.
4. Wandiwash was a battle between the EIC and the Mughal Empire.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3 only. Statement (4) is the trap — Wandiwash was French vs EIC, not EIC vs Mughal Empire. ⚠ Alert — Prelims 1995 trap: UPSC asks "match the battle to who fought it" and swaps opponents to fool half-memory. The correct pair is Battle of Wandiwash (1760) = French vs the East India Company. The trap pairs include Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir Qasim (not Mir Jafar); Chilianwala (1849) = EIC vs Sikhs (not Marathas); Kharda (1795) = Nizam vs Marathas (not EIC). ◆ How to spot the trap: look at the year first — if the year does not match when the opponent was active, the pairing is wrong.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to why France lost the 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Tactical mistake — Bussy abandoned the Northern Sarkars to reinforce Lally in Carnatic; Robert Clive57-67 arrived from Bengal and took over Northern Sarkars in 1759.
2. Poor leadership — Lally was despised by his own officers and sepoys for his rude conduct, which demoralised the army.
3. Financial weakness — French soldiers went unpaid for months; the French EIC had spent heavily in earlier wars without commensurate gains.
4. Superior British navy — Britain dominated the Coromandel coast, giving decisive advantages in the coastal warfare of the Northern Sarkars and Carnatic.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why (c) All four is correct: Statement 1 ✓ — tactical mistake. Bussy abandoned the Northern Sarkars to reinforce Lally in Carnatic; Robert Clive57-67 came from Bengal and took the Northern Sarkars in 1759. Statement 2 ✓ — poor leadership. Lally was rude and despised by his own officers and sepoys, which sapped morale. Statement 3 ✓ — financial weakness. French soldiers went unpaid for months; the French EIC had spent heavily in earlier wars without commensurate gains. Statement 4 ✓ — superior British navy. Britain dominated the Coromandel coast, giving decisive advantages in the coastal warfare of the Northern Sarkars and Carnatic.
(a)(b)(d) all undercount; all four statements are correct, so (c) is the only valid answer.
*Memory hook: Bussy + Lally + Money + Navy — France lost the 3rd Carnatic War on all four counts.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes why the EIC won the Carnatic Wars (1746–48, 49–54, 56–63)?

options.text: The EIC won because it had the largest army in India and overwhelmed the French in pitched battles.

The EIC won for several connected reasons: France starved Dupleix42-54 of reinforcements to preserve its 1748 Treaty gains; Dupleix42-54's recall after the 2nd Carnatic War hurt French strategic continuity, while Robert Clive57-67 and Eyre Coote provided British leadership across all three wars; British capitalism was mature and could finance long wars while French feudalism plus revolutionary disruption (1789) starved the French EIC of resources; British naval supremacy (which led directly to the Industrial Revolution 1750–1850) made coastal warfare British-favoured.
The EIC won because the Mughal Emperor sided with the British against the French.
The EIC won because the Marathas attacked the French simultaneously from the west.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: The EIC won the Carnatic Wars for several connected reasons. France starved Dupleix42-54 of reinforcements to preserve its 1748 Treaty gains. Dupleix’s recall after the 2nd Carnatic War broke French strategic continuity, while Robert Clive57-67 and Eyre Coote provided British leadership across all three wars. British capitalism was mature and could finance long wars, while French feudalism plus revolutionary disruption (1789) starved the French EIC of resources. British naval supremacy (which led directly to the Industrial Revolution 1750–1850) made coastal warfare British-favoured.

(a) ✗ — The EIC did not have the largest army in India; it won via leadership continuity + finance + navy, not by sheer numbers. (c) ✗ — the Mughal Emperor played no role in the Carnatic; the Carnatic was a southern theatre. (d) ✗ — the Marathas did not coordinate an attack on the French; they had their own theatre.
*Memory hook: Money + Navy + Leadership continuity — the EIC’s three structural advantages over the French.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the Treaty of Paris (1763)?

options.text: The Treaty ended Mughal authority in India and recognised the EIC as the legal sovereign of Bengal.

The Treaty of Paris (1763) ended the global Seven Years' War and, by extension, the 3rd Carnatic War in India; under its terms, the French got back their factories and Pondicherry but lost their political ambitions in India — the French were no longer a serious empire-building rival to the British in India after 1763.
The Treaty divided India between France and Britain along the Eastern Ghats.
The Treaty was signed in Pondicherry and gave the French sovereignty over the Carnatic.

body: Mains-style FYQs (with B1 answer guidance)
explanation: (Treaty of Paris (1763)

Why (b) is correct: The Treaty of Paris (1763) ended the global Seven Years’ War and, by extension, the 3rd Carnatic War in India. Under its terms, the French got back their factories and Pondicherry but lost their political ambitions in India — they could not fortify Pondicherry or maintain a political establishment. After 1763 the French were no longer a serious empire-building rival to the British in India.

(a) ✗ — Mughal authority was not ended by this treaty; EIC sovereignty over Bengal came via the Diwani grant of 1765, not Paris 1763. (c) ✗ — there was no India-division along the Eastern Ghats. (d) ✗ — the treaty was signed in Paris, not Pondicherry; France received Pondicherry back as a trading post only.
*Memory hook: France got the factories back — but lost the empire.*

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: How did Dupleix invent the blueprint for empire in India during the 2nd Carnatic War?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"During the 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54), Dupleix invented the blueprint for European empire-building in India. Examine the components of that blueprint and their long-term significance."

Demand of the question: Identify Dupleix’s strategic innovations during the 2nd Carnatic War + show how those moves became a model the EIC later copied at Plassey 1757 and during the Subsidiary Alliance era.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Dupleix’s blueprint had four parts — intervene in succession disputes, back a puppet, secure revenue districts, and use trained Indian troops officered by Europeans. The EIC later copied all four.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Intervention in succession disputes — Dupleix exploited Hyderabad and Carnatic succession quarrels (see 'The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?').

2. Puppet rulers — Muzaffar Jung in Hyderabad, Chanda Sahib in Carnatic; European-backed candidates who paid back in cash, jagirs, and trade privileges (see 'The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?').

3. Revenue districts (the Northern Sarkars / Circars) — the French secured territorial revenue from Hyderabad as the price of backing Muzaffar Jung; this was the first European territorial revenue grant in India (see 'The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?').

4. Sepoys — Indian foot-soldiers trained in European drill and officered by Europeans; the original model of the EIC sepoy army (see 'The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?').

5. EIC copies the blueprint — Clive at Plassey 1757 (puppet Mir Jafar + Bengal revenue + sepoy army) was applying exactly Dupleix’s 1749 model on a much bigger canvas (see 'The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?' and 'The 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63)').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): France won the methodology of empire — and lost the empire. The EIC copied Dupleix’s blueprint and built British India.
revise: The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?
The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Why did the French lose the Carnatic Wars and the EIC win?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"Both the French and the English fought three Carnatic Wars in India between 1746 and 1763. The French lost and the English won. Examine the reasons."
Demand of the question: Cover BOTH the French weaknesses (why France lost) AND the EIC strengths (why EIC won). Conclude with the long-term consequence — the Treaty of Paris 1763.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The French lost the Carnatic Wars because home-government support was weaker, the French navy was outclassed, and finance was thinner; the EIC won on all three counts.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):
1. Home-government support — the British State (Royal Navy + Parliament) backed the EIC; the French monarchy under-funded the French Compagnie (see 'The 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63)').
2. Naval power — the Royal Navy controlled the Atlantic and Indian Ocean sea-lanes; the French lost control of reinforcement routes after 1758 (see 'The 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63)').
3. Financial depth — EIC raised capital through joint-stock + Bank of England credit; French Compagnie was a State monopoly with thinner pockets (see 'The 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63)').
4. Bengal annexation 1757 — Plassey gave the EIC Bengal revenues, funding the Carnatic wars without drawing on London. France had no such windfall (see 'The 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63)').

5. Treaty of Paris 1763 — ended the global Seven Years War + the Indian Carnatic War; France retained Pondicherry as a non-fortified trading post; EIC dominance in India was now uncontested (see 'The 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63)').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): The Carnatic Wars were lost on the seas + in the treasury, not on the battlefield alone. The EIC won India because Britain backed it.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Mir Jafar conspiracy at Plassey
questions.stem: Consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the Third Battle of Panipat, Ahmed Shah Abdali defeated Ibrahim Lodi.
2. Tipu Sultan was killed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
3. Mir Jafar entered into conspiracy with the English for the defeat of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula in the Battle of Plassey.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
explanation: Answer: (b)

Why (b) is correct: Only Statement 3 is correct — and it sits in 'Robert Clive, the Conspiracy & the Battle'. Mir Jafar57-60 — technically the Bakhshi (war paymaster + head of military intelligence), but the de facto commander since Siraj56-57 was young — entered into a conspiracy with Robert Clive57-67 and the EIC. Jafar wanted the Subahdarship for himself; he made a deal with EIC to remove Siraj56-57. At the Battle of Plassey (1757), Mir Jafar ensured that the bulk of the Bengal army did not fight and turned back. Siraj56-57 was easily defeated, fled, and was later captured and beheaded on Mir Jafar's son Miran's orders.
Why the other options are wrong:

1. Statement 1 wrong — In the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), Ahmed Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas (not Ibrahim Lodi). Ibrahim Lodi was defeated at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) by Babur26-30.
2. Statement 2 wrong — Tipu Sultan was killed in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99) at Srirangapatna, not the Third Anglo-Mysore War (1789–92).

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: Chronological order of 18th-century battles
questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the battles fought in India in the 18th century?

options.text: Battle of Wandiwash, Battle of Buxar, Battle of Ambur, Battle of Plassey
Battle of Ambur, Battle of Plassey, Battle of Wandiwash, Battle of Buxar
Battle of Wandiwash, Battle of Plassey, Battle of Ambur, Battle of Buxar
Battle of Ambur, Battle of Buxar, Battle of Wandiwash, Battle of Plassey

explanation: Answer: (b)

Why (b) is correct: The correct chronological order is Ambur (1749) → Plassey (1757) → Wandiwash (1760) → Buxar (1764). You will find the full chronology table in 'Chronology Box: 18th-Century Battles' — and the analytical synthesis: two French battles frame two English ones (French high at Ambur, French out at Wandiwash; EIC political breakthrough at Plassey, EIC sovereign breakthrough at Buxar).
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) wrong — places Wandiwash (1760) before Buxar (1764) and before Ambur (1749), which is impossible.
2. (c) wrong — places Wandiwash (1760) before Plassey (1757), which is impossible.
3. (d) wrong — places Buxar (1764) before Wandiwash (1760), which is impossible.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Royal Farman of 1717:
items: 1. The Farman was secured by the EIC from Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar13-19 after Dr. William Hamilton successfully treated the Emperor for a serious illness.
2. The Farman granted the EIC three rights — Duty-Free Trade in Bengal, Gujarat and Deccan; the right to use the Royal Mint; and the right to rent 38 villages around Calcutta.
3. Nawab Murshid Quli Khan17-27 accepted the Farman and granted all three rights without any pushback.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only:
Statement 1 ✓ — secured from Farrukhsiyar13-19 after Dr. William Hamilton's medical services.
Statement 2 ✓ — three rights: Duty-Free Trade in Bengal/Gujarat/Deccan + Royal Mint + 38 villages around Calcutta.

Statement 3 ✗ — MQK17-27 accepted the Farman but pushed back on each right: allowed DFT institutionally but refused to let officials misuse Dastaks; refused Royal Mint; allowed renting of villages but not purchase.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: With reference to the Dastak Problem, consider the following statements:
items: 1. By 1750, private trade by EIC officials was worth roughly fifty times their annual salaries.
2. Misuse of Dastaks by EIC officials violated the Royal Charter, which was British law.
3. Cornwallis86-93 was a notable exception — one of the rare honest Governors of that era.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 3 only:
Statement 1 ✓ — by 1750, private trade by EIC officials was worth 1,00,000 pounds per annum, roughly fifty times their annual salaries.

Statement 2 ✗ — misuse of Dastaks by EIC officials violated Indian law (tax evasion under Bengal's customs framework), NOT British law. The Royal Charter was violated by Interlopers (non-EIC British merchants), a different category.
Statement 3 ✓ — Cornwallis86-93 was a rare honest exception among Governors of that era.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem:
Match the following terms with their correct description:
List I (Term)
items: 1. Interlopers
2. Free merchants
3. Dastak misuse
questions.stemTail: List II (Description) A. EIC officials fraudulently passing personal goods as company goods — violated Indian law (customs duty evasion under Bengal's customs framework). B. Non-EIC British merchants who traded with India, violating the Royal Charter — faced court cases in Britain. C. Non-EIC British merchants stationed in India who agreed to sell Indian goods to the EIC inside India rather than exporting independently — artificially legal in the eyes of British law. Codes:
explanation: Term 1 (Interlopers) — non-EIC British merchants trading with India, violated the Royal Charter (British law) and faced court cases in Britain (B).
Term 2 (Free merchants) — British merchants stationed in India who agreed to sell to the EIC inside India rather than export independently — artificially legal in EIC's eyes (C).
Term 3 (Dastak misuse) — EIC officials fraudulently passing personal goods as company goods, also selling Dastaks; violated Indian customs framework (tax evasion) (A).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Black Hole Tragedy (1756):
items: 1. J.Z. Holwell's colonial account claimed that 146 prisoners were locked in and 123 died of suffocation.
2. Modern historians estimate the actual number of dead at approximately 30–40.
3. Holwell built a monument in 1760, demolished in 1821; Viceroy Curzon built a marble replica in 1901; in 1940 Netaji Bose led an agitation that shifted the monument to St. John's Church graveyard.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. (Siraj-ud-daula (Siraj56-57; 1756-57) & the Road to Plassey:
Statement 1 ✓ — Holwell's colonial account: 146 locked in / 123 died.
Statement 2 ✓ — modern historians estimate ~30–40 dead based on room dimensions and circumstantial evidence.
Statement 3 ✓ — full monument-history sequence: Holwell 1760 → ruined and demolished 1821 → Curzon's marble replica 1901 → Netaji Bose's 1940 agitation shifted it to St. John's Church graveyard.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: With reference to the Treaty of Alinagar (February 1757), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Alinagar was a town in Bihar where Robert Clive57-67 defeated Siraj-ud-Daula56-57.
Alinagar was the new name Siraj-ud-Daula56-57 had given to Calcutta after capturing it; the treaty restored EIC privileges in that city.
The Treaty of Alinagar was signed in 1764 and it gave the EIC the Diwani of Bengal Suba.
Alinagar was a French settlement in the Coromandel coast neutralised by Clive57-67.

explanation: "Alinagar" was the new name Siraj-ud-Daula56-57 had given to Calcutta after capturing it. The Treaty of Alinagar (February 1757) was therefore signed at Calcutta-renamed-Alinagar and restored all EIC privileges. The place name in the treaty title is the same city, not a different town.
(a) ✗ — No battle at any "Alinagar" in Bihar; Calcutta was the city.
(c) ✗ — Treaty of Alinagar was 1757, not 1764; the 1764 turning point was the Battle of Buxar; Diwani came via the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765.
(d) ✗ — French settlements neutralised by Clive57-67 included Hugli port and Chandarnagar in Bengal, not any "Alinagar."

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Battle of Plassey (1757):
items: 1. Mir Jafar, the commander of Bengal's army, conspired with Clive57-67 and ensured the bulk of the Bengal army did not fight.
2. Siraj-ud-Daula56-57 was vastly outnumbered in effective combatants and was easily defeated.
3. Mir Jafar57-65 became Nawab and the EIC's puppet, with a break — he ruled 1757–60 and 1763–65.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: Statement 1 ✓ — Mir Jafar, commander of Bengal's army, approached Clive57-67 and ensured the bulk of the army did not fight.
Statement 2 ✓ — Siraj-ud-Daula56-57 was vastly outnumbered in effective combatants (his nominal army was much larger but most of it stood down per Mir Jafar's arrangement).
Statement 3 ✓ — Mir Jafar57-65 (with a break, 1757–60 and 1763–65) became puppet Nawab; the EIC reinstalled him for the second period after Mir Qasim60-63 rebelled.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: With reference to the Plassey Plunder (1757–65), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The immediate financial settlement included Rs 2.25 crore to the EIC, 2,34,000 pounds to Robert Clive57-67 personally, and 2,75,000 pounds to the Royal British military.
2. Between 1757 and 1765, a further 2.5 million pounds were taken by the EIC as political gifts from Bengal.
3. After Plassey, EIC officials conducted private domestic trade through Indian agents called Gomastas who procured goods directly from peasants and artisans, cutting out Indian middlemen.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. (The Plassey Plunder (1757–65):

Statement 1 ✓ — immediate settlement: Rs 2.25 crore to EIC + 2,34,000 pounds to Clive57-67 personally + 2,75,000 pounds to Royal British military, plus a personal jagir of 35,000 pounds per annum to Clive57-67.
Statement 2 ✓ — between 1757 and 1765, a further 2.5 million pounds were taken as political gifts.
Statement 3 ✓ — Gomastas were Indian agents who procured directly from peasants and artisans, cutting out Indian middlemen entirely.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Which one of the following best describes how the Drain of Wealth began after Plassey?

options.text: Indian rulers paid annual tribute in gold to the British Crown.
Bengal's own Diwani revenues were used by the EIC to buy Indian goods for export — meaning India was paying for its own plunder, while surplus gold flowed from India to Britain.
The EIC charged customs duty on every Indian merchant's export, with all revenue sent to London.
The British Parliament imposed a colonial tax on Bengal that began in 1765.

explanation: (The Plassey Plunder (1757–65):

Drain of Wealth = Bengal's own Diwani revenues used by the EIC to buy Indian goods for export. India was paying for its own plunder; surplus gold flowed from India to Britain (gold-outflow replacing the pre-1757 gold-inflow). This is the substantive meaning of the Drain of Wealth — not Crown tribute, not customs duty, not parliamentary tax.
(a) ✗ — there was no annual tribute paid by Indian rulers to the British Crown until much later; the EIC promised tribute to Shah Alam II60-06 (not the reverse).
(c) ✗ — customs duty was being evaded via Dastak misuse, not collected to London.
(d) ✗ — No parliamentary tax began in 1765; what began was the Diwani-funded extraction.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding Mir Qasim60-63's reforms:
items: 1. He shifted his base from the capital Murshidabad to Bihar.
2. He abolished all internal duties on domestic trade — creating a level playing field for Indian merchants who had been squeezed out by EIC officials.
3. The autonomous behaviour was tolerated by the EIC as long as financial demands were met.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only:
Statement 1 ✓ — Mir Qasim60-63 shifted his base from Murshidabad to Bihar to escape EIC supervision.
Statement 2 ✓ — abolishing internal duties was clever; it created a level playing field for Indian merchants squeezed by EIC officials' untaxed Gomasta-mediated domestic trade since 1757.
Statement 3 ✗ — the autonomous behaviour was intolerable to the EIC; Mir Qasim60-63 was attacked, defeated in Bihar, and forced into the Buxar coalition.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: With reference to Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk (also known as Gaddar-ul-Mulk), consider the following statements:
items: 1. He blinded Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur in 1754.
2. He murdered Emperor Alamgir II in 1759.
3. Shah Alam II60-06 left Delhi for Awadh partly to escape his court factionalism and to set his sights on Bengal — which had stopped sending revenue to Delhi since 1751.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: Statement 1 ✓ — Imad-ul-Mulk blinded Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur in 1754.
Statement 2 ✓ — Imad-ul-Mulk murdered Emperor Alamgir II in 1759.
Statement 3 ✓ — Shah Alam II60-06 fled Delhi for Awadh fearing the Wazir's pattern; he had set his sights on Bengal which had stopped sending revenue to Delhi since 1751.
(Note: Imad-ul-Mulk and Gaddar-ul-Mulk are the same person — gaddar = "traitor," a derisive nickname earned from these acts.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to the Battle of Buxar (1764), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The Indian coalition won decisively under the leadership of Mir Qasim60-63.

The allied coalition (Mir Qasim60-63 + Shuja-ud-Daula54-75 + Shah Alam II60-06) had prepared a defensive strategy, but Shuja54-75 lost patience and switched to an offensive direct attack against Mir Qasim's advice; EIC commander Hector Munroe's final charge then turned the tables.
Robert Clive57-67 personally led the EIC forces to victory at Buxar.
Shah Alam II60-06 was beheaded after the battle to prevent any future Mughal claim.

explanation: The allied coalition (Mir Qasim60-63 + Shuja54-75 + Shah Alam II60-06) had prepared a defensive strategy — laying siege to the fort. Shuja54-75 lost patience, switched to offensive direct attack against Mir Qasim's explicit advice — handing the advantage to the EIC. Hector Munroe's final charge turned the tables. (Clive57-67 was in London at the time.)
(a) ✗ — The coalition lost.
(c) ✗ — Clive57-67 was in London; Munroe commanded.
(d) ✗ — Shah Alam II60-06 was deliberately spared and treated with respect — the EIC needed his sovereign legitimacy as legal cover.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) clauses on the Emperor:
items: 1. The EIC promised to pay Shah Alam II60-06 an annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees.
2. The EIC promised to militarily help Shah Alam II60-06 recapture Delhi from the Rohilla Afghans, who had held Delhi since 1761.
3. Shah Alam II60-06 was given Allahabad and Kora — taken from Awadh — as a seat of dignity.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: Statement 1 ✓ — annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees promised to Shah Alam II60-06.
Statement 2 ✓ — military help promised to recapture Delhi from the Rohilla Afghans, who had held Delhi since 1761.
Statement 3 ✓ — Allahabad and Kora given (taken from Awadh) as a seat of dignity for the Emperor whose Red Fort was under Rohilla control.
(Important caveat: in practice the EIC paid neither the Rs 26 lakh nor supplied an army to recapture Delhi — it was all legal formality. What mattered was the Diwani.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: With reference to the Diwani granted by the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Diwani included revenue administration, control of the revenue/treasury, and control of Civil Courts.
2. The Diwani granted to the EIC covered Bengal, Orissa and Bihar.
3. The Diwani included welfare duties such as health and education.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only.
Statement 1 ✓ — Diwani = revenue administration + control of revenue/treasury + control of Civil Courts.
Statement 2 ✓ — Diwani of Bengal Suba covered Bengal, Orissa and Bihar.

Statement 3 ✗ — Diwani did not include modern welfare duties (health/education), because those were traditionally handled by private/religious patronage and local Zamindars, not the Mughal government.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: With reference to the Dual Government in Bengal (1765–72), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The Diwani was with the Nawab and the Nizamat was with the EIC.
The EIC controlled the Diwani while the Nawab controlled the Nizamat; the Dual Government was wound up in 1772 under Warren Hastings73-85, triggered by the Great Bengal Famine of 1770.
Both Diwani and Nizamat were with the EIC from 1765 onwards.
The Dual Government continued until 1858, when the Crown took over.

explanation: The EIC controlled the Diwani while the Nawab controlled the Nizamat, with the EIC appointing a Deputy Nawab (Naib Nazim — Md Reza Khan) as its Diwan in practice. The Dual Government (1765–72) was wound up in 1772 under Warren Hastings73-85, triggered by the catastrophic Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (one crore people / one-third of Bengal's population dead) which the Dual Government's split-responsibility had supercharged.
(a) ✗ — reverse arrangement; the Diwani was with the EIC, not the Nawab.
(c) ✗ — Direct Rule (both Diwani + Nizamat with EIC) only began in 1772, not from 1765.
(d) ✗ — The Dual Government was ended in 1772, not 1858.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Awadh clauses of the Treaty of Allahabad (1765):
items: 1. Shuja-ud-Daula54-75 was made to pay 50 lakh rupees to the EIC as compensation; Benaras was separated from Awadh and the EIC formally annexed it in 1775.
2. The Policy of Ring Fence was initiated with Awadh — creating a military buffer around the EIC's Bengal core.

3. A mini Subsidiary Alliance was signed: an EIC army was permanently stationed in Awadh and was to be paid for by Awadh via annual subsidy. The architecture had been pioneered by Dupleix42-54 in Hyderabad in 1751.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: Statement 1 ✓ — Shuja54-75 paid 50 lakh rupees compensation; Benaras was separated and formally annexed by the EIC in 1775.

Statement 2 ✓ — the Policy of Ring Fence was initiated with Awadh; under the alliance, if anyone attacked the EIC in Bengal, Awadh was treaty-bound to help. (Mainly associated with Warren Hastings73-85 later, but Clive57-67 planted its seed in this treaty.)

Statement 3 ✓ — a mini Subsidiary Alliance was signed: EIC army permanently stationed in Awadh, paid by Awadh via annual subsidy. The architecture had been pioneered by Dupleix42-54 in Hyderabad in 1751 — the EIC adopted the French model.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_16
questions.stem: With reference to the 1717 Imperial Farman of Farrukhsiyar13-19, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It was issued by Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar13-19 (reigned 1713–1719).
2. It is often called the "Magna Carta of the Company" because of the sweeping privileges it granted.
3. The EIC received dastaks — duty-free trade passes — across Bengal, along with extensive commercial rights.
4. The Farman was obtained through a remarkable piece of diplomacy: Dr. William Hamilton, an English surgeon, successfully treated the Emperor for a serious illness.
5. The 1717 Imperial Farman was a provincial-level farman issued by the Subahdar of Bengal, like the 1691 farman of Ibrahim Khan.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: 1, 2, 3 and 4 only. — Statements (1)–(4) all correct: Farrukhsiyar13-19 issued + "Magna Carta of the Company" + dastaks across Bengal + Dr. William Hamilton's medical treatment of the Emperor. Statement (5) is the trap — the 1717 Farman was the truly imperial farman issued directly by the Emperor; it is distinct from the 1691 provincial-level farman issued by Ibrahim Khan, the Subahdar of Bengal, under approval of Aurangzeb58-07. Confusing the two is the recurring exam trap.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Why does Plassey 1757 mark the beginning of British conquest in India?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"The Battle of Plassey (1757) was the start of the British conquest of India — not because it was a great military victory, but because of what it gave the EIC. Examine."
Demand of the question: Show WHY Plassey began the conquest — even though it was militarily a small affair, it gave the EIC the financial and political base from which to fight every later war.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Plassey 1757 was not a great battle. But it gave the EIC Bengal — the richest province of India — and turned a trading company into a territorial State.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. The conspiracy, not the battle — Clive57-67 won Plassey through pre-arranged defections (Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh, Jagat Seths), not by overwhelming force (see 'Robert Clive, the Conspiracy & the Battle [ ▲ Index ]').

2. Mir Jafar as puppet — the EIC installed its own Nawab who paid huge sums to Clive and the EIC; the Dupleix blueprint perfected (see 'Robert Clive, the Conspiracy & the Battle [ ▲ Index ]' and 'The Plassey Plunder (1757–65) [ ▲ Index ]').

3. The Plassey Plunder (1757–65) — systematic extraction of Bengal wealth: nazarana, free trade exemptions, currency manipulation; transferred to England as the Drain (see 'The Plassey Plunder (1757–65) [ ▲ Index ]').

4. From trader to ruler — the EIC now had territorial revenue from Bengal that funded its later wars: Anglo-Mysore, Anglo-Maratha, Subsidiary Alliance era (see 'Plassey Marks the Beginning of Conquest [ ▲ Index ]').

5. Setup for Buxar 1764 — Plassey gave the EIC Bengal; Buxar would give it the legal right to rule. The two together made the EIC a sovereign State in India (see 'Battle of Buxar (1764): EIC Gets the Right to Rule [ ▲ Index ]' and 'Treaty of Allahabad (*ToA1765): [ ▲ Index ]').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): Plassey 1757 was the start of conquest not by force of arms but by conspiracy + revenue — a trading company became a State.
revise: Plassey Marks the Beginning of Conquest [ ▲ Index ]
Siraj-ud-daula (Siraj56-57; 1756-57) & the Road to Plassey (1757) [ ▲ Index ]
Robert Clive, the Conspiracy & the Battle [ ▲ Index ]

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Compare the Battle of Plassey 1757 with the Battle of Buxar 1764. Which mattered more for British conquest?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"While Plassey 1757 began British conquest, the Battle of Buxar 1764 was the decisive turning point. Examine both battles and their consequences."
Demand of the question: Cover BOTH battles — the conspiracy at Plassey + the pitched battle at Buxar — and assess which gave the EIC the deeper foundation.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Plassey 1757 gave the EIC Bengal’s wealth through conspiracy. Buxar 1764 gave the EIC the legal right to rule Bengal through a pitched military victory.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Plassey 1757 — conspiracy-led victory; Mir Jafar installed as puppet Nawab; EIC gained financial access to Bengal but no legal sovereignty (see 'Robert Clive, the Conspiracy & the Battle [ ▲ Index ]').

2. Buxar 1764 — pitched battle against a confederation of Mir Qasim60-63 (Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daula54-75 (Nawab of Awadh), and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II60-06; the three combined armies of ~50,000 lost to Hector Munro’s ~7,000 EIC force (see 'Battle of Buxar (1764): EIC Gets the Right to Rule [ ▲ Index ]').

3. Treaty of Allahabad 1765 — the legal consequence of Buxar: Mughal Emperor granted Diwani (revenue collection rights) of Bengal-Bihar-Orissa to the EIC — legalising what Plassey had only made possible (see 'Treaty of Allahabad (*ToA1765): [ ▲ Index ]').

4. Why Buxar mattered more — it converted the EIC from a de facto power into a de jure ruler under Mughal sanction; the Mughal Emperor’s seal made EIC rule legitimate in Indian law (see 'Treaty of Allahabad (*ToA1765): [ ▲ Index ]').
5. Awadh as buffer — the Treaty also turned Awadh into a buffer State paying tribute, securing the EIC’s northern flank without annexation (see 'Treaty of Allahabad (*ToA1765): [ ▲ Index ]').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): Plassey gave the EIC Bengal’s wealth; Buxar gave it Bengal’s law. Together they made the EIC a sovereign in India.
revise: Robert Clive, the Conspiracy & the Battle [ ▲ Index ]
Battle of Buxar (1764): EIC Gets the Right to Rule [ ▲ Index ]

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Governor General who kept the British flag flying high vs Napoleon
questions.stem: At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors General kept the British flag flying high in India?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Lord Wellesley.

Why (c) is correct: Lord Wellesley (Richard Wellesley98-05, GG 1798–1805) was the Governor General who pursued an aggressive expansion policy in India precisely when Napoleon was sweeping through Europe (Egypt 1798, Austria, Italy). Wellesley used the Subsidiary Alliance to add Hyderabad, Mysore, Awadh, the Carnatic, and the Marathas to the British orbit — keeping the British flag flying high in India even as Napoleon humbled monarchies in Europe. 'Who Were the Wellesleys?'.
(a) ✗ — Warren Hastings73-85 was GG 1773–85, well before the Napoleonic era.
*Memory hook: Wellesley98-05 = the Napoleonic-era GG who kept India British while Europe crumbled.*

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: Which does NOT apply to Subsidiary Alliance
questions.stem: Which does NOT apply to Subsidiary Alliance?
explanation: Answer: (c)

Why (c) is correct: “Secure fixed income for the Company” is the NOT-a-feature option. The other three DO apply: (a) large standing army at others' expense (yes), Napoleonic danger (yes), paramountcy (yes).

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.title: Which statement does NOT apply to Wellesley's SA
questions.stem: Which one of the following statements does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley?

options.text: To maintain a large standing army at others' expense
To keep India safe from Napoleonic danger
To secure a fixed income for the Company
To establish British paramountcy over the Indian states

explanation: Answer: (c)

Why (c) is correct (i.e. (c) does NOT apply to SA): Same trap-anchor as Prelims 2018 — the subsidy was earmarked for the EIC army's maintenance, not for the Company's general revenue. The four-option set is a near-verbatim repeat of Prelims 2018 (slightly more polished phrasing). The trap is identical: subsidy ≠ surplus income. See 'What the EIC Got' (term 4 with the "not surplus income" clarifier).
Why the other options DO apply to SA: Same reasoning as PYQ_Pre.2.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.title: Fort William College institution-founder pair
questions.stem:
With reference to educational institutions during colonial rule in India, consider the following pairs:
Institution — Founder
items: 1. Sanskrit College at Banaras — William Jones
2. Calcutta Madarsa — Warren Hastings
3. Fort William College — Arthur Wellesley
questions.stemTail: Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched?
explanation: Answer: (b)

Why (b) is correct: Only Pair 2 is correctly matched. The Fort William College detail ('Who Were the Wellesleys?') is the foundation: Wellesley98-05 — i.e. Richard Wellesley, Governor General of Bengal — established Fort William College in 1800. NOT Arthur Wellesley (Richard's brother, who was a British Royal Army commander, not a Governor General). The 2018 stem deliberately swaps Richard for Arthur to test whether the student knows the founder by full name.
Why the other pairs are wrong:
Pair 1 wrong — Sanskrit College at Banaras was founded by Jonathan Duncan in 1791, NOT by William Jones. (Asiatic Society of Bengal 1784 was Jones's institution.)
Pair 3 wrong — Fort William College was founded by Richard Wellesley98-05, NOT Arthur Wellesley. Arthur was the military commander brother.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.title: Why Wellesley established Fort William College
questions.stem: Wellesley established the Fort William College at Calcutta because:

options.text: he was asked by the Board of Directors at London to do so
he wanted to revive interest in oriental learning in India
he wanted to provide William Carey and his associates with employment
he wanted to train British civilians for administrative purpose in India

explanation: Answer: (d)

Why (d) is correct: The Fort William College detail ('Who Were the Wellesleys?') gives the verdict: Wellesley98-05 established the College in 1800 to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs before posting them to the districts. The college's purpose was administrative — Wellesley wanted his EIC officers to be linguistically and legally competent before they began ruling Indian districts.
Why the other options are wrong:
(a) The Board of Directors did NOT ask. Wellesley98-05 set the college up as his own initiative — part of the empire-builder's instinct to professionalise the EIC's administrative cadre.

(b) Reviving oriental learning was NOT Wellesley's purpose. (Asiatic Society of Bengal under William Jones from 1784 was the institutional home of oriental learning revival; Fort William College's mandate was administrative training, not scholarly revival.)

(c) William Carey was a Baptist missionary linguist who later became a teacher at Fort William College — but employment for Carey was NOT the founding purpose. Carey joined after the college was established.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.title: Why Wellesley established Fort William College (near-verbatim repeat of 2020)
questions.stem: Wellesley established the Fort William College at Calcutta because:

options.text: he was asked by the Board of Directors at London to do so
he wanted to revive interest in oriental learning in India
he wanted to provide William Carey and his associates with employment
he wanted to train British civilians for administrative purpose in India

explanation: Answer: (d)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: With reference to Pitt's India Act 1784, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The Act allowed the Governor-General to declare offensive war at his own discretion, without prior approval.
The Act banned offensive war by the Governor-General without the express command of the Court of Directors of the EIC or the Board of Control of the British State, but permitted defensive war.
The Act gave the Governor-General full sovereignty over the Indian princely States.
The Act mandated that the EIC pursue direct conquest as the primary policy in India.

explanation: Pitt's India Act 1784 banned offensive war by the Governor-General without express authorisation from the Court of Directors of the EIC or the Board of Control of the British State; defensive war was permitted. The reason was ruinous war expenditure from the Three Carnatic Wars (1746–63), Battle of Buxar (1764), Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–69 and 1780–84), and 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82).
(a) ✗ — opposite of what the Act did. (c) ✗ — Act did not grant sovereignty over princely States. (d) ✗ — Act mandated balance of power + Indirect Rule, NOT direct conquest.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: With reference to the two roots of the Subsidiary Alliance, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The SA was a complete invention of Wellesley98-05, with no prior precedent.

The French root was Dupleix42-54's installation of a French force at Hyderabad in 1751 (Salabat Jung as Nizam, Marquis de Bussy at court); the British root was Robert Clive57-67's mini Subsidiary Alliance with Awadh in the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), upgraded by Wellesley98-05 into a full contractual treaty.
The SA was developed by Cornwallis86-93 during his tenure (1786–93).
The SA was first signed at Mysore in 1799 with no earlier precedent.

explanation: +. Why (b) is correct: The Subsidiary Alliance had two prior roots that Wellesley98-05 only formalised, not invented. The French root was Dupleix42-54's installation of a French force at Hyderabad in 1751 — Salabat Jung was made Nizam, Marquis de Bussy was stationed at his court, and the host State paid for the French troops. The British root was Robert Clive57-67's mini Subsidiary Alliance with Awadh in the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) — an EIC army permanently stationed in Awadh, paid by Awadh via annual subsidy. Wellesley98-05 in 1798 took this two-strand template and turned it into a full contractual treaty with a standard Model. (a) ✗ — SA was not Wellesley's invention; he formalised existing Dupleix + Clive precedents. (c) ✗ — Cornwallis86-93's tenure focused on the Permanent Settlement (1793) and judicial reform, not SA. (d) ✗ — Mysore 1799 was a signatory, not the first precedent; the precedents go back to Hyderabad 1751 and Awadh 1765. *Memory hook: Dupleix 1751 + Clive 1765 → Wellesley 1798 (formalisation, not invention).*

2. The Indian State's army was disbanded and replaced by an EIC-maintained army permanently stationed in the State.
3. The EIC took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy — decisions on war, peace, diplomacy, defence budget, and foreign trade.
4. The Indian State paid an annual subsidy that became the EIC's surplus general revenue, available for any company purpose.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3 only. +. Why (a) is correct: Statement 1 ✓ — a British Resident was stationed permanently in the Indian ruler's court, reducing the ruler to a nominal figurehead while the Resident took the real decisions. Statement 2 ✓ — the Indian State's army was disbanded; an EIC-maintained army was stationed in the State permanently, paid for by the ruler's own subsidy. Statement 3 ✓ — the EIC took over the Indian State's foreign policy and external defence — the heart of sovereignty was transferred to the EIC. Statement 4 ✗ — the annual subsidy was earmarked for the EIC army's maintenance, NOT surplus general revenue available for any company purpose. This is the same trap-anchor as Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021: subsidy ≠ surplus income. *Memory hook: Resident + EIC army + foreign policy = SA's three transfers of sovereignty; subsidy funds the army, NOT general revenue.*
All three statements are core terms of the SA per 'Model Treaty of Subsidiary Alliance + Legal Logic'. The model treaty was the same template for every signatory.
*Memory hook: Resident + EIC army + foreign policy = SA's three transfers of sovereignty.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Why did the EIC specifically demand Foreign Policy as part of the Subsidiary Alliance?

options.text: Because the EIC wanted to control trade with European powers in India.
Because the legal right to deploy the army could otherwise still belong to the Indian ruler.
Because Pitt's India Act 1784 mandated the EIC to control all foreign relations of Indian States.
Because the British Crown directly required it under the Royal Charter.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: The EIC maintained the army using the host State's own subsidy money. Without Foreign Policy in the EIC's hands, the legal right to deploy that army could still belong to the Indian ruler. By taking Foreign Policy, the EIC ensured it alone could declare war or peace using the troops it commanded — converting the Indian State's army into an EIC instrument with the ruler footing the bill.

(a) ✗ — controlling European trade was a separate concern; Foreign Policy in the SA was about military deployment. (c) ✗ — there was no Mughal Emperor restriction the EIC needed to evade in 1798. (d) ✗ — the EIC was not seeking to internationalise the conflict; it was localising military control.
*Memory hook: EIC paid the army with the ruler's money; Foreign Policy let it ALSO command the army legally.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Which one of the following is the correct reason Wellesley98-05 was recalled to London in 1805?

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: How did Wellesley98-05 evade the conquest ban of Pitt’s India Act 1784 to build British paramountcy through the Subsidiary Alliance?
body: 150 words · 10 marks

"Pitt’s India Act 1784 banned the EIC from territorial conquest. Yet under Wellesley98-05 (Governor-General 1798–1805) the EIC absorbed half the subcontinent. Examine the Subsidiary Alliance as the legal-political device that made this possible."
Demand of the question: Show how Wellesley used the Subsidiary Alliance to expand WITHOUT formally conquering — the legal trick that turned ban into expansion.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Pitt’s India Act 1784 banned conquest. Wellesley98-05 used the Subsidiary Alliance — a "voluntary" treaty that transferred foreign policy to the EIC — to expand without conquering.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Two roots of the SA — Dupleix42-54’s 1751 Hyderabad model (French root) + Clive’s 1765 Treaty of Allahabad (British root); Wellesley98-05 codified both into the Model Treaty (see 'Two Roots of the SA: Dupleix42-54 + ToA1765 [ ▲ Index ]' and 'Model Treaty of Subsidiary Alliance + Legal Logic [ ▲ Index ]').

2. Legal trick — the Indian ruler kept his throne but surrendered foreign policy and external defence to the EIC; the EIC stationed its own troops paid for by the ruler — protectorate without annexation (see 'Model Treaty of Subsidiary Alliance + Legal Logic [ ▲ Index ]').

3. Foreign-policy logic — by taking control of foreign policy, the EIC could fight wars in the Indian ruler’s name; conquest formally remained absent because no annexation document was signed (see 'Model Treaty of Subsidiary Alliance + Legal Logic [ ▲ Index ]').

4. Vicious-chain consequences — SA crippled Indian States: their armies disbanded, finances drained to pay the subsidy, court factions left to scheme; many States collapsed within a generation (see 'Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States [ ▲ Index ]').

5. Nine signatories (1798–1818) — Hyderabad, Mysore, Awadh, Tanjore, Surat, Carnatic, Peshwa, Sindhia, Bhonsle of Berar; covered most of southern + eastern India by Wellesley’s recall in 1805 (see 'Which States Signed and Under What Circumstances [ ▲ Index ]' and 'Direct Annexations + Wellesley98-05’s Recall [ ▲ Index ]').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): The Subsidiary Alliance turned Pitt’s conquest ban into expansion law — the EIC ruled India without formally conquering it.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Examine the vicious-chain consequences of the Subsidiary Alliance for the Indian States that signed it.
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"The Subsidiary Alliance was sold to Indian rulers as protection. In practice it triggered a vicious chain of consequences that hollowed out the States that signed. Examine."
Demand of the question: Show the chain — step by step — of how SA crippled the State that signed it. Each link feeds the next; the result is internal collapse without external invasion.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Subsidiary Alliance was a slow vivisection — army disbanded, fisc drained, court paralysed, succession compromised. Most signatories collapsed within a generation.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Disbanded army — the ruler’s own army was disbanded; only EIC troops remained — the ruler lost the ability to defend himself or even police his own State (see 'Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States [ ▲ Index ]').

2. Fiscal drain — the ruler paid for the EIC troops stationed in his State; the subsidy was huge and ate revenue surplus; this destroyed the ability to fund education, irrigation, infrastructure (see 'Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States [ ▲ Index ]').

3. Court paralysis — with foreign policy removed, the ruler’s court lost its strategic function; factions schemed over palace politics only; talented administrators left (see 'Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States [ ▲ Index ]').

4. EIC Resident as real ruler — the EIC posted a Resident at the court; the Resident decided what the ruler could and could not do; the ruler became a figurehead (see 'Model Treaty of Subsidiary Alliance + Legal Logic [ ▲ Index ]' and 'Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States [ ▲ Index ]').

5. Eventual annexation — when the State was bankrupt + the ruler weak, the EIC could annex with little resistance (Awadh 1856, Doctrine of Lapse cases). SA was the slow fuse; annexation was the explosion (see 'Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States [ ▲ Index ]' and 'Direct Annexations + Wellesley98-05’s Recall [ ▲ Index ]').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): The Subsidiary Alliance was the EIC’s slow poison: army gone, money gone, court gone, ruler gone. Annexation finished the process.
