explanation: All three statements verbatim from chapter source — Pollilur 1780 = worst defeat of European army in India + iron-cased rocket artillery + Colonel Baillie defeat + Indian military innovation overcame European tactical advantages.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: With reference to the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780–84) coalition diplomacy, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Warren Hastings73-85 broke the Indian coalition by returning Guntur to Hyderabad (removing their grievance) and signing the Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with the Marathas — which both ended the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) and converted the Marathas into EIC military allies.
Warren Hastings73-85 declared war on Hyderabad to break the coalition.
The coalition was broken by Tipu82-99's death in 1782.
The Treaty of Salbai (1782) was signed between Mysore and the EIC.

explanation: Warren Hastings73-85's coalition-breaking diplomacy: Guntur returned to Hyderabad (removing their grievance) + Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with Marathas — which both ended the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) AND converted Marathas into EIC military allies. Indian coalition dismantled and reassembled against Mysore.
(b) ✗ — No war declared on Hyderabad; opposite of strategy.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Treaty of Seringapatam / Srirangapatnam (1792):
items: 1. Mysore lost half its empire — including the rich territories of Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal.
2. Tipu82-99 paid a war fine of 3 crore rupees and surrendered two of his own sons as hostages to guarantee compliance with treaty terms.
3. The treaty restored status quo with both sides returning conquered territories.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only.
Statement 1 ✓ — Mysore lost half its empire including Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal.
Statement 2 ✓ — 3 crore rupees war fine + two sons surrendered as hostages.
Statement 3 ✗ — that describes Treaty of Mangalore 1784 (after 2nd war), not Seringapatam 1792 (after 3rd war). Seringapatam was territorial loss, not status quo restoration.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: With reference to the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The EIC fought alone against Mysore.

Wellesley98-05 used Tipu82-99's negotiations with Napoleon as a political pretext; Hyderabad had already signed the first Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC in 1798; Arthur Wellesley led a Royal regiment alongside EIC forces in the Siege of Srirangapatnam; Tipu82-99 died defending his capital.
Tipu82-99 retained Mysore's territory after a stalemate.
Wellesley98-05 was killed in the Siege of Srirangapatnam.

explanation: All elements verbatim from chapter: Wellesley98-05 used Napoleon-Tipu82-99 correspondence as London pretext + Hyderabad's first SA 1798 pre-aligned a southern power + Arthur Wellesley at Siege of Srirangapatnam + Tipu82-99 dies defending capital.

(a) ✗ — EIC fought alongside Marathas + Hyderabad. (c) ✗ — Mysore lost most territory; Wodeyar core only retained under SA. (d) ✗ — Wellesley98-05 was the GG ordering the war from Calcutta, not on the battlefield.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: After the 4th Anglo-Mysore War, the central core of Mysore was given back to:

options.text: The old Wodeyar dynasty, with five-year-old Krishnaraja III placed on the throne under a Subsidiary Alliance.

explanation: Wodeyar dynasty restored to Mysore's central core; five-year-old Krishnaraja III placed on the throne under a Subsidiary Alliance. The best parts of remaining Mysore territory (Kanara, Coimbatore, others) were divided between EIC and Hyderabad.
(a) ✗ — Tipu82-99's sons were hostages from 1792; not a restoration option.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding Dhondia Wagh and post-1799 consolidation:
items: 1. Dhondia Wagh was a former prisoner of Tipu82-99 who escaped after Seringapatam (1799) and raised a mounted force from demobilised Mysore soldiers.
2. He styled himself "King of Two Worlds" and threatened EIC supply lines in the Mysore–Maratha borderlands during 1799–1800.
3. Colonel Arthur Wellesley was sent to hunt him down and killed Dhondia in action in 1800.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three statements are correct — Dhondia Wagh as former Tipu prisoner + "King of Two Worlds" + Mysore-Maratha borderlands raids 1799-1800 + Colonel Arthur Wellesley kills Dhondia in 1800.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: With reference to the Carnatic Debts mechanism, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The Carnatic Debts referred to formal EIC-Carnatic treaty obligations.
Successive Nawabs of Carnatic borrowed from private EIC officials at high interest rates.
The Carnatic Debts were paid off by the British Parliament from London.
The Carnatic Debts were a Mughal-era institution.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: Successive Nawabs of Carnatic — most notably Md Ali Wallajah52-95 — borrowed massive sums from private EIC officials at high interest rates, using the land revenue of Carnatic as collateral. EIC officials then collected land revenue from those fertile lands directly. The Nawab couldn't pay; debts compounded; EIC creditors became the de facto rulers of the Carnatic countryside even before formal annexation in 1801.

(a) ✗ — The Carnatic Debts were private loans from EIC officials, NOT formal EIC-Carnatic treaty obligations. (c) ✗ — the Carnatic Debts were never paid off by the British Parliament from London; they became the legal pretext FOR direct annexation in 1801, with the Nawab pensioned and Carnatic lands taken in lieu of debt. (d) ✗ — the Carnatic Debts were a late-18th-century mechanism involving EIC private creditors, NOT a Mughal-era institution.
*Memory hook: Carnatic Debts = private EIC officials' high-interest loans → land revenue siphoned → Carnatic hollowed out.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: With reference to the Carnatic Treaty (1801) and Carnatic annexation, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Wellesley98-05 annexed Carnatic in 1801 outright, using two justifications — maladministration and the accusation that the Nawab had been secretly communicating with Tipu Sultan82-99.
2. Carnatic was annexed directly as EIC territory, not converted into a Subsidiary Alliance state like Awadh or Hyderabad.
3. The Carnatic Treaty 1801 was the first Subsidiary Alliance signed in South India.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only.

Why (a) is correct: Statement 1 ✓ — Wellesley98-05 annexed Carnatic in 1801 outright, using TWO justifications: maladministration AND the accusation that the Nawab had been secretly communicating with Tipu Sultan82-99. Statement 2 ✓ — Carnatic was annexed directly as EIC territory, NOT converted into a Subsidiary Alliance state (unlike Hyderabad, Awadh, Mysore which signed SAs). Statement 3 ✗ — the Carnatic Treaty 1801 was NOT a Subsidiary Alliance at all — it was an outright annexation. Hyderabad's SA (1798) was the first SA signed in South India, not the Carnatic Treaty. The Nawab of Carnatic was pensioned off after Wellesley took the territory directly.
*Memory hook: Carnatic 1801 = direct annexation (not SA) on grounds of maladministration + secret Tipu communications; Hyderabad 1798 was the first South-India SA, not Carnatic.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to Travancore's pre-SA history, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Marthanda Varma29-58 built modern Travancore in the 18th century and decisively defeated the Dutch at the Battle of Colachel (1741).
2. Rama Varma58-98 maintained the EIC alliance as a hedge against Mysore.
3. Tipu82-99's attack on Travancore in 1789 gave Cornwallis86-93 the political pretext to declare the 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1790–92).
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: Why (d) is correct: Statement 1 ✓ — Marthanda Varma29-58 built modern Travancore in the 18th century and decisively defeated the Dutch at the Battle of Colachel (1741), ending Dutch political ambitions in Kerala. Statement 2 ✓ — Rama Varma58-98 (1758–98) maintained the EIC alliance as a hedge against Mysore's expansion southwards. Statement 3 ✓ — Tipu82-99's attack on Travancore in 1789 gave Cornwallis86-93 the political pretext to declare the 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1790–92), since the Travancore-EIC alliance was already in place. 'Travancore Before the SA'.
*Memory hook: Marthanda Varma 1741 Colachel → Rama Varma EIC alliance → Tipu's 1789 attack → 3rd Anglo-Mysore War.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: With reference to the Travancore Subsidiary Alliance (1805), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The SA was signed at sword-point after a military defeat by the EIC.
The SA was extracted by the EIC for helping the king crush his mutinous Nair troops; a British Resident had been in Travancore since 1800.
The Travancore SA was signed in 1798, before Hyderabad's SA.
The Travancore SA gave the king full control over Foreign Policy.

explanation: Why (b) is correct: The Travancore SA (1805) was extracted by the EIC in exchange for helping the king crush a revolt by his own Nair troops, who had mutinied over non-payment of salary. A British Resident had already been stationed in Travancore's court from 1800. The 1805 mutiny gave the EIC its opening: the king accepted SA terms in exchange for British military intervention against his own soldiers.

(a) ✗ — The SA was not signed at sword-point after a military defeat — Travancore was not militarily defeated by the EIC. (c) ✗ — the SA preceded Velu Thampi's revolt (1809), not followed it. (d) ✗ — the SA was not voluntary; it was extracted under crisis pressure.
*Memory hook: Nair mutiny 1805 → king begs EIC for help → EIC charges Subsidiary Alliance as the price.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: With reference to the Velu Thampi Dalawa revolt and the Kundara Proclamation (January 1809), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Velu Thampi Dalawa was the Prime Minister (Dalawa) of Travancore who signed the "Treaty of Perpetual Friendship" with the EIC in 1795.
2. From the town of Kundara in January 1809, Velu Thampi issued a public call to all Travancoreans to rise against British paramountcy.
3. The Kundara Proclamation 1809 is widely regarded as one of the most significant early revolts against the British in South India.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 2 and 3 only.

Why (b) is correct: Why (b) is correct: Statement 1 ✗ — the "Treaty of Perpetual Friendship" with the EIC was signed in 1795, during Rama Varma58-98's reign; Velu Thampi Dalawa was Prime Minister of Travancore only from 1802 to 1809 (Dalawa = PM + Chief of Armed Forces), so the 1795 treaty cannot be his. Statement 2 ✓ — From the town of Kundara in January 1809, Velu Thampi issued a public call to all Travancoreans to rise against British paramountcy — the Kundara Proclamation. Statement 3 ✓ — the Kundara Proclamation 1809 is widely regarded as one of the most significant early revolts against the British in South India; the revolt was crushed within months and Velu Thampi died later the same year. 'Velu Thampi Dalawa & the Kundara Proclamation (1809)'.

Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — retains the false Statement 1: the 1795 Treaty of Perpetual Friendship predates Velu Thampi's 1802–09 term as Dalawa. (c) ✗ — same error, and it also drops the correct Statement 2, which is the Kundara Proclamation itself. (d) ✗ — "all three" fails because Statement 1 is false; the 1795 treaty belongs to Rama Varma58-98's reign, not to Velu Thampi's ministry.
*Memory hook: Velu Thampi 1809 Kundara — first organised Indian-State revolt against the SA.*

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding Tipu82-99's religious policy:
items: 1. Tipu82-99 patronised the Sringeri Sharada Math, wrote letters to its Shankaracharya seeking blessings, and made generous grants to several Hindu temples in Mysore.
2. He carried out forced conversions of Nairs and Christians in the Malabar region and destroyed churches and temples during his military campaigns there.
3. His religious policy was uniformly tolerant across all regions of his empire.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only:
Statement 1 ✓ — Sringeri Sharada Math patronage + Hindu temple grants in Mysore heartland.
Statement 2 ✓ — forced conversions of Nairs and Christians + church/temple destruction in Malabar.

Statement 3 ✗ — Tipu82-99's religious policy was syncretic yet contradictory, NOT uniformly tolerant. The Mysore-heartland-patronage / Malabar-coercion split is the key analytical point — UPSC tests this with one-dimensional-treatment trap ('A Note on Tipu82-99's Religious Policy' ⚠ Alert).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Arrange the following southern consolidation events in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Carnatic Treaty (Carnatic annexation)
2. Travancore signs Subsidiary Alliance
3. 4th Anglo-Mysore War concludes (Mysore reorganised under Wodeyar SA)
4. Kundara Proclamation issued
explanation: Why (b) is correct: Chronology of southern consolidation: 3. 4th Anglo-Mysore War concludes (Mysore reorganised under Wodeyar SA) — 1799 (May 1799, Tipu killed at Seringapatam) → 1. Carnatic Treaty (Carnatic annexation) — 1801 (under Wellesley98-05) → 2. Travancore signs Subsidiary Alliance — 1805 (after the Nair mutiny) → 4. Kundara Proclamation issued — January 1809 (Velu Thampi's revolt). 'Legacy: Southern Consolidation Completed'.
(a)(c)(d) place events in wrong sequences.
*Memory hook: Mysore 1799 → Carnatic 1801 → Travancore SA 1805 → Kundara 1809.*

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Why did Mysore lose the four Anglo-Mysore Wars despite being one of the most modernised States in 18th-century India?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"Mysore under Haider Ali61-82 and Tipu82-99 was the most modernised Indian State of its time — yet it lost all four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–99). Examine the reasons."
Demand of the question: Explain why modernity alone did not save Mysore. Cover military, diplomatic, financial, and geo-political factors.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Mysore was modernising fast — but the EIC had continental capital, sea power, and the ability to break Indian alliances. Modernity could not compensate for these disadvantages.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. EIC broke alliances — in the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780–84), Mysore allied with the Marathas and the Nizam; the EIC bought off the Marathas via Treaty of Salbai 1782 + Nizam via separate diplomacy (see '2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780–84): How EIC broke Mysore-Marathas-Hyderabad Alliance?').
2. Naval supremacy — the EIC controlled the Coromandel coast through the Carnatic Wars (1746–63); Mysore had no answer to British sea power (see 'Why Did Mysore Lose?').

3. Financial depth — the EIC could draw on Bengal revenues (Plassey 1757 + Diwani 1765) and London capital markets; Mysore’s Military Fiscalism, however efficient, drained faster than it could replenish (see 'Why Was Mysore Such a Serious Threat?' and 'Why Did Mysore Lose?').

4. Tactical decisions — Tipu’s decision to over-fortify Seringapatam rather than fight in the open in 1799 narrowed his options; British siege capability + artillery decided the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (see '4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): How Did Mysore Finally Fall?').

5. Diplomatic isolation — Tipu’s 1790s outreach to France + Khalifa + Egypt drew British alarm without delivering material aid; Napoleon’s Egypt expedition (1798) was contained at the Nile and never reached India (see '4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): How Did Mysore Finally Fall?' and 'Why Did Mysore Lose?').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): Mysore had the right ideas; it did not have the resources or the allies. The EIC had both.
revise: Why Was Mysore Such a Serious Threat?
2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780–84): How EIC broke Mysore-Marathas-Hyderabad Alliance?
4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): How Did Mysore Finally Fall?
4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): How Did Mysore Finally Fall?

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: How did the Subsidiary Alliance and direct annexation complete the EIC’s southern consolidation (1799–1809)?
body: 150 words · 10 marks

"By 1799 the EIC had defeated Mysore. By 1809 it had crushed Velu Thampi’s revolt in Travancore. Examine how the Subsidiary Alliance + direct annexation combined to complete southern consolidation in this decade."
Demand of the question: Show how the EIC moved across the southern map using TWO tools simultaneously — SA for some States, annexation for others. Cover Mysore, Carnatic, Travancore.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The post-1799 decade saw the EIC use the Subsidiary Alliance where the State accepted protection, and direct annexation where it did not. Both tools finished southern consolidation.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):
1. Mysore 1799 — Wodeyar dynasty restored as Subsidiary Ally; Tipu’s territories partitioned between EIC, Hyderabad, and Mysore (see '4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): How Did Mysore Finally Fall?').
2. Carnatic 1801 — directly annexed by Wellesley98-05; the Carnatic Debts (loans to Nawab Md Ali52-95 from EIC officials) became the legal pretext (see 'Carnatic Annexed (1801)').

3. Travancore SA 1805 — signed under pressure after the 1805 Nair mutiny over unpaid salaries; Rama Varma58-98 had earlier presided over the decline of Marthanda Varma29-58’s strong state (see 'Travancore: What Happens When the SA Breaks Its Own Promises?').

4. Velu Thampi’s revolt 1809 — the Dalawa’s Kundara Proclamation challenged the SA terms; the revolt was crushed by the EIC, ending Travancorean resistance (see 'Velu Thampi Dalawa & the Kundara Proclamation (1809)').
5. Southern map completed — Mysore as SA + Carnatic annexed + Travancore as SA = no independent State left south of the Krishna by 1809 (see 'Legacy: Southern Consolidation Completed').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): SA + direct annexation worked together — the Carnatic was eaten, Mysore and Travancore tied down. Southern India was British by 1809.
revise: 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): How Did Mysore Finally Fall?
Travancore: What Happens When the SA Breaks Its Own Promises?

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Match Year to War
questions.meta: Prelims 1999 · Match List I with List II
questions.stem: Match List I (Years) with List II (Events) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists.
explanation: (c) ✓ — A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2. Why (c) is correct: The correct match is A-3 (1775 = 1st Anglo-Maratha War, Treaty of Surat), B-4 (1780 = 2nd Anglo-Mysore War, Pollilur era), C-1 (1824 = 1st Anglo-Burmese War), D-2 (1838 = 1st Anglo-Afghan War). The trap-anchor is year-of-outbreak (start year); students who memorise wars by their end year (1782 / 1784 / 1826 / 1842) often pick wrong. (a) ✗ — pairs B-2 (1780 = 1st Anglo-Afghan), but 1780 is 2nd Anglo-Mysore; 1st Anglo-Afghan started in 1838. (b) ✗ — pairs A-4 (1775 = 2nd Anglo-Mysore), but 1775 is 1st Anglo-Maratha (Treaty of Surat).

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: Match AD Range to War
questions.meta: Prelims 2004 · Match List I with List II
questions.stem: Which of the following pairs are correctly matched?
explanation: (a) 2 and 4
(b) 3 and 4
(c) 1 and 2
(d) 2 and 3

(d) ✓ — 2 and 3. Why (d) is correct: Pairs B-2 (1790–92 = 3rd Anglo-Mysore War) and C-3 (1824–26 = 1st Anglo-Burmese War) are correctly matched. Trap features: A. 1767–69 is the 1st Anglo-Mysore War (NOT 1st Anglo-Maratha — that started 1775); D. 1845–46 is the 1st Anglo-Sikh War (NOT 2nd — 2nd Anglo-Sikh was 1848–49). (a) ✗ — pair D (1845–46 = 2nd Sikh War per List II) is incorrect; 1845–46 was 1st Anglo-Sikh. (b) ✗ — same D-pairing error. questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.title: Abdali's Invasion: Maratha Punjab Expansion
questions.stem: What was the immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali to invade India and fight the Third Battle of Panipat?

options.text: He wanted to avenge the expulsion by Marathas of his Viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore
The frustrated Governor of Jullandhar Adina Beg Khan invited him to invade India
He wanted to punish Mughal administration for non-payment of agreed annual tribute
He wanted to annex all the fertile plains of Punjab upto the borders of Delhi to his kingdom

explanation: (a) ✓ — The immediate provocation was the Maratha thrust into the north-west: the Marathas had seized Lahore and driven out Abdali's son and viceroy Timur Shah from the Punjab, so Abdali invaded to recover the province and avenge that expulsion — the campaign that culminated in the Third Battle of Panipat (1761).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about why the Deccan mattered to the EIC:
items: 1. The Deccan and Konkan coast were commercially critical — large coastline, significant cotton trade from Gujarat with China.
2. The Maratha Confederacy was the last major Indian power capable of checking EIC expansion across the subcontinent.
3. Three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–82, 1803–05, 1817–19) decided the outcome.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three statements verbatim from chapter source — Deccan/Konkan commercial significance + Maratha Confederacy as last challenger + 3 wars (1775–82, 1803–05, 1817–19).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: With reference to the trigger of the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Hyder Ali61-82 attacked the Maratha territories, drawing the EIC into war.

The Baarbhai Conspiracy (1774) removed Raghunath Rao73-74; he then approached the EIC's Governor of Bombay William Hornby and signed the Treaty of Surat (1775) for EIC military help in regaining the Peshwaship in exchange for Salsette and Bassein.
Tipu Sultan82-99 invaded the Konkan coast.

explanation: Baarbhai Conspiracy 1774 removed Raghunath Rao73-74; he approached William Hornby (Governor of Bombay) and signed Treaty of Surat 1775 in exchange for Salsette + Bassein + revenue from Bharuch/Surat. EIC agreed to help him regain the Peshwaship.
(a) ✗ — Hyder Ali61-82 was Mysore, not connected to 1st Anglo-Maratha trigger. (c) ✗ — Tipu82-99 not involved here. (d) ✗ — French navy not involved.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: With reference to the Treaty of Purandhar (1776), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Negotiated by Warren Hastings73-85 with Nana Fadnis.
2. The EIC would recognise Madhav Rao II74-95 as the legitimate Peshwa, and Raghunath Rao73-74 would be pensioned off.
3. The EIC would receive Salsette and Bharuch; Marathas would not allow any French presence in their domain.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three statements verbatim — Treaty of Purandhar 1776 negotiated by Warren Hastings73-85 with Nana Fadnis; recognised Madhav Rao II74-95 as Peshwa; Raghunath Rao73-74 pensioned off; EIC got Salsette + Bharuch; no French presence allowed.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: With reference to the Treaty of Salbai (1782), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: It was signed by Robert Clive57-67.

It ended the 1st Anglo-Maratha War; established a military alliance between EIC and Marathas; the Marathas switched sides in the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780–84); the EIC retained Salsette and Bharuch; PoRF was established with the Marathas.
It annexed half of Maratha territory to the EIC.

explanation: Treaty of Salbai 1782 (negotiated at Gwalior, represented on the Maratha side by Mahadji Scindhia) ended the 1st Anglo-Maratha War + military alliance between EIC and Marathas + Marathas switched sides in 2nd Anglo-Mysore War + EIC retained Salsette and Bharuch + no French settlements + PoRF established with Marathas.

(a) ✗ — Robert Clive57-67 was Bengal-era, not Salbai 1782. (c) ✗ — Salbai did not annex Maratha territory; EIC returned all captured territory. (d) ✗ — Wellesley98-05 came in 1798, sixteen years after Salbai.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the inter-war period (1782–1803):
items: 1. Mahadji Scindhia dominated Maratha politics until his death in 1794.
2. Madhav Rao II74-95 committed suicide in 1795; Bajirao II96-18 then became Peshwa.
3. Nana Fadnis died in 1800, removing the one figure who had held the Confederacy together.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three preserved verbatim from chapter source — Mahadji Scindhia died 1794 + Madhav Rao II74-95 suicide 1795 + Bajirao II96-18 becomes Peshwa 1796 + Nana Fadnis dies 1800.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: With reference to the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Bajirao II96-18 signed it after defeating Yashwantrao Holkar in battle.

Bajirao II96-18 had been defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar (avenging the execution of his stepbrother Vithoji Rao Holkar by the Peshwa); fled and signed the SA with the EIC in exchange for help to regain the Peshwaship; this triggered the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05).
The Treaty of Bassein was signed by Tipu Sultan82-99 with the Marathas.
The Treaty of Bassein ended the 1st Anglo-Maratha War.

explanation: Vithoji Rao Holkar's brutal execution by Peshwa Bajirao II96-18 (1801) → Yashwantrao Holkar revenge defeat of Bajirao II96-18 + Daulat Rao Scindhia (October 1802) → Bajirao II96-18 fled and signed Treaty of Bassein (December 1802) for SA + EIC help to regain Peshwaship → triggered 2nd Anglo-Maratha War.

(a) ✗ — opposite (Bajirao II96-18 was defeated, not the victor). (c) ✗ — Tipu82-99 not involved. (d) ✗ — Bassein triggered the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War; it did not end the 1st (Salbai 1782 ended the 1st).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Battle of Assaye (1803):
items: 1. Arthur Wellesley, commanding his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces, fought against the Marathas at Assaye.
2. Arthur Wellesley later described Assaye as the toughest fight of his entire military career — harder than anything he faced against Napoleon in Europe.
3. The man who eventually defeated Napoleon at Waterloo found the Marathas a harder military challenge.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three statements verbatim from chapter source — Arthur Wellesley led Royal regiment + Battle of Assaye 1803 + his "toughest fight" verdict + Marathas-vs-Napoleon analytical aside.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to the consequences of the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Bajirao II96-18 regained the Peshwaship.
2. Scindhia lost all territory north of the River Yamuna — including Delhi and Agra, and all his territory in Gujarat — and signed a Subsidiary Alliance.

3. A British Resident stationed in Delhi established PoIR over Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II60-06; from this point the legal fiction of Mughal sovereignty since the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 continued, but its substance was gone entirely.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three preserved verbatim — Bajirao II96-18 reinstated + Scindhia loses N of Yamuna + Delhi + Agra + Gujarat + SA + PoIR over Shah Alam II60-06 + Mughal-sovereignty fiction (since ToA 1765) hollowed out.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: With reference to the Policy of Paramountcy (PoP, 1813–58) under Francis Hastings13-23, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: PoP restored the EIC's policy of non-interference with Indian States.

PoP = PoSA + Indian States lost all rights previously promised under SA. The EIC now openly declared that its own interests overrode any treaty commitments to Indian rulers — what had earlier happened in practice was now declared openly.
PoP was abolished by Wellesley98-05 in 1805.
PoP applied only to the Maratha Confederacy.

explanation: PoP (1813–58) under Francis Hastings13-23 = PoSA + Indian States lost all rights previously promised under SA. EIC openly declared its interests overrode treaty commitments — what had happened in practice was now declared openly.

(a) ✗ — opposite of restoration; PoP was re-initiated expansion after Cornwallis86-93 second-stint non-interference. (c) ✗ — PoP started 1813, after Wellesley98-05 had already been recalled (1805); not abolished by him. (d) ✗ — PoP applied broadly, not just Marathas.

questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three statements verbatim — Appa Sahib + Treaty of Nagpur 1816 + power-grab as regent for Parsoji Bhonsle + Arab/Rohilla mercenaries loophole + Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817) + EIC Subsidiary Force already stationed in Nagpur defeated Appa Sahib's larger force.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12

2. Maharashtra — the Svarajya, the original Maratha homeland — was annexed into the Bombay Presidency.
3. Satara (seat of the Chhatrapati) and Kolhapur were not annexed; the EIC maintained the Chhatrapati's line as a symbolic gesture.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three statements verbatim — Peshwaship abolished + Bajirao II96-18 → Bithur near Kanpur + adopted son Nana Sahib → Kanpur revolt 1857 + Maharashtra (Svarajya) annexed into Bombay Presidency + Satara (Chhatrapati) + Kolhapur preserved as symbolic gesture.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding why the Marathas lost (4-factor diagnostic):
items: 1. Factionalism at every stage — Surat vs Purandhar treaties of 1775–76; Bajirao II96-18's flight to Bassein 1802; Holkar–Scindhia split during the 2nd war; united too late in the 3rd.
2. Absence of unified command — Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle and Gaikwad of Baroda never coordinated effectively.
3. The Marathas had military superiority over the EIC throughout the three wars; their defeat came purely from political betrayal.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only:
Statement 1 ✓ — factionalism at every stage (Surat-Purandhar 1775-76 + Bassein 1802 + Holkar-Scindhia 2nd war split + united too late in 3rd).
Statement 2 ✓ — absence of unified command among Scindhia + Holkar + Bhonsle + Gaikwad of Baroda.

Statement 3 ✗ — the opposite of the true diagnosis. The Marathas had strong individual military (Pollilur-style at the unit level + Battle of Assaye reputation) but political organisational gaps. Their defeat was political (factionalism + no unified command + EIC financial depth + naval/logistics gap), NOT a "purely political betrayal" of an otherwise-superior military force. Mysore also fought well and modernised seriously. It lost because it fought largely alone — the same diagnostic applies to the Marathas.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: With reference to the annexation of Sindh (1843), which one of the following is correct?

Annexed by Dalhousie48-56 in 1843 under the Doctrine of Lapse.
Annexed by Hardinge44-48 in 1843 after the 1st Anglo-Sikh War.

explanation: Sindh annexed in 1843 by Ellenborough42-44 from the "Char Yaar" (four Baloch chiefs of the Talpur dynasty) without credible justification. Sir Charles Napier was the military commander; his "Peccavi" anecdote captures the brazenness.

(a) ✗ — Wellesley98-05 was recalled 1805, well before Sindh 1843. (c) ✗ — Dalhousie48-56's Doctrine-of-Lapse era began 1848, five years after Sindh annexation. (d) ✗ — Hardinge44-48 dealt with 1st Anglo-Sikh War 1845–46, not Sindh.

2. In 1848, Dalhousie48-56 annexed Satara under the Doctrine of Lapse — ending the residual Maratha presence on the political map 29 years after the Confederacy collapsed.
3. The Satara annexation opened the Doctrine-of-Lapse sequence that culminated in Awadh 1856 and the trigger environment of 1857.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
body: End of Practice Set. Answer Key follows.
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. (Dalhousie’s Annexations and Policies):

All three statements verbatim — Chhatrapati line preserved as symbolic figurehead from 1819; Dalhousie48-56 annexed Satara under Doctrine of Lapse in 1848 (29-year gap); Satara opened the Doctrine-of-Lapse sequence (Jhansi 1853 → Nagpur 1854 → Awadh 1856 → 1857 trigger environment).

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Why did the Marathas lose the three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–82, 1803–05, 1817–19) despite their numerical strength?
body: 150 words · 10 marks
"The Maratha Confederacy was the largest indigenous power in India at the start of the Anglo-Maratha Wars. Yet by 1819 it was completely broken. Examine the reasons."
Demand of the question: Show why the Marathas’ numerical and territorial advantage failed against the EIC. Cover structural, leadership, and tactical reasons.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Marathas were militarily strong but politically fragmented. The EIC exploited their internal disunity, financial weakness, and tactical inferiority to win all three wars.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Internal disunity — the Maratha Confederacy was nominally led by the Peshwa, but real power was split among four Sardars (Scindia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaekwad). EIC isolated them one at a time (see 'Why Did the Marathas Lose?').

2. Peshwa Bajirao II96-18’s blunder — signed the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802) after losing to Holkar; this sold out the Confederacy and triggered the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (see '2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) — Wellesley98-05's War').

3. Tactical inferiority — the Marathas relied on heavy cavalry; EIC infantry squares + artillery (Wellesley98-05 at Assaye 1803) outclassed them on the field (see '2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) — Wellesley98-05's War').
4. Financial weakness — Maratha treasury was small relative to EIC’s Bengal revenue base; sustained war drained them faster than they could replenish (see 'Why Did the Marathas Lose?').

5. Pindari menace — the Pindaris (irregular raiders attached to Maratha Sardars) gave the EIC a pretext for the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War; Francis Hastings13-23’s paramountcy policy converted the war into final destruction of Maratha sovereignty (see 'The Pindaris, Francis Hastings 13-23 (1813-23) & his Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58)' and '3rd Anglo-Maratha War + Pindari War (1817–19)' and 'Consequences of 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19)').
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): Maratha defeat was political, not military. The EIC won because the Marathas were not one polity but many quarrelling ones.
revise: The Pindaris, Francis Hastings 13-23 (1813-23) & his Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58)

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Compare Francis Hastings13-23’s Policy of Paramountcy (1813–58) with Wellesley98-05’s Subsidiary Alliance — how did the EIC’s frontier doctrine evolve?
body: 150 words · 10 marks

"Wellesley98-05’s Subsidiary Alliance and Francis Hastings13-23’s Policy of Paramountcy were both designed to extend British control over Indian States. Compare the two doctrines and explain how the EIC’s frontier policy evolved."
Demand of the question: Show what each doctrine did + how Paramountcy extended/replaced SA. Conclude with the trajectory: SA → Paramountcy → direct annexation.
Suggested intro (~25 words): SA promised protection; Paramountcy demanded subordination. Each phase of EIC policy made Indian States more dependent and the EIC more sovereign.
Guiding themes (pick 4-5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley98-05, 1798–1805) — Indian ruler surrendered foreign policy + external defence; EIC stationed troops paid by the ruler ('2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) — Wellesley98-05's War' background; Ch 11 detail).

2. Policy of Paramountcy (Francis Hastings13-23, 1813–58) — EIC was declared the paramount power over ALL Indian States; principalities now had to accept EIC supremacy in both internal and external matters (see 'The Pindaris, Francis Hastings 13-23 (1813-23) & his Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58)').

3. Pindari pretext — Francis Hastings used the Pindari raids as justification to break Maratha sovereignty in the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817–19); annexation and direct control followed (see '3rd Anglo-Maratha War + Pindari War (1817–19)' and 'Consequences of 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19)').

4. EIC Army overhyping — 'Wars due to EIC Army overhyping threat to borders' notes that the EIC Army repeatedly inflated border threats to justify wars; this was the structural pattern across multiple decades (see 'Wars due to EIC Army overhyping threat to borders').
5. Trajectory — SA (soft control) → Paramountcy (declared supremacy) → Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie48-56, outright annexation on heirless succession). Each step removed more Indian sovereignty.
Suggested conclusion (~20 words): SA was the bait; Paramountcy was the trap; Lapse was the kill. The EIC’s frontier doctrine ratcheted up through three phases.

questions.label: PYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Mains 2013 — "Lord Dalhousie was the founder of modern India"
body: "In many ways, Lord Dalhousie was the founder of modern India." Elaborate.

Demand of the question: Elaborate on the claim that Lord Dalhousie was the founder of modern India — which calls for substantiation with specific evidence of how Dalhousie48-56's tenure built the modern Indian infrastructure that survived into the post-1947 nation. The "in many ways" framing tells you the prompt accepts a qualified affirmative — you must enumerate the ways and explain why they qualify as foundational. The directive verb Elaborate asks for examples + analytical reasoning, not a yes/no debate.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Lord Dalhousie48-56 (1848–56) was, in many ways, the founder of modern India — the physical and institutional infrastructure he built for colonial purposes outlasted them, and India inherited it.
Guiding themes (pick 4–5 for a 200-word answer):
1. Railways (1853) — first line Bombay–Thane; by 1856 extended to Calcutta–Raniganj + Madras–Arakkonam
2. Telegraph Department (1853) — 4,000 miles connecting major Indian cities
3. Post Office Act (1854) — uniform half-anna rate from Peshawar to Calcutta
4. Public Works Department (PWD) — separated from military; Grand Trunk Road revival
5. Wood's Despatch (1854) — "Magna Carta of Indian Education"; vernacular schools + universities + structured education administration
6. Three universities (Bombay, Madras, Calcutta) — established 1857 under Lord Canning, but the groundwork was Dalhousie48-56's

Suggested conclusion (~25 words): In many ways, Dalhousie48-56's colonial infrastructure became the skeleton of modern India — the irony being that what he built for empire became the bones of an independent nation.

Reconciliation note for Mains-grade rigour: Dalhousie48-56 built this infrastructure for colonial purposes — easier troop movement, cheaper administration, raw material extraction, market creation. The Mains 2013 quote is true and the colonial-purpose framing matters. The reconciliation: the infrastructure outlasted its colonial purpose. India inherited a colonial skeleton and made it the bones of a postcolonial state. The strongest single anchor for this argument is Wood's Despatch (1854) — its education-administration blueprint is what most directly shaped modern India's civil service + university + literacy infrastructure.

(a) — that's the Post Office Act 1854. (c) — Doctrine of Lapse was abolished only after 1858 by Queen Victoria's Proclamation. (d) — that's Wood's Despatch 1854 + Lord Canning 1857 establishment.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: With reference to Nana Sahib and the 1857 link, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Peshwa Bajirao II96-18 died in 1851; Dalhousie48-56 refused to continue the State pension of Rs 8 lakh per annum to his adopted son Nana Sahib.
2. The argument was that while Nana Sahib could legally inherit Bajirao II96-18's private wealth, he had no right to inherit a political title or a State pension.
3. This financial ruin and loss of status was a direct cause of Nana Sahib becoming one of the fiercest leaders of the 1857 revolt — with his base at Bithur, near Kanpur.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: All three statements verbatim from chapter source — Bajirao II96-18 dies 1851 + Rs 8 lakh pension refused + private-vs-political distinction + Nana Sahib leads 1857 Kanpur revolt.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: With reference to the annexation of Berar (1853), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Berar was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse.
Berar was annexed in lieu of subsidy from Hyderabad — which had signed the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798 and could not pay by 1853.
Berar was annexed by Wellesley98-05 in 1801.
Berar was annexed after the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War.

explanation: Berar 1853 = Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy from Hyderabad — first SA signatory 1798 + escalating subsidy demands + 1853 default + Berar taken as permanent payment.

(a) — not Lapse; this was a separate instrument. (c) — Wellesley98-05 dealt with Awadh 1801 in lieu of subsidy, NOT Berar; Wellesley98-05 was recalled 1805. (d) — 2nd Anglo-Maratha War concluded with Treaty of Bassein/Assaye-aftermath SAs in 1803-05, not Berar 1853.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: With reference to the annexation of Awadh (1856), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Awadh was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse because Wajid Ali Shah had no biological heir.

Awadh was annexed on the pretext of misgovernance — Wajid Ali Shah had children (so Lapse did not apply); Dalhousie48-56 used a different pretext. The British Resident had already established Indirect Rule, leaving the Nawab "no powers but all the blame".
Awadh was annexed after the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War.
Awadh was annexed in lieu of subsidy.

explanation: Awadh 1856 was annexed on misgovernance pretext because Wajid Ali Shah had children (Lapse couldn't apply). British Resident had established Indirect Rule — Nawab "no powers but all the blame". Prelims 2008 directly tests this distinction.

(a) — Lapse didn't apply because Wajid Ali Shah had heirs. (c) — 2nd Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49) is unrelated to Awadh annexation 1856. (d) — that was Berar 1853 (see 'Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy: Berar (1853)'), not Awadh.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to the two Treaties of Amritsar, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Treaty of Amritsar 1809 was signed between Maharaja Ranjit Singh01-39 and the EIC; it established the Sutlej River as the boundary between the Sikh State and EIC territory.

2. The Treaty of Amritsar 1846 was signed between the EIC and Gulab Singh Dogra; under it, Kashmir and Hazara were sold to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees, recognising him as Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir.
3. Both treaties were signed in the same year by the same parties.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only. ⚠ Alert:
Statement 1 ✓ — Treaty of Amritsar 1809 = Ranjit Singh01-39 + EIC, Sutlej boundary.
Statement 2 ✓ — Treaty of Amritsar 1846 = EIC + Gulab Singh Dogra, Kashmir + Hazara sold for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees, J&K creation.
Statement 3 ✗ — opposite; 1809 vs 1846 are 37 years apart and signed by different parties (Ranjit Singh01-39 vs Gulab Singh Dogra).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: With reference to the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War (1848–49), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The Sikh State decisively defeated the EIC and retained Punjab.

The Sikh Governors of Haripur and Multan revolted; this gave Dalhousie48-56 the opportunity. Punjab was annexed from Maharaja Duleep Singh, who had ascended the throne in 1843 at the age of just 5 years (ruled 1843–49).
The war was fought under Hardinge44-48.
The war ended with Treaty of Lahore 1849.

explanation: 2nd Anglo-Sikh War triggered by Sikh Governors of Haripur and Multan revolt → Dalhousie48-56 opportunity. Punjab annexed from Maharaja Duleep Singh (1843-49 child king age 5).

(a) — opposite; EIC won. (c) — Hardinge44-48 fought the 1st Anglo-Sikh War (1845-46), not the 2nd. The 2nd was under Dalhousie48-56. (d) — Treaty of Lahore was 1846 (after 1st Anglo-Sikh War), not 1849.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: With reference to the Treaty of Kalat (1854) and the Treaty of Jacobabad (1876), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Treaty of Kalat (1854) was signed by the EIC under Dalhousie48-56 (PoP era); Treaty of Jacobabad (1876) was signed by the British State under Viceroy Lytton76-80 after the Government of India Act 1858 abolished the EIC (Policy of Subordinate Union era). The shift between the two mirrors what happened to all 565 Indian princely States in 1858.
Both were signed under the Government of India Act 1858.
Both were treaties with the Sultanate of Oman.

explanation: Treaty of Kalat 1854 = EIC under Dalhousie48-56 (PoP era — pre-1857 EIC authority). Treaty of Jacobabad 1876 = British State under Viceroy Lytton76-80 (Policy of Subordinate Union era — post-1858 GOI Act). The shift mirrors the 1858 transition for all 565 princely States from EIC subordinates to British Crown subjects.

(a) — Dalhousie48-56 was recalled 1856; could not have signed Jacobabad 1876. (c) — 1854 Kalat predated GOI Act 1858. (d) — Sultanate of Oman was the Gwadar enclave context ('Britain's Maritime Ring Fence' ⚠ Alert), not Kalat treaties.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to Gwadar's status as an Omani enclave, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In 1783, the Khan of Kalat gifted the port of Gwadar to a prince of Oman.
2. Gwadar remained an overseas territory of the Sultanate of Oman for over 170 years, sitting inside the Balochistan coast.
3. Pakistan purchased Gwadar from Oman in 1958 — eleven years after independence.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. ⚠ Alert:

All three statements verbatim from chapter source — 1783 Khan of Kalat gifts Gwadar to Omani prince + 170-year Omani enclave inside Balochistan + Pakistan purchases 1958 (eleven years post-Independence).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: With reference to Wood's Despatch (1854), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: It was the formal ending of the Doctrine of Lapse.

Sometimes called the "Magna Carta of Indian Education", it laid the blueprint for mass education — recommending vernacular elementary schools, universities, and a structured education administration. Dalhousie48-56 supported and implemented it.
It established the Telegraph Department in India.
It was issued by Lord Canning in 1857.

explanation: Wood's Despatch (1854) = "Magna Carta of Indian Education"; mass-education blueprint = vernacular elementary schools + universities + structured education administration. Dalhousie48-56 supported and implemented it.

(a) — Doctrine of Lapse ended only via Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858. (c) — Telegraph Department established 1853, separate from Wood's Despatch. (d) — Wood's Despatch was 1854 under Dalhousie48-56, not 1857 under Canning.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: With reference to the three Presidency Universities (Bombay, Madras, Calcutta), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: They were officially established in 1854 under Dalhousie48-56.
They were officially established in 1857 under Lord Canning, but the groundwork was Dalhousie48-56's via Wood's Despatch (1854).
They were established in 1858 under Queen Victoria's Proclamation.
They were established in 1853 by Lord Hardinge.

explanation: Three universities (Bombay, Madras, Calcutta) officially established 1857 under Lord Canning, but the groundwork was Dalhousie48-56's via Wood's Despatch (1854). UPSC trap — students often credit Dalhousie48-56 directly with the universities (he laid the groundwork) or Lord Canning entirely (he formally established them).

(a) — universities were established in 1857, not 1854. (c) — Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858 was about Doctrine of Lapse reversal, not universities. (d) — Hardinge44-48 was 1844-48; universities came in 1857 under Canning.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Arrange the following British India policies in correct chronological order of formal initiation:
items: 1. Policy of Paramountcy (PoP)
2. Policy of Subsidiary Alliance (PoSA)
3. Policy of Subordinate Union
4. Policy of Relative Isolation
explanation: Policy of Relative Isolation (until 1813) → Policy of Subsidiary Alliance / PoSA (1798-1858) → Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58) → Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1947).
(Note: PoIR + PoRF run concurrently with the others; they are not numbered in the strict chronological-init sequence above.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: With reference to the post-Dalhousie reversal of the Doctrine of Lapse, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The Doctrine of Lapse continued under Lord Canning until 1862.

Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 — issued after the Government of India Act 1858 abolished the EIC and transferred power to the British Crown — formally ended the Doctrine of Lapse and pledged that the treaties and rights of Indian rulers would be respected. This was the explicit reversal of Dalhousie48-56's core policy.
The Doctrine of Lapse was replaced by the Doctrine of Subordinate Annexation in 1860.
Viceroy Lytton76-80 reinstated the Doctrine of Lapse in 1876.

explanation: Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 — issued after Government of India Act 1858 abolished the EIC and transferred power to the British Crown — formally ended the Doctrine of Lapse and pledged respect for Indian rulers' treaties and rights. Explicit reversal of Dalhousie48-56's core policy. PoP replaced by Policy of Subordinate Union.

(a) — Lapse was ended in 1858 by Queen Victoria's Proclamation, not continued under Canning. (c) — no such doctrine; the replacement was Policy of Subordinate Union. (d) — Viceroy Lytton76-80 did not reinstate Lapse; he tightened Paramountcy-era instruments (e.g. Treaty of Jacobabad 1876) but did not annex.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_16
questions.stem: With reference to Lord Dalhousie48-56 (1848-56) and Bethune School at Calcutta, consider the following statements:
items: 1. J.E. Drinkwater Bethune was Law Member of Dalhousie's Council.
2. Bethune School (1849) was the the first successful secular school for girls in India.
3. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar was associated with the Bethune School and became Principal of Sanskrit College in 1851 under Dalhousie's tenure.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: Why (d) is correct: all three statements are confirmed. Bethune was Law Member of Dalhousie's Council; the school (1849) was the first successful secular school for girls in India; Vidyasagar's 1851 Sanskrit College principalship + 1856 Inspector of Schools both fell under Dalhousie's tenure.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Only 1 and 2 — incomplete; statement 3 about Vidyasagar's 1851 Sanskrit College principalship is also correct.
2. (b) Only 2 and 3 — incomplete; statement 1 (Bethune as Law Member of Dalhousie's Council) is also correct.
3. (c) Only 1 and 3 — incomplete; statement 2 (first successful secular school for girls) is also correct.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Discuss the role of the Doctrine of Lapse in fuelling the 1857 revolt.
body: Demand: Link DoL annexations to specific 1857 grievances; show causal chain from policy to revolt.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Doctrine of Lapse, applied by Dalhousie48-56 to thrones, pensions & land titles from 1848, created the aggrieved leadership that fuelled the 1857 revolt.
Guiding themes:

1. DoL refused Hindu adoption (see 'Doctrine of Lapse: Legal Principle vs Pretext') → 7 States annexed 1848-54 with Jhansi and Nagpur as flashpoints (see 'Annexations via Lapse: Chronology (1848–54)').
2. Pension refusal to Nana Sahib (see 'Doctrine of Lapse Applied to Pensions: Nana Sahib + 1857 Link') and threat to Bahadur Shah Zafar37-57's titular dignity (see 'Critique + Post-Dalhousie').
3. Talukdars and inam-holders dispossessed (see 'The Inam Commission (1852)' and 'Annexation of Awadh (1856)') — created landed grievance coalition.
4. annexation-aggrieved leaders formed the spine of the 1857 revolt — Lakshmibai (Lapse 1854), Nana Sahib (pension 1851), Bahadur Shah Zafar (Mughal dignity).
Closing verdict: The Doctrine of Lapse mattered less as law than as grievance — it supplied the 1857 revolt with leaders who had already lost everything.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Examine Dalhousie48-56's annexations as instruments of Sub-Imperialism.
body: Demand: Show that annexations were driven by EIC-on-ground decisions (sub-imperialism), with concrete examples.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Dalhousie48-56's annexations — Punjab 1849, Lower Burma 1852-53, Berar 1853, Awadh 1856 & the seven Lapse States — were instruments of Sub-Imperialism, decided in India, not London.
Guiding themes:
1. Sub-Imperialism = policies driven by senior EIC officials in India, not British Parliament (see Chapter 17: 'Conquest in India: Policy vs Drift').
2. DoL formulated by Court of Directors 1847 but implemented systematically by Dalhousie48-56 (see 'Doctrine of Lapse: Legal Principle vs Pretext').
3. Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy: Berar 1853 from Hyderabad (see 'Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy: Berar (1853)').
4. Sikh Wars + Punjab annexation 1849 (see 'Sikh State Annexation: 1st + 2nd Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–49)').
5. 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 → Lower Burma annexed (see '2nd Anglo-Burmese War (1852–53): Lower Burma / Pegu').
6. Awadh 1856 on misgovernance pretext — NOT under DoL (see 'Annexation of Awadh (1856)').
Closing verdict: Dalhousie48-56's annexations were instruments of Sub-Imperialism — the empire-builder on the spot, not Parliament in London, drove the Company State to 63% of India.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Suppression of Thugs
questions.stem: Who among the following was associated with suppression of Thugs?
explanation: Why (b) is correct: Sir William Henry Sleeman ran the Thuggee and Dacoity Department (set up 1835) under William Bentinck28-35. His informant networks + approver testimony + swift judicial commissions secured over 3,000 Thug convictions between 1831 and 1841. You will find this in 'Law & Order Paternalism'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) General Henry Prendergast — led the annexation of Upper Burma 1885–86 (see 'Dufferin's Upper Burma (1886)'), NOT Thuggee suppression.
2. (c) Alexander Burnes — Afghan-frontier political agent killed in the 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1841 (see 'Forward Policy in Afghanistan: Ellenborough → Lytton'), NOT Thuggee suppression.
3. (d) Captain Robert Pemberton — Assam/Burma frontier officer, NOT Thuggee suppression.
Memory hook: *Sleeman = Thugs; Prendergast = Burma; Burnes = Afghanistan.*

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: Last Major Territorial Extension
questions.stem: The last major extension of British Indian territory took place during the time of:
explanation: Why (a) is correct: Dufferin84-88 added Upper Burma in January 1886 after the 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885–86. This was the last major territorial extension of British India before independence. You will find this in 'Dufferin's Upper Burma (1886)'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (b) Dalhousie48-56 was the big annexation-era GG (Punjab 1849, Awadh 1856, Doctrine of Lapse) — but his last major extension was Awadh 1856. Dufferin came later (1886) and added Upper Burma.
2. (c) Lytton76-80 carried forward the Forward Policy (see 'Forward Policy in Afghanistan: Ellenborough → Lytton') but did NOT make territorial extensions.
3. (d) Curzon99-05 came later; his Partition of Bengal 1905 was administrative reorganisation, NOT territorial extension.

Nuance on Burma: Dufferin84-88 added Upper Burma to British India & Burma was ruled as a province of British India until 1937. Burma is not traditionally part of India — hence if we are talking about India then the answer is Dalhousie48-56, but if we are talking about the political entity (territory of the British State in India) then the answer is Dufferin84-88. Such questions are weird. Legally the answer should be Dufferin84-88 because the PYQ mentions British India. But the famous answer is Dalhousie48-56 — so the UPSC answer key may say Dalhousie48-56.
Memory hook: *Dufferin = 1886 = Upper Burma = last major extension.*

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.title: Five Antiquarians + ASI (See Chapter 19: 'Education Reforms' — Archaeological Survey of India)
questions.stem: Alexander Rea, A.H. Longhurst, Robert Sewell, James Burgess and Walter Elliot were associated with:
explanation: Why (a) is correct: All five were field antiquarians of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) — founded by Alexander Cunningham in 1861 and reorganised as a permanent department in 1871. Alexander Rea excavated at Amaravati and Bhattiprolu; A.H. Longhurst at Nagarjunakonda and Hampi; Robert Sewell wrote A Forgotten Empire (Vijayanagara); James Burgess was the first Director of the Archaeological Survey of Western and Southern India; Walter Elliot of the Madras Civil Service catalogued Andhra Buddhist sites and coins. You will find this in 'Foreign Ideologies Motivating India's Anti-Colonial Struggle'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (b) English Press — wrong. None of the five was a press editor or journalist.
2. (c) Churches in Princely States — wrong. None was a missionary.
3. (d) Railways — wrong. None was a railway engineer.
Memory hook: *Five British surnames + late-19th-century activity + you don't know any individually = ASI archaeological work.*

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.title: What is the correct chronological sequence of the following
questions.stem: What is the correct chronological sequence of the following?
items: 1. Wood's Education Despatch
2. Macaulay's minute on education
3. The Sargent Education Report
4. Indian Education (Hunter Commission )
explanation:
Why (a) is correct: Macaulay's minute on education (1835) - In this English policy was introduced as a important feature for education and was supported.
Charles Wood's despatch (1854) - Primary school to adopt vernacular language, high school to adopt Anglo vernacular language and English on college level.
Hunter Commission (1882) - To look into the complaints of the non-implementation of Wood's despatch of 1854.
Sargenta plan on Education (1944) - Future development of education in India. (covered in future chapters — Ch 19 Social Reforms, Education Reforms and Print Culture, see relevant section)
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (b) Wrong — places Sargent (1944) before Hunter (1882). Hunter Commission is the earlier landmark.
2. (c) Wrong — opens with Wood's Despatch 1854 ahead of Macaulay's Minute 1835.
3. (d) Wrong — opens with Hunter Commission 1882 instead of Macaulay's Minute 1835.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.title: Wellesley98-05 + Press Regulation Act 1799
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Lord Wellesley imposed Press Regulation Act or Censorship Act in 1799.
Reason (R): The Government became convinced of the role played by the Press towards Indian Renaissance and growth of Indian nationalism.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

explanation: (C) ✓ — A is true but R is false. Wellesley98-05 DID impose the Press Regulation Act (also called Censorship Act) in 1799 — A is correct. R is false: the 1799 regulation was a wartime censorship measure during the French Revolutionary Wars era (anxiety about French sympathisers and revolutionary ideas spreading through Calcutta's Anglo-Indian press), NOT about anticipating Indian Renaissance or Indian nationalism — which were not yet political phenomena in 1799 (Brahmo Samaj was 1828; INC was 1885). The pre-1857 colonial state was worried about European-language print, not Indian-language nationalist print. See Ch 19 (Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture) 'How the Press Began in India' — the new ⚠ Alert (Prelims 1998 A/R) bullet expands on this.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (b) Wrong — when both A and R are true and R clearly explains A, this option (R does NOT explain A) does not apply.
2. (c) Wrong — R is also true in the underlying question.
3. (d) Wrong — A is true in the underlying question.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.title: Which one of the following provisions was not made in the Ch
questions.stem: Which one of the following provisions was not made in the Charter Act of 1833?

options.text: The trading activities of the East India Company were to be abolished
The designation of the supreme authority was to be changed as the Governor-General of India in Council
All law-making powers to be conferred on Governor-General in Council
An Indian was to be appointed as a law member in the Governor-General's Council

explanation: Why (d) is correct: The Charter Act of 1833 did not provide that an Indian was to be appointed as a law member in the Governor-General Council. The other provisions are. It redesignated the Governor-General of Bengal as the Governor-General of India. Under this provision Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India. It deprived the Governors of Bombay and Madras of their legislative powers. The Governor-General was given exclusive legislative powers for the whole of British India. It ended the activities of the British East India Company as a commercial body and became a purely administrative body. In particular, the company lost its monopoly on trade with China and other parts of the Far East. It attempted to introduce a system of open competitions for the selection of civil servants. However, this provision was negated after opposition from the court of directors who continued to hold the privilege of appointing company officials. The Island of Saint Helena was vested in his Majesty. (covered in future chapters — Ch 17 1773 Regulating Act to 1858 GOI Act, see relevant section)
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Was provided — the Charter Act 1833 ended the EIC's commercial activities, leaving it only administrative functions.
2. (b) Was provided — the Act re-designated the GG of Bengal as the GG of India (Bentinck became the first GG of India).
3. (c) Was provided — all law-making powers were centralised in the GG-in-Council under the Act.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.title: Consider the following statements 1. Robert Clive was the fi
questions.stem: Consider the following statements
items: 1. Robert Clive was the first Governor-General of Bengal.
2. William Bentinck was the first Governor- General of India.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
explanation: Why (b) is correct: According to Regulating Act of 1773, Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal. This provision was changed through the Charter Act of 1833, according to which Lord William Bentinck was made the first Governor-General of India. Thus, the first statement is wrong and the second is correct. (covered in future chapters — Ch 17 1773 Regulating Act to 1858 GOI Act, see relevant section)
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Wrong — Robert Clive was not the first GG of Bengal. Warren Hastings73-85 was, under the Regulating Act 1773.
2. (c) Wrong — Statement 1 is false (Hastings73-85, not Clive).
3. (d) Wrong — Statement 2 is true (Bentinck was the first GG of India under Charter Act 1833).

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.title: The first Factory Act for restricting the working hours of w
questions.stem: The first Factory Act for restricting the working hours of women and children and authorising local government to make necessary rules was adopted during whose time?
explanation: Why (c) is correct: During the period of Lord Ripon (1880-84), there was a phase of progress with the Factory Act 1881, which tried to improve the position of factory workers. The first Factory Act was passed in 1881. This Act prohibited the employment of children below 7 years of age and the employment of children under 12 years of age for more than 9 hours. Other chief events of his period were : end of Second Anglo Afghani War; the Vernacular Press Act repealed in 1882; and policy of free trade introduced. The most important constructive work of Lord Ripon was the enactment of a series of Acts, which made Local Self-government more effective. The Ilbert Bill was introduced during his time. The Hunter Commission Report on education came in 1882. Lord Ripon and Lord William Bentinck was the most liked among the British Viceroys. (covered in future chapters — Ch 23 Pre-1885 INM, see relevant section)
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Wrong — Lytton76-80 is associated with the Vernacular Press Act 1878 & the Arms Act 1878, not factory reform.
2. (b) Wrong — Bentinck28-35 ran social-reform legislation (Sati abolition 1829 etc.), but the first Factory Act came decades later under Ripon.
3. (d) Wrong — Canning56-62 was the GG/Viceroy who oversaw the 1857 Revolt suppression and the GOI Act 1858 transition, not factory legislation.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.10
questions.title: Who of the following was/were economic critic/critics of col
questions.stem: Who of the following was/were economic critic/critics of colonialism in India?
items: 1. Dadabhai Naoroji
2. G Subramaniam Iyer
3. RC Dutt
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
explanation: Why (d) is correct: The National Movement was built around a very sophisticated ideological discourse, most of which was developed by the first generation of nationalists, simultaneously called Moderates, who were towering intellectuals. Dadabhai Naoroji, RC Dutt, Ranade, Gokhale, G Subramaniam Iyer, were among those who grounded Indian nationalism firmly on the foundation of anti-imperialism by fashioning the world's first economic critique of colonialism, before Hobson and Lenin. Drain Theory was the core of nationalist critique of colonialism and the acknowledge high-priest of this critique was Dadabhai Naoroji who, as early as 1867, put forward the idea that Britain was draining and bleeding India and that, too, for nothing in return. R C Dutt made this theme the subject of his 'Economic History of India'. Subramaniam Iyer was known for his fiery articles with plenty of sting. Subramaniam Iyer actively supported the cause of India's freedom and used his newspaper The Hindu to protest British Imperialism. Hence, option (d) is correct. (covered in future chapters — Ch 27 Moderates Positives and Drain Theory, see relevant section)
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Wrong — drops G Subramaniam Iyer and RC Dutt, both major Drain-Theory voices.
2. (b) Wrong — drops RC Dutt, whose Economic History of India (1902, 1904) is a foundational drain-critique text.
3. (c) Wrong — drops Dadabhai Naoroji, the original Drain-Theory architect (Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901).

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.11
questions.title: Which of the following led to the introduction of English Ed
questions.stem: Which of the following led to the introduction of English Education in India?
items: 1. Charter Act of 1813
2. General Committee of Public Instruction, 1823
3. Orientalist and Anglicist Controversy
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
Why (d) is correct: The first humble beginning with respect to education in India was made by the Charter Act of 1813 , which directed the East India Company to sanction ₹ 1 lakh annually to encourage learned Indians and for promotion of Modern Sciences.
A decade before Lord Macaulay arrived in India, the General Committee of Public Instruction was formed in 1823, which was to guide the company on the matter of education. The General Committee of Public Instruction had two groups viz Orientalists and Anglicists on the issue of the Development of Education of India. Orientalists supported the use of vernacular languages and Anglicists supported the use of English.
Finally, In 1835, the education policy of Lord Macaulay was published titled "Minute on Indian Education" in which he advocated educating Indians through English and also enrich Indian Languages' so that they become the vehicles of European scientific, historical and literary expression. (covered in future chapters — Ch 19 Social Reforms, Education Reforms and Print Culture, see relevant section)
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Wrong — drops the Orientalist-Anglicist Controversy, the policy debate that crystallised the English-medium decision.
2. (b) Wrong — drops Charter Act 1813 & the Orientalist-Anglicist Controversy.
3. (c) Wrong — drops the General Committee of Public Instruction 1823, which forwarded the issue to Macaulay.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.13
questions.title: Imperial Preference
questions.stem: The term "Imperial Preference" was applied to the:

options.text: Special privileges on British imports in India
Subordination of Indian interest to that of the British
Preference given to British political agents over Indian Princes

explanation: Why (a) is correct: Imperial Preference was a commercial-tariff arrangement — constituent units of the British Empire (Britain, the Dominions and India) granted one another preferential lower tariff rates denied to non-Empire competitors. Formalised at the Ottawa Conference of 1932. The operational effect on India: British goods entered Indian ports at lower tariff than German, Japanese or American competitors. This is option (a) verbatim. You will find this in 'Imperial Preference'.
Why the other options are wrong:

1. (b) Racial discrimination — wrong. Racial discrimination was a separate phenomenon (covered in 'Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)' — Racism + Authoritarianism Post 1857), not the same as Imperial Preference.

2. (c) Subordination of Indian interest in general — wrong. This is the general description of colonialism, not the specific definition of Imperial Preference. The specific definition is the tariff arrangement.
3. (d) Preference given to British political agents over Indian Princes — wrong. This is Political Department protocol (a separate administrative-ceremonial matter), NOT Imperial Preference.
Memory hook: *Imperial Preference = tariff = British imports get special treatment in India.*

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.14
questions.title: Forward Policy in Afghanistan
questions.stem: The Governor-General who followed a spirited Forward Policy towards Afghanistan was:
explanation: Why (d) is correct: Lytton76-80 carried forward the Forward Policy initiated by Ellenborough42-44 — and launched the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War 1878–80, forcing the Treaty of Gandamak 1879 and (after the massacre of Cavagnari at Kabul) a second occupation. You will find this in 'Forward Policy in Afghanistan: Ellenborough → Lytton'.
Why the other options are wrong:
1. (a) Minto — Minto II (1905–10) was a Viceroy of a different era (post-Curzon), NOT associated with the spirited Forward Policy.
2. (b) Dufferin84-88 — famous for Upper Burma 1886 (see 'Dufferin's Upper Burma (1886)'), NOT the Afghanistan Forward Policy.
3. (c) Elgin — Either Elgin I (1862–63) or Elgin II (1894–99) — different era; not Forward Policy.
Memory hook: *Lytton = Forward; Ripon = Retreat.* (Ripon80-84 reversed the Forward Policy and withdrew British forces from Afghanistan.)

questions.label: PYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Mains 2014 — Foreign Ideologies Motivating India's Anti-Colonial Struggle
body: "What were the major political, economic and social developments in the world which motivated the anti-colonial struggle in India?"

Demand of the question: The question asks for major political, economic and social developments in the world that motivated India's anti-colonial struggle — not domestic Indian developments. The directive verb is implicit ("What were..."), calling for an enumeration with explanation across the 3 categories named in the prompt — political + economic + social. The trap: students who focus on Indian developments alone miss the prompt's world-developments anchor.

Suggested intro (~25 words): India's anti-colonial struggle was motivated by major political, economic and social developments worldwide — Enlightenment-era revolutions, deindustrialisation under empire, Russian Revolution, and the post-WWI principle of self-determination.
Guiding themes (pick 4–5 for a 150-word answer):

1. Political — Pre-1900 Revolutionary Currents — American Revolution (1765–83) + French Revolution 1789 + European revolutions 1830 + 1848 + Irish Home Rule (1870–1914) and Irish armed struggle (1916–21) all challenged imperial superiority and inspired colonised peoples.
2. Economic — Industrial Revolution Deindustrialisation — destruction of Indian handloom + deindustrialisation fed Drain Theory of Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt.
3. Social — Russian Revolution 1917 — gave the Indian left a peasant-worker mobilisation model and an anti-imperial vocabulary.
4. Social — Wilson's Self-Determination 1918 — post-WWI Fourteen Points + rising anti-racism made continued British rule indefensible in international forums.

5. Returning Indian leaders brought currents home — Gandhi from South Africa (1893–1915) + Nehru from Cambridge — Indian-diaspora struggles + Western liberal-democratic theory absorbed and applied in India.

Suggested conclusion (~25 words): The major political, economic and social world developments — from American/French Revolutions through Russian Revolution to Wilson's self-determination — together motivated India's anti-colonial struggle as part of a worldwide conversation about freedom.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: With reference to the White Man's Burden (WMB) ideology, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: WMB was a specifically British religious doctrine.

WMB was the foundational belief that Western European civilisation was superior, and that the British therefore had a responsibility to civilise the rest of the world; it was the architectural roof under which Orientalism, Authoritarianism, the Three New Ideologies, and post-1857 Racism all rested.
WMB was abolished by Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858.
WMB applied only to Indian subjects, not to other colonies.

explanation: 'Foundation: White Man's Burden (WMB)':

WMB = Western European civilisation superior + responsibility to civilise others; foundational belief; the architectural "roof" under which Orientalism, Authoritarianism, the Three New Ideologies, and post-1857 Racism all rested.

(a) — WMB was a civilisational/political ideology, not specifically religious. (c) — Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858 ended the Doctrine of Lapse, NOT WMB; the post-1857 shift kept WMB but expressed it through racial contempt (see 'Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)'). (d) — WMB was a generalised European-imperial ideology; not India-specific.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: With reference to Orientalism (1765–1813), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Warren Hastings73-85 was Orientalism's most prominent champion.
2. William Jones discovered that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin belong to the same language family — what we today call the Indo-European language family.

3. Orientalism's institutional foundations included the Calcutta Madrasa (1781), the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784), the Sanskrit College in Banaras (1791), and Fort William College, Calcutta (1800).
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. 'Orientalism (1765–1813): Rule India, the India Way':

All three statements verbatim from chapter source — Warren Hastings73-85 + William Jones Indo-European discovery + 4 Orientalist institutions (Calcutta Madrasa 1781 + Asiatic Society 1784 + Sanskrit College Banaras 1791 + Fort William College Calcutta 1800).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: With reference to Cornwallis86-93's Authoritarianism, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Cornwallis86-93 promoted Indians to senior administrative positions for the first time.

Cornwallis86-93 replaced all Indians in senior administrative positions with British officials, introduced the Cornwallis Code (Charter Act 1793), the Permanent Settlement of 1793 in Bengal, and the concept of the Aloof Elite — keeping rulers separate from the ruled, motivated by his personal experience commanding the British defeat in the American War of Independence (1776–83).

explanation: 'Authoritarianism: Cornwallis86-93 + Conservatism':

Cornwallis86-93's Authoritarianism — replace Indians in senior admin + Cornwallis Code (Charter Act 1793) + Permanent Settlement 1793 + Aloof Elite + American-Independence personal motivation (1776–83).
(a) — opposite (Cornwallis86-93 removed Indians). (c) — he introduced Permanent Settlement, not abolished. (d) — 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775–82 was under Warren Hastings73-85, not Cornwallis86-93.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: With reference to the Conservative school within British Imperial Ideology, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Thomas Munro, John Malcolm, Mountstuart Elphinstone and Charles Metcalfe represented the Conservative school.
2. Thomas Munro's Ryotwari Settlement (1801–07, 1820+) in Madras Presidency exemplified "Orientalist in form, Authoritarian in substance".
3. The Conservatives believed India should be governed entirely by Indian leaders without British interference.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only. 'Authoritarianism: Cornwallis86-93 + Conservatism':
Statement 1 ✓ — Conservative school: Munro/Malcolm/Elphinstone/Metcalfe.
Statement 2 ✓ — Munro's Ryotwari Settlement (1801–07, 1820+) = Orientalist form + Authoritarian substance.

Statement 3 ✗ — opposite of chapter analytical thesis. Conservatives believed India should be governed through Indian traditions — but the British would govern, with no leadership role for Indians whatsoever. Total power centralised in EIC hands.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: With reference to Liberalism in British India (post-1813), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Thomas Macaulay was the most prominent Liberal; he served as legal member of the Governor General's council under the Charter Act 1833.
2. His Law Commission (1834) codified western-style laws for British India by 1837; his Minute on Indian Education (1835) proposed western education in English to create "Brown Sahibs".
3. Liberalism cited the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 as proof that the EIC had governed India badly under Orientalism.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. 'Three New Ideologies (Post 1813): Liberalism + Utilitarianism + Evangelicalism':
