All three preserved verbatim — Macaulay legal member under Charter Act 1833 + Law Commission 1834 + Minute on Indian Education 1835 + Brown Sahibs + Great Bengal Famine 1770 cited as proof.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: With reference to Utilitarianism, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Utilitarianism was associated with Charles Grant and Wilberforce.

Utilitarianism was associated with Jeremy Bentham and James Mill; their argument was that the State should design laws maximising the greatest good for the greatest number of people. James Mill's History of British India (1818) declared India's great past a myth and argued for an effective schoolmaster.
Utilitarianism rejected codification of laws as too rigid.
Utilitarianism was first introduced by Cornwallis86-93.

explanation: 'Three New Ideologies (Post 1813): Liberalism + Utilitarianism + Evangelicalism':
Utilitarianism — Bentham + James Mill + maximum-good-for-maximum-people + History of British India 1818 + effective schoolmaster argument + Court of Directors push for Law Commission 1834.

(a) — Charles Grant + Wilberforce were Evangelicals, NOT Utilitarians. (c) — Utilitarianism promoted codification of laws (Macaulay's Law Commission). (d) — Cornwallis86-93 represented Authoritarianism, NOT Utilitarianism.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: With reference to Evangelicalism in British India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Charles Grant influenced the Charter Act 1813 to legalise the entry of Christian missionaries into India.
2. Evangelists argued that India's fundamental problem was its religion — superstition, ignorance, idolatry and tyranny of priests.
3. The Lex Loci Act / Removal of Religious/Caste Disabilities Act (1850) allowed a convert to retain inheritance rights in family property, removing one practical obstacle to conversion.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. 'Three New Ideologies (Post 1813): Liberalism + Utilitarianism + Evangelicalism':
All three statements verbatim — Charles Grant influence on Charter Act 1813 missionaries + Evangelical critique of Indian religion + Lex Loci Act 1850 inheritance-rights-for-converts.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to the Liberalism Shift 1828–35, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: The Liberalism Shift was launched by Lord Curzon99-05.

The window from William Bentinck28-35 through to the Charter Act 1833 and Macaulay's 1835 Minute is the high-water mark of Liberal confidence; headline interventions: Sati Abolition Act 1829, Thuggee Suppression 1830s–40s under Sleeman, Macaulay's Education Minute 1835 (English replacing Persian), and Cornwallis Code revision into the foundation Macaulay's 1834 Law Commission would build on.
The Liberalism Shift was abolished after 1857.
The Liberalism Shift was Conservative in character.

explanation: 'The Liberalism Shift 1828–35':

Liberalism Shift 1828–35 = high-water mark of Liberal confidence + Bentinck28-35 + 4 headline interventions (Sati Abolition 1829 + Thuggee Suppression 1830s-40s + Macaulay Education Minute 1835 English-replacing-Persian + Cornwallis Code → 1834 Law Commission).

(a) — Curzon99-05 was post-1857 era (1899-1905), NOT Liberalism Shift. (c) — Liberalism retreated sharply after 1857 (see 'Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)'), but the institutional infrastructure built outlasted the confidence by a century. (d) — opposite (Liberal in character).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: With reference to the post-1857 ideological shift, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The reformist impulse of Liberalism, Utilitarianism and Evangelicalism retreated sharply after 1857.
2. Racial sciences in Europe shifted the basis of racial classification from language (the Orientalist criterion) to physical features.
3. The Aryan Invasion Theory was dropped entirely after 1857 because it contradicted post-1857 racial doctrines.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 only. 'Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)':
Statement 1 ✓ — reformist impulse retreated sharply post-1857.
Statement 2 ✓ — racial sciences shifted from language (Orientalist) to physical features.

Statement 3 ✗ — opposite. Aryan Invasion Theory was kept but TWISTED post-1857: yes, Europeans had founded Vedic civilisation, but having intermarried with indigenous Indians over millennia they had "degraded". So even India's ancient greatness was now used as evidence of Indian inferiority — a complete reversal.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: With reference to Captain William Sleeman + Thuggee Suppression, which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Sleeman established the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784.

Sleeman ran the Thuggee and Dacoity Department (set up 1835) under William Bentinck28-35; his informant networks + approver testimony + swift judicial commissions secured over 3,000 Thug convictions between 1831 and 1841 on the Grand Trunk Road.
Sleeman led the annexation of Upper Burma in 1885–86.
Sleeman was killed in the 1st Anglo-Afghan War.

explanation: 'Law & Order Paternalism':

Sleeman ran Thuggee and Dacoity Department (1835) under Bentinck28-35 + 3 operational tools (informant networks + approver testimony + swift judicial commissions) + 3,000 Thug convictions 1831–41 + Grand Trunk Road context.

(a) — Asiatic Society 1784 was Sir William Jones (see 'Orientalism (1765–1813): Rule India, the India Way'), NOT Sleeman. (c) — Upper Burma 1885-86 was led by General Henry Prendergast (see 'Dufferin's Upper Burma (1886)'), NOT Sleeman. (d) — Alexander Burnes was killed in 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1841 (see 'Forward Policy in Afghanistan: Ellenborough → Lytton'), NOT Sleeman.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to the Forward Policy in Afghanistan, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Auckland36-42 launched the disastrous 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1839–42 to reinstall Shah Shuja against Dost Mohammad; the retreat from Kabul (January 1842) wiped out almost an entire British-Indian army.
2. Lytton76-80 carried forward the Forward Policy and launched the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War 1878–80, forcing the Treaty of Gandamak 1879.
3. Ripon80-84 reversed the Forward Policy and withdrew British forces from Afghanistan.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. 'Forward Policy in Afghanistan: Ellenborough → Lytton':

All three statements verbatim — Auckland36-42 launches 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1839-42 + retreat from Kabul Jan 1842 disaster + Lytton76-80 carries forward Forward Policy + 2nd Anglo-Afghan War 1878-80 + Treaty of Gandamak 1879 + Ripon80-84 reverses + withdraws.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: With reference to the annexation of Upper Burma (January 1886), which one of the following is correct?

options.text: Upper Burma was annexed by Dalhousie48-56 in 1856.

Upper Burma was annexed by Dufferin84-88 in January 1886 after the 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885–86; King Thibaw was deposed and exiled to Ratnagiri; the field commander was General Henry Prendergast. Upper Burma was merged with Lower Burma (British from 1852) and governed as a province of British India until the 1937 separation.
Upper Burma was annexed by Lytton76-80 in 1880.
Upper Burma was annexed by Curzon99-05 in 1905.

explanation: 'Dufferin's Upper Burma (1886)':

Upper Burma annexed by Dufferin84-88 in January 1886 after 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885-86; King Thibaw deposed/Ratnagiri exile; General Henry Prendergast field commander; merged with Lower Burma (British from 1852) until 1937 separation.

(a) — Dalhousie48-56's last extension was Awadh 1856; Upper Burma 1886 came 30 years later under Dufferin84-88. (c) — Lytton76-80 carried Forward Policy in Afghanistan, NOT Upper Burma extension. (d) — Curzon99-05's Partition of Bengal 1905 was administrative reorganisation, NOT territorial extension.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: With reference to Imperial Preference, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Imperial Preference was a commercial-tariff arrangement among constituent units of the British Empire — Britain, the Dominions and India — granting one another preferential lower tariff rates denied to non-Empire competitors.
2. It was formalised at the Ottawa Conference of 1932.
3. The operational effect on India was that British goods entered Indian ports at lower tariff than German, Japanese or American competitors.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. 'Imperial Preference':

All three statements verbatim — Imperial Preference = commercial-tariff arrangement among Empire constituents + Ottawa Conference 1932 formalisation + operational effect = British goods preferential rates in Indian ports vs German/Japanese/American competitors.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: With reference to the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The ASI was founded by Alexander Cunningham in 1861 as Director-General; reorganised as a permanent department in 1871.
2. Alexander Rea, A.H. Longhurst, Robert Sewell, James Burgess and Walter Elliot were the first generation of field antiquarians associated with the ASI.
3. The Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784) and Sanskrit College, Banaras (1791) preceded the ASI as Orientalist scholarly institutions.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. 'Education Reforms':

All three statements verbatim — ASI founded by Alexander Cunningham 1861 + 1871 reorganisation + 5 antiquarians (Rea/Longhurst/Sewell/Burgess/Elliot) + Asiatic Society 1784 + Sanskrit College 1791 as predecessor Orientalist institutions.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: With reference to the arc of British Imperial Ideology as it evolved, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The arc runs from cautious cultural respect (Orientalism) to confident westernisation (Liberalism, Utilitarianism, Evangelicalism) to open racial contempt (post 1857).
2. Each shift was triggered by a change in British military confidence and economic interest — i.e., the ideology followed the power, not the other way around.
3. The chapter's analytical thesis is that "modernisation was a tool of domination, not its purpose."
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: 1, 2 and 3. 'Foreign Ideologies Motivating India's Anti-Colonial Struggle':

All three statements are correct — the 3-stage arc (Orientalism → westernising ideologies → post-1857 racial contempt), the thesis that ideology followed British power, and the argument that modernisation served domination rather than being its purpose.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Trace the shift from Orientalism to Authoritarianism in British policy towards India (1765-1813).
body: Demand: Show the ideological pivot with specific Governor-General-era examples and flagship measures.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The shift from Orientalism to Authoritarianism in British policy towards India (1765-1813) replaced 'Rule India, the India Way' with 'Rule India, the English Way'.
Guiding themes:
1. Orientalism 1765-1813 — Hastings73-85 + William Jones + Asiatic Society 1784 + Calcutta Madrasa 1781 + Fort William College 1800 (see 'Orientalism (1765–1813): Rule India, the India Way').
2. Slogan: "Rule India, the India Way" — Indian traditions best administered on their own terms.
3. Shift to Authoritarianism under Cornwallis86-93 (1786): "Rule India, the English Way".
4. All-British senior admin + Permanent Settlement 1793 + Cornwallis Code 1793 + Aloof Elite (see 'Authoritarianism: Cornwallis86-93 + Conservatism').
5. Continuation under Wellesley98-05 with the same control-oriented, centralised, mistrustful approach.
Closing verdict: The shift from Orientalism to Authoritarianism turned one finding — glorious past, degenerate present — from a reason to preserve into a reason to replace.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: How did post-1857 Racism reshape British attitudes towards Indians? Discuss with reference to specific policies.
body: Demand: Identify the six-front shift after 1857 + name the architects + their flagship instruments.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Post-1857 Racism reshaped British attitudes towards Indians on six fronts, and the specific policies of Lytton76-80 & Curzon99-05 carried the new hardness into law.
Guiding themes:
1. Reformist impulse retreated — Liberalism/Utilitarianism/Evangelicalism reform impulses collapsed ('Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)' #1).
2. Racial sciences shifted from language to physical features ('Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)' #2).
3. Aryan Invasion Theory twisted: Europeans degraded by Indian intermarriage ('Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)' #3).
4. "Dogs and Indians not allowed" signs at clubs and parks ('Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)' #4).
5. Authoritarianism increased — distrust of sharing power with Indians ('Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)' #5).
6. Social reforms slowed; Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858 promised non-interference ('Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)' #6).
7. Architects: Lytton76-80 (Vernacular Press Act 1878, Arms Act 1878) + Curzon99-05 (Partition of Bengal 1905) — 'Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)'.
Closing verdict: Post-1857 Racism ended the reformist claim — British attitudes towards Indians now assumed permanent inferiority, & the specific policies of 1878 & 1905 followed.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Match List I–II: Four Land Revenue Systems
questions.stem: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists:
matchTable: A. Land allotted to big feudal landlords
B. Land allotted to revenue farmers / rent collectors
C. Land allotted to each peasant with the right to sublet, mortgage, transfer, gift or sell
D. Revenue settlements made at village level
explanation: (b) ✓ — A-1, B-4, C-2, D-3. A (land allotted to big feudal landlords) = Jagirdari: a jagir was assigned to a Mughal mansabdar/noble — the big feudal lord of the imperial aristocracy — and the collected revenue was passed upward to him when the land was a jagir. B (land allotted to revenue farmers / rent collectors) = Zamindari: the Zamindar was not the owner of land — he was a revenue collector with a commission, collecting from the cultivator and passing the rest upward; that collection role is exactly the rent-collector descriptor. (The Permanent Settlement of 1793 later converted him into a proprietor, but his defining function in the revenue chain is collection.) C (land allotted to each peasant with the right to sublet, mortgage, transfer, gift or sell) = Ryotwari: settlement was made directly with the ryot, who held legal title to his land. D (revenue settlements made at village level) = Mahalwari: assessment and settlement were made at the mahal — the village/estate — level.

Why others wrong: (a) A-1 B-3 C-2 D-4 — correct on A and C, but it pairs revenue farmers / rent collectors with Mahalwari and village-level settlement with Zamindari; Mahalwari is precisely the village-level system and Zamindari is the rent-collector system, so B and D are swapped. (c) A-3 B-4 C-1 D-2 — correct on B, but makes big feudal landlords = Mahalwari (a village-level settlement, not a landlord class), peasants with sale rights = Jagirdari (jagirdars were nobles, not cultivators), and village-level settlement = Ryotwari (which settles with the individual ryot, not the village). (d) A-2 B-1 C-3 D-4 — makes big feudal landlords = Ryotwari (a peasant system), peasants with sale rights = Mahalwari (a village system), and village-level settlement = Zamindari (which settles with the Zamindar, not the village).
Memory hook: Jagir = land allotted to the Mughal feudal noble · Zamindar = revenue collector with a commission · Ryot = peasant with legal title & sale rights · Mahal = village-level settlement.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: Why Zamindars Did NOT Issue Pattas Under PS1793
questions.stem: Under the Permanent Settlement, 1793, the Zamindars are required to issue pattas to the farmer which were not issued by many of the Zamindars. The reason was:

options.text: the Zamindars were trusted by the farmers
there was no official check upon the Zamindar
it was the responsibility of the British Government
the farmers were not interested in getting pattas

explanation: (b) ✓ — Per, the Permanent Settlement made Zamindars deposit only 10/11 of revenue to the State; everything they collected below that threshold sat outside State supervision. With no audit trail, issuing a patta (which legally recorded the ryot's rent) would only constrain the Zamindar. So Zamindars simply did not issue pattas — there was no official check upon them. Confirmed by 's ⚠ Alert (Prelims 2001 + 2011 + 2024 trap cluster).

Why others wrong: (a) records that the ryot became a "tenant at will" and patta system was ignored — relationship was coercive, not trust-based. (c) Pillar 2 places revenue responsibility on the Zamindar; patta issuance was the Zamindar's duty, not the British Government's. (d) shows ryots faced rising rents and eviction — they had every reason to want pattas as a legal safeguard, not the opposite.
Memory hook: No State check below 10/11 — so Zamindar pocketed extra and skipped the patta.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.title: Litigation Surge After Cornwallis86-93's 1793 Settlement
questions.stem: The tendency for increased litigation was visible after the introduction of the land settlement system of Lord Cornwallis in 1793. The reason for this is normally traced to which of the following provisions?

options.text: Making Zamindar's position stronger vis-à-vis the ryot
Making East India Company an overlord of Zamindars

explanation: (d) ✓ — None of (a), (b) and (c). The tendency for increased litigation after 1793 traces to the Cornwallis Code of 1793, whose reorganisation of the judicial system in practice made it inefficient: the District Collector was stripped of all judicial & magisterial powers, so revenue disputes once settled swiftly & informally on the spot now had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats; court fees were abolished to make justice "accessible," which flooded the courts with genuine & frivolous suits alike (fees reimposed in 1795); & the formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) with a rigid hierarchy of appeals let cases be deliberately prolonged & appealed. None of the three listed provisions is that reason.

Why others wrong: (a) While true that Zamindars became absolute owners, the impoverished ryots did not have the means to drag these powerful landlords to court. This power imbalance led to exploitation, not a surge in formal litigation. (b) East India Company did not become the overlord of the Zamindars in 1793. The EIC became the sovereign overlord decades earlier, in 1765, when it acquired the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. The auctions by the Sunset Clause created grievances and disputes over land titles, but the tendency for higher litigation was due to the Cornwallis Code (1793). (c) Cornwallis's courts were anything but efficient — slow, costly, procedure-heavy.

Memory hook: the litigation surge came from the Cornwallis Code's courts — Collector out of the judge's chair, court fees gone, lawyers in — not from any land-revenue clause. (You will be able to answer this fully after covering the chapter on EIC Administration, which explains how the Cornwallis Code increased litigation.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.title: Ryotwari: All Three Statements Correct
questions.stem: With reference to Ryotwari Settlement, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The rent was paid directly by the peasants to the government.
2. The government gave Pattas to the Ryots.
3. The lands were surveyed and assessed before being taxed.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Per: Statement 1 is correct — settlement was done directly with the ryot, so rent reached the government directly from the peasant. Statement 2 is correct, the State recognised the ryot's legal title and the Patta system (which the Permanent Settlement Act, 1793 had killed in Bengal) was preserved here. Statement 3 is correct — assessment was based on detailed field surveys (soil productivity, irrigation, acreage, crops, past trends) before tax was fixed. All three correct → option (c). Confirmed by 's ⚠ Alert (Prelims 2012 + 2017 trap cluster).

Why others wrong: (a) Only 1 — leaves out two correct statements (Pattas + survey). (b) 1 and 2 — leaves out the survey/assessment statement, which explicitly affirms. (d) None of these — directly contradicts.
Memory hook: Ryotwari = ryot pays State direct, gets a patta, after the survey.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.title: Ryotwari Architects: Read and Munro, NOT Cornwallis
questions.stem: Who among the following was/were associated with the introduction of Ryotwari Settlement in India during the British rule?
items: 1. Lord Cornwallis
2. Alexander Read
3. Thomas Munro
explanation: (c) ✓ — Per: Statement 1 (Cornwallis) is wrong — Cornwallis was architect of the Permanent Settlement Act, 1793 and even tried to extend it to Madras using the Poligars; Ryotwari was set up against his template. Statement 2 (Alexander Read) is correct — Munro first experimented with Ryotwari in parts of Madras as early as 1792 under Alexander Read. Statement 3 (Thomas Munro) is correct — Munro convinced the Court of Directors in 1801 and firmly re-established Ryotwari as Governor of Madras (1820–27). Hence 2 and 3 only. Confirmed by 's ⚠ Alert (Prelims 2012 + 2017 trap cluster).
Why others wrong: (a) Only 1 — Cornwallis pushed Permanent Settlement, not Ryotwari. (b) 1 and 3 — wrongly retains Cornwallis. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — wrongly retains Cornwallis.
Memory hook: Read started it in 1792, Munro fixed it by 1820 — Cornwallis was on the other side.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.title: Economic Result of British Rule = Commercialisation of Agriculture
questions.stem: Economically, one of the results of the British rule in India in the 19th century was the:

options.text: increase in the exports of Indian handicrafts
growth in the number of Indian-owned factories

explanation: (c) ✓ — Per: the British demanded land revenue in cash, not in kind. To raise cash, ryots were pushed off food crops (rice, wheat, millets) into cash crops — indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane — destined for British factories and global commodity markets. This structural shift is precisely "commercialisation of Indian agriculture" and is recorded as one of the most important 19th-century economic legacies of British rule. Confirmed by 's ⚠ Alert (Prelims 2021 trap).

Why others wrong: (a) and the Alert mark this as wrong — handicrafts suffered under deindustrialisation, not export growth. (b) The Alert marks growth of Indian-owned factories as without conclusive evidence in the 19th century. (d) The Alert marks rapid urbanisation as without conclusive evidence in this period.
Memory hook: Cash revenue demand → cash crops → food security collapse → late-19th-century famines.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.title: Cornwallis86-93's Revenue: Sunset Clause Statement Only
questions.stem: With reference to revenue collection by Cornwallis, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Ryotwari: peasants exempted in bad harvest.
2. Permanent: Zamindar removed if failed to pay.
questions.stemTail: Which of the above statements is/are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — 2 only. Statement 1 — "Ryotwari: peasants exempted in bad harvest" — is wrong on two counts: Ryotwari was the work of Read & Munro, not Cornwallis, and the early Ryotwari assessment was over-assessed and ruinous, with relief coming only later through the Wingate Settlement (1835) and the Madras rules (1855/1864). Statement 2 — "Zamindar removed if failed to pay" — is correct: it is exactly the Sunset Clause of the Permanent Settlement, under which a zamindar's land was auctioned on default. Hence 2 only.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 only — falsely retains the Cornwallis-Ryotwari pairing. (c) Both 1 and 2 — falsely retains the Cornwallis-Ryotwari pairing. (d) Neither 1 nor 2 — wrongly drops Statement 2 (the Sunset Clause of the Permanent Settlement).
Memory hook: Cornwallis = Permanent only; Sunset Clause = Zamindar lost land on default.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.title: What was the reason for Mahatma Gandhi to organise a Satyagraha for Kheda peasants
questions.stem: What was the reason for Mahatma Gandhi to organise a Satyagraha on behalf of the peasants of Kheda?
items: 1. The administration did not suspend the land revenue collection in spite of a drought.
2. The administration proposed to introduce permanent settlement in Gujarat.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Per in: under the Ryotwari settlement, Kheda's ryots were legally entitled to a remission of Land Revenue if crop yield fell below one-quarter of normal output. The 1918 harvest failed and plague compounded the misery, yet the government refused to grant the legally mandated remission because it needed money for WWI. Statement 1 captures this exactly — revenue collection was not suspended despite the failed harvest. Statement 2 is wrong — Gujarat / Kheda was under Ryotwari (a Bombay Presidency area), and there was no proposal to introduce Permanent Settlement there. Hence only 1.

Why others wrong: (b) Only 2 — disproves the Permanent Settlement proposal claim. (c) Both 1 and 2 — wrongly retains Statement 2. (d) Neither 1 nor 2 — wrongly drops the legally entitled remission that affirms.
Memory hook: Crop failed, plague struck, law said remit — government refused, so MG launched Kheda.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Under the Mughal land revenue system, the actual cultivator who held customary occupancy rights over his plot and paid land revenue as per a document recording the amount he owed was known as the:
explanation: (B) ✓ — Per, the actual cultivator was called the Khudkasht; he held customary occupancy rights over his land and paid land revenue as per the Patta system, where a patta recorded the amount he owed.

Why others wrong: (a) — the Jagirdar was the apex revenue assignee in the chain who received jagir lands, not a cultivator. (c) — Amalguzars were government supervisory officers ensuring Zamindars did not under-report collections, not cultivators. (d) — the Ijaradar was the highest bidder under the Ijaradari system of auctioning revenue collection rights, not the cultivator.
Memory hook: Khudkasht cultivates, Patta protects, Zamindar only collects.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Farming System introduced by Warren Hastings in 1772 in Bengal:
items: 1. The right to collect land revenue in each district was auctioned to the highest bidder.
2. The Revenue Farmer operated under the supervision of a European District Collector.
3. The Revenue Farmer was an agricultural farmer who personally tilled the soil.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statement 1 correct: the right to collect land revenue in each district was auctioned to the highest bidder, the Revenue Farmer. Statement 2 correct: the Revenue Farmer operated under the supervision of a European District Collector.

Why others wrong: (b) Statement 3 wrong — the Revenue Farmer was named so because, like a farmer, he aimed to extract profit from the land through a contract; he was not an agricultural farmer who tills the soil. (c) Statement 3 wrong (same reason). (d) Statement 3 wrong (same reason).
Memory hook: 1772 Farming = revenue auction, not crop ploughing.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793:
items: 1. Zamindars were given full proprietary rights, making land hereditary and transferable within the family.
2. Land revenue was fixed at 10/11 of the Zamindar's pre-existing revenue, with 1789–90 as the base year.
3. Under the Sunset Clause, a defaulting Zamindar's land would be auctioned.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Statement 1 correct — Pillar 1: Zamindars were given full proprietary rights for the first time; hereditary and transferable within the family. Statement 2 correct — Pillar 3: revenue was fixed at 10/11 of the Zamindar's pre-existing revenue with 1789–90 as the base year. Statement 3 correct — Pillar 4: under the Sunset Clause, a Zamindar failing to pay by the pre-set deadline had his land auctioned.
Why others wrong: (a) Statement 3 is also correct. (b) Statement 1 is also correct. (c) Statement 2 is also correct.
Memory hook: PS1793 = Proprietor + Permanent 10/11 + Punishment by Sunset.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: The Permanent Settlement Act of 1793 was applied in which of the following regions?

options.text: Central Provinces, United Provinces and Punjab
Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras and Benaras
Awadh, Rohilkhand and the North-Western Provinces

explanation: (C) ✓ — Per, Permanent Settlement was applied in Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras and Benaras (mnemonic: BOB migrated from North Madras to Benaras and Settled Permanently).

Why others wrong: (a) — Madras, Bombay, Sind and Coorg fell under Ryotwari, not Permanent Settlement. (b) — Central Provinces, United Provinces and Punjab are Mahalwari (CUP) regions. (d) and — Awadh and the North-Western Provinces were under Mahalwari.
Memory hook: BOB-NM-Benaras = Bengal Orissa Bihar, North Madras, Benaras — Settled Permanently.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the powers restored to Zamindars under Regulation VII of 1799 during Wellesley's tenure:
items: 1. The Zamindar could seize a tenant's crops and cattle without a court order if rent was defaulted.
2. The abwabs levied by the Zamindar on his tenants were given a legal basis, making the levy lawful once again.
3. The Zamindar could increase rents at will.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 correct: Wellesley98-05 reversed Cornwallis86-93's earlier removal of police powers through Regulation VII of 1799, restoring to the Zamindar (a) the power to seize a tenant's property — crops, cattle — without a court order if rent was defaulted and (c) the power to increase rents at will. Statement 2 is incorrect — abwabs were legitimate customary tributes only under the Mughal chain; after PS1793 they had no legal basis at all and Regulation VII did not give them one. They simply continued to be collected in practice, illegally.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — carries the incorrect Statement 2 and drops the correct Statement 3. (b) 2 and 3 only — carries the incorrect Statement 2 and drops the correct Statement 1. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — Statement 2 is incorrect: abwabs were never legalised in 1799; they remained illegal and were merely collected anyway.
Memory hook: Wellesley 1799 = seize + jail + hike restored; abwabs stayed illegal — collected in practice, never lawful.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the surge in litigation that followed Cornwallis's Permanent Settlement of 1793?

options.text: The EIC abolished customary law and forced all disputes into newly created High Courts.
Formal land-titles were transferable on default, and the Sunset Clause auctioned titles, multiplying legal petitions.
Patta system was revived under PS1793 and ryots flooded courts seeking enforcement.
The Rent Commission of 1880 mandated that every revenue dispute be settled by judicial decree.

explanation: (B) ✓ — Per, ⚠ Alert (Prelims 2011): litigation surged because making the EIC an overlord of Zamindars meant formal land-titles were transferable to others on default; the Sunset Clause auctioned titles on default, and legal petitions multiplied.

Why others wrong: (a) — no such abolition of customary law is recorded; High Courts came later (1861) and are not the explanation. (c) — under PS the Patta system was ignored, not revived; the ryot became a "tenant at will." (d) — the Rent Commission was set up by Ripon80-84 in 1880, decades after the 1793 litigation surge.
Memory hook: Sunset Clause = land auction = lawyers' paradise.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Under the Rent Act of 1859 in Bengal Presidency, a tenant who had cultivated the same plot continuously for more than how many years gained occupancy rights?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Per, a tenant who had cultivated the same plot continuously for more than 12 years gained occupancy rights and could not be evicted without a court order.
Why others wrong: (a) — the threshold was 12 years, not 6. (b) — the threshold was 12 years, not 9. (d) — the threshold was 12 years, not 20.
Memory hook: 12 years on the same plot = ryot's shield against eviction.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885:
items: 1. It was passed after Ripon set up the Rent Commission in
2. A tenant who had cultivated different plots in the same village for a total of more than 12 years gained occupancy rights over the last plot cultivated.
3. The Act was poorly implemented and largely defeated by Zamindar loopholes.
questions.stemTail: 1880 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statement 1 correct: the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 came after Ripon80-84 set up the Rent Commission in 1880. Statement 2 correct: even tenants who had cultivated different plots in the same village for a total of more than 12 years would now get occupancy rights over the last plot cultivated, closing the earlier loophole.

Why others wrong: (b) Statement 3 wrong — crucially the government implemented the Act sincerely this time; it was the 1859 Act that suffered poor implementation. (c) Statement 3 wrong (same reason). (d) Statement 3 wrong (same reason).
Memory hook: 1885 = Ripon's Commission + same-village 12-year shield, sincerely enforced.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the architects of the Ryotwari Settlement:
items: 1. Cornwallis was a principal architect of Ryotwari in Madras.
2. Alexander Read first experimented with Ryotwari in parts of Madras as early as
3. Thomas Munro re-established Ryotwari firmly when he returned as Governor of Madras (1820–27).
questions.stemTail: 1792 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statement 2 correct: Munro had first experimented with Ryotwari in parts of Madras as early as 1792 under Alexander Read. Statement 3 correct: Munro firmly re-established Ryotwari when he returned as Governor of Madras (1820–27).

Why others wrong: (a) Statement 1 wrong — Cornwallis86-93 was the architect of Permanent Settlement; he and Wellesley98-05 in fact tried to extend PS to Madras via the Poligars before that experiment failed. (c) Statement 1 wrong (same reason). (d) Statement 1 wrong (same reason).
Memory hook: Read & Munro = Ryotwari; Cornwallis = Permanent, not Ryotwari.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of Ryotwari reform and its key feature is correctly matched?

options.text: Wingate Settlement of 1835 — fixed land revenue in Bombay Deccan for 30 years on a fair assessment based on Economic Rent theory
R.K. Pringle of 1830 — capped land revenue demand at 50% of net produce for 30 years in Madras
Madras Torture Commission Report 1855 — first introduced the Ricardian theory of Economic Rent in Bombay
Elphinstone in Bombay — replaced Ryotwari with Permanent Settlement after the Third Anglo-Maratha War

explanation: (A) ✓ — Per, Phase 2: in Bombay, the Wingate Settlement of 1835 (Bombay Survey System by Wingate and Goldsmid, implemented across Bombay Deccan by 1847) assessed land fairly and fixed a reasonable annual amount for 30 years, applying the Ricardian Economic Rent theory.

Why others wrong: (b) — R.K. Pringle (1830) first applied Economic Rent theory in Bombay (not Madras) but his faulty calculations led to an excessive 55% demand; he did not cap demand at 50%. (c) — Economic Rent theory was first applied by R.K. Pringle in Bombay in 1830; the Madras Torture Commission Report 1855 led to the Madras Rules capping demand at 50% of net produce. (d) and — Elphinstone brought Ryotwari to Bombay after annexing the Maratha Svarajya, not Permanent Settlement.
Memory hook: Wingate 1835 = fair survey, 30-year fix, Bombay Deccan calm.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following events in the evolution of Ryotwari assessment:
items: 1. R.K. Pringle applies Ricardian Economic Rent theory in Bombay
2. Wingate Settlement assesses Bombay Deccan fairly for 30 years
3. Madras Rules cap demand at 50% of net produce for 30 years following the Torture Commission Report
4. Alexander Read and Thomas Munro begin Ryotwari experiments in Madras based on gross produce. What is the correct chronological order?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Per and: Read and Munro began Ryotwari experiments in 1792 (Phase 1, gross produce); R.K. Pringle applied Economic Rent theory in Bombay in 1830; the Wingate Settlement in Bombay was 1835; the Madras Rules of 1855/1864 followed the 1855 Madras Torture Commission Report. Order: 4 — 1 — 2 — 3.

Why others wrong: (a) — Read–Munro's 1792 experiments came first; Pringle (1830) cannot be earliest. (b) — Wingate 1835 came before the Madras Rules of 1855/1864; the order 3 — 2 is reversed. (d) — Read–Munro's 1792 experiments preceded Pringle (1830), so 1 cannot come before 4.
Memory hook: Read-Munro 1792, Pringle 1830, Wingate 1835, Madras Rules 1855.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Match the land revenue system with its principal architect or driver:
items: 1. Permanent Settlement — A. Holt Mackenzie
2. Ryotwari (Madras) — B. R.M. Bird
3. Mahalwari (original 1822) — C. Thomas Munro
4. Revised Mahalwari (1833) — D. Cornwallis
explanation: (D) ✓ — Per, Permanent Settlement was passed by Cornwallis86-93 (1-D). Per, Thomas Munro was the chief architect of Ryotwari in Madras (2-C). Per, Holt Mackenzie's recommendations were implemented through Regulation VII of 1822 (3-A). Per, in 1833, R.M. Bird introduced the Revised Mahalwari System (4-B).

Why others wrong: (a) — PS was Cornwallis's work, not Holt Mackenzie's. (b) — Ryotwari was Munro's, not Cornwallis's. (c) and — PS was Cornwallis's and Ryotwari was Munro's; the pairings are inverted.
Memory hook: Cornwallis-PS, Munro-Ryotwari, Holt-Mackenzie-1822, Bird-1833.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Holt Mackenzie's recommendations were implemented through which Regulation to create the Mahalwari Settlement, and the term Mahal in this system refers to:

options.text: Regulation VII of 1799 — a fortified residence of the Taluqdar
Regulation VII of 1822 — a community of people at the village, estate or district level
Regulation VII of 1833 — a tax-paying joint family
Regulation XII of 1828 — a Mughal-era assessment circle of 12 villages

explanation: (B) ✓ — Per, Holt Mackenzie's recommendations were implemented through Regulation VII of 1822, creating the Mahalwari Settlement; Mahal = a community of people at the village, estate or district level.

Why others wrong: (a) — Regulation VII of 1799 was Wellesley98-05's measure restoring Zamindar coercive powers under PS, not the Mahalwari Settlement. (c) and — Mahalwari was created by Regulation VII of 1822; 1833 is the year R.M. Bird revised the system, not its founding regulation. (d) — There were no Regulation XII of 1828; Mahalwari was created by Regulation VII of 1822 and Mahal is a community, not a 12-village circle.
Memory hook: 1822 + Holt Mackenzie = Mahal (community) wari (settlement).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Revised Mahalwari System introduced by R.M. Bird in 1833 in the North-Western Provinces:
items: 1. Assessment was done at the Mahal level, not at the individual plot level.
2. Individual contribution within the Mahal was decided by the community itself.
3. Land revenue was capped at a maximum of 50% of the Rental Value for 30 years, subject to State revision.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 correct: (1) assessment done at the Mahal level, not at individual plot level — respecting the community's collective character; (2) individual contribution within the Mahal decided by the community itself. Statement 3 is incorrect — Bird's Revised Mahalwari fixed land revenue at 66% of the Rental Value (Net Assets) for 30 years; the 50% cap on rental value / net produce is Ryotwari Madras under the Madras Rules (1855/1864).

Why others wrong: (b) 2 and 3 only — carries the incorrect Statement 3 and drops the correct Statement 1. (c) 1 and 3 only — carries the incorrect Statement 3 and drops the correct Statement 2. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — Statement 3 is incorrect: the Revised Mahalwari rate was 66% of Rental Value, not the 50% Madras Ryotwari cap.
Memory hook: Bird 1833 = Mahal assesses, community shares, 66% for 30 years — the 50% cap is Madras Ryotwari, not Mahalwari.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Match the following regions with the principal land revenue system applied there:
items: 1. Bengal, Orissa, Bihar — A. Ryotwari
2. Madras and Bombay — B. Mahalwari
3. Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab — C. Permanent Settlement
explanation: (C) ✓ — Per, Permanent Settlement was applied in Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras and Benaras (1-C). Per, Ryotwari was applied in Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras and Bombay (2-A). Per, Mahalwari was applied in Central Provinces, United Provinces and Punjab (3-B).

Why others wrong: (a) — Bengal, Orissa, Bihar was PS country, not Ryotwari. (b) and — Bengal-Orissa-Bihar was PS, Madras-Bombay was Ryotwari and CUP was Mahalwari; pairings are scrambled. (d) — Madras and Bombay were Ryotwari, not Mahalwari; CUP was Mahalwari, not Ryotwari.
Memory hook: BOB = Permanent · SCAM-B = Ryotwari · CUP = Mahalwari.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Compare the Permanent Settlement and the Ryotwari Settlement in terms of their impact on the cultivating class.
body: Demand: Show how the choice of landowner shaped ryot outcomes; cite specific corrective Acts.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Permanent Settlement and the Ryotwari Settlement chose opposite landowners — Zamindar & ryot. Their impact on the cultivating class, however, converged on ruin.
Guiding themes:
1. PS1793 — Zamindar as legal owner; ryot became "tenant at will"; Patta system collapsed; abwabs continued; absentee landlordism emerged (see 'Bengal — Three Experiments').
2. Corrective: Rent Act 1859 + Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 restored occupancy rights (see 'Bengal — Three Experiments').
3. Ryotwari — ryot as legal owner; direct State settlement; but over-assessment → indebtedness → Mirasidars became new big landowners (see 'Ryotwari Settlement').
Closing verdict: Compared in terms of their impact on the cultivating class, both settlements failed the ryot — one through the Zamindar, the other through over-assessment & debt.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Explain how the British policy of cash-revenue demand led to the commercialisation of Indian agriculture and its consequences.
body: Demand: Trace the policy-to-outcome chain — cash demand → cash-crop shift → food security collapse → late-19th-century famines.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The British policy of cash-revenue demand pushed ryots from food grain to cash crops. The commercialisation of Indian agriculture that followed was paid for in famine.
Guiding themes:
1. Mughal system allowed payment in kind; the British demanded cash (see 'Commercialization of Agriculture').
2. Ryots compelled — or induced by moneylenders and traders — to shift to cash crops: indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane.
3. Land that had historically grown rice, wheat and millets now given over to commodity crops destined for British factories or global markets.
4. Food security declined — less food grain in reserve when droughts/floods hit.
5. Directly fed the famines of the late 19th century (link to Drain Theory chapter).
6. Prelims 2021 anchor: commercialisation as the documented economic result of British rule (see 'Commercialization of Agriculture').
Closing verdict: The British policy of cash-revenue demand did not merely change crops; its consequence was a food-insecure countryside that could not survive the late-19th-century droughts.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: Match List I-II: Acts to Provisions
questions.stem: Match List I (Acts of Colonial Government of India) with List II (Provisions):
matchTable: 1. Set up a Board of Control in Britain to fully regulate the EIC
2. Company's trade monopoly in India was ended
3. Power to govern was transferred from EIC to British Crown
4. Company's Directors asked to present to British Government all correspondence and documents pertaining to administration
explanation: (a) ✓ — alert (Prelims 2002 trap cluster), the mapping is A. Charter Act 1813 = (2) Company's trade monopoly in India was ended; B. Regulating Act 1773 = (4) Directors to present all correspondence to British Government; C. Act of 1858 = (3) Power transferred from EIC to British Crown; D. Pitt's India Act 1784 = (1) Board of Control set up. Match: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1.

Why others wrong: (b) A-1 wrong (BoC was 1784, not 1813); (c) B-3 wrong (1773 did not transfer power to Crown — that was 1858); (d) C-3 in (d) is correct but A-1 and B-4 pairing breaks (A-1 wrongly assigns BoC to Charter 1813).
Memory hook: 1813-trade, 1773-letters, 1858-Crown, 1784-BoC — 2-4-3-1 the canonical chain.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.title: Pair NOT Correctly Matched
questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs is not correctly matched?
explanation: (c) ✓ — alert (Prelims 2004 trap cluster): (a) Pitt's India Act: Warren Hastings is factually wrong (Hastings73-85 was under Regulating Act 1773, not Pitt's Act 1784) but UPSC's official key marks (c) as the answer; (b) Doctrine of Lapse: Dalhousie48-56 is correctly matched; (c) Vernacular Press Act: Curzon is wrongly matched — the Vernacular Press Act 1878 was Lytton76-80's, not Curzon's (cross-ref — Vernacular Press Act 1878 under Lytton);

Why others wrong: (a) Pitt's Act–Hastings pairing is also factually loose (Hastings = Regulating Act 1773), but UPSC chose the more flagrant Lytton/Curzon mismatch as the intended answer; (b) Doctrine of Lapse–Dalhousie is a textbook correct pair; (d) Ilbert Bill–Ripon is a textbook correct pair.
Memory hook: Vernacular Press Act 1878 = Lytton76-80 (NOT Curzon); Curzon = Partition of Bengal 1905.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.title: Hastings + Calcutta SC + IPC
questions.stem: Consider the following statements:
items: 1. Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General who established a regular police force in India on the British pattern.
2. A Supreme Court was established at Calcutta by the Regulating Act, 1773.
3. The Indian Penal Code came into effect in the year 1860.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — alert (Prelims 2005 trap): Statement 1 WRONG — Hastings73-85 did NOT establish a regular police force on British pattern; that was Cornwallis86-93's reform under the Cornwallis Code 1793. Statement 2 CORRECT — Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta was established by the Regulating Act 1773. Statement 3 CORRECT — Indian Penal Code came into effect in 1860. Hence 2 and 3 only.

Why others wrong: (a) includes statement 1 which is wrong (Hastings did not set up the regular police force); (c) includes statement 1 which is wrong (Cornwallis86-93, not Hastings, set up the police); (d) includes statement 1 which is wrong.
Memory hook: Hastings73-85 ≠ police force (Cornwallis86-93 did it); SC Calcutta = 1773 Act ✓; IPC = 1860 ✓.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.title: Charter 1833 + GOI 1858
questions.stem: Consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Charter Act, 1833 abolished East India Company monopoly of Indian trade.
2. Under the Government of India Act, 1858, the British Parliament abolished the East India Company altogether and undertook the responsibility of ruling India directly.
explanation: (b) ✓ — alert (Prelims 2006 two-statement): Statement 1 WRONG — Charter Act 1833 ended EIC's remaining commercial monopolies (Tea + Opium + China), but the EIC's monopoly over Indian trade itself had already been ended by Charter Act 1813. So statement 1's claim that 1833 abolished EIC's Indian trade monopoly is technically wrong (1813 did that). Statement 2 CORRECT — under GOI Act 1858, EIC rule was replaced by direct rule of the British Crown; EIC was formally dissolved in 1874. Hence only 2.

Why others wrong: (a) statement 1 wrongly credits 1833 for ending EIC's Indian-trade monopoly which was actually 1813's act; (c) statement 1 is wrong (1813 did it, not 1833); (d) statement 2 is correct (Crown takeover under GOI Act 1858 is textbook fact).
Memory hook: 1813 ended India-trade monopoly; 1833 ended residual tea+opium+China; 1858 abolished EIC altogether.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.title: Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858 Objects
questions.stem: What was/were the object/objects of Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858)?
items: 1. To disclaim any intention to annex Indian states.
2. To place the Indian administration under the British Crown.
3. To regulate East India Company's trade with India.
explanation: (a) ✓ — alert (Prelims 2014 — Objects of Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858): Statement 1 CORRECT — Proclamation disclaimed any intention to annex Indian states. Statement 2 CORRECT — Proclamation placed Indian administration under the British Crown. Statement 3 WRONG — Proclamation had nothing to do with regulating EIC's trade; by 1858 EIC's commercial function had already been ended (Charter 1833) and EIC itself was being dissolved. Hence 1 and 2 only.

Why others wrong: (b) statement 1 is also correct (no-annexation pledge), so "only 2" is incomplete; (c) statement 3 is wrong (Proclamation did not regulate EIC trade); (d) statement 3 is wrong (EIC trade had already ended by 1833).
Memory hook: Proclamation 1858 = no-more-annexation pledge + Crown takeover; trade-regulation was NOT its job.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.title: Charter Act of 1813
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about 'The Charter Act of 1813':
items: 1. It ended the trade monopoly of the East India Company in India except for trade in tea and trade with China.
2. It asserted the sovereignty of the British crown over the Indian territories held by the Company.
3. The revenues of India were now controlled by the British Parliament.
explanation: (a) ✓ — alert (Prelims 2019 trap on Charter 1813): Statement 1 CORRECT — Charter Act 1813 ended EIC's monopoly over India trade except tea, opium and China. Statement 2 CORRECT — Charter Act 1813 re-clarified undoubted sovereignty of Crown over Indian territorial possessions. Statement 3 WRONG — control of Indian revenues by the British Parliament was NOT a Charter 1813 provision; the supervisory power over Civil, Military and Revenue government of British territorial possessions was given to the Board of Control under Pitt's India Act 1784, and revenues of British India were placed under Parliament's control only by the Charter Act 1853. Hence 1 and 2 only.

Why others wrong: (b) statement 3 is wrong (revenue control was Pitt's Act 1784 / Charter 1853, not Charter 1813); (c) statement 2 is correct (Crown sovereignty re-asserted in 1813), so excluding it is wrong; (d) statement 3 is wrong.
Memory hook: Charter 1813 = end India-trade monopoly (tea+opium+China retained) + Crown sovereignty re-clarified + missionaries + ₹1 lakh education; revenue control NOT here.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.10
questions.title: Act that Designated GG/Bengal as GG/India
questions.stem: By which Act was the Governor General of Bengal designated as the Governor General of India?
explanation: (d) ✓ — alert (Prelims 2023 — By which Act was GG of Bengal designated GG of India): The Charter Act 1833 elevated GG(Bengal)-in-Council to GG(India)-in-Council. Bentinck28-35 was the holder of that re-designated office. Hence (d) Charter Act 1833.

Why others wrong: (a) Regulating Act 1773 only created the office of GG/Bengal, it did not redesignate it as GG/India; (b) Pitt's India Act 1784 created the Board of Control and Double Government, it did not redesignate the GG; (c) Charter Act 1793 increased GG's power over his council and over Bombay/Madras Governors but did not redesignate GG.
Memory hook: 1773 made GG/Bengal; 1833 promoted him to GG/India; Bentinck28-35 = first GG/India.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.11
questions.title: Who was the Governor-General of India during the Sepoy Mutiny
questions.stem: Who was the Governor-General of India during the Sepoy Mutiny?
explanation: (a) ✓ — #8 (Title: @Br State — provisions shaping EIC–British State relationship), "In 1858, Canning56-62 became the 1st Viceroy." Canning was GG 1856–62. The Sepoy Mutiny of 1857 falls within Canning's tenure (1856–62). Hence (a) Lord Canning.

Why others wrong: (b) Bentinck28-35 was GG of India 1828–35, well before 1857; (c) Hardinge was GG before Dalhousie48-56 (1844–48), not during 1857; (d) Lytton76-80 was Viceroy 1876–80, two decades after the Mutiny, and is associated with the Vernacular Press Act 1878 (cross-ref Ch 19) — not with 1857.
Memory hook: Canning56-62 = GG during 1857 Mutiny + 1st Viceroy after GOI Act 1858 (same man, two titles).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Which provision was first introduced by the Regulating Act of 1773?

options.text: Board of Control with six members in London
Supreme Court at Calcutta with one Chief Justice and three puisne judges
Open competitive examination for Covenanted Civil Services

explanation: (B) ✓ — The 1773 Act mandated a Supreme Court at Calcutta with one Chief Justice and three puisne judges, all chosen by the Crown; Sir Elijah Impey was first CJ in 1774. See — Regulating Act 1773 @Br State.

Why others wrong: (a) Board of Control was created by Pitt's India Act 1784; (c) GG/India designation came under Charter Act 1833; (d) Open competitive ICS examination was introduced by Charter Act 1853.
Memory hook: 1773 = SC Calcutta + CJ + 3 puisne; BoC = 1784; GG/India = 1833; open ICS = 1853.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding Pitt's India Act of 1784:
items: 1. It created the Board of Control as the supreme political authority over the East India Company.
2. It merged the offices of Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief into a single post.
3. It declared that conquest in India was repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of the British nation.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are correct: BoC was created in 1784 to supervise EIC's political affairs, and the Act stated conquest was repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of the nation. Statement 2 is wrong — Pitt 1784 made CIC an ex-officio ORDINARY member of GG's council (one of 3 seats), but the offices of GG and CIC were NOT merged into a single post.

Why others wrong: (b) Statement 2 alone is wrong — the GG and CIC offices were not merged; Pitt 1784 only made CIC ex-officio ordinary member of GG's council; (c) Statement 2 is incorrect for the same reason; (d) Statement 3 is also correct, so 'only 1' is incomplete.
Memory hook: Pitt 1784 = BoC + 'conquest repugnant' + CIC as ex-officio ordinary member of GG's council (NOT a merger of offices).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: The Charter Act of 1813 is associated with which of the following changes?
items: 1. Ended the East India Company's monopoly over trade with India, retaining its monopoly over tea and trade with China
2. Permitted Christian missionaries to enter India for conversions with a licence
3. Mandated EIC expenditure of Rs 1 lakh per annum on education. Select the correct answer
explanation: (D) ✓ — All three are correct: EIC's monopoly over India trade ended in 1813, with tea and China trade retained; missionaries could enter with a CoD or BoC licence; Rs 1 lakh per annum was earmarked for education. See — Charter Act 1813 @Br State.
Why others wrong: (a) Missionaries and Rs 1 lakh education are also correct; (b) End of India trade monopoly is also a 1813 feature; (c) Missionary entry is also a 1813 feature.
Memory hook: 1813 = end India-trade monopoly (tea + China retained) + missionaries with licence + Rs 1 lakh education.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: By which Act was the Governor-General of Bengal redesignated as the Governor-General of India?
explanation: (C) ✓ — The Charter Act of 1833 elevated GG(Bengal)-in-Council to GG(India)-in-Council, and made GG/India the executive and legislative head of all British India. William Bentinck was the first GG/India. See — Charter Act 1833 @GG, point #1.

Why others wrong: (a) Regulating Act 1773 created GG/Bengal; (b) Pitt's Act 1784 created the BoC and Double Government, no redesignation; (d) GOI 1858 renamed GG as "Viceroy & GG", not GG/Bengal to GG/India.
Memory hook: GG/Bengal → GG/India = Charter 1833; Viceroy & GG = 1858; BoC = 1784; GG/Bengal created = 1773.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Which one of the following provisions was NOT introduced by the Charter Act of 1833?

options.text: Abolition of the East India Company's commercial functions
Centralisation of all law-making power in the GG(India)-in-Council
Promise of no bar to EIC service on grounds of religion, race, birth or colour
Appointment of an Indian as a Law Member in the Governor-General's Council

explanation: (D) ✓ — The 1833 Law Member appointed was Thomas Macaulay, an Englishman; the appointment of an Indian Law Member came much later. The other three were 1833 provisions. See — Charter Act 1833 @GG, points #1, #2, #5, #7.

Why others wrong: (a) EIC's commercial function was fully ended in 1833; (b) Legislative powers of Bombay and Madras Governors were withdrawn and centralised in GG-in-Council; (c) Racial-equality clause regarding EIC service is verbatim from the 1833 Act.
Memory hook: 1833 Law Member = Macaulay (English), NOT Indian; commerce end + central legislature + racial-equality clause all 1833.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Which of the following changes was introduced by the Charter Act of 1853?

options.text: Covenanted Civil Services were opened to Indians through an open competitive examination
The Governor-General of Bengal was given a casting vote in his Council
A Supreme Court was established at Calcutta
Christian missionaries were permitted to enter India for conversions

explanation: (A) ✓ — Charter Act 1853 ended EIC patronage by introducing an open Civil Services Examination — first held in London in 1855 — and opened the Covenanted Civil Services to Indians. See — Charter Act 1853 @Br State, points #2 and #3.

Why others wrong: (b) GG's casting vote came from Regulating Act 1773 and an additional regular + casting vote from Pitt's Act 1784; (c) Supreme Court at Calcutta was set up under Regulating Act 1773; (d) Missionary entry was under Charter Act 1813.
Memory hook: 1853 = open ICS exam (London, 1855) + CCS to Indians; SC Calcutta = 1773; missionaries = 1813.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Government of India Act, 1858:
items: 1. The East India Company's rule in India was replaced by direct rule of the British Crown.
2. The Board of Control was replaced by a Council of India headed by the Secretary of State for India.
3. Lord Dalhousie became the first Viceroy and Governor-General.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 hold: Company rule was replaced by direct rule of the British State, and the Board of Control gave way to a 15-member Council of India headed by the Secretary of State for India, seven of the old Court of Directors being absorbed for continuity. Statement 3 names the wrong man. Dalhousie's term as Governor-General ran 1848–1856 and his Indian legacy in this period is the Lieutenant-Governorship of Bengal, created to lighten the GG's workload and first held by Frederick James Halliday from 1854. It was Canning, Governor-General from 1856, who took the new style of Viceroy and Governor-General in 1858 and thereafter reported only to the Secretary of State.

Why others wrong: (b) Statement 3 fails — the first Viceroy and Governor-General was Canning in 1858, while Dalhousie had already demitted office in 1856. (c) Statement 1 is sound: the 1857 revolt and the charge of mismanagement ended Company rule and brought direct rule of the British State, so dropping it is wrong while statement 3 remains the defective one. (d) Statement 2 is sound: the Board of Control of 1784 was superseded by the Council of India under the Secretary of State, ending the dual control the GG had lived under since 1784 — and statement 3 still misnames the first Viceroy.
Memory hook: GOI 1858 = Crown takeover + Secretary of State + 15-member India Council; Canning = 1st Viceroy (Dalhousie 1848–56 = 1st LG of Bengal in 1854, not the 1st Viceroy).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Which of the following objects was/were declared in Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858?
items: 1. To confer on Queen Victoria the title of Kaesar-i-Hind, Empress of India
2. To place the Indian administration under the British Crown
3. To grant amnesty to those who had taken part in the 1857 revolt, with limited exceptions
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statements 2 and 3 were declared objects: the Proclamation announced the transfer of governance from the Company and placed the Indian administration under the British Crown, and it granted amnesty to those who had taken part in the 1857 revolt, with limited exceptions. Statement 1 belongs to a later instrument. The imperial title was conferred by the Royal Titles Act of 1876, which empowered Victoria to take the style Kaesar-i-Hind, and it was proclaimed at Lytton's Imperial Darbar at Delhi in 1877; before that she had used it only unofficially. On the princes the 1858 Proclamation did the opposite of asserting a new title — it disclaimed any intention to annex Indian States, walking back the Doctrine of Lapse and the Awadh annexation of 1856.

Why others wrong: (a) Statement 1 fails — the Empress of India title came by the Royal Titles Act of 1876 and the Delhi Darbar of 1877, not by the 1858 Proclamation. (c) Statement 1 is the defective one, and it discards statement 2, which is the Proclamation's central announcement — Indian administration passing to the British Crown. (d) Amnesty in statement 3 is rightly a Proclamation object, but the imperial title in statement 1 is not, and the transfer of administration to the Crown in statement 2 plainly was.

Memory hook: QVP 1858 = no-annexation walkback + Crown rule + religious non-interference + race/creed-blind service + amnesty; Empress of India / Kaesar-i-Hind title = Royal Titles Act 1876, Delhi Darbar 1877.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Match the Acts in List I with the provisions in List II:
items: 1. Regulating Act 1773 — A. Board of Control created in London;
2. Pitt's India Act 1784 — B. Supreme Court established at Calcutta;
3. Charter Act 1813 — C. EIC's commercial functions fully ended;
4. Charter Act 1833 — D. Christian missionaries permitted to enter India
matchTable: A. Board of Control created in London
B. Supreme Court established at Calcutta
C. EIC's commercial functions fully ended
D. Christian missionaries permitted to enter India
explanation: (B) ✓ — Correct mapping: 1773 set up the SC at Calcutta; 1784 created the BoC; 1813 admitted Christian missionaries with a licence; 1833 ended EIC's commercial functions entirely. See, 3.1, 5.2 and 6.1.

Why others wrong: (a) BoC is 1784, not 1773; SC Calcutta is 1773, not 1784; missionaries are 1813, not 1833; commerce-end is 1833, not 1813 — every pair flipped; (c) Pairs 3 and 4 are flipped — missionaries are 1813 and commerce-end is 1833; (d) BoC is 1784 not 1773, SC Calcutta is 1773 not 1784, and pairs 3-4 are flipped.
Memory hook: 1773 = SC Calcutta; 1784 = BoC; 1813 = missionaries + India-trade monopoly ends; 1833 = commerce fully ends.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Under the Charter Act of 1833, the Governor-General-in-Council was empowered to make laws applicable to which of the following?

options.text: The whole of British India, applicable equally to Indians and Britishers
The whole of British India and the Princely States

explanation: (C) ✓ — Charter Act 1833 empowered GG(India) as the executive and legislative head of British India to make and administer laws for the whole of British India, equally applicable to Indians and Britishers alike. The legislative powers of the Bombay and Madras Governors were taken away under the same Act. See — Charter Act 1833 @GG, points #2 and #3.

Why others wrong: (a) Bengal-only legislative reach was the 1773 Council's scope; (b) The 1833 laws applied equally to Indians and Britishers, not only British subjects; (d) Princely States only came under Crown paramountcy via the GOI Act 1858, and even then domestic affairs remained with the Princes.
Memory hook: 1833 = uniform laws for whole British India, Indians + Britishers equal; Princely States = Paramountcy from 1858.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1793:
items: 1. It declared that subjects of the Crown could not acquire sovereign powers over territory on their own but only on behalf of the Crown.
2. It mandated that the salaries of the members of the Board of Control would be paid by the East India Company.
3. It renewed the East India Company's Charter for forty years.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Act declared that Crown subjects could acquire sovereign powers only on behalf of the Crown — making EIC merely an agent of the British State — and the BoC members' salary was now to be paid by EIC, later linked to Home Charges. Statement 3 is wrong — the Charter was renewed for twenty years, not forty.

Why others wrong: (a) Statement 2 — BoC salary paid by EIC — is also correct; (c) Statement 1 — sovereignty of Crown clause — is also correct, and Statement 3 is wrong because the renewal was 20 years; (d) Statement 3 is wrong — renewal was for 20 years, not 40.
Memory hook: 1793 = EIC = mere agent of Crown + BoC salaries paid by EIC + 20-year renewal (NOT 40).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the Supreme Council of Bengal under the Regulating Act 1773 is correct?

options.text: The Council comprised the Governor-General and four councillors, deciding by majority vote
The Governor-General had both a regular vote and a casting vote
The Commander-in-Chief of the army was an ex-officio member
The Council had the power to make laws for the whole of British India

explanation: (A) ✓ — Under the Regulating Act 1773, the Supreme Council of Bengal was created with four councillors (GG + 4), and all decisions were by majority vote; the GG had only a casting vote — a tiebreaker. See — Regulating Act 1773 @GG, point #4.

Why others wrong: (b) The regular + casting vote was granted by Pitt's India Act 1784; (c) The mandate to include the C-i-C as a Council member came under Pitt's India Act 1784; (d) Law-making power in 1773 was limited to Bengal and matters of war and peace; whole of British India came under Charter Act 1833.
Memory hook: 1773 Council = GG + 4 councillors, casting-vote-only GG; regular+casting = 1784; CIC seat = 1784; all-India laws = 1833.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Which of the following pairs is/are correctly matched?
items: 1. Warren Hastings — first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act 1773;
2. William Bentinck — first Governor-General of India under Pitt's India Act 1784;
3. Charles Canning — first Viceroy and Governor-General under the Government of India Act
1858. Select the correct answer
explanation: (c) ✓ — Pairs 1 and 3 are correctly matched: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal created by the Regulating Act 1773, and Canning, Governor-General since 1856, became the first Viceroy and Governor-General in 1858. Pair 2 joins the right man to the wrong statute. Pitt's India Act 1784 created the Board of Control and the Double Government of Company affairs, reduced the GG's council to three and gave him a casting vote as well as a regular one, but it left the designation untouched. The elevation of Governor-General of Bengal to Governor-General of India came with the Charter Act 1833, and Bentinck, in office from 1828, was the first holder of that higher title.

Why others wrong: (a) Pair 3 is correctly matched, and pair 2 is the flawed one — it credits Bentinck's elevation to 1784 instead of the Charter Act 1833. (b) Pair 1 is correctly matched — Hastings held the newly created Bengal Governor-Generalship from 1773 — while pair 2 is the mismatch. (d) Pair 2 is not correctly matched: Pitt's Act 1784 built the Board of Control and Double Government; the GG/India designation was the Charter Act 1833's contribution.
Memory hook: Firsts: Hastings = GG/Bengal 1773 (Regulating Act); Bentinck = GG/India 1833 (Charter Act — Pitt's 1784 only built the Board of Control); Canning = 1st Viceroy 1858.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Board of Control set up under Pitt's India Act, 1784:
items: 1. It was placed under the supreme control of the President of the Board, who was a Secretary of State
2. It could send confidential orders directly to India through a Secret Committee of three directors within the Court of Directors
3. Its supervisory power was extended to all administrative affairs in India by the Charter Act of 1793
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are sound: the Board's six members were headed by one of the Secretaries of State as President, sitting with the Chancellor of the Exchequer and four Privy Councillors; and a Secret Committee of three directors inside the Court of Directors let the Board send confidential orders straight to India on sensitive military and diplomatic business, bypassing the full Court. Statement 3 attaches the right reform to the wrong Act. What the Charter Act 1793 did to the Board was shrink it — the President left with two junior members who need not be Privy Councillors, with their salaries thereafter paid by the Company. The widening of the Board's supervision to every administrative matter, including implementation of laws and officers' transfers and postings, came only with the Charter Act 1833.

Why others wrong: (a) Statement 2 is also correct — the Secret Committee of three directors was exactly the channel through which the Board's confidential orders reached India without passing the full Court of Directors. (c) Statement 1 is correct: a Secretary of State, that is a Cabinet minister, presided over the six-member Board — and statement 3 still dates the extension of supervisory power to the wrong Act. (d) Statement 3 fails: the 1793 Act reduced the Board to a President plus two junior members; the extension of its supervision to all administrative affairs belongs to the Charter Act 1833.

Memory hook: BoC 1784 = Secretary of State as President + Secret Committee of 3 inside CoD; 1793 shrinks the Board (President + 2 juniors, EIC pays salaries), 1833 extends it to all administrative affairs.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Which one of the following was a feature of the policy of Subordinate Union introduced by the Government of India Act, 1858, towards the Indian Princely States?

options.text: Princely States were formally annexed and merged into British India
Princely States were placed under Mughal sovereignty, with the Crown acting as a guarantor
Sovereignty, Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs rested with the Crown while domestic affairs remained with the Prince
Princely States were given full internal and external sovereignty, subject only to a tribute to the Crown

explanation: (C) ✓ — Under the policy of Subordinate Union (Paramountcy), Sovereignty, Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs (Sov, D, C, FA) rested with the Crown while domestic affairs remained with the Prince. Mughal sovereignty was legally ended in 1858 and the Crown became sovereign over all of India. See — GOI Act 1858 @Br State, point #2.ii.

Why others wrong: (a) Princely States were ruled by Indian Princes under Paramountcy, not annexed — the Proclamation explicitly disclaimed annexation; (b) Mughal sovereignty was legally ended in 1858, not preserved; (d) Princes did not retain external sovereignty — Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs rested with the Crown.
Memory hook: Paramountcy 1858 = Sov + D + C + FA with Crown; domestic with Prince; Mughal sovereignty legally ended.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Trace the evolution of the EIC-British State relationship from the Regulating Act 1773 to the GOI Act 1858.
body: Demand: Show the sequential tightening of British State control over EIC across the major Acts.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The EIC-British State relationship moved one way only. From the Regulating Act 1773 to the GOI Act 1858, every Act took powers from the Company.
Guiding themes:
1. Regulating Act 1773 — Parliamentary oversight initiated; GG of Bengal Presidency created (see 'Regulating Act of 1773').
2. Pitt's India Act 1784 — Board of Control created in London (see 'Pitt's India Act / East India Company Act (1784)').
3. Charter Act 1813 — trade monopoly ended (except Tea/Opium/China) (see 'Charter Act (1813)').
4. Charter Act 1833 — EIC commercial functions ended; GG/India + Law Commission (see 'Charter Act (1833) / St. Helena Act').
5. Charter Act 1853 — Indian Civil Service via open competition (see 'Charter Act (1853)').
6. GOI Act 1858 — EIC abolished, Crown direct rule (see 'Government of India Act (1858) / Act for Better Government of India').
Closing verdict: Traced from the Regulating Act 1773 to the GOI Act 1858, the EIC-British State relationship ends where it was always headed — the Company abolished.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Discuss the constitutional significance of Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858.
body: Demand: Identify the Proclamation's main promises + their political significance for British-Indian relations.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 announced the Crown's takeover. Its constitutional significance lies in three promises — no annexation, religious non-interference & public service without discrimination.
Guiding themes:
1. End of EIC rule → direct Crown rule via GOI 1858 (see 'Government of India Act (1858) / Act for Better Government of India').
2. Proclamation explicitly ended the Doctrine of Lapse (see 'Government of India Act (1858) / Act for Better Government of India').
3. Pledged respect for treaties and rights of Indian rulers — reversal of Dalhousie48-56's annexationist policy.
4. Promised religious tolerance and non-interference in Indian customs — direct acknowledgement that religious interference had been a major 1857 grievance.

5. GOI 1858 introduced the Policy of Subordinate Union — implemented through Paramountcy — replacing Mughal sovereignty over Princely States ('Government of India Act (1858) / Act for Better Government of India' #2).
Closing verdict: The constitutional significance of Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 is that it set the terms of Crown rule for the next 89 years, until 1947.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.title: Cornwallis86-93's Separation of Judicial Powers from DC
questions.stem: By a regulation in 1793, the District Collector was deprived of his judicial powers and made the collecting agent only. What was the reason for such regulation?

options.text: Lord Cornwallis felt that the District Collector's efficiency of revenue collection would enormously increase without the burden of other work
Lord Cornwallis felt that judicial power should compulsorily be in the hands of Europeans, while Indians can be given the job of revenue collection in the districts
Lord Cornwallis was alarmed at the extent of power concentrated in the District Collector and felt that such absolute power was undesirable in one person
The judicial work demanded a deep knowledge of India and a good training in law and Lord Cornwallis felt that District Collector should be only a revenue collection agent

explanation: (c) ✓ — Cornwallis was alarmed that one officer combining revenue + judicial powers held absolute power over the very people whose appeals he would hear; the Permanent Settlement of 1793 had just created a new zamindar landowner class who needed independent courts they could trust against revenue officials. Per (Why Did Cornwallis86-93 Reform the Judiciary?), an officer who collected your tax should not also be the judge hearing your appeal against his own actions — so the DC was stripped of all judicial powers & confined to revenue collection.

Why others wrong: (a) revenue-efficiency was a side-benefit, not the principal motivation — frames the change around separation of powers, not collection efficiency; (b) wrong on facts — Cornwallis86-93 in fact removed Indians from ALL senior positions, so the European-judge / Indian-collector framing inverts what he actually did; (d) the "DC lacked legal knowledge" reason is a partial truth at best — Chapter nowhere flags lack of India-knowledge or law-training as the trigger; the trigger was structural conflict of interest post-PS1793.
Memory hook: Tax-man can't be judge of his own tax — PS1793 zamindars needed clean courts, so Cornwallis split the hat.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.title: Cornwallis86-93 as Founder of CCS
questions.stem: Who among the following Governor-Generals created the Covenanted Civil Service of India which later came to be known as the Indian Civil Service?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Cornwallis86-93 reorganised EIC officers into the two-tier Covenanted Civil Service (CCS, senior, European-only, signed a "covenant" with the Court of Directors before sailing) + Uncovenanted Civil Service (UCS, junior, hired locally). Per, he is "called the founder of civil services in India" because he converted a corrupt, patronage-ridden set of employees into a structured, professionalised service. The CCS was later renamed Indian Civil Service (ICS) in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne88-94 on the Aitchison Commission 1887 recommendations — NOT by ICA 1892.
