(A) ✗ — Peasant resistance (Indigo Revolt 1859–63) ended forced cultivation in Bengal and limited Indigo expansion, but did not by itself cause the early-20th-century DECLINE — the synthetic-indigo breakthrough did. Per: the long-term death blow to natural indigo, however, came not from peasant resistance but from chemistry.

(C) ✗ — National leaders' opposition is associated with the 1917 Champaran Satyagraha (Mahatma Gandhi) and the Champaran Agrarian Act 1918, which ended the Bihar Tinkathia System — but the GLOBAL DECLINE of natural indigo was already underway from 1897 (BASF synthetic indigo) and well-advanced by the time of Champaran.

(D) ✗ — Government control over planters (e.g. the Indigo Commission 1860 ruling) did not cause the early-20th-century DECLINE — that ruling addressed contract terms in 1860, decades before the global market collapse.

Note: Indigo cultivation declined by the early 20th century because of its unprofitability in the world market after BASF developed synthetic indigo in 1897. The Bihar Tinkathia System chapter of this story closed only in 1918 with the Champaran Agrarian Act, following Mahatma Gandhi's 1917 satyagraha.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: In which year did the East India Company begin promoting Indigo cultivation in Bengal by giving loans to ten European planters?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Per, In 1788, the East India Company (EIC) began promoting Indigo cultivation in Bengal by giving loans to ten European planters.
Why others wrong: (a) 1757 was Plassey, not Indigo loans; (b) 1772 is the year of Warren Hastings' reforms, unrelated; (d) 1793 is the Permanent Settlement, which post-dated the Indigo loans.
Memory hook: Ten planters, one year — 1788, the trap is laid.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Under the Ryoti System of Indigo cultivation in Bengal, the ryot was contractually bound to grow Indigo on a minimum portion of his occupied land. What was that minimum portion?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Per, the Ryoti System contract stipulated that The ryot had to grow Indigo on at least 25% of the land he occupied.
Why others wrong: (b) 3/20th was the Tinkathia System in Bihar, not Bengal's Ryoti System; (c) 10% has no basis; (d) 50% has no basis.
Memory hook: Quarter of the field, all of the misery.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: With reference to the Indigo Revolt (1859–63), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Nij System failed because buying land and arranging labour was expensive and complicated.
2. Under the Ryoti System, the planter himself bought the land and cultivated Indigo directly.
3. The Permanent Settlement of 1793 had made land a commodity that could be sold, rented, leased, or mortgaged.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Per, Statement 1 matches The Nij System... faced a practical problem. Buying large tracts of land, organising labour, and arranging bullocks & ploughs was expensive & complicated. Statement 3 matches after the Permanent Settlement of 1793, zamindars were large landowners & land had become a commodity that could be sold, rented, leased, or mortgaged. Statement 2 is wrong — under the Ryoti System the planter LEASED land from zamindars and signed contracts with tenant ryots; he did not buy and cultivate directly (that was the Nij System).
Why others wrong: (a) includes Statement 2 which inverts Nij and Ryoti; (c) includes the same wrong Statement 2 and drops correct Statement 1; (d) includes wrong Statement 2.
Memory hook: Nij = own & cultivate; Ryoti = lease & contract.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Who wrote the 1860 Bengali play Neel Darpan (Blue Mirror), depicting the oppression of ryots by Indigo planters?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Per, 1860 — Neel Darpan (Blue Mirror): Playwright DeenBandhu Mitra wrote this powerful play depicting the oppression of ryots by Indigo planters.

Why others wrong: (a) Michael Madhusudhan Datta translated the play into English, did not author it; (c) James Long was the Christian missionary who published the English version and was convicted of libel; (d) Kaliprasanna Sinha paid Long's Rs 1,000 fine, did not author the play.
Memory hook: Mitra wrote, Datta translated, Long published, Sinha paid.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following pairs concerning the Indigo Revolt:
items: 1. James Long — convicted of libel, fined Rs 1,
2. Kaliprasanna Sinha — paid the fine imposed on James Long
3. Michael Madhusudhan Datta — translated Neel Darpan into English. How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Per, all three are textually correct: Long was convicted, fined Rs 1,000 (paid by Kaliprasanna Sinha), and sentenced to one month's imprisonment; the record also states Bengali poet Michael Madhusudhan Datta translated Neel Darpan into English.
Why others wrong: (b) under-counts — all three are matched; (c) under-counts; (d) contradicts the record explicit attribution of all three roles.
Memory hook: Three names, three roles — all correct.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Which of the following Acts gave the Bengal ryot the legal protection he later invoked in court to enforce his occupancy rights against Indigo planters?

options.text: The Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act of 1879

explanation: (C) ✓ — Per, When planters attempted eviction, ryots went to court to enforce their occupancy rights under the Rent Act of 1859.

Why others wrong: (a) The Permanent Settlement of 1793 turned zamindars into large landowners; it did not grant occupancy rights to ryots; (b) The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 came much later, out of the Pabna agitation; (d) The Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act of 1879 dealt with Maharashtra moneylender debt, not Bengal Indigo.
Memory hook: 1859 Rent Act — the ryot's shield in court.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why Indigo cultivation in India declined by the beginning of the 20th century?

options.text: Peasant resistance to the oppressive conduct of planters.
Its unprofitability in the world market because of new inventions.
National leaders' opposition to the cultivation of indigo.

explanation: (B) ✓ — Per, In 1897, the German company BASF developed synthetic indigo, which was cheaper & more consistent than the natural product. As synthetic indigo flooded global markets, the demand for natural indigo collapsed — destroying whatever economic logic had remained in the plantation system.

Why others wrong: (a) The Indigo Revolt of 1859–63 only shifted cultivation from Bengal to Bihar; it did not cause national decline; (c) National leaders' opposition came much later (Champaran 1917) and only ended the Tinkathia System; (d) Government control of planters did not drive the global collapse — chemistry did.
Memory hook: Chemistry, not Champaran, killed natural indigo.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: The Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918 brought to an end which of the following systems?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Per, The Bihar chapter of this story would close only in 1917, when Mahatma Gandhi (MG) launched the Champaran Satyagraha, leading to the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918, which brought the Tinkathia System to its end.

Why others wrong: (a) The Permanent Settlement of 1793 was not ended by the 1918 Act; (b) The Ryotwari System operated in Madras and Bombay Presidencies, not Bihar; (c) The Nij System had already failed commercially in Bengal long before; the 1918 Act addressed the Bihar Tinkathia arrangement.
Memory hook: Champaran 1918 — Tinkathia's tombstone.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: With reference to the Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The grievances arose because zamindars violated the occupancy rights granted by the Rent Act of
2. Illegal extra cesses called Abwabs were being collected from the ryots.
3. The Bengalee newspaper edited by Surendra Nath Bannerjea supported the ryots.
questions.stemTail: 1859 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Per, all three statements are textually correct: the Rent Act of 1859 had granted occupancy rights "But zamindars were routinely violating these rights"; "illegal extra cesses called Abwabs were being collected"; and Bengalee (English), edited by Surendra Nath Bannerjea (SNB), supported the ryots.
Why others wrong: (a) drops correct Statement 3; (b) drops correct Statement 1; (c) drops correct Statement 2.
Memory hook: Pabna trio — rights, Abwabs, Bengalee.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 granted occupancy rights to ryots who had cultivated different plots of land in the same village continuously for more than how many years?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Per, This act gave occupancy rights to ryots who had cultivated different plots of land in the same village continuously for more than twelve years.
Why others wrong: (a) Six years has no basis; (b) Ten years has no basis; (d) Twenty years has no basis.
Memory hook: Twelve years tilled — occupancy sealed.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: During the Bombay Deccan Riots of 1875, the ryots, when violence broke out, did NOT attack the lives of moneylenders. What did they attack instead?

options.text: The debt bonds held by moneylenders

explanation: (B) ✓ — Per, The ryots did not attack moneylenders' lives. They burned debt bonds. (An awareness of the instrument of oppression, not just its wielder.)

Why others wrong: (a) Grain warehouses are not mentioned; (c) British revenue offices were not the target — the 1875 riot was directed at moneylenders, not revenue staff; (d) Village headmen's houses are not mentioned.
Memory hook: Burn the bond, spare the man.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Which Act was passed in 1879 to give protection against loss of land due to indebtedness and to regulate interest rates in the Bombay Deccan?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Per, The Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act of 1879 was passed. It gave protection against loss of land due to indebtedness & regulated interest rates.

Why others wrong: (a) The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 dealt with Bengal occupancy rights, not Deccan indebtedness; (b) The Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918 ended the Tinkathia System in Bihar; (c) The Rent Act of 1859 dealt with Bengal ryots' occupancy rights.
Memory hook: Deccan 1875 riots — 1879 Relief Act.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Match List I with List II: List I (Organisation/Body): A. Poona Sarvajanik Sabha B. British Indian Association C. Namdhari Sect D. Indigo Commission. List II (Year established / set up):
items: 4. Led by Baba Ram Singh. Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
explanation: (A) ✓ — Per the record: places the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha at 1870; places the British Indian Association at 1851; names Baba Ram Singh as head of the Namdhari Sect; places the Indigo Commission at 1860.
Why others wrong: (b) swaps A and B; (c) swaps B and D; (d) swaps A and D.
Memory hook: 1851 BIA, 1860 Indigo Commission, 1870 PSS, Ram Singh's Namdharis.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Why did the British quietly withdraw the bill underlying the Punjab Canal Colony Agitations of 1907 after initial repression?

options.text: Because the Lahore Indian Association, Arya Samaj, and Singh Sabha threatened a national boycott.
Because the Lieutenant Governor of Punjab considered the bill against the spirit of free market economics.
Because the Indian Army was heavily recruited from Punjab, and peasant disaffection could spread to the army.
Because Mahatma Gandhi launched a Satyagraha against the bill.

explanation: (C) ✓ — Per, The withdrawal was driven by a specific calculation: post-1857, the Indian Army was heavily recruited from Punjab, particularly from the Sikh community. Disaffection among Punjab's peasantry could spread to the army — a risk the British simply could not afford.

Why others wrong: (a) The three organisations mobilised the peasantry, but the record attributes the withdrawal specifically to army-recruitment calculations, not boycott threats; (b) The "free market" reasoning belongs to the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal during the Indigo Revolt, not Punjab 1907; (d) Gandhi's Satyagraha had no role in the 1907 Canal Colony withdrawal — Champaran was a decade later.
Memory hook: Soldiers' fathers were the ryots — bill withdrawn.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Which of the following are correctly listed as features that distinguished post-1857 peasant revolts from earlier uprisings, according to the Chapter?
items: 1. Peasants used the colonial legal system as a tool against colonial rule
2. The Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC) began to take up peasant causes
3. Peasants increasingly relied on armed mercenaries from princely states. Select the correct answer:
explanation: (A) ✓ — Per, the two named changes are (i) peasants now had a greater awareness of British laws & institutions... They used the legal system that colonial rule had imposed on them as a tool against that very rule and (ii) the Western Educated Middle Class — or WEMC — began to take up peasant causes. Statement 3 is not.
Why others wrong: (b) includes fabricated Statement 3; (c) drops correct Statement 2 and includes fabricated Statement 3; (d) includes fabricated Statement 3.
Memory hook: Courts + Class — the two new weapons after 1857.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The peasant revolts after 1857 were the rehearsal for the methods that the Indian National Movement would later perfect." Examine this view with specific reference to non-cooperation, no-tax, boycott, and legal-challenge methods used in these revolts.
body: Demand: Defend the "rehearsal" framing by mapping each INM method to a specific pre-INM peasant-revolt instance.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The peasant revolts after 1857 were the rehearsal. Non-cooperation, no-tax, boycott, and legal-challenge methods were all tried before the Indian National Movement would later perfect them.
Guiding themes:
1. Open with 'A Thread Running Through All These Revolts' verdict — these revolts are "the soil in which that movement would grow" + ◆ box "rehearsal" framing.
2. Non-cooperation — Indigo Revolt 1859-63 (see 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)'): social boycott of Indian agents of planters = Non-Cooperation decades before Gandhi.

3. No-tax campaign — Maharashtra 1873-74 (see 'Maharashtra') + Maharashtra 1896-97 (see 'Maharashtra') + Punjab 1907 Canal Colony agitation (see 'Punjab'). Three separate no-tax campaigns before the INM made it a signature method.
4. Boycott — Indigo Revolt social boycott (see 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)') + no-rent campaign in court (see 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)').

5. Legal challenge — Indigo ryots using Rent Act 1859 occupancy rights (see 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)'); Pabna Agrarian Leagues pooling money for court cases ('Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal' ¶2); Poona Sarvajanik Sabha collecting 17,000 powers-of-attorney (see 'Maharashtra').
Closing verdict: The Indian National Movement did not invent these methods. It scaled and pan-Indianised what the peasant revolts after 1857 had already rehearsed regionally.
revise: A Thread Running Through All These Revolts

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: "The Indigo Revolt (1859–63) marked the entry of the Western Educated Middle Class into peasant causes." Examine the contribution of the WEMC to the revolt and assess its long-term significance for Indian political life.
body: Demand: Trace the WEMC's specific contributions to the Indigo Revolt + judge what this entry meant for the trajectory of Indian politics.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Indigo Revolt (1859–63) marked the entry of the Western Educated Middle Class into peasant causes. Playwrights & editors now spoke for the ryot in public.
Guiding themes:

1. Open with 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)' framing — the WEMC's involvement represents "the spirit of Fraternity at work here — a key element of Modern Nationalism. The educated class standing up for the oppressed peasant was a new phenomenon in Indian public life."
2. Specific contributions per 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)':
(i) Neel Darpan (Blue Mirror, 1860) by DeenBandhu Mitra — public-awareness play.

(ii) Michael Madhusudhan Datta's English translation + James Long's publication; libel case + Rs 1,000 fine paid by Kaliprasanna Sinha + 1 month imprisonment — turning the Indigo issue into an international public-opinion event.
(iii) Hindu Patriot (English) + Somprakash (Bengali) — sustained editorial advocacy.
(iv) British Indian Association 1851 (educated zamindars) — class-interest convergence with peasants against European planter dominance.
3. Long-term significance — 'What Changed After 1857': "The peasant was no longer alone." This is the Fraternity element of Modern Nationalism beginning to take shape in concrete practice.

4. Caveat — 'Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal' ¶3 (Pabna) shows the WEMC was not monolithic; it could side with zamindars against ryots when the landlord was Indian. So WEMC entry into peasant causes was real, but conditional.
Closing verdict: The entry of the Western Educated Middle Class into peasant causes was real but conditional — Pabna showed it could side with the Indian zamindar.
revise: The Role of the Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC)

questions.label: FYQ_M.3
questions.stem: "Post-1857 peasant resistance was characterised by an awareness of the instruments of oppression, not just the wielders of oppression." Discuss with reference to specific revolts in Bengal, Maharashtra, and Punjab.
body: Demand: Show how peasants targeted SYSTEMS (debt bonds, contracts, fiscal mechanisms) rather than PERSONS (moneylenders, planters); cite specific revolts.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Deccan ryots in 1875 burned debt bonds, not moneylenders. Post-1857 peasant resistance showed an awareness of the instruments of oppression, not just the wielders of oppression.
Guiding themes:

1. Open with the Chapter's analytical insight — 'Action': "The ryots did not attack moneylenders' lives. They burned debt bonds. (An awareness of the instrument of oppression, not just its wielder.)" This framing recurs across the chapter.

2. Bombay Deccan Riots 1875 — 'Maharashtra': ryots burned the debt bonds, not the moneylenders themselves. Specific target: the legal instrument (debt bond) that perpetuated the cycle of dispossession via the Limitation Law 1859 workaround.

3. Indigo Revolt 1859-63 — 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)': ryots refused contracts (the legal instrument of forced cultivation) + went to court under Rent Act 1859 (a different legal instrument that gave them occupancy rights). Two legal instruments — one rejected, one wielded — both consciously chosen.

4. Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873 — 'Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal': ryots organised legal-action structures (Agrarian Leagues + pooled-money court funds) rather than attacking zamindars directly. The instrument targeted was the legal-rights mechanism in Rent Act 1859 (already won) plus the new Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 (still being shaped).
5. Punjab 1907 Canal Colony — 'Punjab': peasants targeted the proposed BILL (legal instrument) through a no-tax campaign — and the British withdrew the bill. The instrument was the law itself.
Closing verdict: This awareness of the instruments of oppression separates post-1857 peasant resistance from the pre-1857 revolts, and points forward to the INM's focus on laws.

questions.label: FYQ_M.4
questions.stem: "The Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 was the legislative resolution of a peasant struggle that had begun decades earlier." Trace this from the Rent Act 1859 onwards, with reference to the Indigo Revolt, Pabna, and Ripon80-84's 1880 Rent Commission.
body: Demand: Walk the legislative arc from Rent Act 1859 to Bengal Tenancy Act 1885, showing how peasant agitation drove each step.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Zamindars evaded the Rent Act 1859. The Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 was the legislative resolution of a peasant struggle that had begun decades earlier.
Guiding themes:
1. Open with the legislative arc verdict — 'Result'. The BTA 1885 closed the same-plot loophole in Rent Act 1859 that zamindars had exploited via eviction-before-12-years.
2. Rent Act 1859 — set up after decades of peasant agitation. Granted occupancy rights to ryots who cultivated the SAME plot continuously for 12+ years. 'Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal' ¶1.
3. Indigo Revolt 1859-63 (see 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)') — ryots wielded Rent Act 1859 in court against eviction by planters. The Act's protective potential demonstrated.

4. Zamindar workaround — eviction before 12-year continuity completed ('Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal' ¶1, 'The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)' background). Rent Act 1859 became a loophole-vulnerable shield.

5. Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873 ('Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal' ¶2) — formal organisation + court cases + Ishan Chandra Roy replication. Sustained legal pressure highlighting the Rent Act 1859 enforcement failures.

6. Ripon80-84's Rent Commission 1880 (see 'Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal') — the British response. Commission led to Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 — closing the loophole by extending occupancy rights to DIFFERENT plots in same village + 12-year threshold.

7. Implementation difference — 'Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal' closes: "The Act was properly implemented and finally brought genuine relief to Bengal's ryots." The 1885 Act succeeded where the 1859 Act had been defeated by zamindar workarounds, because the political pressure built up over two decades made enforcement unavoidable.
Closing verdict: The Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 shows the pattern — agitation, law, loophole, renewed agitation, revised law. Peasant struggle, not colonial goodwill, drove each step.

questions.label: FYQ_M.5
questions.stem: "The 1907 Punjab Canal Colony agitations were withdrawn not out of liberal sympathy but out of strategic calculation about the Indian Army." Examine this proposition with reference to the post-1857 Army recruitment policy.
body: Demand: Show why the British backed down in 1907 — anchor in the post-1857 army restructuring's Punjab-recruitment focus.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The British answered the 1907 Punjab Canal Colony agitations with repression, then withdrew the bill — not out of liberal sympathy but out of strategic calculation.
Guiding themes:

1. Open with 'Punjab' framing — the British response was "twofold — repression, and then quiet withdrawal of the bill" — and the closing strategic calculation: "post-1857, the Indian Army was heavily recruited from Punjab, particularly from the Sikh community. Disaffection among Punjab's peasantry could spread to the army — a risk the British simply could not afford."

2. Post-1857 Army recruitment context — cross-reference Ch 21 'Changes in the Army — Peel Commission'. Post-1857 army was deliberately recruited from "martial races" (Jats, Rajputs, Sikhs, Gurkhas) from REGIONS THAT STAYED LOYAL IN 1857. Punjab was the centrepiece of this recruitment policy.

3. The risk in 1907 — if Punjab's peasantry rose in agitation, the Sikh soldiers (whose families were peasants) would face conflicting loyalties between their farmer kin and their British employer. A repeat of the Bengal Army's 1857 fate, with the dominant martial race playing the part the Bengal Army had played 50 years earlier.

4. Bill contents ('Punjab' ¶1) — government control of inheritance + water rate hikes + fine increases. Each provision directly affected peasant land + peasant household economics. The bill was carefully designed to maximise revenue — but ill-considered against the Punjab-Army-recruitment lens.

5. Three organisations ('Punjab' ¶2) — Lahore Indian Association 1877 + Arya Samaj 1875 + Singh Sabha 1873. The presence of the Singh Sabha — a Sikh religious-reform body — particularly worried the British because it intersected directly with the Sikh-soldier community.
6. Outcome — the bill was withdrawn. Not because the British conceded the principle, but because the strategic cost of pursuing it exceeded the revenue benefit.
Closing verdict: Post-1857 Army recruitment policy from Punjab had become a constraint on British fiscal power. The withdrawal was strategic calculation about the Indian Army, not sympathy.
revise: Changes in the Army — Peel Commission

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: Which one of the following submitted in 1875 a petition to the House of Commons demanding India's direct representation in the British Parliament?
explanation: (D) ✓ — "The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870), set up by M.G."
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — In 1875, the Sabha sent a petition to the British House of Commons demanding direct Indian representation. No such petition by the Deccan Association is recorded.
(B) ✗ — The Indian Association did not yet exist in 1875 — Surendranath Banerjee founded it only in 1876.. (Its own House-of-Commons petition was a different, later episode.)
(C) ✗ — The Madras Mahajan Sabha was founded only in 1884 — nine years after the 1875 petition.
(Note: It was Indian Association that submitted a petition to the House of Commons demanding direct representation in the British Parliament.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: With reference to colonial rule India, what was sought by the Ilbert Bill in 1883?

options.text: To bring Indians and Europeans on par as far as the criminal jurisdiction of courts was concerned
To impose severe restrictions on the freedom of the native press as it was perceived to be hostile to colonial rulers
To encourage the native Indians to appear for civil service examinations by conducting them in India
To allow native Indians to possess arms by amending the Arms Act

explanation: (A) ✓ — The British were not going to treat Indians as equals — not in courts, not in civil services, not in political life.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Restrictions on the native press describe the Vernacular Press Act 1878 under Lytton76-80 — not the Ilbert Bill, which dealt with the criminal jurisdiction of Indian judges.

(C) ✗ — Holding the ICS examination in India was a separate, rejected demand: Lytton cut the age limit to 19 in 1876 and the exam stayed London-only; a simultaneous India exam came only under GOI Act 1919.. The Ilbert Bill said nothing about civil service examinations.
(D) ✗ — Arms licensing was the Arms Act 1878 (Indians required a licence; Europeans and Eurasians exempt). The Ilbert Bill proposed no change to arms law; it was a judicial-jurisdiction measure.
(Note: The main aim of Ilbert Bill introduced in 1883, during the viceroyalty of Lord Ripon, was to bring Indians and Europeans on par as far as the criminal jurisdiction of courts was concerned.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: The Ilbert Bill controversy was related to the

options.text: imposition of certain restrictions to carry arms by the Indians
imposition of restrictions on newspapers and magazines published in Indian languages
removal of disqualifications imposed on the Indian magistrates with regard to the trial of the Europeans
removal of a duty on imported cotton cloth

explanation: (C) ✓ — The bill proposed to extend the jurisdiction of Indian district judges to try cases involving Britons in the mofussil (rural) areas. This would end an existing privilege by which a Briton in rural India could not be tried before an Indian judge — i.e., removal of the disqualification on Indian magistrates trying Europeans.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Restrictions on carrying arms came from the Arms Act 1878 under Lytton76-80 — a different controversy, five years before the Ilbert Bill.
(B) ✗ — Restrictions on Indian-language newspapers came from the Vernacular Press Act 1878 — not from the Ilbert Bill, which was a judicial measure.
(D) ✗ — The Ilbert Bill contained nothing about customs duties on cotton; it dealt solely with which judges could try Britons.

(Note: The Ilbert Bill was introduced in 1883, by Viceroy Ripon to amend the existing laws to allow the Indian judges to try British offenders in criminal cases at the district level. It was named after Sir Courtenay Ilbert.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.stem: Pairs:1. Radhakanta Deb - British Indian Assoc2. Gazulu Chetty - Madras Mahajana Sabha3. S.N. Banerjee - Indian Assoc
explanation: (B) ✓ — Pairs 1 and 3 are correct: Radhakanta Deb was the first president of the British Indian Association [BrIA1851]; Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association (1876).
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "Only 1" undercounts: pair 3 is also correct — Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association in 1876.

(C) ✗ — Pair 2 is the wrong one: the Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884) was founded by M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Anandacharlu — not by Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty; and this option also drops the correct pair 1.

(D) ✗ — Overcounts: pair 2 fails — the record lists the Madras Mahajan Sabha's founders as M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Anandacharlu, and Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty is not among them.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: The first major voluntary organisation in India, set up at Calcutta in 1851, was the:
explanation: (b) ✓ — The British Indian Association [BrIA1851] was set up in Calcutta in 1851 with Radhakanta Deb as first president; it was the first all-Indian organisation in character. Why others wrong: (a) Dwarkanath Tagore's Landholders' Society dates to 1838 and included many non-official Anglo-Indians, so it was not all-Indian in character;
Memory hook: BrIA1851 = Bengal's first president was Radhakanta Deb.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: The immediate trigger for the founding of the British Indian Association (1851), the Bombay Association (1852), and the Madras Native Association (1852) was:

options.text: the British Parliament's debate on the Charter Act of 1853
the introduction of the Vernacular Press Act

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The British built many of the very tools that would eventually be used against them." Examine this statement with reference to the growth of the Indian national movement between 1857 and 1885.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine this statement" asks you to test the claim, not merely narrate. The time anchor is India between 1857 and 1885 — the years before the INC was born. "Tools ... used against them" means every theme must name a British creation & then show its nationalist use. Hold the irony frame from start to finish.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Between 1857 and 1885 the British built railways, schools & courts to rule better. Indians turned the very tools of empire into weapons used against them.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. Western education created the critics (see 'Western Education'). The rapid expansion of Western higher education after 1857 produced the WEMC. The British had wanted loyal 'Brown Sahibs'. Once it was clear that power would not be shared, admiration turned to criticism & then to a demand for Indian rights. Growth was uneven: the Downward Filtration Theory (1835) served only the elites of the Presidency Towns, and the Census of 1921 still showed 8% literacy & 2% female literacy despite Wood's Dispatch (1854) & the Hunter Commission (1882–83).

2. The press & the new communications grid (see 'The Press' + 'Railways and Telegraphs'). By 1875 India had over 400 newspapers in English & vernacular languages, with a combined readership of more than 1.5 lakh. From the 1850s railways & the electric telegraph let leaders of Bombay, Bengal, Madras & Punjab meet & coordinate. The infrastructure of empire became the infrastructure of anti-colonial politics.

3. Racism was the accelerant (see 'British Racism and Authoritarianism'). The 'Black Acts' of 1850 ended the European privilege of trial only in a Presidency Town — European protest, the 'white rebellion', got them suspended. The Lex Loci Act (1850) was read as a tool to promote conversion. Income tax, once withdrawn, was re-introduced in 1868 while famines swept India — the WEMC replied with No Taxation Without Representation. In 1870 the answer to WEMC criticism was a cut in higher education spending in Bengal.

4. Lytton76-80 antagonised every educated section (see 'The Lytton Years (1876–1880)'). The ICS age limit was cut from 21 to 19 in 1876 while the exam stayed in London; the Statutory Civil Services Act (1878) filled posts by nomination, so only loyalists entered; the Delhi Durbar (1877) was staged while the Great Madras Famine of 1876–78 killed approximately one crore Indians; the Vernacular Press Act (1878) pushed the Amrita Bazar Patrika to turn English overnight; the Arms Act (1878) exempted Europeans & Eurasians.

5. Even the reformist interlude proved the point (see 'Ripon's Interlude (1880–1884)' + 'Local Self-Government (1882)'). Ripon80-84 repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882, amended the Arms Act, restored the ICS age to 21 & passed the Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882 — elected District Boards in rural areas, at least two-thirds elected members in municipalities & a non-official chairperson. Yet his simultaneous ICS exam proposal failed against European opposition. Indians were being trained in a self-government they were not trusted with.

6. The Ilbert Bill settled the remaining doubt (see 'The Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883–84)'). C.P. Ilbert's bill would have let Indian district judges try Britons in the mofussil. European agitation forced its withdrawal & a mixed-jury version. Massive press campaigns followed across the country. The lesson was plain — no equality in courts, in the civil services or in political life. Organisation was the only answer, and the INC followed in 1885.
Closing verdict: The claim holds. Between 1857 and 1885 education, press, rail & law became the very tools that colonial rule handed to its own critics.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: To what extent did the Indian political associations founded after 1870 mark a break from the British Indian Association (1851) and its contemporaries? Analyse.
body: Demand of the question: "To what extent" wants a graded judgment, not a yes or no. The anchor is the shift from the associations of 1851–52 to the bodies founded after 1870. Weigh three things — who led them, what they demanded, what they actually did. Show the continuity as well as the change.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The British Indian Association (1851) petitioned as a landed lobby. The associations founded after 1870 claimed to speak for the people — a real but partial break.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Who the first associations were (see 'The First Associations (1851–52)'). The British Indian Association [BrIA1851] was set up in Calcutta in 1851, with Radhakanta Deb as its first president & members drawn from the educated landed class. The Bombay Association (1852) & the Madras Native Association (1852) shared that profile — educated, landed, conservative. All three were formed for the same immediate reason: Parliament was deliberating on the Charter Act of 1853.

2. Their demands showed their limits (see 'Their Demands'). They sent separate petitions, not a joint one — three regional lobbies, not one national fraternity. Common grievances: high taxes, expensive & incompetent administration, neglect of education & public works. Elite interests: opposition to the salt & opium monopolies. They attacked 'un-British rule', never British rule itself. No demand was met.

3. New leadership after 1870 (see 'The Rise of WEMC-Led Associations (Post-1870)'). The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) of M.G. Ranade aimed to represent all sections of society & in 1875 petitioned the House of Commons for direct Indian representation. Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association (1876) to 'represent the people'. Then the Lahore Indian Association (1877) under Sardar Dyal Singh Majithia, and the Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884) of M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer & P. Anandacharlu.

4. New work — and the continuity (see 'What These New Associations Did'). They led peasants during the Indigo Revolt (1859–63), the Bombay Deccan Riots (1875) & the Punjab Canal Colony Agitations (1907); the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha ran famine relief & arbitration courts; they protested the Plantation Labour & Inland Emigration Act (1859); they demanded representation in the Legislative Councils set up by the Indian Councils Act of 1861, separation of powers & lower Home Charges. But the old Bombay Association was itself revived in 1876 under Dadabhai Naoroji, the two types coexisted through the 1870s–90s, and leadership still rested with an educated elite.
Closing verdict: The break was real but gradual — bodies founded after 1870 widened the base, yet the British Indian Association model faded only across the 1870s–90s.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: The Congress is tottering to its fall and one of my great ambitions while in India, is to assist it to a peaceful demise. This statement is attributed to
explanation: (B) ✓ — The statement is Lord Curzon's, from his viceroyalty (1899–1905): he saw the Congress as "tottering to its fall" and hoped to assist its "peaceful demise" — a prediction the INC's later history proved spectacularly wrong.
Wrong options:

(C) ✗ — Lytton76-80 left India in 1880 — five years BEFORE the INC was born (Bombay, December 1885). He could not have spoken of assisting the demise of an organisation that did not yet exist.
(D) ✗ — "None of these" fails because the attribution is settled: the words are Curzon's (Viceroy 1899–1905), not an anonymous remark.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Indian National Congress
items: 1. Sarojini Naidu was the first woman to be the President of the Congress.
2. CR Das was in prison when he functioned as the President of the Congress.

questions.stemTail: Which of these statements are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statements 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 1 (Naidu first woman President) is WRONG — Annie Besant was first woman INC President at Calcutta Session 1917. Statement 2 (C.R. Das as President while in prison) is CORRECT — Das presided over Gaya Session 1922 from prison. Statement 3 (A.O. Hume first Britisher INC President) is WRONG — Hume was Founder/General Secretary, never President; George Yule was first Britisher INC President at Allahabad Session 1888. Statement 4 (Alfred Webb 1894) is CORRECT. Therefore answer is (B) 2 and 4.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Both its statements are the false ones: the first woman INC President was Annie Besant (Calcutta 1917), not Sarojini Naidu (Kanpur 1925, the second); and A.O. Hume never presided — the 1st British President was George Yule (Allahabad 1888).
(C) ✗ — Statement 3 contaminates it: Hume served as the INC's General Secretary and never held the presidency; the first Britisher in the chair was George Yule (1888).
(D) ✗ — Includes both false statements: 1 (Besant, not Naidu, was the first woman President) and 3 (Hume never presided).

(Note: Sarojini Naidu was second woman to be the President of Congress, first being Annie Besant in 1917. A O Hume was the founder of Congress, but he never became its President. Hence statement 2 and 4 is correct.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: Where was the First Session of the Indian National Congress held in December, 1885?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The Indian National Congress was founded in Bombay in December 1885.
Wrong options:
