(C) ✗ — Calcutta is the classic trap: it hosted the SECOND session (1886, under Dadabhai Naoroji), not the first.
(D) ✗ — Delhi was not the venue; the first session met at Bombay in December 1885 with Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee as President.

(Note: In December, 1885, the Indian National Congress was established by AO Hume; an ex-ICS officer, dominated the INC till 1892 as its General Secretary. The INC met for the first time on 28th December, 1885.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: What was the purpose which Sir William Wedderburn and WS Caine had set-up the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893?

options.text: To agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of commons
To campaign for the entry of Indians into the Imperial Judiciary
To facilitate a discussion on India's Independence in the British Parliament
To agitate for the entry of eminent Indians into the British Parliament

explanation: (A) ✓ — The Indian Parliamentary Committee (set up by Wedderburn & Caine, 1893) was a pressure group of sympathetic British MPs; its purpose was to raise and press Indian political reforms in the House of Commons.
Wrong options:

(B) ✗ — The Committee's arena was the House of Commons and its object Indian political REFORM; entry of Indians into the imperial judiciary was never its brief — Wedderburn's own record shows the judiciary issue ran the other way: his pro-Indian positions cost him a Bombay High Court judgeship.

(C) ✗ — In 1893 the vocabulary was reform WITHIN British rule, not independence: as an MP, Wedderburn supported INC demands through the 1890s in partnership with Gokhale — demands for representative reform.
(D) ✗ — The Committee was a pressure group OF sympathetic British MPs inside Parliament, not a vehicle for sending eminent Indians INTO Parliament.
(Note: The purpose of Sir William Wedderburn and WS Caine was to agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons in 1893.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.stem: Consider the following statements :
items: 1. The first woman President of the Indian National Congress was Sarojini Naidu.
2. The first Muslim President of the Indian National Congress was Badruddin Tyabji.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statement 2 is correct: Badruddin Tyabji was the first Muslim President of the INC (Madras Session, 1887). Statement 1 is wrong: the first woman President was Annie Besant (Calcutta, 1917); Sarojini Naidu came second (Kanpur, 1925).
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Statement 1 is the false one — Annie Besant (1917), not Sarojini Naidu (1925), was the first woman in the INC chair.
(C) ✗ — "Both 1 and 2" fails on statement 1: Naidu was the SECOND woman President (Kanpur 1925), after Annie Besant (Calcutta 1917).
(D) ✗ — "Neither" fails on statement 2, which is true: Tyabji presided at Madras in 1887 as the first Muslim INC President.
(Note: Annie Besant was the first woman President of Indian National Congress. She presided over the 1917 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress. Annie Besant was of Irish origin.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: With reference to the foundation of the Indian National Congress, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The INC was founded in Bombay in December 1885.
2. Its first President was Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee.
3. The retired British civil servant credited with the most active role in bringing it together was A.O. Hume.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: **(d) ✓ — All three statements are correct.** The INC was founded in Bombay in December 1885 (Statement 1 ✓); its first President was Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee (Statement 2 ✓); and the man credited with the most active role in bringing it together was Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant who toured India in the early 1880s and persuaded political leaders in Bombay, Madras, and Calcutta to gather for a common conference (Statement 3 ✓). Why others wrong: (a), (b), (c) each drop one verified statement — see 'The Birth of the INC'.
Memory hook: Bombay · 1885 · WC Bonnerjee · Hume — the four-word seed of the Congress.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: The first non-Indian President of the Indian National Congress was:
explanation: **(c) ✓ George Yule.** George Yule holds the distinction of being the 1st non-Indian President of the INC, presiding over the Allahabad Session in 1888. Why others wrong: (a) A.O. Hume served as General Secretary of the INC, never President (A.O. Hume — The Founder); (b) William Wedderburn was the **2nd** Non-Indian President (1889 and again 1910) per 'William Wedderburn — The Co-Founder Who Became a Biographer'; (d) Alfred Webb was the **3rd** Non-Indian President (Madras 1894) per 'Alfred Webb — The Irish Friend'.
Memory hook: Yule first (1888) · Wedderburn second (1889) · Webb third (1894) — Y-W-W.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: With reference to the "Safety Valve Theory" associated with the founding of the Indian National Congress, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The theory originated in a biography of A.O. Hume written by William Wedderburn in 1913.
2. The seven volumes of secret reports allegedly described a conspiracy by the educated middle class.
3. R.P. Dutt, the noted historian, supported the reading that the INC was formed to prevent a mass uprising.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — **(c) ✓ 1 and 3 only.** The theory's origin lies in Wedderburn's 1913 biography of Hume (Statement 1 ✓); and R.P. Dutt also supported the reading that the INC was formed to prevent a mass uprising (Statement 3 ✓). Statement 2 is FALSE — per 'What does the Safety Valve Theory say?', the seven volumes allegedly described a conspiracy by the **lower classes** to overthrow British rule, not by the educated middle class. The educated Indian elite are the opposite end of the same theory: they are the group the INC was supposed to hand a peaceful outlet to, not the group said to be plotting.

Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — 1 and 2 only: includes the false Statement 2 and drops the verified Statement 3 about R.P. Dutt. (b) ✗ — 2 and 3 only: includes the false Statement 2 and drops the verified Statement 1 about Wedderburn's 1913 biography. (d) ✗ — 1, 2 and 3: includes Statement 2, which names the wrong class; the alleged conspiracy was by the lower classes — see 'What does the Safety Valve Theory say?'.
Memory hook: Wedderburn 1913 biography · R.P. Dutt seconds it — but the 7 gurus' volumes named the LOWER classes plotting; the educated elite were the ones being handed the valve.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Why is the Safety Valve Theory regarded as historically unreliable? Consider the following reasons:
items: 1. The seven volumes of secret reports have no reference anywhere except in Wedderburn's biography.
2. Viceroy Dufferin84-88 called the Moderates a "microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest".
3. Dufferin84-88 said the Congress was "tottering to its fall" and hoped to assist it to a peaceful demise.
questions.stemTail: Which of the reasons given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — **(a) ✓ 1 and 2 only.** The seven volumes of secret reports were never found in any archive and have no reference anywhere except in Wedderburn's biography (Reason 1 ✓); and Dufferin84-88 did not see the Moderates as leaders of the Indian masses, calling them a "microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest" (Reason 2 ✓). Reason 3 is FALSE — per the Prelims 1998 ⚠ Alert in 'The Birth of the INC', the "tottering to its fall … peaceful demise" line belongs to **Lord Curzon99-05**, not to Dufferin (UPSC itself offered Dufferin as the trap option). Dufferin's own recorded reaction was quieter and is the reason that actually works: he asked the Governor of Bombay to stay alert about the INC, fearing it would grow into something like the Irish Home Rule League.

Why others wrong: (b) ✗ — 2 and 3 only: includes the false Reason 3 and drops the verified Reason 1 about the unfindable seven volumes. (c) ✗ — 1 and 3 only: includes the false Reason 3 and drops the verified "microscopic minority of Babus" remark. (d) ✗ — 1, 2 and 3: includes Reason 3, which puts Curzon99-05's words in Dufferin84-88's mouth — see the Prelims 1998 ⚠ Alert in 'The Birth of the INC'.
Memory hook: Unfindable 7 volumes · "microscopic minority of Babus" = Dufferin84-88 · "peaceful demise" = Curzon99-05 — two hostile viceroys, two different lines; never swap them.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Which of the following pre-1885 campaigns or protests were undertaken by Indian regional associations before the founding of the INC?
items: 1. The setting up of the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893
2. Nationwide protests against the Income Tax of 1868
3. A campaign in 1877 for Indianisation of the Civil Services
4. Active support for the Ilbert Bill (1883–84)
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the code given below:
explanation: (b) ✓ — **(b) ✓ 2, 3 and 4 only.** Nationwide protests against the Income Tax of 1868 (item 2 ✓), a campaign in 1877 for Indianisation of the Civil Services (item 3 ✓) and active support for the Ilbert Bill 1883–84 (item 4 ✓) all appear in the pre-1885 list under 'What were these pre-1885 associations doing?'. Item 1 is FALSE for this question — the Indian Parliamentary Committee was set up in **1893**, eight years AFTER the INC was founded, and it was set up in Britain by Sir William Wedderburn and W.S. Caine to work on the House of Commons (Prelims 2011 ⚠ Alert). It was not a pre-1885 campaign by Indian regional associations. Read the stem's time-window before ticking an item that is true in itself.

Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — 1 and 2 only: includes item 1, which falls outside the pre-1885 window, and drops the verified 1877 Civil-Services campaign and Ilbert Bill support. (c) ✗ — 1, 3 and 4 only: includes the out-of-window item 1 and drops the verified 1868 Income Tax protests. (d) ✗ — 1, 2, 3 and 4: includes item 1; the Indian Parliamentary Committee is 1893 and London-based — see the Prelims 2011 ⚠ Alert and 'What were these pre-1885 associations doing?'.

Memory hook: Pre-1885 fronts = Lex Loci 1850 · Income Tax 1868 · Civil-Services 1877 · Ilbert Bill 1883–84. Indian Parliamentary Committee = 1893, London, Wedderburn + Caine — AFTER the INC, not before.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Match the following pre-1885 all-India organisational efforts (List I) with the year associated (List II):
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the code given below:
matchTable: A. British India Association's attempt to open branches in Bombay & Madras
B. Native Press Association formed by journalists at the Imperial Darbar
C. National Conference held by the Indian Association in Calcutta
D. All-India gathering at the Theosophical Society's annual convention in Madras
A. British India Association's attempt to open branches in Bombay & Madras
B. Native Press Association formed by journalists at the Imperial Darbar
C. National Conference held by the Indian Association in Calcutta
D. All-India gathering at the Theosophical Society's annual convention in Madras
explanation: **(a) ✓ A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3.** The British India Association (1851) attempted to open branches in Bombay & Madras to submit a joint petition during the Charter renewal of 1853 (A-4 ✓); journalists invited to the 1877 Imperial Darbar formed the Native Press Association and elected Surendranath Banerjea as President (B-1 ✓); the Indian Association held a National Conference in Calcutta in 1883, with another scheduled for 1885 (C-2 ✓); and in 1884, delegates from across India gathered at the Theosophical Society's annual convention in Madras (D-3 ✓). Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) shuffle at least one pairing — see 'Were efforts for an all-India body already underway?'.
Memory hook: 1851 BIA · 1877 Press · 1883 Calcutta Conference · 1884 Theosophical — the dress rehearsal for 1885.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: The Indian National Conference, held in Calcutta in 1883 and 1885, was launched by:

options.text: Dadabhai Naoroji through the East India Association
Surendranath Banerjea through the Indian Association (1876)
A.O. Hume through the Indian Telegraph Union
Pherozeshah Mehta through the Bombay Presidency Association

explanation: **(b) ✓ Surendranath Banerjea through the Indian Association (1876).** The Indian Association (1876) of Surendranath Banerjea was the lead actor in many pre-1885 agitations; Banerjea used the Indian Association as a permanent organisational body to launch the Indian National Conference (1883) — a periodic gathering that brought delegates from across British India together. The Conference met in 1883 & 1885, then merged into the INC in 1886. Why others wrong: (a) Naoroji's East India Association is not mentioned in the Chapter as the launcher of the Indian National Conference; (c) Hume's role was bridging regional bodies for the 1885 conference, not launching the Indian National Conference (So What Was Hume's Real Usefulness?); (d) the Chapter does not attribute the Indian National Conference to Mehta or the Bombay Presidency Association.
Memory hook: Banerjea + Indian Association (1876) → Indian National Conference (1883, 1885) → merged into INC (1886).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: According to the chapter, Hume's "real usefulness" in 1885 lay in the fact that:

options.text: he had access to seven volumes of secret intelligence reports
he mediated between competing regional associations and lent a British founder's protective cover
he was personally appointed by Viceroy Dufferin84-88 to organise an Indian assembly
he financed the early sessions of the INC through his personal wealth

explanation: **(b) ✓** Hume's actual contribution was more practical than mythological — he acted as a mediator, helping to bridge differences among the various regional organisations competing for leadership of a future national body; getting Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras to sit together was not simple, and Hume helped make it happen. Gopal Krishna Gokhale put it plainly in 1913: the British would never have allowed an all-India organisation under an Indian's leadership, so a British founder gave the INC a protective cover in its early years. Why others wrong: (a) the seven volumes of secret reports belong to the Safety Valve Theory and were never actually found in any archive (Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?); (c) Dufferin84-88 did not take Hume seriously and quietly asked the Governor of Bombay to watch the INC (Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?); (d) the Chapter does not attribute INC finances to Hume's personal wealth.
Memory hook: Mediator + lightning conductor — bridging Bombay-Calcutta-Madras and shielding a young INC from British reflex.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: The viceroy who described the early Indian Moderates as a "microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest" was:
explanation: **(c) ✓ Lord Dufferin84-88.** Dufferin84-88 did not take Hume seriously; he hated the Moderates, did not see them as leaders of the Indian masses, and called them a "microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest" — hardly the language of a man who thought they could prevent a mass revolt. Why others wrong: (a) Lytton76-80's heavy expenditure on the Afghan War (1878–80) is referenced in 'A.O. Hume — The Founder', but the "microscopic minority" remark is Dufferin's; (b) Ripon80-84 is associated with the Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882, which Hume supported (see 'Key English Figures Behind the INC'); (d) Curzon99-05 is associated with the separate statement about "assisting the INC to a peaceful demise", not the "microscopic minority" remark.
Memory hook: Dufferin84-88's "microscopic minority of Babus" — the safety-valve myth dies in his own words.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: With reference to A.O. Hume's career before the INC, consider the following statements:
items: 1. He served as Secretary of the Department of Revenue, Agriculture & Commerce in 1871 under Viceroy Mayo69-72.
2. He was dismissed from his post for opposing Lord Lytton76-80's heavy expenditure on the Afghan War 1878–80.
3. He served as the first President of the INC at the Bombay Session in December 1885.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: **(a) ✓ 1 and 2 only.** Hume served as Secretary of the Department of Revenue, Agriculture & Commerce in 1871 under Viceroy Mayo69-72 (Statement 1 ✓) and was dismissed from his post for opposing Lytton76-80's heavy expenditure on the Afghan War 1878–80 (Statement 2 ✓). Statement 3 is FALSE — per 'A.O. Hume — The Founder' and 'The Birth of the INC', Hume served as **General Secretary** Of the INC and was never President; the first President of the 1885 Bombay Session was Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee. Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) all include Statement 3 about Hume being President, which is false — see 'A.O. Hume — The Founder'.
Memory hook: Mayo's Secretary 1871 · sacked over Afghan War spending · General Secretary (never President) of the INC.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to William Wedderburn, consider the following statements:
items: 1. He had served as Chief Secretary of Bombay and as a Judge of the Bombay High Court.
2. He was the 2nd non-Indian President of the INC, serving in 1889 and again in 1910.
3. He favoured the establishment of Cooperative Banks to provide cheap loans to farmers.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — **(c) ✓ 2 and 3 only.** Wedderburn became the 2nd non-Indian President of the INC, serving in 1889 and again in 1910 (Statement 2 ✓); and he favoured the establishment of Cooperative Banks to provide cheap loans to farmers (Statement 3 ✓). Statement 1 is FALSE — per 'Justice John Jardine — The Liberal Lawyer', the Chief Secretaryship of Bombay and the judgeship on the Bombay High Court belong to **John Jardine**, the other British co-founder of 1885. Wedderburn was ex-Secretary to the Bombay Government, and far from sitting on the Bombay High Court he was **denied** a judgeship there because of his pro-Indian positions.

Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — 1 only: rests entirely on the false Statement 1, and drops both verified statements. (b) ✗ — 1 and 2 only: includes the false Statement 1 and drops the verified Cooperative Banks statement. (d) ✗ — 1, 2 and 3: includes Statement 1, which gives Wedderburn Jardine's Bombay offices — see 'Justice John Jardine — The Liberal Lawyer' and 'William Wedderburn — The Co-Founder Who Became a Biographer'.

Memory hook: Wedderburn = ex-Secretary to the Bombay Government, DENIED the High Court judgeship · 2nd non-Indian President (1889 & 1910) · Cooperative Banks. Chief Secretary + Judge of Bombay HC = Jardine.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: George Yule, who became the 1st non-Indian President of the INC in 1888, is associated with which of the following?
items: 1. The Allahabad Session of the INC, 1888
2. The Agency House "Andrew Yule & Company" in Calcutta
3. The General Secretaryship of the Indian National Congress
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the code given below:
explanation: (b) ✓ — **(b) ✓ 1 and 2 only.** Yule presided over the Allahabad Session of the INC in 1888 (item 1 ✓); and he was a merchant and businessman, founder of the Agency House "Andrew Yule & Company" in Calcutta (item 2 ✓). Item 3 is FALSE — per 'A.O. Hume — The Founder' and the Prelims 2000 ⚠ Alert, the General Secretaryship of the INC belongs to **A.O. Hume**, who was General Secretary and never President. Yule's non-Congress office was the Presidency of the Indian Chamber of Commerce; the two men sit on opposite sides of the same line — Hume the Secretary who never presided, Yule the President who never held the secretaryship.

Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — 1 only: drops the verified item 2, the Agency House "Andrew Yule & Company" in Calcutta. (c) ✗ — 2 and 3 only: includes the false item 3 and drops Yule's defining credential, the Allahabad Session of 1888. (d) ✗ — 1, 2 and 3: includes item 3, which hands Yule the post Hume actually held — see 'A.O. Hume — The Founder' and the Prelims 2000 ⚠ Alert.
Memory hook: Yule = Allahabad 1888 + Andrew Yule & Co (+ Indian Chamber of Commerce). General Secretary of the INC = Hume — Secretary never President, President never Secretary.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Alfred Webb, who presided over the Madras Session of the INC in 1894, was:

options.text: a retired British civil servant who had served as ex-Secretary to the Bombay Government
an Irish politician and MP in the 1890s, invited personally by Dadabhai Naoroji
a merchant and founder of an Agency House in Calcutta
a Liberal lawyer who served as Chief Secretary of Bombay and a Judge of the Bombay High Court

explanation: **(b) ✓** Alfred Webb was an Irish politician who served as an MP in the 1890s and holds the distinction of being the 3rd non-Indian President of the INC, presiding over the Madras Session of 1894; he was invited personally by Dadabhai Naoroji, with whom he shared a close friendship. Why others wrong: (a) describes William Wedderburn (William Wedderburn — The Co-Founder Who Became a Biographer); (c) describes George Yule (George Yule — The Merchant President); (d) describes Justice John Jardine (Justice John Jardine — The Liberal Lawyer).
Memory hook: Irish MP · Naoroji's friend · Madras 1894 — Webb's three identifiers.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: The "Congress is tottering to its fall and one of my great ambitions while in India, is to assist it to a peaceful demise" — this statement is attributed to which of the following Viceroys?
explanation: **(c) ✓ Lord Curzon99-05.** Prelims 1998 ⚠ Alert — the correct answer to "The Congress is tottering to its fall…" is Lord Curzon. The remark reflects Curzon's hostile attitude towards the INC during his viceroyalty. Why others wrong: (a) Dufferin84-88's documented hostility (Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?) was the "microscopic minority of Babus" remark, not the "peaceful demise" line; (b) Lytton76-80 is associated with the Vernacular Press Act and Afghan War (What were these pre-1885 associations doing? + 'Key English Figures Behind the INC' — A.O. Hume — The Founder), not this statement; (d) Ripon80-84 was a reformist whom Hume actively supported (A.O. Hume — The Founder) — he would not have made this remark.
Memory hook: "Peaceful demise" = Curzon99-05 — the viceroy who wanted to bury the Congress.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: With reference to the Indian Parliamentary Committee set up in 1893, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It was set up by Sir William Wedderburn and W.S. Caine.
2. Its purpose was to agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons.
3. It was established in the same year that Wedderburn served his first term as INC President.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: **(a) ✓ 1 and 2 only.** Prelims 2011 ⚠ Alert — the Indian Parliamentary Committee was set up in 1893 by Sir William Wedderburn and W.S. Caine (Statement 1 ✓) to agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons (Statement 2 ✓). Statement 3 is FALSE — per 'William Wedderburn — The Co-Founder Who Became a Biographer', Wedderburn served as the 2nd non-Indian INC President in **1889** (and again in 1910), not in 1893. Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) include the false Statement 3 about Wedderburn's first INC presidency being in 1893 — see 'William Wedderburn — The Co-Founder Who Became a Biographer'.
Memory hook: Wedderburn + Caine (1893) → Indian Parliamentary Committee → reforms via House of Commons.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The 'safety valve' thesis tells us more about A.O. Hume's biographer than about the founding of the Indian National Congress." Critically examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" means you must state the thesis fairly, then test the evidence behind it, then deliver a verdict. The time anchor is double - the INC's founding in December 1885 and Wedderburn's biography of 1913. The framing phrase "tells us more about A.O. Hume's biographer" tells you the answer must judge the source, not only the claim.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The 'safety valve' thesis rests on William Wedderburn's 1913 biography of Hume. It was written 28 years after the founding of the Indian National Congress.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. What the thesis claims (see 'What does the Safety Valve Theory say?'). Hume founded the INC as a deliberate British strategy, not out of sympathy for Indians. The educated Indian elite would air grievances peacefully & a violent mass uprising would be prevented. Wedderburn's version - in 1878 Hume saw seven volumes of secret reports compiled by religious gurus, describing a lower-class conspiracy, & then met Viceroy Dufferin84-88. R.P. Dutt supported this reading.

2. The evidence fails (see 'Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?'). Those seven volumes were never found in any archive. They have no reference anywhere except in Wedderburn's biography - a book by a close personal friend, written nearly four decades after the supposed events, about events he did not witness.

3. Dufferin was no co-designer (see 'Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?'). Dufferin84-88 did not take Hume seriously. He hated the Moderates & did not see them as leaders of the Indian masses. He called them a "microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest" - not the language of a man who thought they could stop a revolt.

4. Dufferin's alarm, not his satisfaction (see 'Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?'). He did not welcome the INC's formation. He quietly asked the Governor of Bombay to be alert about it. He feared it would grow into something like the Irish Home Rule League, led by Charles Parnell in the 1870s-80s. The comparison was a warning, not a compliment.

5. The biographer's motive (see 'Then Why Did Wedderburn Write What He Wrote?'). Wedderburn wanted to show Hume as a patriot who sacrificed his career to save the British Empire from its own folly. The safety-valve story made Hume look prescient & heroic. It was written for a friend's legacy, not as history.

6. What is left of Hume once the myth goes (see 'So What Was Hume's Real Usefulness?'). He was a mediator who helped the competing regional bodies of Bombay, Calcutta & Madras sit together. Gokhale said plainly in 1913 that the British would never have allowed an all-India organisation under Indian leadership - so a British founder gave the INC protective cover.
Closing verdict: The 'safety valve' thesis rests on one unverifiable source. It tells us more about A.O. Hume's biographer than about the founding of the Indian National Congress.
revise: What does the Safety Valve Theory say?
Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?
Then Why Did Wedderburn Write What He Wrote?

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: The Indian National Congress of 1885 was less a British creation than the natural culmination of decades of organised Indian political work. Discuss.
body: Demand of the question: "Discuss" asks you to build the case with evidence & then weigh it. The time anchor runs backwards from December 1885 to the associations of the 1850s-1870s. The phrase "less a British creation" means you must not deny Hume's role - you must place it in proportion.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Indian National Congress of 1885 was less a British creation than the natural culmination of decades of organised Indian political work, begun with the British India Association in 1851.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. A long agitation record (see 'What were these pre-1885 associations doing?'). Protests against the Lex Loci Act of 1850. Nationwide protests against the Income Tax of 1868. A campaign in 1877 for Indianisation of the Civil Services.

2. A widening political agenda (see 'What were these pre-1885 associations doing?'). Campaigns against the Afghan War (1878-80) & the Vernacular Press Act (1878). Active support for the Ilbert Bill (1883-84). A demand for the right to join Volunteer Corps, then restricted to Europeans. In 1885, an appeal to British voters to elect pro-Indian candidates.

3. The Bengal engine (see 'What were these pre-1885 associations doing?'). The Indian Association (1876) of Surendranath Banerjea, editor of Bengalee, was a permanent organisational body. It launched the Indian National Conference (1883), which met in 1883 & 1885 & merged into the INC in 1886 - while the Indian Association itself continued separately.

4. All-India machinery already being built (see 'Were efforts for an all-India body already underway?'). The British India Association (1851) tried to open branches in Bombay & Madras for a joint petition during the Charter renewal of 1853. Journalists at the 1877 Imperial Darbar formed the Native Press Association & elected Banerjea President. Delegates gathered at the Theosophical Society's convention in Madras in 1884. By 1885 a National Fund existed for political campaigns in India & London.

5. Hume's proportionate share (see 'So What Was Hume's Real Usefulness?'). His contribution was practical - mediating between regional organisations competing for leadership of a future national body. Getting Bombay, Calcutta & Madras to sit together was not simple. Gokhale (1913) added the other half: a British founder gave the body protective cover.
Closing verdict: No pre-1885 demand had been met, so an all-India body was the logical next step - a natural culmination, not a British creation.
revise: What were these pre-1885 associations doing?
Were efforts for an all-India body already underway?

questions.label: FYQ_M.3
questions.stem: How far does A.O. Hume's own record as a British official explain the shape he wanted the Indian National Congress to take?
body: Demand of the question: "How far" demands a measured judgement - establish the link first, then mark its limit. The time anchor is 1871 to 1885, from Mayo69-72 to Ripon80-84. The phrase "the shape he wanted" points at Hume's design for the body, not merely at his motives.

Suggested intro (~25 words): A.O. Hume's own record as a British official ran from 1871 to his dismissal under Lytton76-80. It largely explains the shape he wanted the Indian National Congress to take.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The reformist official (see 'A.O. Hume — The Founder'). As Secretary of the Department of Revenue, Agriculture & Commerce in 1871, he worked under Mayo69-72 to improve agricultural yields. His instincts were reformist, whatever the safety-valve story later claimed.

2. The cost of dissent (see 'A.O. Hume — The Founder'). He opposed Lytton76-80's heavy expenditure on the Afghan War (1878-80) & was dismissed from his post for it. He supported Ripon80-84's reforms, especially the Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882.

3. The design that followed (see 'A.O. Hume — The Founder'). He was a Liberal in the British tradition who believed in representative governance. He wanted the INC to function like "His Majesty's Opposition" - a formal, legitimate channel of political dissent. In 1885 he published a direct appeal to British voters to elect pro-Indian candidates to Parliament.

4. Where the explanation stops (see 'So What Was Hume's Real Usefulness?'). Hume shaped the form, not the demand. His real work was mediating between competing regional organisations. He served as General Secretary, never President. Gokhale (1913) read his Britishness as protective cover for an Indian-led project.
Closing verdict: Hume's record as a British official explains the loyal, opposition-style shape of the INC - but the political demand behind it was already Indian.

questions.label: FYQ_M.4
questions.stem: Evaluate the role played by British and Irish liberals in the early years of the Indian National Congress (1885-1894).
body: Demand of the question: "Evaluate" requires a balance sheet - contribution on one side, limits on the other. The bracket 1885-1894 fixes the span from the founding to Alfred Webb's Madras Session. Cover organisers, presidents & the London end of the work.

Suggested intro (~25 words): British and Irish liberals founded, organised & presided over the Congress between 1885 and 1894. Their role in the early years of the Indian National Congress was real but bounded.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. The organiser (see 'A.O. Hume — The Founder'). Hume toured India in the early 1880s & brought leaders together. He served as General Secretary, never President. He wanted the INC to work like "His Majesty's Opposition" & in 1885 appealed to British voters to elect pro-Indian candidates.

2. The co-founder who worked Westminster (see 'William Wedderburn — The Co-Founder Who Became a Biographer'). Ex-Secretary to the Bombay Government & co-founder in 1885. He became the 2nd non-Indian INC President - 1889 & again 1910. He favoured Cooperative Banks for cheap farm loans. His pro-Indian positions cost him a judgeship at the Bombay High Court. With W.S. Caine he set up the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893 to agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons, working closely with Gokhale.

3. The liberal lawyer (see 'Justice John Jardine — The Liberal Lawyer'). Jardine was also a co-founder in 1885. He had served as Chief Secretary of Bombay & as a Judge of the Bombay High Court, & later became an MP (1906-1918).

4. The merchant president (see 'George Yule — The Merchant President'). Yule was the 1st non-Indian INC President, at the Allahabad Session of 1888. He founded the Agency House "Andrew Yule & Company" in Calcutta & headed the Indian Chamber of Commerce. That a man at the top of colonial commerce presided over the INC was itself politically significant.

5. The Irish friend (see 'Alfred Webb — The Irish Friend'). Webb, an Irish MP of the 1890s, was the 3rd non-Indian INC President, at the Madras Session of 1894. Dadabhai Naoroji invited him personally. He opposed racism & the opium trade into China. Ireland's own Home Rule struggle shaped his sympathy.

6. The limits (see 'So What Was Hume's Real Usefulness?'). Gokhale said in 1913 that the British would never have allowed an all-India organisation under Indian leadership. The liberals supplied cover, contacts & a London platform. The demands, the agitation & the organisation were Indian.
Closing verdict: In the early years of the Indian National Congress, British and Irish liberals gave protective cover & access to Westminster - never the political direction.
revise: William Wedderburn — The Co-Founder Who Became a Biographer
Justice John Jardine — The Liberal Lawyer

questions.label: FYQ_M.5
questions.stem: "The Indian National Congress was born under British suspicion, not British sponsorship." Analyse the colonial state's response to the Congress in its early years.
body: Demand of the question: "Analyse" means break the official response into its parts - private opinion, surveillance, the fear of precedent - & show how they fit. The anchor is the Congress's founding in December 1885 & the years that follow. The contrast "suspicion, not sponsorship" is the hinge of the answer.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Indian National Congress was born under British suspicion, not British sponsorship. Dufferin84-88 quietly asked the Governor of Bombay to stay alert about the new body.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. The Viceroy's private verdict (see 'Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?'). Dufferin84-88 did not take Hume seriously. He hated the Moderates & did not see them as leaders of the Indian masses at all. He called them a "microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest".

2. Watched from the start (see 'Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?'). He did not welcome the formation of the INC. He quietly asked the Governor of Bombay to be alert about it - surveillance, not sponsorship.

3. The Irish precedent (see 'Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?'). He feared the INC would grow into something like the Irish Home Rule League, led by Charles Parnell in the 1870s-80s, which had pressured & embarrassed the British government. The comparison was a warning signal.

4. Why a British founder mattered (see 'So What Was Hume's Real Usefulness?'). Gokhale said in 1913 that the British would never have allowed an all-India organisation under Indian leadership. Hume gave the INC protective cover in its early years - Indians used him as a lightning conductor.

5. Where the hostility ended (see 'The Birth of the INC'). Lord Curzon later declared the Congress "tottering to its fall" & made it an ambition to assist it "to a peaceful demise" - the plainest statement of the official mind.
Closing verdict: The colonial state watched the Congress from birth. British suspicion, not British sponsorship, defined its early years - and later hardened into open hostility.
revise: Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong?

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: Which one of the following Acts of British India strengthened the Viceroy's authority over his executive council by substituting 'portfolio' or departmental system for corporate functioning?
explanation: (A) ✓ — The ICA 1861 gave legal recognition to the Portfolio System introduced by Canning56-62 in 1859 — the practice of allocating specific departments... to individual VEC members, whose decisions on their portfolios would be final, subject to the Viceroy's veto. This formalised cabinet-style administration at the centre.
Wrong options:

(B) ✗ — The Government of India Act 1858's subject was the transfer of rule from the Company to the Crown — it reorganised control in London, not the working of the executive council in India; the portfolio system entered the law only with ICA 1861.

(C) ✗ — ICA 1892's contribution lay on the LEGISLATIVE side — gradually growing the council's outer ring — not in executive working: the portfolio system had already been legally recognised three decades earlier, by ICA 1861. +.

(D) ✗ — ICA 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) again expanded the legislative outer ring with marginal new powers — by then the portfolio system had been in legal force for nearly half a century (ICA 1861, formalising Canning56-62's 1859 practice). +.

(Note: The Indian Councils Act, 1861 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Canning strengthened the viceroy authority over his executive council by substituting 'portfolio' or departmental system for corporate functioning.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: The phrase "despotism controlled from home" — used to describe the operating principle of the Government of India under British rule — is most closely associated with which of the following?

options.text: Lord Canning, Viceroy at the time the Indian Councils Act, 1861 was enacted
Charles Wood, Secretary of State for India
Lord Dalhousie, the architect of pre-1857 centralisation
James Wilson, the first Finance Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council

explanation: (B) ✓ — The Secretary of State for India, Charles Wood, described the Government of India as a "despotism controlled from home." This one line captured the fundamental feature of British Indian governance, and remained the operating principle right until 1947. Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — Lord Canning (Canning56-62) was Viceroy when ICA 1861 was passed and is associated with the Portfolio System (1859), not with this phrase. (c) ✗ — Lord Dalhousie's name does not appear in in this connection. (d) ✗ — James Wilson is mentioned in as the first Finance Member (1859), not as the author of this phrase.
Memory hook: Wood spoke; the "Home" was London; the "despot" was the Secretary of State himself.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: With reference to the restructure carried out by the Indian Councils Act, 1861, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Act created two separate, independent institutions — a Viceroy's Executive Council and an Imperial Legislative Council.
2. Every Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC) member was automatically part of the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC).
3. The Commander-in-Chief was an extraordinary member of the VEC and therefore also sat in the ILC.
4. The expanded-council model created by the Act continued until the Government of India Act, 1919.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — - Statement 2 is correct — "Every VEC member was automatically part of the ILC." - Statement 3 is correct — the Commander-in-Chief (C-I-C), already an extraordinary member of the VEC, by virtue of his military office, thus also sat in the ILC. - Statement 4 is correct — the record states the arrangement continued until 1919 (the Government of India Act 1919 / Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms); the 1909 Morley-Minto Reforms only added marginal new powers to the outer ring, not true separation. Why others wrong: - Statement 1 is incorrect — the record is explicit: the ICA 1861 did not create two separate, independent institutions. The VEC was expanded by adding "additional members" specifically for law-making sessions; the same council wore two hats.
Memory hook: One council, two hats — executive hat (VEC) and legislative hat (ILC). The hats changed; the council did not.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Match the following bodies under the Indian Councils Act, 1861 with their functions:
questions.stemTail: Choose the correct match:
matchTable: A. Day-to-day executive work at the centre
C. Day-to-day executive work in a province
A. Day-to-day executive work at the centre
C. Day-to-day executive work in a province
explanation: (A) ✓ — The Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC) for day-to-day executive functions, and the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) for law-making. At the province level, a parallel structure was created: Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) and Governor's Executive Councils (GECs) — so the PLC is the law-making body in the province and the GEC handles day-to-day executive work in the province. - 1-A ✓ VEC → executive at centre - 2-B ✓ ILC → law-making at centre - 3-D ✓ PLC → law-making in province - 4-C ✓ GEC → executive in province Why others wrong: The other options either swap the centre pair (b, c) or the province pair (b, d). Only option (a) keeps both pairs in the correct executive-vs-legislative direction.
Memory hook: Letter "E" in VEC and GEC = Executive; letter "L" in ILC and PLC = Legislative.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: With reference to the Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC) as it stood after the Indian Councils Act, 1861, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It consisted of the Governor-General, five ordinary members, and the Commander-in-Chief as an extraordinary member.
2. A 5th ordinary member, dedicated to Finance, was added constitutionally in 1861.
3. A 6th ordinary member, dedicated to Public Works, was added in 1874.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — - Statement 1 is correct — the record states the VEC was now structured as: GG + 5 ordinary/regular members + C-I-C as extraordinary member. - Statement 2 is correct — the record states A 5th Ordinary Member was added constitutionally in 1861 to handle Finance. It also notes the post was introduced in practice in 1859 with James Wilson; constitutional backing came in 1861. - Statement 3 is correct — the record states a 6th Ordinary Member was added in 1874 to handle the portfolio of Public Works. All three statements are correct.

Why others wrong: (a) Statement 1 alone is incomplete — Statements 2 and 3 are also correct. (b) Statement 2 alone misses 1 and 3. (c) Combining 1 and 2 still excludes the correct Statement 3 about the 1874 Public Works addition.
Memory hook: 1857 revolt → debt → Finance Member (1861); 1870s railways/canals → Public Works (1874).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: The Portfolio System, which allotted specific departments to individual members of the Viceroy's Executive Council, was first introduced in which year and by which Viceroy?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The ICA 1861 gave legal recognition to the Portfolio System introduced by Canning56-62 in 1859. So the Portfolio System was introduced in 1859 by Canning56-62; the ICA 1861 only formalised what was already an in-house practice. Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — Wrong year. 1858 was the year of the Government of India Act, not the Portfolio System. (c) ✗ — Wrong year. 1861 is when the system received legal recognition through ICA 1861, not when it was introduced. (d) ✗ — Wrong person. Canning56-62, not Elgin, introduced the practice in 1859.
Memory hook: Canning practised it in 1859; the Act recognised it in 1861. Practice first, law later.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Who among the following was the first Finance Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council, and is also remembered for introducing income tax in India in 1860?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The first to hold this post in 1859 was James Wilson, who introduced income tax in 1860 (he died in 1860). The post was institutionalised in practice in 1859 and given constitutional backing through ICA 1861. Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — Charles Wood was Secretary of State for India (London), not Finance Member of the VEC (India). (c) ✗ — The Maharaja of Patiala was one of the three Indians nominated to the ILC in 1862, not a Finance Member. (d) ✗ — Dinkar Rao of Gwalior was likewise nominated to the ILC in 1862; he was not Finance Member.
Memory hook: Wilson → 1859 Finance post → 1860 income tax → died 1860.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: With reference to the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) created under the Indian Councils Act, 1861, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Act fixed at six the number of additional members nominated by the Viceroy.
2. Of these additional members, at least half had to be non-officials.
3. The official majority in any legislative vote was constitutionally guaranteed.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — - Statement 1 is incorrect — the ICA 1861 did not fix the number at six; the record states that now 6 to 12 additional law members could be nominated by the Viceroy for the ILC. A fixed six belongs to the earlier arrangement — in 1853, 6 legal members were added for law-making (Legislative Meetings of GG's Council = [VEC + 6 legal members]). - Statement 2 is correct — "of which half must be non-officers." - Statement 3 is correct — the record explains: the official majority was guaranteed. The VEC alone (GG + 5 + CIC = 7) already outnumbered or matched even the maximum possible non-officials (6 out of 12 additional members). The British could afford this gesture because the math was rigged. Hence only Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — Includes the incorrect Statement 1 and drops the correct Statement 3 on the guaranteed official majority. (c) ✗ — Includes the incorrect Statement 1 and drops the correct Statement 2 on the half-non-official rule. (d) ✗ — Statement 1 is wrong (6 to 12, not a fixed six), so all three cannot be correct.

Memory hook: Memory hook: 1853 = a fixed 6 legal members; 1861 = a flexible 6 to 12 additional members, half non-official — but the math stayed rigged, the VEC's 7 always outvoting a maximum of 6 non-officials.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to the first Indians nominated to the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) in 1862, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The three nominees were the Raja of Banaras, the Maharaja of Patiala, and Dinkar Rao of Gwalior.
2. All three were drawn from the Zamindars and moneylenders of the British Indian Association (BrIA, 1851).
3. The British logic for these nominations was to reward and secure the cooperation of elite Indians who had stayed loyal during 1857.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — - Statement 1 is correct — In 1862, 3 Indians were nominated to the ILC: the Raja of Banaras, the Maharaja of Patiala, and Dinkar Rao of Gwalior. - Statement 2 is incorrect — the record ties the Zamindars & moneylenders of the British Indian Association (BrIA, 1851) to the wider pool of the only 45 Indians nominated in total until ICA 1892, not to the three of 1862, of whom it says "All were elites, some from Princely States" — the Rulers of Princely States are listed as a separate category from the BrIA zamindars & moneylenders. - Statement 3 is correct — The British logic was simple: since the elite Indians had stayed loyal during 1857, their cooperation should be rewarded & secured. Hence only Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — Includes the incorrect Statement 2 and drops the correct Statement 3 on the British logic of rewarding 1857 loyalty. (b) ✗ — Includes the incorrect Statement 2 and drops the correct Statement 1 naming the three nominees. (d) ✗ — Statement 2 is wrong (the BrIA zamindars & moneylenders describe the wider pre-1892 pool of 45, not the 1862 three), so all three cannot be correct.

Memory hook: Memory hook: Three loyal elites in 1862 — Banaras (Raja), Patiala (Maharaja), Gwalior (Dinkar Rao); the BrIA zamindars & moneylenders belong to the wider list of just 45 Indians nominated up to 1892. Co-opt the elites; exploit the masses.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the British rationale for permitting half of the additional members of the ILC to be non-officials (potentially including Indians) under the Indian Councils Act, 1861?

options.text: The British wished to give Indians a genuine share of legislative power, however small, as a first step toward responsible government.
The British were under pressure from Indian political bodies such as the Indian National Congress, which had begun demanding representation.
The official majority was guaranteed in any vote, so the British could safely offer a token of representation without risking control.
The Charter Act 1853 had already mandated this proportion, and the British were merely fulfilling that legal obligation.

explanation: (C) ✓ — The record asks "Why?" and answers explicitly — Because the official majority was guaranteed. The VEC alone (GG + 5 + CIC = 7) already outnumbered or matched even the maximum possible non-officials (6 out of 12 additional members). The British could afford this gesture because the math was rigged. Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — the record describes this as "a tiny element — of popular & representative governance," not a first step toward responsible government. "no responsible government anywhere." (b) ✗ — The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885, well after ICA 1861. No such pressure existed in 1861. (d) ✗ — The Charter Act 1853 did not mandate non-official quotas; the record attributes the 6-to-12 with half non-official rule to ICA 1861 itself.
Memory hook: Token offered because the math was rigged — VEC of 7 always outvoted a maximum of 6 non-officials.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: With reference to the powers of the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) under the Indian Councils Act, 1861, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The ILC could ask questions to the Executive on government policy.
2. The ILC could bring and pass resolutions on matters of public importance.
3. The ILC could not discuss or vote on the Budget.
4. The Viceroy held absolute veto power over all bills passed by the ILC.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — - Statement 3 is correct — "Budget Discussion/Vote: NOT allowed." - Statement 4 is correct — "The Viceroy held absolute veto power over all bills." Why others wrong: - Statement 1 is incorrect — the record lists "Ask Questions to Executive: NOT allowed." - Statement 2 is incorrect — the record lists "Bring & Pass Resolutions: NOT allowed." The record concludes by saying the ILC had a small membership, entirely nominated (no elections), and no control whatsoever over the Executive.
Memory hook: ILC could do almost nothing — no questions, no resolutions, no budget vote. The Viceroy held all the strings.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1861, the Viceroy was granted Ordinance power. Which of the following best describes this power?

options.text: The power to dissolve the ILC and call fresh nominations.
The power to make law by executive order, valid for a period of 6 months.
The power to delegate legislative authority to the Governor of any province for a period of 6 months.
The power to amend any Act passed by the British Parliament, subject to the approval of the Secretary of State for India.

explanation: (B) ✓ — The Viceroy also had Ordinance power — the power to make law by executive order, valid for 6 months. (An Ordinance is essentially law made by the Executive, bypassing the Legislature.) Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — the record does not describe Ordinance power as dissolution power. The ILC was nominated, not elected, so dissolution language does not apply in the way the option implies. (c) ✗ — Ordinance power is the Viceroy's own law-making power, not a delegation to Governors. (d) ✗ — The Viceroy could not amend Acts of the British Parliament; that would invert the entire chain of authority described in.
Memory hook: Ordinance = Viceroy legislates by executive order; valid 6 months; bypasses the ILC entirely.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: The Indian Councils Act, 1861 restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras. Which earlier Act had originally taken away these legislative powers and concentrated them at the centre?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Centralisation had peaked in 1833, when the legislative powers of Bombay & Madras were taken away & concentrated at the centre. ICA 1861 began reversing that. It restored the legislative powers of Bombay & Madras. Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — The Regulating Act, 1773 began the process of centralisation but it did not specifically strip Bombay and Madras of legislative powers; that came at the 1833 peak. (b) ✗ — Charter Act, 1813 is not the Act named in for this stripping action. (d) ✗ — Charter Act, 1853 added 6 legal members to the GG's Council but did not perform the Bombay-Madras stripping.
Memory hook: 1773 began → 1833 peaked (Bombay-Madras stripped) → 1861 began reversing → 1935 Provincial Autonomy peaked.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1861, new Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) were set up in Bengal, the North-Western Provinces (NWP) and Punjab. Which of the following correctly lists these in the order in which their PLCs were established?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The new PLCs were set up in: - Bengal — 1862 - NWP — 1886 - Punjab — 1897 the record also explains the delays: NWP was delayed because memories of 1857 were still raw, and the British were cautious about loosening executive grip; Punjab was delayed because it was a frontier province — the British preferred strong executive control there rather than the slower deliberation of a legislative body. Why others wrong: All three other options scramble at least one of the year-to-province pairings given in.
Memory hook: Bengal first (1862), NWP next (1886, 1857 hangover), Punjab last (1897, frontier caution).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Match the following powers held by the Viceroy under the Indian Councils Act, 1861 over the provinces with the later legislation that diluted or ended them:
questions.stemTail: Choose the correct match:
matchTable: List I (Viceroy's province-level power under ICA 1861)
1. Requirement of Viceroy's sanction on the Governor's nomination of non-official members of a PLC
2. One Country, One Budget (no separate provincial budget)
3. Rule-making power over the functioning of the ILC, PLCs, VEC and GECs
List I (Viceroy's province-level power under ICA 1861)
1. Requirement of Viceroy's sanction on the Governor's nomination of non-official members of a PLC
2. One Country, One Budget (no separate provincial budget)
3. Rule-making power over the functioning of the ILC, PLCs, VEC and GECs
explanation: (A) ✓ — - 1-A ✓ By ICA 1892, this requirement for Viceroy's sanction on provincial nominations was ended, shifting more genuine power to the Governors. - 2-B ✓ There was no separate provincial budget — only one budget for British India as a whole … This was ended by GOI 1919, which separated the provincial budget from the central budget for the first time. - 3-C ✓ Rule-making power was ended only by GOI 1935, which brought Provincial Autonomy. Why others wrong: Each of the other options misaligns at least one power with the wrong terminating Act. Match-list questions of this kind reward year-anchored recall — once you fix any one pair correctly, the others fall into place.
Memory hook: Sanction → 1892. Budget → 1919. Rule-making → 1935.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Which of the following best characterises the nature of government established by the Indian Councils Act, 1861?

options.text: A federal government with two clearly bicameral legislatures at the centre and the provinces.
A parliamentary government in which the executive was accountable to a legislature dominated by elected Indian members.
A despotic, non-responsible government in which all members of the legislature were nominated and the Viceroy held absolute veto and ordinance powers.
A dyarchical government in which "transferred" subjects were placed in the hands of Indian ministers responsible to the provincial legislature.

explanation: (C) ✓ — - 8.10 — "Election Method: All members nominated — no elections" - 8.9 — Viceroy Powers: Absolute veto, ordinance (6 months), prior approval for bills - 8.12 — Nature of Govt: Despotism — no responsible government anywhere Option (c) captures all three facts and matches — "despotism controlled from home." Why others wrong: (a) ✗ — Per, the structure was Not federal — decentralisation from 1833 peak, Centre made budget. A bicameral Central Legislature came only with the Government of India Act, 1919. (b) ✗ — There were no elections; the executive was not accountable to the legislature. (d) ✗ — Dyarchy was introduced at the provincial level by the Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms), not by ICA 1861.
Memory hook: All nominated + absolute veto + no responsible government = despotism, plain and simple.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "Charles Wood wanted a 'despotism controlled from home'; the Indian Councils Act of 1861 built exactly that, and then softened its edges with nominated Indians." Critically examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" wants both sides — what the Act conceded & what it withheld. The anchor is 1861, the first restructuring of the British Indian State after the 1857 revolt. The framing phrase "softened its edges" is the hinge: show that nominating Indians changed how the Act looked, not how it worked. A one-sided answer will not score.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Charles Wood wanted a "despotism controlled from home". The Indian Councils Act of 1861 built exactly that, then softened its edges with nominated Indians.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. The governing idea (see 'Core Philosophy'). Secretary of State for India Charles Wood called the Government of India a "despotism controlled from home" — "home" meant Britain, & the dictator sat in London. This principle held till 1947. ICA 1861 restructured the Legislature & Executive; the Indian High Courts Act of 1861 reorganised the Judiciary. Two laws, one year.

2. The despotism built into the design (see 'ICA 1861's Restructure of Legislature & Executive'). One council wore two hats — the VEC for day-to-day executive work, the ILC (= VEC + Additional Members) for law-making. Every VEC member was automatically part of the ILC. That guaranteed a built-in official majority in every legislative vote. The model ran until 1919.

3. The Executive was strengthened, not checked (see 'Evolution of the Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC)'). The Portfolio System introduced by Canning56-62 in 1859 got legal recognition — a member's decision on his portfolio was final, subject to the Viceroy's veto. A 5th Ordinary Member for Finance was added in 1861 (post begun 1859 with James Wilson, income tax 1860). VEC = GG + 5 Ordinary Members + CIC as extraordinary member.

4. The softening (see 'The Legislature (now called ILC)'). The Viceroy could nominate 6 to 12 additional members for the ILC, half of them non-officials. In 1862 three Indians came in — the Raja of Banaras, the Maharaja of Patiala & Dinkar Rao of Gwalior. All elites, whose loyalty in 1857 was being rewarded. Till ICA 1892 only 45 Indians were nominated — mainly Zamindars & moneylenders of the British Indian Association (BrIA, 1851), British businessmen & Princely rulers.

5. Why the gesture cost the British nothing (see 'Powers of the ILC'). No questions to the Executive, no resolutions, no budget discussion or vote. Discussion & bills needed the Viceroy's prior approval. He held absolute veto over all bills & ordinance power valid for 6 months. The math was rigged: VEC alone (GG + 5 + CIC = 7) matched or outnumbered the maximum 6 non-officials.
Closing verdict: ICA 1861 was a despotism controlled from home, written into law. The nominated Indians softened its edges; they never touched its power.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: To what extent did the Indian Councils Act of 1861 begin the reversal of legislative centralisation in British India?
body: Demand of the question: "To what extent" needs a measured verdict, not a yes or no. Anchor the answer to 1861 & to the 1833 peak of centralisation that the Act began to undo. Weigh what was restored to the provinces against what the Viceroy kept for himself. Do not call this federalism.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Indian Councils Act of 1861 began the reversal of legislative centralisation. Bombay & Madras got their law-making powers back. The Viceroy kept every lever.
Body guidance — 4 themes:
1. What was being reversed (see 'At the Province Level'). Centralisation began in 1773 & peaked in 1833, when the legislative powers of Bombay & Madras were taken away & concentrated at the centre.

2. The real restoration (see 'At the Province Level'). ICA 1861 restored the legislative powers of Bombay & Madras. PLCs & GECs were created, & new PLCs were proposed for Bengal, Punjab & the North-Western Provinces (NWP). Each PLC = Governor (or Lt Governor) + Executive Council members + additional members nominated for law-making. New PLCs came up in Bengal 1862, NWP 1886, Punjab 1897 — the delays came from raw memories of 1857 & from frontier caution in Punjab.

3. What the Viceroy kept (see 'True Federalism — Just a Small Beginning'). A Governor's nomination of non-officials to his PLC was not valid without the Viceroy's sanction (ended by ICA 1892). The Viceroy framed the rules for the ILC, PLCs, VEC & GECs (ended only by GOI 1935). Certain bills needed his approval before introduction. He could create new provinces & appoint Lieutenant-Governors.

4. One country, one budget (see 'True Federalism — Just a Small Beginning'). There was no separate provincial budget — only one budget for British India as a whole, ended by GOI 1919. So provinces got councils without money power (see 'ICA 1861 Summary': not federal, decentralisation from the 1833 peak, Centre made the budget).
Closing verdict: The reversal of legislative centralisation was real but shallow. 1861 gave provinces councils, not power; that arrived with Provincial Autonomy under GOI 1935.
revise: True Federalism — Just a Small Beginning

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: Assertion [A] The basic weakness of the early nationalist movement lay in its narrow social base. Reason [R] If fought for the narrow interests of the social groups which joined it.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanaiton of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

explanation: (C) ✓ — A is true: the record calls uneven representation and the total exclusion of non-elites "the most serious structural weakness of the early INC". R is false: although its MEMBERS were elites, the movement's demands went well beyond elite interests — decrease of Land Revenue, end of the Salt Tax, repeal of the Arms Act 1878, trial by jury. A true + R false = (c).
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Fails twice over: R is false — the demand list in (land-revenue cuts, salt-tax abolition, Arms Act repeal) served the common people, not merely the groups that joined — so R can neither be true nor "explain" A.

(B) ✗ — Also requires R to be TRUE — but the record demand list contradicts R: a movement fighting for lower land revenue and an end to the salt tax was not fighting only for "the narrow interests of the social groups which joined it."
(D) ✗ — Inverts the truth values: A is exactly what — a narrow, elite, Presidency-dominated social base — while R is the false statement.

questions.label: PYQ_M.1
questions.stem: Mains — Moderates: Failure to Carry Conviction (See Chapter 'Weaknesses of the Moderates and the INC' — Negatives of Moderate Methods)
body: "Why did the 'Moderates' fail to carry conviction with the nation about their proclaimed ideology and political goals by the end of the nineteenth century?"

Demand of the question: Explain why the 'Moderates' failed to carry conviction with the nation about their proclaimed ideology and political goals by the end of the nineteenth century. The question accepts the failure as given — supply reasons, do not argue whether they failed. The phrase "with the nation" fixes the test: judge them by reach beyond the Western-educated middle class. Produce causes drawn from their social base, their methods and their results.

Suggested intro (~25 words): By the end of the nineteenth century the Moderates could not carry conviction with the nation — their proclaimed ideology and political goals never travelled beyond an English-educated elite.
Themes to bring out:
1.  Limited political mobilisation — Moderates confined activity to educated middle class and professional elite; never reached peasants, workers, women.
2.  Constitutional methods alone — petitions, memorials, prayers; British indifference exposed by 1892 (ICA1892's indirect-election fraud).
3.  Narrow social base — anglicised vocabulary, English-medium meetings; alienated rural India.
4.  Ideological vacuum — refused to demand independence; "Home Rule within the Empire" rang hollow after Bengal Famine 1900 & Partition 1905.
5.  Failure of results — three decades of agitation produced ICA 1892 (a sham), Lord Curzon's Partition (1905), and the cultural humiliation of being called "microscopic minority" by Dufferin.
Closing line: by the late 1890s the next generation (Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai) had concluded Moderate constitutionalism could not deliver — Extremism + Swadeshi were the answer.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Which two Western philosophical traditions formed the intellectual foundation of the Moderates in the INC?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Per, the Moderates were shaped by Utilitarianism (greatest good for the greatest number through law and good governance) and Liberalism (individual rights, rule of law, constitutional governance). Together these underwrote their faith in gradual constitutional reform.

Why others wrong: (a) Romanticism/Nationalism — not the intellectual foundation at issue; (b) Socialism/Marxism — never embraced; Moderates supported Capitalism and Industrialisation on British lines; (d) Conservatism/Mercantilism — opposite of the liberal-utilitarian framework they actually held.
Memory hook: Two L-shaped pillars hold up the Moderate roof — Liberalism left, utiLitarianism right.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Who, as the first President of the INC, declared that the Congress was "loyal to the British and well-wishers of the British"?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Per, the first President of the INC, W.C. Bonnerjee, captured the Moderate stance by declaring the INC was "loyal to the British & well-wishers of the British."

Why others wrong: (a) Naoroji — Drain of Wealth theorist, not the source of this declaration; (b) Banerjea — coined "Un-British Rule," a related but distinct phrase; (d) Gokhale — defended the Moderates in 1913 but did not author this opening declaration.
Memory hook: Bonnerjee opened the bonhomie — "loyal & well-wishers" was his line.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Surendranath Banerjea's famous phrase "Un-British Rule" was meant to describe:

options.text: Rule by Indians that copied British institutions
British rule unsupported by any Indian collaborators
The gap between Britain's stated liberal values and its actual conduct in India
The administration of Princely States outside direct British control

explanation: (c) ✓ — Per, "Un-British Rule" meant the gap between Britain's own stated liberal values and its actual conduct in India; Moderates wanted that gap removed, not British rule itself.

Why others wrong: (a) Indian rule copying British institutions — not the meaning; (b) Rule without Indian collaborators — chapter does not define the phrase this way; (d) Princely States — outside the scope of the phrase, which targeted British conduct in British India.
Memory hook: "Un-British" = Britain not living up to Britain's own brochure.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Moderates' goal:
items: 1. Their ultimate vision was full independence from Britain.
2. They sought Self-Government on the model of Canada or Australia.
3. They believed the Indian masses were not yet ready for full self-rule.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Per and, the Moderates' ultimate vision was Self-Government like Canada or Australia (dominion status), not independence; and they held that Indians, lacking widespread Western education, were not yet ready for full self-rule. Statement 1 is therefore wrong.
Why others wrong: (a) includes wrong Statement 1; (c) includes wrong Statement 1 and omits correct Statement 2; (d) includes wrong Statement 1.
Memory hook: Canada-Australia dream, not flag-independence scream.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: With reference to the Moderates' demand for Indianisation of services, consider the following statements:
items: 1. They demanded that the Civil Services examination be held simultaneously in India and Britain.
2. They demanded that the upper age limit for the examination be raised to
3. They demanded immediate appointment of Indians to officer rank in the military.
questions.stemTail: 23 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (d) ✓ — Per.4 lists all three: simultaneous Civil Services exam in India and Britain, raising the age limit to 23, and the demand for Indians at officer rank in the military (which was rejected as the British could not imagine taking orders from Indians).
Why others wrong: (a), (b), (c) each omit at least one of the three demands explicitly listed under Indianisation in.
Memory hook: Exam-here, age-23, officers-too — Moderates asked, British said no.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Which of the following demands by the Moderates was framed as a "Right to Bear Arms for self-defence" rather than as a call to violence?

options.text: End to indentured labour in Assam tea plantations

explanation: (b) ✓ — Per.8, the Moderates demanded repeal of the Arms Act 1878 (which had disarmed ordinary Indians) and framed it as a Right to Bear Arms for self-defence, not as a call to violence.

Why others wrong: (a) Trial by Jury — concerned the right to be judged by peers, unrelated to bearing arms; (c) Volunteer Army — demand to open recruitment beyond "Martial Races", not a self-defence framing; (d) Assam indentured labour — labour-exploitation demand, no arms element.
Memory hook: Arms Act 1878 repealed — for self-defence, not war-call.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Why did the Moderates demand the abolition of the India Council?

options.text: Because it was dominated by Indian Princes who opposed reform
Because the Council was draining Indian revenue to Britain
Because lobbying one Secretary of State was easier than lobbying fifteen Council members
Because the Council blocked the Indianisation of the Civil Services

explanation: (c) ✓ — Per.1, the Moderates wanted abolition of the 15-member India Council sitting in London around the Secretary of State because lobbying one Secretary of State was easier than lobbying fifteen members of a Council.

Why others wrong: (a) Indian Princes — Council was a British advisory body, not princely-dominated; (b) Drain of revenue — this was not the abolition rationale; (d) Blocking Indianisation — not cited; the rationale was decision-making efficiency.
Memory hook: Lobby one, not lobby fifteen.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the social composition of the INC in the period 1892-1905:
items: 1. Landlords made up about 40% of members.
2. Muslims made up about 6.5% of members.
3. Brahmins alone constituted roughly 40% of Hindu membership.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — The landlord share was about 20%; the 40% block belonged to the lawyers, who were the single largest professional group in the early INC, with traders at roughly 15%. Statements 2 and 3 stand — Muslims accounted for only about 6.5% of members, and within the Hindu 90% majority the Brahmins alone made up roughly 40%.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — endorses the 40% landlord figure. Landlords were around 20% of the membership; 40% was the lawyers' share, which is why the early INC behaved like a bar association rather than a landlords' lobby. It also sets aside the Brahmin concentration inside the Hindu majority. (c) 1 and 3 only — repeats the same landlord-for-lawyer swap and additionally rejects the 6.5% Muslim figure, which is the sharpest single measure of how narrow the early INC's communal base had become after the 1890s. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — needs landlords to have been 40% of the membership. The occupational break-up ran roughly 20% landlords, 40% lawyers and 15% traders, so statement 1 fails even though 2 and 3 are exact.
Memory hook: Lawyers 40, landlords 20 — briefs outnumbered estates; and inside the ledger, Hindus 90, Muslims 6.5, Brahmins 40 of the Hindu share.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Who became the first Muslim President of the INC, at the Madras session of 1887?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Per, Bombay's Badruddin Tyabji became the first Muslim President of the INC at the Madras session of 1887, and was cited as a notable exception to otherwise low Muslim participation.

Why others wrong: (b) Syed Ahmed Khan — opposed the INC; (c) Aga Khan — associated with the 1906 Muslim deputation, not early INC presidency; (d) Jinnah — entered politics much later and was not president in 1887.
Memory hook: Tyabji of Bombay, Madras chair 1887 — the early Muslim exception.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Why did the Moderates oppose the Factories Acts and the Indian Mines Act 1901?

options.text: Because the Acts did not extend to Indian-owned factories
Because the Lancashire Lobby pushed the Acts to raise Indian production costs and weaken Indian textiles
Because the Acts mandated trade union recognition
Because the Acts increased the working age above what Indian families could afford

explanation: (b) ✓ — Per, the Moderates argued that British textile manufacturers in Lancashire were lobbying for factory regulations in India so that stricter rules would raise Indian production costs and reduce the competitiveness of Indian textiles, keeping India a supplier of raw materials rather than a manufacturing economy.

Why others wrong: (a) Coverage of Indian-owned factories — not the stated reason; (c) Trade union recognition — the Acts did not turn on this; (d) Working age vs household affordability — this was not the Moderate rationale.
Memory hook: Lancashire's lobby, not labour's welfare — that was the British game.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following pairs of Factory/Mines legislation and Viceroy in office:
items: 1. Factories Act 1881 — Ripon80-84
2. Factories Act 1891 — Ripon80-84
3. Indian Mines Act 1901 — Curzon99-05
questions.stemTail: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
explanation: (c) ✓ — The 1891 Factories Act — the one that pulled in factories of 50 or more workers, lifted the minimum working age from 7 to 9 and capped women's hours at 11 — came under Lansdowne, not Ripon, whose viceroyalty had closed in 1884. Ripon's own factory law is the 1881 Act of pair 1, and the Indian Mines Act of 1901, the first real regulation of mining, falls squarely in Curzon's term, so pairs 1 and 3 are correctly matched.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — lets Ripon keep both factory laws, which would need him in office in 1891, seven years after he left; it also discards the Mines Act 1901–Curzon pairing, which is sound. (b) 2 and 3 only — holds on to the mis-paired 1891 Act while rejecting the one factory law that genuinely is Ripon's, the Act of 1881 covering factories with 100 or more workers. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — would make Ripon responsible for the 1881 and the 1891 Acts alike; the 1891 measure was Lansdowne's, so the set cannot be wholly correct.
Memory hook: 81 Ripon, 91 Lansdowne, 1901 Curzon — one law a decade, a different Viceroy each time; Ripon owns only the first.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Why did the Moderates support extending the Permanent Settlement of 1793 outside Bengal?

options.text: To raise State revenue for famine relief
To protect Zamindars from arbitrary increases in Land Revenue
To convert ryotwari peasants into landlords
To centralise revenue collection in the hands of the Government of India

explanation: (b) ✓ — Per.1, the Moderates wanted PS1793 extended outside Bengal because it prevented the State from raising Land Revenue and thus protected Zamindars (the class many INC members came from) from higher taxation.

Why others wrong: (a) Famine relief — opposite intent; PS1793 capped revenue, not raised it; (c) Ryotwari to landlord conversion — not the stated logic; (d) Centralising revenue — PS1793 fixed revenue, the opposite of arbitrary central control.
Memory hook: Fix the rent, freeze the Zamindar's fear.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Position / Stance)
A. "Strategy of Mendicancy" label
B. "Un-British Rule" coinage
C. Defended Moderates in 1913, noting British would not have allowed INC to form otherwise
D. First Muslim President of the INC

List II (Person)
items: 1. Surendranath Banerjea
2. Critics and later the Extremists
3. Badruddin Tyabji
4. Gopal Krishna Gokhale
matchTable: C. Defended Moderates in 1913, noting British would not have allowed INC to form otherwise
D. First Muslim President of the INC

Why others wrong: (b) swaps A and B and misassigns C, D; (c) misassigns B and C; (d) misassigns A.
