questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Demand)
A. Repeal of the Arms Act 1878
B. End exploitation of Indentured Labourers
C. Open Army recruitment beyond "Martial Races"
D. End the Salt Tax

List II (Description)

2. Right to Bear Arms for self-defence

B. End exploitation of Indentured Labourers

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Consider the following statements explaining why the Moderates' methods failed to produce results:
items: 1. They were a narrow demographic, roughly 90% Hindu and drawn overwhelmingly from lawyer and landlord classes.
2. They distrusted the masses and refused to mobilise them, fearing popular agitation would spiral out of control.
3. The British government had legally banned petitions from political associations.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Per, the two structural problems that reinforced each other were a narrow demographic (90% Hindu, lawyer/landlord-dominated) and a fundamental distrust of the masses (a refusal to mobilise them for fear of uncontrolled agitation). Statement 3 is fabricated; petitions were the Moderates' chosen method, not a banned one.
Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) each include the fabricated Statement 3; (b) and (c) also drop a correct statement.
Memory hook: Narrow base + masses kept out = petitions ignored.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The Moderates did not want the removal of British rule; they wanted the removal of 'Un-British Rule'." Examine how this belief shaped the goals & the methods of the early Indian National Congress.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine how this belief shaped" asks you to run one idea through two outputs — the goals & the methods. The framing phrase is Surendranath Banerjea's "Un-British Rule": the gap between Britain's stated liberal values & its actual conduct in India. The anchor is the INC's first two decades from 1885. Do not write a list of demands; show cause & effect.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Moderates did not want the removal of British rule. Banerjea asked only for the removal of 'Un-British Rule'. This belief shaped both the goals & the methods of the early INC.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. The intellectual root (see 'Moderates' Ideology'). Utilitarianism & Liberalism gave them Constitutionalism — Responsible Government, protection of citizens' rights, Rule of Law. From this came Constitutional Methods: use only the institutions & mechanisms the State itself provides.

2. The premise of loyalty (see 'Did the Moderates oppose British Rule?'). They knew British rule was exploitative. But they believed in the Providence of British Rule — that if sufficiently pressurised, the British could be made to modernise India. W.C. Bonnerjee, the first INC President, declared the INC "loyal to the British & well-wishers of the British."

3. The goal that followed (see 'Goals & Methods'). Not independence — Limited Self-Government within British rule, & in the long run Self-Government like Canada or Australia. They argued the masses, without widespread Western education, were not yet ready for full self-rule.

4. The methods that followed (see 'Goals & Methods'). Prayers & petitions, resolutions at annual sessions, use of the press, a rich culture of debates. No mass action, no street agitation — Gradualism. Critics & later the Extremists called it the "Strategy of Mendicancy."

5. The demands that followed (see 'Moderates' Demands'). Every demand repaired the machinery of the Raj instead of removing it — abolish the India Council, expand the ILC & PLCs, Indianise the services, cut Military Expenditure, repeal the Arms Act 1878. Outcome: no demands were met.
Closing verdict: Seeking the removal of 'Un-British Rule' & not the removal of British rule gave the Moderates a strong moral case, but no leverage — & so no results.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Analyse the demands raised by the Moderates on governance, the public services & the economy, & explain why two decades of such demands produced no result.
body: Demand of the question: "Analyse ... & explain why" is a two-part directive. First map the demands under the three heads named in the question — governance, the public services & the economy. Then supply causes for the nil outcome. The anchor is the INC's first two decades from 1885. Marks are lost if the second half is left as an afterthought.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Moderates raised careful demands on governance, the public services & the economy. Two decades of such demands produced no result — not one was conceded.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. Governance & the legislature (see 'On the question of Governance & Legislative Reform'). Abolish the India Council — the 15-member advisory body around the Secretary of State in London. Expand the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) & Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) with at least 50% indirectly elected members. Give both real legislative authority, not advisory roles.

2. The public services (see 'On the question of Governance & Legislative Reform'). Indianisation of the Civil & Military Services — hold the Civil Services examination simultaneously in India & Britain & raise the age limit to 23. Officer rank for Indians was refused: the British could not imagine taking orders from Indians. Indian officer appointments began only after the 1st Round Table Conference of 1931, with IMA Dehradun in 1932.

3. The economic demands (see 'On the question of Economics'). Decrease & share Military Expenditure — the Indian Army was used for imperial adventures like the Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901). A Volunteer Army against the "Martial Races" doctrine; Trial by Jury; repeal of the Arms Act 1878; lower Land Revenue & an end to the Salt Tax; extension of PS1793 outside Bengal; an end to indentured labour exploitation in the Assam Tea Plantations.
4. Why nothing moved — the method (see 'Goals & Methods'). Prayers, petitions & resolutions created little pressure on the British. The label "Strategy of Mendicancy" captured that reality.

5. Why nothing moved — the base (see 'Weaknesses of the Moderates and the INC'). The colonial government could safely ignore petitions from a few hundred educated professionals with no mass base behind them.

Closing verdict: The demands on governance, the public services & the economy were reasonable & well-argued. Two decades of such demands produced no result because argument without pressure moves no colonial state.

questions.label: FYQ_M.3
questions.stem: "The early Congress neither represented the people nor threatened to unleash them." Critically examine this assessment of the Indian National Congress in its first two decades.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" wants both sides — establish the charge with evidence, then weigh the defence. The proposition has two distinct halves: representation is about who was inside the INC; unleashing is about whom it refused to mobilise. The anchor runs from the Bombay session of 1885 through the INC's first two decades.

Suggested intro (~25 words): In its first two decades the early Congress neither represented the people nor threatened to unleash them. Its composition explains the first half of the charge, its fear of the masses the second.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. The representation charge — the numbers (see 'Not a truly representative organization'). Of the 72 delegates at the first session (Bombay, 1885), 38 came from the Bombay Presidency & 21 from Madras, but only 3 from the whole Bengal-Bihar-Orissa-Assam region & 10 from Punjab & the North-Western Provinces & Oudh. Note the Bengal reason: the 2nd Indian National Conference of the Indian Association (1876) had just been held in Calcutta, keeping leaders like SNB away.

2. The representation charge — social composition (see 'Not a truly representative organization'). Western-educated middle-class professionals — lawyers, doctors, journalists, teachers — plus merchants, bankers & landowners; upper castes; concentrated in the three Presidencies. In 1892-1909 membership was roughly 20% landlords, 40% lawyers & 15% traders (see 'Social Background affected Moderate Politics').

3. The communal gap (see 'Low Muslim participation'). In 1892-1909 Hindus were 90% of members & Muslims only about 6.5%; Brahmins alone were roughly 40% of the Hindu membership. Badruddin Tyabji, first Muslim President at the Madras session of 1887, was the exception. The 1886 decision to keep social questions off the agenda until 1907 protected the coalition, but produced INC silence during the cow-killing riots of 1893.

4. The refusal to unleash (see 'Not full-time politicians'). Most leaders were part-time politicians with lucrative legal practices, & the INC worked like a three-day annual conference rather than a political party. They also distrusted the masses & refused to mobilise them, fearing that popular agitation would turn violent & uncontrolled.

5. The defence (see 'Goals & Methods'). Gokhale noted in 1913 that had the Moderates not used these methods, the British would not have allowed the INC to function. The culture of mass politics in direct confrontation with the colonial government had not yet developed anywhere in India.
Closing verdict: The charge largely holds. A Congress that neither represented the people nor threatened to unleash them could be ignored — which is exactly what the colonial state did.

questions.label: FYQ_M.4
questions.stem: The Moderates opposed the Factories Act 1881, the Factories Act 1891 & the Indian Mines Act 1901. Evaluate the reasoning behind this opposition & its consequences for Indian labour.
body: Demand of the question: "Evaluate" asks for a judgement, not a description. Two things must be weighed — the reasoning behind the opposition & its consequences for Indian labour. The three named Acts fix the span, Ripon80-84 to Curzon99-05. Do not reduce the opposition to class selfishness alone; there was a second, economic-nationalist motive.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Moderates opposed the Factories Act 1881, the Factories Act 1891 & the Indian Mines Act 1901. The reasoning was economic nationalism; the consequences for Indian labour were harsh.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. What the three Acts did (see 'Social Background affected Moderate Politics'). Factories Act 1881 (Ripon80-84): factories with 100 or more workers, no employment of children under 7, children aged 7-12 capped at 9 hours a day, fencing of hazardous machinery. Factories Act 1891 (Lansdowne88-94): cover extended to factories with 50 or more workers, minimum working age raised from 7 to 9, definition of a child raised from 12 to 14, women capped at 11 hours with a 1.5-hour rest interval. Indian Mines Act 1901 (Curzon99-05): first major regulation of mining, a minimum age for child labour & better conditions for women & children underground.

2. The Lancashire Lobby argument (see 'Social Background affected Moderate Politics'). British textile manufacturers in Lancashire lobbied heavily for factory regulation in India so that Indian production costs would rise & Indian textiles would lose competitiveness against British goods. The British were not passing these laws out of sympathy for Indian workers.

3. The infant-industry case (see 'Social Background affected Moderate Politics'). The Moderates held that only Indian Capitalism could remove poverty & industrialise India, & that heavy regulation imposed prematurely would crush indigenous industrialisation — leaving India a permanent supplier of raw materials & a market for British manufactures.

4. The other side of the ledger — class interest (see 'Social Background affected Moderate Politics'). They took no anti-Zamindar stand; they wanted PS1793 extended outside Bengal, which barred the State from raising Land Revenue & favoured big landlords; they opposed the Punjab Land Alienation Bill of 1900 meant to stop indebted peasants losing land to moneylenders. They did back the Assam Tea Garden workers — but against European planters.

5. The consequence for labour (see 'Social Background affected Moderate Politics'). Indian workers, including children, continued to labour under harsh conditions for longer than desired. This social background prevented the Moderates from becoming popular among the masses.

Closing verdict: The reasoning behind this opposition was real anti-colonial economics, not mere selfishness. But the consequences for Indian labour were paid by workers & children in factories & mines.
revise: Weaknesses of the Moderates and the INC

questions.label: FYQ_M.5
questions.stem: "The methods of the Moderates created little pressure on the British, yet they built the culture & institutions of modern politics in India." How far do you agree?
body: Demand of the question: "How far do you agree" asks for a graded verdict, not a yes or a no. Both halves of the proposition are partly true, so test each separately. Keep the focus on methods — do not drift into ideology or the list of demands.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The methods of the Moderates created little pressure on the British — no demand was conceded. Yet they built the culture & institutions of modern politics in India.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. What the methods were (see 'Goals & Methods'). Sending prayers & petitions, passing resolutions at annual sessions, using the press to express opinion, building a rich culture of debates. No mass action, no agitation on the streets — Gradualism.

2. The pressure they failed to create (see 'Moderates' Demands'). Outcome: no demands were met. Two decades of petitions & prayers produced, in practice, zero. Critics & the Extremists called it the "Strategy of Mendicancy," i.e. begging.

3. Gokhale's defence (see 'Goals & Methods'). Gokhale noted in 1913 that had the Moderates not followed these methods, the British would not have allowed the INC to function. A movement that begins with petition & prayer is building the institutions & culture of modern politics for a country that had only just begun a modern national movement.

4. The structural limit (see 'Weaknesses of the Moderates and the INC'). The Moderates neither represented the masses nor were willing to mobilise them, fearing violent & uncontrolled agitation. So the colonial government could ignore them without cost.
Closing verdict: Agree in part. The methods created little pressure on the British, but the debates, press & annual sessions built the institutions of modern politics later leaders inherited.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: Who among the following leaders did not believe in the drain theory of Dadabhai Naoroji?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Sir Syed Ahmed Khan stood apart: he was loyal to the British and opposed the INC's politics of self-rule — he did not subscribe to the Drain Theory, unlike the Moderate economists who built it. names the theory's architects: R.C. Dutt, Dadabhai Naoroji, and M.G. Ranade.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Tilak stood inside the nationalist camp that embraced the economic critique of British rule; the question seeks the one leader OUTSIDE it — Sir Syed, who opposed the INC and its politics altogether.
(B) ✗ — R.C. Dutt is one of the theory's ARCHITECTS — His work gave the Drain Theory its historical depth and empirical backbone.
(C) ✗ — M.G. Ranade likewise built the theory — the record lists him among its architects and calls him "the father of Indian economics."
(Note: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan did not believe in the Drain Theory. He was loyal to British and was opposed to Congress' idea of self rule and end of British empire.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: M.C Setalvad, B.N. Rao and Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer were distinguished members of the
explanation: (B) ✓ — M.C. Setalvad, B.N. Rau, and Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer were distinguished members of the All India National Liberal Federation, the post-1918 Moderate splinter party from the INC (founded after the Surat Split aftermath; many Moderates left INC to form the Federation alongside Surendranath Banerjea and Tej Bahadur Sapru). All three were noted constitutional lawyers; B.N. Rau later drafted the initial Indian Constitution; Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer was a Constituent Assembly member.

◆ Legacy-PYQ note. While legacy PYQ compilations blindly accept (d) Servants of India Society as the answer to the 1997 question, it is a historically flawed key (likely due to the examiner confusing B.N. Rau with his brother, B. Shiva Rao, who was an actual member). These men were wealthy jurists and civil servants, not missionaries bound by the Society's strict vow of poverty. They were, however, closely aligned with the constitutional and moderate ideology of the All India National Liberal Federation, making it the most historically logical choice.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — The Swaraj Party (1923) was the Council-entry party of C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru — a post-Non-Cooperation formation, not the Moderates' Liberal Federation where these three constitutional lawyers belonged.

(D) ✗ — The Servants of India Society (1905) was Gokhale's order of full-time social workers — not the political home of Setalvad, Rau, and Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer, whom the record places in the All India National Liberal Federation (1918).
(C) ✗ — The Madras Labour Union (1918) was a workers' trade union — no connection to these three jurists of the Liberal Federation.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: A graduate at 18, professor and associate editor of the Sudharak at 20, Secretary of the Sarvajanik Sabha and of the provincial conference at 25, Secretary of the National Congress at 29, leading witness before an important Royal Commission at 31, Provincial legislator at 34, Imperial legislator at 36, President of the Indian National Congress at 39, ......a patriot whom Mahatma Gandhi himself regarded as his master. This is how a biographer describes
explanation: (C) ✓ — The biography fits Gopal Krishna Gokhale point by point: associate editor of the Sudharak, Secretary of the Sarvajanik Sabha, then Secretary of the INC — the career ladder of Ranade's protégé; Gandhi himself regarded Gokhale as his political master.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Malaviya belonged to the Allahabad school of nationalism — not to the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha-Sudharak circle this biography describes.

(B) ✗ — Ranade is the MENTOR in this story, not the subject: the Sudharak-Sarvajanik Sabha apprenticeship describes his protégé Gokhale; Ranade himself, a sitting judge, stayed out of front-line Congress office.
(D) ✗ — Tilak's path ran through Kesari and confrontational mass politics — not through the reformist Sudharak or Royal Commission testimony.
(Note: Gopal Krishna Gokhale was born in Kohlapur (Maharashtra) in 1866. Gandhiji himself regarded Gokhale as his Political Master in India.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: There was no independent development of industries in India during British rule because of the

options.text: preference of the rich to invest in land

explanation: (A) ✓ — The record account of why no independent industry grew: there was no industrialisation of India — no Indian factories came up to replace the handicrafts — British rule built no capital-goods (heavy-industry) base, so independent industrial development was impossible.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Capital scarcity is not the record explanation — the drain shipped India's own surplus OUT (Home Charges, dividends, interest); what India lacked was the factory base itself.
(C) ✗ — Resources were never the obstacle — India was Britain's raw-material source, exporting cotton, indigo, jute, and opium in bulk; a resource-scarce country could not have played that role.

(D) ✗ — The drift back to land was the CONSEQUENCE of having no factories to absorb displaced artisans (the record "disguised unemployment in agriculture"), not the cause of missing industrial development.
(Note: The absence of heavy industries during British period in India was due to the negligence and high-handedness of British regime.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: Who among the following used the phrase 'Un-british' to criticise the English colonial control of India?
explanation: (C) ✓ — The phrase is Dadabhai Naoroji's: his book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) was "the most systematic presentation" of the Drain Theory — exploitation indicted as conduct unworthy of Britain's own professed principles.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Anandamohan Bose was a Bengal Moderate organiser, not the economist of the drain; the 'Un-British' coinage is fixed in the title of Naoroji's 1901 book.
(B) ✗ — Badruddin Tyabji's place in the era is the INC presidency (first Muslim President, Madras 1887); the 'Un-British' indictment belongs to Naoroji's economic critique.
(D) ✗ — Pherozeshah Mehta was an INC founder-figure of the Bombay school, not the author of the drain critique — the phrase comes from Naoroji's Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.

(Note: Dadabhai Naoroji (1865-1917) in his book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" described an economic critique of British polices by alleging them of home charges. He was the first Indian to be elected to the British House of Commons.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: Who among the following rejected the title of 'Knighthood' and refused to accept a position in the Council of the Secretary of State for India?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Gokhale declined both the Knighthood and a seat on the Council of the Secretary of State — consistent with the ethic of self-denying public service he institutionalised in the Servants of India Society (1905).
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Motilal Nehru's renunciations belong to a LATER era — he gave up his legal practice during Non-Cooperation (1920–22); the Knighthood-and-Council refusal is Gokhale's story.
(B) ✗ — Ranade, as a sitting judge, HELD government office his whole career — the opposite of refusing a position; the refusal belongs to his protégé Gokhale.
(D) ✗ — Tilak was never offered such honours — the Raj prosecuted and jailed him rather than courted him; only a Moderate the British wished to co-opt could refuse a Knighthood, and that was Gokhale.

(Note: In 1905, Gopal Krishna Gokhale had established the Servants of India Society. He had also rejected the title of 'Knighthood' and refused to accept a position in the Council of the Secretary of State for India.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.stem: With reference to the period of colonial rule in India, 'Home Charges' formed an important part of drain of wealth from India. Which of the following funds constituted 'Home Charges'?
items: 1. Funds used to support the Indian office in London.
2. Funds used to pay salaries and pensions of British personnel engaged in India.
3. Funds used for waging wars outside India by the British.
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below
explanation: (D) ✓ — All three sat in the drain's London ledger: Home Charges covered goods and services supposedly provided to India by Britain or the Secretary of State — the India Office establishment (statement 1); salaries, pensions, and training costs of British officials and soldiers (statement 2); and India was billed even for Britain's campaigns beyond India — its army fought imperial wars like the Boxer Rebellion (1899–1901) at Indian expense (statement 3).
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "Only 1" undercounts severely: officials' salaries, pensions and training costs (statement 2) head the record own Home-Charges list.
(B) ✗ — "1 and 2" stops short: India was also charged for wars waged outside India — the Boxer Rebellion deployment is the record own example of Indian money spent on Britain's external campaigns.
(C) ✗ — "2 and 3" drops statement 1 — but the India Office in London was the most direct of the charges India paid "for goods and services supposedly provided" by Britain.
(Note: All wars waged in defence of India was put under Home Charges. In fact, the suppression of the 1857 Revolt itself was put under the 'Home Charges'.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.stem: Consider the following statements The most effective contribution made by Dadabhai Naoroji to the cause of Indian freedom Movement was that he
items: 1. exposed the economic exploitation of India by the British.
2. interpreted the ancient Indian texts and restored the self-confidence of Indians.
3. stressed the need for eradication of all the social evils before anything else.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statement 1 is Naoroji's exact contribution: the Drain Theory exposed how Britain used political power to extract India's wealth. Statements 2 and 3 describe other streams: textual revivalism was not his work, and "social evils first" inverts his record — Naoroji's 1886 rule kept social questions OFF the INC agenda.
Wrong options:

(B) ✗ — Contains neither of Naoroji's actual contributions: he was the economist of the drain, not a textual revivalist (statement 2), and his 1886 rule deliberately excluded social questions from the Congress platform (statement 3).
(C) ✗ — Statement 3 directly contradicts Naoroji's record: he laid down the informal rule that the INC would take up only political questions, not social or class questions.
(D) ✗ — Overcounts: only statement 1 survives — statements 2 (revivalism) and 3 (social-evils-first) belong to other streams of the movement, not to the economist of the drain. +.

(Note: Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian to show that India was being drained of its wealth under the British rule and thus was fast succumbing to poverty. In 1876, he published a paper titled 'Poverty of India'.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.10
questions.stem: Economic result of British rule in 19th century:
explanation: (C) ✓ — Indian agriculture was reoriented away from food crops and towards cash crops and raw materials meant for export to British factories — the commercialisation of agriculture, the record named economic result of the 19th century.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Reversed: handicraft exports COLLAPSED — artisans "lost both domestic and export markets" as India turned from net exporter of finished goods into a raw-material supplier.
(B) ✗ — The record is categorical: "no Indian factories came up to replace the handicrafts" — industrial growth was precisely what 19th-century British rule denied India.
(D) ✗ — Displaced artisans were forced BACK onto agriculture — rural disguised unemployment, not urban growth, was the century's drift.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: At the very first INC session in 1885 at Bombay, the Congress declared which of the following as its first goal?
explanation: (B) ✓ — at the first INC session in 1885 in Bombay, the Congress declared its goal as "building national unity," because India in 1885 had no pre-existing sense of a single political community.

Why others wrong: (a) Swaraj as a goal came much later (1906 Calcutta), not in 1885; (c) Separate electorates were a colonial concession, not an INC goal — the INC's own 1889 Minority Clause demanded reserved seats, not separate electorates; (d) Social-reform questions like untouchability were consciously kept off the INC agenda under the 1886 Naoroji rule.
Memory hook: 1885 Bombay first call — not Swaraj, just "unity above all."

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: The informal INC rule that the Congress would take up only political questions and not social or class questions was laid down in 1886 by:
explanation: (B) ✓ — The record states that in 1886, Dadabhai Naoroji laid down what became an informal INC rule — that the Congress would take up only political questions, not social or class questions, because social issues could divide Indians against each other.

Why others wrong: (a) Banerjea was a leading Moderate but is not credited with this 1886 rule; (c) Bonnerjee presided over the 1885 founding session but did not author the political-only rule; (d) Mehta was a Bombay Moderate but the 1886 rule is attributed specifically to Naoroji.
Memory hook: 1886 Naoroji's filter — Indians vs British only, no in-house quarrels.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the early INC's effort at building Hindu–Muslim unity:
items: 1. The 1888 INC decision held that no resolution would be passed if the majority of Hindu or Muslim members disagreed.
2. The 1889 Minority Clause demanded that the British government reserve seats in the Imperial and Provincial Legislative Councils for religious minorities in proportion to their population.
3. The demand for minority representation in legislative councils was first formally raised by the Muslim League.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are taken verbatim from the record. Statement 3 is wrong because the 1889 Minority Clause was raised by the INC itself, not by the Muslim League.

Why others wrong: (b) Statement 3 is wrong — it was the INC, not the Muslim League, that first formally demanded minority representation; (c) Same reason — Statement 3 is wrong; (d) Statement 3 inverts the record actual point.
Memory hook: 1888 veto + 1889 reservation — Moderates, not Muslim League, opened the minority-seat door.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Why did the INC make it a structural rule that the President of each annual session would not be from the host region?

options.text: Because the British government required the President to be a non-resident of the host city
Because the host region's leaders were busy with logistical arrangements
Because a non-local President speaking to local concerns built inter-regional bonds and an all-India leadership
Because it gave the session the appearance of a national gathering for British observers

explanation: (C) ✓ — The record explains the logic in plain words: a Bengali leader presiding in Calcutta builds nothing new, but a Marathi leader presiding in Calcutta — speaking to Bengali concerns — builds an all-India leadership and creates inter-regional bonds that would not exist otherwise.

Why others wrong: (a) No such British requirement is on record; (b) Logistical convenience is not the reason given — the rule is explicitly about nation-building, not workload; (d) The purpose was internal nation-building, not appearance management for British observers.
Memory hook: Marathi in Calcutta, Bengali in Bombay — each session stitched another inter-regional bond.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Drain Theory and its key architects:
items: 1. Romesh Chandra Dutt argued that the 2% drain was surplus capital lost to India.
2. Dadabhai Naoroji's Poverty and Un-British Rule in India was published in
3. M.G. Ranade is often described as the father of Indian economics.
questions.stemTail: 1901 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — The surplus-capital reply belongs to Naoroji, not Dutt. When the British defended themselves by saying the drain was only about 2% of export value, it was Naoroji who answered that the figure was surplus capital, and that surplus invested at home would have compounded over decades into substantial growth. Dutt's distinct contribution was the two-volume economic history that gave the theory its data and historical depth, so Statement 1 hands one architect the signature argument of another. Statement 2 is right on the date — Poverty and Un-British Rule in India appeared in 1901 — and Statement 3 is right on the epithet, Ranade being the figure commonly called the father of Indian economics.

Why others wrong: (a) Accepts the surplus-capital argument as Dutt's and simultaneously denies Ranade the title of father of Indian economics; both readings are inverted, since that rejoinder to the '2% only' defence is Naoroji's and the Ranade description is accurate. (c) Endorses every statement, which requires Dutt to have authored the compounding-surplus reply. That reply is Naoroji's, so any combination containing Statement 1 fails. (d) Retains the misassigned argument while doubting 1901 as the publication year of Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, which is in fact the correct year for Naoroji's landmark text.
Memory hook: Dutt supplied the two volumes of data, Naoroji supplied the '2% was surplus capital' comeback, Ranade is the father of Indian economics — same trinity, three different jobs.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: The Drain Theory gained particular prominence after the bitter disappointment with which of the following measures?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The record states that the Drain Theory gained particular prominence after the bitter disappointment with the Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA1892), which failed to deliver any meaningful reform.

Why others wrong: (a) ICA 1861 pre-dates the INC itself and is not linked to the Drain Theory's rise; (c) GOI 1858 only transferred power from EIC to Crown — it was not the proximate trigger; (d) ICA 1909 came much later and is associated with separate electorates, not the rise of Drain Theory.
Memory hook: 1892 ICA flopped — Drain Theory took the stage.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the core argument of the Drain Theory in one sentence, as articulated in the Moderates' framework?

options.text: The use of free trade and the absence of protective tariffs to crush native industry
The substitution of barter trade by monetised exchange under colonial rule
The misuse of political power over the State of the Colony for the economic benefit of the Colonial Power
The redirection of colonial savings into European banking institutions

explanation: (C) ✓ — This is the record one-line statement of Drain Theory: The misuse of political power over the State of the Colony for the economic benefit of the Colonial Power.

Why others wrong: (a) Free trade is one mechanism (Absence of Protective Tariffs) — not the whole core argument; (b) Monetisation versus barter is not the record framing of the drain; (d) the record speaks of surplus extraction, not banking-channel routing as the central definition.
Memory hook: Political control to economic plunder — one sentence, the whole theory.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the impact of British industrial capitalism on India:
items: 1. India shifted from being a net exporter of finished goods to a net exporter of raw materials.
2. Indian agriculture was reoriented from food crops towards cash crops and raw materials for British factories.
3. Indian artisans who lost their trade were absorbed quickly into newly built Indian factories.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 reflect the record account of the commercialisation of agriculture and the inversion of India's trade structure. Statement 3 is the opposite of the truth — the record says explicitly that there was no industrialisation of India, no Indian factories came up to replace the handicrafts, and artisans were forced back onto agriculture.
Why others wrong: (b) Statement 3 inverts the record actual account of artisan displacement; (c) Same reason — Statement 3 is wrong; (d) Statement 3 is the opposite of what the record records.
Memory hook: Finished-goods exporter to raw-material exporter — and the artisan fell back to the field, not forward to the factory.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Which of the following infrastructural change, in the second half of the 19th century, cut the sea distance between India and Britain by about 4,500 miles and intensified the drain by making raw-material extraction and finished-goods import cheaper and faster?

options.text: Introduction of the steam locomotive in Indian railways
Modernisation of Indian ports under Dalhousie
Construction of the Suez Canal between 1859 and 1869
Opening of the Bombay–Aden submarine telegraph line

explanation: (C) ✓ — The construction of the Suez Canal between 1859 and 1869 cut the sea distance between India and Britain by 4,500 miles, making it cheaper and faster to extract raw materials from India and ship finished goods back.

Why others wrong: (a) Steam locomotives helped extraction internally but the 4,500-mile sea-distance cut specifically belongs to the Suez Canal; (b) Port modernisation is part of the broader transport revolution but not the specific 4,500-mile fact; (d) The telegraph is not cited for the 4,500-mile distance figure.
Memory hook: Suez 1859 to 1869 — 4,500 miles shaved off, drain accelerated.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the components of the Drain from India in the 19th century:
items: 1. No import duty was imposed on British goods entering India until World War I (1914–19), when protective tariffs were first applied.
2. Under the Council Bills mechanism, foreign importers paid in foreign exchange to a London office and used the resulting vouchers to obtain rupees from the Government of India for Indian goods.
3. Home Charges included salaries and pensions of British officials, dividends to EIC shareholders, and expenses of the Secretary of State for India.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — All three statements are drawn directly from the record account of the drain components — Absence of Protective Tariffs, Tax-Financed Trade via Council Bills, and Home Charges.
Why others wrong: (a) Omits Statement 3 on Home Charges, which is correct; (b) Omits Statement 1 on protective tariffs, which is correct; (c) Omits Statement 2 on Council Bills, which is correct.
Memory hook: Tariffs absent + Council Bills routed + Home Charges loaded — three pipes, one drain.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (Mechanism of the Drain)
items: 1. Council Bills (post-1833)
2. Home Charges
3. 5% Guaranteed Interest Scheme

4. Absence of Protective Tariffs
List II (Description)
A. Dividends, salaries, pensions and SoS expenses charged to India
B. Risk-free assured return paid by Indian taxpayers to British railway investors
C. Foreign importer's forex stayed in London while India paid out rupees from taxpayer money
D. British goods flooded Indian markets as no import duty was imposed until WWI
matchTable: A. Dividends, salaries, pensions and SoS expenses charged to India
B. Risk-free assured return paid by Indian taxpayers to British railway investors
C. Foreign importer's forex stayed in London while India paid out rupees from taxpayer money
D. British goods flooded Indian markets as no import duty was imposed until WWI
explanation: (A) ✓ — Council Bills routed forex to London while India paid rupees domestically (C); Home Charges covered British salaries, pensions, dividends, SoS expenses (A); the 5% guaranteed-interest scheme assured risk-free return to British railway companies, with losses borne by Indian taxpayers (B); the absence of protective tariffs let British goods flood India until WWI (D). and.
Why others wrong: (b) Swaps Council Bills with Home Charges; (c) Wrongly pairs Home Charges with the 5% scheme; (d) Mismatches every pair.
Memory hook: CB to London forex, HC to British salaries, 5% to railway shield, no tariff to import flood.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: With reference to the Strachey Commission (1880), which of the following is correct?

options.text: It was a Royal Commission appointed to enquire into Indian expenditure and recommend reduction of Home Charges
It was a commission appointed to review the working of the Indian Councils Act of 1861
It was a commission to investigate the tariff structure between Britain and India after the 1858 transfer of power
It was a Famine Commission appointed by the British government to recommend measures against recurring famines in India

explanation: (D) ✓ — The record lists the Strachey Commission (1880) among the famine commissions appointed in response to recurring famines, along with the Lyall Commission (1897) and the MacDonnell Commission (1900), noting that their recommendations were rarely implemented seriously.

Why others wrong: (a) Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure is a different body; the record ties Strachey 1880 to famines; (b) Strachey 1880 is not linked to ICA 1861 review; (c) the record does not link Strachey 1880 to tariff investigation.
Memory hook: Strachey 1880 — Famine Commission, not expenditure commission.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding British canal-building in 19th-century India:
items: 1. Canals were built mostly in non-Permanent-Settlement 1793 regions such as Punjab, western UP and coastal Madras.
2. By 1947, only about a quarter of the cultivated area was under public irrigation.
3. Water from British-built canals was supplied free of cost to peasants.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — The record says canals were built only in non-Permanent Settlement 1793 areas (Statement 1) and that by 1947 only 25% of cultivated area was under public irrigation (Statement 2). Statement 3 is the opposite, which states that canal water was not free and only rich farmers could afford it.
Why others wrong: (b) Statement 3 inverts the record "not free / only rich farmers" account; (c) Same reason; (d) Same reason.
Memory hook: Canals only outside PS-1793 zones, only 25% covered, never free — three strikes against the British claim.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (Personality)
items: 1. Dadabhai Naoroji
2. R.C. Dutt
3. M.G. Ranade

4. Gopal Krishna Gokhale
List II (Identifier from the Chapter)
A. Often called the father of Indian economics
B. Former ICS officer turned economic historian, author of The Economic History of India (1901 & 1903)
C. Author of Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901)
D. Rejected the title of Knighthood and refused a position in the Council of the Secretary of State for India
matchTable: A. Often called the father of Indian economics
B. Former ICS officer turned economic historian, author of The Economic History of India (1901 & 1903)
C. Author of Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901)
D. Rejected the title of Knighthood and refused a position in the Council of the Secretary of State for India
explanation: (D) ✓ — Naoroji authored Poverty and Un-British Rule in India 1901 (C); Dutt is the ICS-officer-turned-historian who wrote The Economic History of India in two volumes 1901 and 1903 (B); Ranade is called the father of Indian economics (A); Gokhale, per the Alert entry, rejected the Knighthood and refused the SoS Council position (D). and.
Why others wrong: (a) Misplaces Naoroji as the father of Indian economics; (b) Swaps Naoroji with Dutt and Ranade with Gokhale; (c) Swaps Dutt and Ranade.
Memory hook: Naoroji-book, Dutt-volumes, Ranade-economist, Gokhale-no-Sir — line them up in this order.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: The Moderates' counter-argument to the British claim that "the drain was only 2% of India's export value, which paid for real development" rested most centrally on which of the following propositions?

options.text: The 2% figure was statistically inflated and the actual drain was much smaller
The drained surplus, if invested in India, would have compounded over decades into substantial GDP growth
The 2% drain was offset by the gains from railway construction, making it economically neutral
The drain estimate of 2% ignored gold and bullion outflows from India to China

explanation: (B) ✓ — Dadabhai Naoroji's argument as the centrepiece of the rejoinder — even if 2% sounds small, it was surplus capital that, if invested in India instead of drained to Britain, would have compounded over decades and generated significant GDP growth. It is what the surplus could have become, not the absolute percentage, that matters.

Why others wrong: (a) The Moderates did not contest the 2% figure as inflated — they accepted it and reframed its significance; (c) the record counter-arguments specifically reject the idea that railways offset the drain; (d) Gold outflows to China are not the basis of the 2%-rejoinder; the compounding-surplus argument is.
Memory hook: 2% small? Compound it for fifty years — Naoroji's savings-account answer to the British defence.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The Drain Theory made the economic critique of colonialism inseparable from the political demand for Swaraj." Examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" asks you to test the claim, not merely describe the Drain Theory. The anchor is Moderate economic writing from the 1890s & the early 1900s, after the Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA1892) failed to deliver reform. The framing phrase "inseparable from the political demand for Swaraj" carries the load. Show how an economic argument produced a political conclusion.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Drain Theory was the Moderates' central intellectual contribution. By proving colonial extraction with data, it made the economic critique of colonialism inseparable from the political demand for Swaraj.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. Context & architects (see 'Drain Theory'). The theory gained prominence after the bitter disappointment with the Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA1892). Its architects were Romesh Chandra Dutt - a former ICS officer who wrote The Economic History of British India (Vol. I, 1902) & India in the Victorian Age (Vol. II, 1904) - Dadabhai Naoroji & MG Ranade, often called the father of Indian economics.

2. The core claim in one line (see 'Drain Theory'). The misuse of political power over the State of the Colony for the economic benefit of the Colonial Power. Mark the word 'political' - the cause named is political control, so the cure must also be political.

3. The evidence base (see 'Components of the Drain'). Name the mechanisms briefly - absence of protective tariffs until World War I (1914-19), exchange rate manipulation, Council Bills (post-1833) & Home Charges. Data & argument, not sentiment, made the critique difficult to counter.

4. The ideological kill (see 'Drain Theory'). The theory showed that the entire claim of the White Man's Burden was false - British rule was exploiting India, not developing it. Naoroji's Poverty & Un-British Rule in India (1901) was its most systematic presentation.

5. Why the economics forced politics (see 'Did British Rule Modernise India — The Debate'). Answer the British defence that the drain was only 2% of export value. Naoroji's reply: this was surplus capital, which would have compounded over decades had it stayed in India. Without self-rule the drain could never be stopped.
Closing verdict: By locating the cause in political control, the Drain Theory made the economic critique of colonialism inseparable from the political demand for Swaraj.
revise: Did British Rule Modernise India — The Debate

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: "India was made to pay for its own exploitation." Discuss the mechanisms of the drain of wealth, & how they changed from the eighteenth to the nineteenth century.
body: Demand of the question: "Discuss" wants a mechanism-by-mechanism account, not a general lament. The stem fixes a time axis - eighteenth century versus nineteenth - so the body must be periodised. The phrase "pay for its own exploitation" points you to the mechanisms where Indian taxpayer money financed the transfer, chiefly Council Bills & Home Charges.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The drain worked through named mechanisms, not slogans. From the eighteenth to the nineteenth century their form changed, but India was still made to pay for its own exploitation.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. Pre-19th century mechanisms (see 'Components of the Drain'). Misuse of the Dastaks - duty-free trade passes granted for the EIC's own goods but used by Company servants for private trade. Add the Plassey plunder of 1757-65 & Land Revenue extraction from Bengal, Orissa & Bihar beginning 1765 under the Treaty of Allahabad 1765.

2. The reversal of the gold flow (see 'Components of the Drain'). Earlier gold flowed into India as payment for Indian goods. After Plassey & the acquisition of LR rights, gold flowed out of India. This is the hinge between the two periods.

3. The nineteenth-century structure, 1813 onwards (see 'Impact of British Industrialisation on India'). Colony = source of raw materials & export market. Commercialisation of agriculture pushed peasants towards cotton, indigo, jute & opium. The Suez Canal, built between 1859 & 1869, cut the India-Britain sea distance by 4,500 miles & made extraction cheaper.

4. Trade-regime mechanisms (see 'Components of the Drain'). No import duty protected Indian manufacturers until World War I (1914-19), so British goods flooded Indian markets. Exchange rate manipulation kept British business competitive in India.

5. Council Bills, post-1833 (see 'Components of the Drain') - the sharpest proof of the stem. The Secretary of State held India's forex in London. A foreign importer bought CBs there with his forex, cashed them in India, & the GOI paid him rupees. The forex stayed in London; Indian taxpayers financed the trade.

6. Home Charges & the net effect (see 'Components of the Drain'). 'Home' means Britain - salaries & pensions of British officials, EIC shareholder dividends, interest on EIC loans & foreign debt, India Council expenses in London, stores bought by the SoS, War Office payments & interest on FDI. Result: a double drain - raw material shipped out, export earnings drained too.
Closing verdict: Whether through Dastaks or Council Bills, the mechanisms of the drain of wealth produced one outcome - India was made to pay for its own exploitation.
revise: Impact of British Industrialisation on India

questions.label: FYQ_M.3
questions.stem: "Whatever modernisation British rule brought to India was an unintended byproduct; no part of it was done for India." Critically examine with reference to railways & canals.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" requires both sides - concede the real gains, then deny the intent. Railways & canals are the two named test cases, so the body must cover both. The phrase "unintended byproduct" is your controlling idea: benefit without design.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Railways & canals are the strongest British claims to modernisation. Both brought real gains, yet each gain was an unintended byproduct - no part of it was done for India.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. Set the scale, then take railways (see 'Did British Rule Modernise India — The Debate'). A 2022 estimate by Utsa Patnaik puts the total drain at $45 trillion at 2022 prices. Dalhousie48-56 introduced railways in 1853 primarily for faster movement of the British army. Lines linked Indian markets & raw material sources to ports, not to Indian manufacturers. Technology transfer stayed low - bridge-building & tunnelling.

2. Railways as an investment scheme (see 'Did British Rule Modernise India — The Debate'). British capitalists received a guaranteed 5% annual interest in pound sterling in London, paid from the day of the FDI & topped up by the GOI in deficit years, with a right to sell the line back at the full FDI value. FDI became a fixed deposit - profits private, losses public, construction wasteful.

3. The concession you must make (see 'Did British Rule Modernise India — The Debate'). By 1947 railways covered 78% of India. Feeder roads from Indian factory hubs let Indian businesses use the network, & rail travel increased people-to-people contact, strengthening the inter-regional bonds the national movement depended upon.

4. Canals - the numbers refute the claim (see 'Did British Rule Modernise India — The Debate'). By 1947 only 25% of cultivated area was under public irrigation. Canals were built only in non-Permanent Settlement 1793 areas such as Punjab, western UP & coastal Madras, where land revenue could still be raised. Water was not free, so only rich farmers could buy it.

5. Famines as the verdict on food security (see 'Did British Rule Modernise India — The Debate'). Famines recurred through the 1860s & 1870s & as late as the Bengal Famine of 1943. The Strachey Commission (1880), Lyall Commission (1897) & MacDonnell Commission (1900) reported, but recommendations were rarely implemented seriously.
Closing verdict: Railways & canals brought real gains, but each was an unintended byproduct of extraction - no part of it was done for India.
revise: Did British Rule Modernise India — The Debate

questions.label: FYQ_M.4
questions.stem: "The first achievement of the Indian National Congress was not a concession won from the British, but the making of an Indian political community." Elucidate.
body: Demand of the question: "Elucidate" asks you to explain with concrete illustrations rather than argue against. The anchor is the early Congress from its first session at Bombay in 1885. The framing phrase "an Indian political community" tells you what to illustrate - the deliberate design choices that built unity before rights were demanded.
Suggested intro (~25 words): At its first session in Bombay in 1885 the Congress declared its goal as building national unity. Its first achievement was the making of an Indian political community.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Why unity came first, & the rule that protected it (see 'Nation Building'). India in 1885 was a land of regions, languages, castes & religions with no pre-existing sense of a single political community. In 1886 Dadabhai Naoroji laid down the informal INC rule - take up only political questions, not social or class questions - so the line stayed Indians versus British.

2. Two concrete Hindu-Muslim steps (see 'Nation Building'). The 1888 INC decision - no resolution would be passed if the majority of Hindu or Muslim members disagreed. The 1889 Minority Clause - reserved seats for religious minorities in the ILC & the PLCs in proportion to population. It was the INC, not the Muslim League, that first demanded minority representation.

3. Nation-building by structural design (see 'Nation Building'). Each session was held in a different part of the country & the President was deliberately not from the host region. A Marathi leader presiding in Calcutta built all-India leadership & inter-regional bonds that would not otherwise exist.

4. The parliamentary habit (see 'Building a Culture of Parliamentary Politics'). Sessions were modelled on parliamentary practice - a President functioning like a Speaker, members speaking, debating & voting on resolutions. This is why the modern political era in India began with the INC.
Closing verdict: Before it won any concession from the British, the Congress had achieved the making of an Indian political community.
revise: Building a Culture of Parliamentary Politics

questions.label: FYQ_M.5
questions.stem: Why did the Moderates, speaking for a poor & largely agrarian country, choose to champion the Indian capitalist class? Analyse in the light of the condition of Indian industry in the late nineteenth century.
body: Demand of the question: The stem carries two directives. "Why" wants the Moderates' own reasoning in their own terms; "Analyse" wants you to test that reasoning against the condition of Indian industry. The apparent contradiction - a poor & largely agrarian country with a pro-capitalist leadership - is what you must resolve, not restate.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Moderates were not anti-poor; they were pro-industrialisation. Their choice to champion the Indian capitalist class followed from the condition of Indian industry in the late nineteenth century.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. The industrialisation argument (see 'The Case for Supporting Indian Capitalists'). India had to industrialise like the West, & nineteenth-century industrialisation ran on capitalism. Britain, the US, Germany & Japan had all industrialised on the backs of a capitalist class.

2. No alternative model existed then (see 'The Case for Supporting Indian Capitalists'). Communist-led industrialisation was born only in 1917 in Soviet Russia & showed results only after 1929. In the 1880s & 1890s the Moderates were working with the tools available to them.

3. The Indian capitalist was weak, not dominant (see 'The Case for Supporting Indian Capitalists'). He faced severe competitive pressure from British imports flooding Indian markets & from British businesses operating inside India with the government's backing. An Indian capitalist in 1890 needed support, not criticism.

4. The industrial vacuum they were reacting to (see 'Impact of British Industrialisation on India'). Handicrafts were destroyed & artisans lost both domestic & export markets. With no Indian factories to absorb them they fell back on land, producing disguised unemployment & an overburdened agriculture.

5. The policy that kept industry weak (see 'Components of the Drain'). No import duty protected Indian manufacturers until World War I (1914-19), while exchange rate manipulation favoured British business. Backing Indian capital was therefore an anti-colonial demand, not a class preference.
Closing verdict: The Moderates championed the Indian capitalist class because, given the condition of Indian industry, only Indian capital could industrialise a poor & largely agrarian country.
revise: The Case for Supporting Indian Capitalists
Impact of British Industrialisation on India

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Who was the Secretary of State for India when the Indian Councils Act of 1892 was enacted?
explanation: (d) ✓ — The record explicitly names Secretary of State: Lord Cross | Viceroy: Lansdowne88-94 (1888–1894) and the Act is also called the Lord Cross Act.
Why others wrong: (a) Lansdowne was the Viceroy (1888–94), not the SoS; (b) Salisbury is not the SoS named for ICA 1892; (c) Morley is linked to ICA 1909, not 1892.
Memory hook: Cross at the centre — the SoS, not the Viceroy.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Which Viceroy's tenure (1888–1894) saw the passing of the Indian Councils Act of 1892?
explanation: (c) ✓ — The record fixes the Viceroy as "Lansdowne88-94 (1888–1894)", and reiterates "During Lansdowne88-94's tenure".
Why others wrong: (a) Ripon's tenure ended before 1892; (b) Dufferin preceded Lansdowne; (d) Curzon came much later (1899–1905).
Memory hook: Lansdowne 88–94 — the Cross Act sits in the middle.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the membership mechanism under the Indian Councils Act of 1892:
items: 1. Non-official members were chosen by direct election from the general public.
2. The legal text of the Act explicitly used the word "election".
3. The mechanism was described as "nomination on the basis of recommendation".
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — The record states the word "election" was "deliberately omitted from the text of the Act" and the mechanism was strictly defined as 'nomination on the basis of recommendation'. No direct election existed.

Why others wrong: (a) The Act introduced no direct election by the public, so "1 only" is wrong; (c) Statement 2 is wrong — the word "election" was specifically avoided; (d) Statement 1 is wrong — no direct election.
Memory hook: Nominated, never elected — the word the Act refused to print.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Under the Indian Councils Act of 1892, which body directly recommended non-official members to the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC)?

options.text: Non-official members of the PLCs and the Bengal Chamber of Commerce
Zamindars and Chambers of Commerce across India

explanation: (c) ✓ — The record specifies that for the ILC, the Viceroy nominated non-officials based on recommendations from the non-official members of the PLCs & the Bengal Chamber of Commerce — not directly from local bodies.
Why others wrong: (a) Municipalities and District Boards fed into PLCs, not ILC; (b) Universities and Trade Associations fed into PLCs; (d) Zamindars fed into PLCs, not directly into ILC.
Memory hook: Two tiers: local bodies feed PLCs; PLCs feed ILC.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Which of the following was/were rights granted to non-official members of the Imperial Legislative Council under the Indian Councils Act of 1892?
items: 1. The right to ask questions of the executive
2. The right to ask supplementary questions
3. The right to discuss the Budget
4. The right to vote on the Budget
explanation: (a) ✓ — The record grants questions (with 6 days' notice, no supplementary questions allowed) and Budget discussion (no vote, no amendment). Supplementaries and voting on the Budget were specifically denied.
Why others wrong: (b) Supplementary questions were "not allowed"; (c) Voting on the Budget was denied; (d) Both supplementaries and Budget vote were denied.
Memory hook: Ask once, talk once — never follow up, never vote.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: With reference to the size of the Imperial Legislative Council after the Indian Councils Act of 1892, what was the total number of additional members?
explanation: (d) ✓ — The record states: the total number of additional members was now set at 10 to 16 — and of these, at least half could be non-officials. It also notes the upgrade from 6–12 under ICA 1861.
Why others wrong: (a) 6–12 was the ICA 1861 figure, replaced by 1892; (b) 16–60 was the ICA 1909 (Morley–Minto) range; (c) No such figure appears for ICA 1892.
Memory hook: 10–16 in '92 — up from 6–12 of '61.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 has been seen as a catalyst for the rise of Extremism in Indian politics. Which of the following best explains this consequence?

options.text: It granted Indians elected majorities in legislatures, raising expectations the British did not meet later
It demonstrated to Moderates that prayers and petitions could yield only hollow concessions
It abolished the Viceroy's veto, exposing the executive to direct attack
It introduced separate electorates, fragmenting Indian political opinion

explanation: (b) ✓ — The record states: If 'prayers & petitions' could produce only this, then the method itself was bankrupt. The disillusionment seeded by ICA 1892 was the soil in which Extremism would take root.
Why others wrong: (a) No elected majority was granted; the council had an official majority; (c) The Viceroy's veto was not abolished; (d) Separate electorates came with ICA 1909, not 1892.
Memory hook: Hollow Act, cracked faith — Extremism's seed-bed.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC) under the Indian Councils Act of 1892:
items: 1. The VEC was reconstituted with an Indian majority.
2. The number of Ordinary Members was increased to ten.
3. The composition of the VEC remained unchanged from the position in 1874.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — The record is explicit: The VEC under the Indian Councils Act of 1892 did not change at all, and summarises "VEC: Unchanged from 1874."

Why others wrong: (a) No Indian majority was introduced; (b) Ordinary Members remained six — Home, Revenue/Agriculture, Law, Military, Finance, Public Works — with no increase; (d) Both 1 and 2 are independently false.
Memory hook: VEC frozen since '74 — '92 didn't touch the inner cabinet.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Which one of the following changes was made by the Indian Councils Act of 1892 with respect to Centre–Province relations?

options.text: Provincial legislatures were given the power to vote on their own budgets
Separate provincial budgets were introduced for the first time
The Viceroy lost the power to create new provinces or appoint Lieutenant-Governors
Governors no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate Non-Officers to the PLC

explanation: (d) ✓ — The record states: the Governor no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate Non-Officers to the PLC … This was a small but genuine decentralisation. All other aspects of Viceregal control over provinces remained as under ICA 1861.

Why others wrong: (a) No vote on Budget was given (even at the Centre, only discussion was allowed); (b) "a single unified budget with no separate provincial budget" remained; (c) These powers remained "exactly as they were under ICA 1861."
Memory hook: One small step — Governor freed from Viceregal pre-clearance.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Which of the following civil service changes are correctly attributed to the Aitchison Commission's recommendations implemented during Lansdowne's tenure?
items: 1. Covenanted Civil Services were renamed Imperial Civil Services
2. Uncovenanted Civil Services were renamed Provincial Civil Services
3. The Statutory Civil Services were abolished
4. These changes were enacted as provisions of the Indian Councils Act of 1892
explanation: (a) ✓ — The record lists CCS→ICS, UCS→PCS, and abolition of Statutory CS (created 1878) as administrative orders of Lansdowne's era on Aitchison Commission's recommendations. Crucially, they were administrative orders of the era, not provisions of the Indian Councils Act of 1892.
Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) Statement 4 is the classic trap — these were administrative measures, not provisions of ICA 1892.
Memory hook: Same era, separate file — Aitchison sits outside the Act.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the powers of non-official members in the Imperial Legislative Council under the Indian Councils Act of 1892:
items: 1. They could move resolutions on policy matters.
2. They could demand a vote on a Government resolution.
3. They could discuss the annual Budget.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — The record states opposition members could not bring any resolution before the council, nor could they demand a vote on a government resolution, while "The Budget could be discussed for the first time" without vote or amendment.

Why others wrong: (a) Resolutions could not be brought by non-officials, so 1 is wrong; (c) No vote could be demanded on Government resolutions, so 2 is wrong; (d) Both 1 and 2 are independently false.
Memory hook: Talk to the Budget, but not the resolutions — speech only, no motion.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Match List I (Recommending Body under ICA 1892) with List II (Council to which it fed names) and select the correct answer:
items: 1. District Boards
2. Bengal Chamber of Commerce
3. Universities

4. Non-official members of PLCs
A. Provincial Legislative Council B. Imperial Legislative Council
matchTable: List II (Council to which it fed names)
explanation: (b) ✓ — The record specifies the two tiers: District Boards, Municipalities, Universities, Trade Associations, and Zamindars fed PLCs; Bengal Chamber of Commerce and non-official members of PLCs fed the ILC.

Why others wrong: (a) Misplaces the Bengal CoC with PLC and PLC members with ILC mapping wrong overall; (c) Inverts the tier structure entirely; (d) Wrongly elevates District Boards to ILC and demotes PLC members to PLC.
Memory hook: Local bodies → PLC; Bengal CoC + PLC members → ILC.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Which of the following demands of the Moderates was at least partially conceded by the Indian Councils Act of 1892?

options.text: Indianisation of the Civil Services and Military
Non-official majority in the legislative councils
Expansion of the Imperial and Provincial Legislative Councils
Adoption of a written constitution with a Preamble

explanation: (c) ✓ — The Moderates' scorecard lists "Expansion of ILC & PLCs: ✓ Yes — but dissatisfactory" as the only partially met demand. All other items are marked "✗ No."
Why others wrong: (a) Indianisation: ✗ No; (b) Non-official majority: ✗ No; (d) Constitutionalism with Preamble: ✗ No.
Memory hook: Six asks, one tick — and even that one disappointed.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Consider the following conditions attached to asking questions in the Imperial Legislative Council under the Indian Councils Act of 1892:
items: 1. Six days' prior notice was required
2. Discussion of the answers given was permitted
3. Supplementary questions were allowed. Which of the conditions given above is/are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — The record states: 6 days' prior notice was required, there could be no discussion of the answers given, and no supplementary questions were allowed. Only Statement 1 is correct.
Why others wrong: (b) Discussion of answers was barred; (c) Both 2 and 3 are false; (d) Statements 2 and 3 are both false.
Memory hook: Six days' notice — no follow-up, no chat after.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: With reference to the Indian Councils Act of 1892, which one of the following statements best describes the legislative role of non-official Indian members in the Imperial Legislative Council?

options.text: They formed the decisive bloc on most government bills
They served an advisory and recommendatory role, never a decisive one
They were granted a suspensive veto over government bills
They could legislate independently on subjects transferred to them

explanation: (b) ✓ — The record states: Their presence was advisory, not decisive — the legislative function was recommendatory, not mandatory. The council was recommendatory due to the official majority and the Viceroy's absolute veto.

Why others wrong: (a) Non-officials were outvoted by the official majority on every bill; (c) No suspensive veto was given; (d) No transferred subjects existed — that idea belongs to later reforms (GoI 1919).
Memory hook: Advisory voice, official vote — recommendatory, not mandatory.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_16
questions.stem: Disappointment with the Indian Councils Act of 1892 led the Moderates to formally raise their ceiling of political demand. The new goal — self-government on the lines of Australia and Canada — was officially adopted by the Indian National Congress at which session?
explanation: (c) ✓ — The record states: This officially became the goal of the Indian National Congress at the 1906 Calcutta session, named Swaraj — Self-Government within the Empire, also called Home Rule.
Why others wrong: (a) Madras 1887 predates the demand-shift; (b) Bombay 1904 — no such adoption per Chapter; (d) Surat 1907 is the split session, not the Swaraj-adoption session.
Memory hook: Calcutta 1906 — Moderates raise the bar to Swaraj.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_17
questions.stem: Why did the official majority in the Imperial Legislative Council under the Indian Councils Act of 1892 effectively neutralise the Indian non-official members?

options.text: Non-official members were barred from voting on any matter
Non-official members were appointed only on probation for one year
The Viceroy could dissolve the council whenever the non-official members opposed him
The Viceroy's Executive Council plus the official additional members always outnumbered the non-officials

explanation: (d) ✓ — The record states: the Viceroy's Executive Council plus the official additional members always comfortably outnumbered the non-official Indians. The official majority was not just a political preference — it was mathematically guaranteed by the structure of the Act.
Why others wrong: (a) Non-officials could vote; they were merely outvoted; (b) No such probation existed; (c) Dissolution power as described is not the basis of the official majority.
Memory hook: VEC + official additionals — the maths always wins.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_18
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Indian Councils Act of 1892:
items: 1. It introduced an elected majority in the Imperial Legislative Council.
2. It permitted discussion of the Budget but not voting on it.
3. It made the Provincial Legislative Councils financially independent of the Centre.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Only Statement 2 is correct. The record confirms Budget discussion was allowed but no vote or amendment was permitted.

Why others wrong: (b) Statement 1 is wrong — no elected majority; the word "election" was avoided and an official majority prevailed; (c) Statement 3 is wrong — a single unified budget with no separate provincial budget remained; (d) Both 1 and 3 are independently false.
Memory hook: Talk the Budget, can't touch it — and provinces still on the Centre's purse.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_19
questions.stem: Match List I (Position) with List II (Person) in the context of the Indian Councils Act of 1892 and select the correct answer:
items: 1. Secretary of State for India
2. Viceroy of India
3. Notable Moderate who served on the council under this Act

4. Commission whose civil-service recommendations were implemented in this era
A. Aitchison Commission B. Gokhale C. Lord Lansdowne D. Lord Cross
matchTable: 3. Notable Moderate who served on the council under this Act
4. Commission whose civil-service recommendations were implemented in this era
explanation: (a) ✓ — The record fixes Lord Cross as SoS and Lord Lansdowne as Viceroy; Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta are named as Indians who served under this framework; the Aitchison Commission's recommendations were implemented during Lansdowne's tenure.
Why others wrong: (b) Swaps SoS and Viceroy and misplaces Aitchison; (c) Wrongly places Gokhale with Aitchison and Lansdowne as a moderate; (d) Wrongly assigns the Aitchison Commission to SoS.
Memory hook: Cross-SoS, Lansdowne-Viceroy, Gokhale-on-Council, Aitchison-on-Services.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_20
questions.stem: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 has been described as "simultaneously a result of the Moderates' struggle and proof of its failure." Which of the following best captures the reasoning behind this characterisation?

options.text: The Act granted everything the Moderates demanded, demonstrating their strength
The Act rejected every Moderate proposal, revealing their total irrelevance
The Act split the Moderates into Extremist and Liberal factions immediately upon its enactment
The Act conceded just enough to show the British had listened, and little enough to show no intent to concede power

explanation: (d) ✓ — The record states the Act was an Act that gave just enough to show the British had listened, and little enough to show they had no intention of actually conceding power.

Why others wrong: (a) Most Moderate demands were rejected (six demands, one partially met); (b) The Moderates did secure council expansion, so they were not wholly ignored; (c) The Moderate–Extremist split (Surat) came in 1907, not at the moment of enactment.
Memory hook: Just enough to listen, little enough to refuse — the polite British No.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was at once the achievement of the Moderates & the proof that their method had failed." Critically examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" asks you to argue both halves & then judge. The anchor is 1892 — Lord Cross as Secretary of State, Lansdowne88-94 as Viceroy. The framing phrase "at once" bars a one-sided answer: show the real gains first, then show why each gain was hollow. The judgement must be about the Moderate method, not only about the Act.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was the achievement of the Moderates — bigger councils, questions, a budget debate. Each gain also showed their method had failed.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. The achievement side (see 'ICA 1892 — Significance'). The Act was the fruit of years of petitions, memorials & reasoned argument. It gave just enough to show the British had listened. Pair with 'Size of the Councils' — the ILC now had 10 to 16 additional members, at least half of them non-officials, against only 3 to 6 non-officials out of the 6–12 additional members of 1861. Gokhale & Pherozeshah Mehta served under this framework.

2. Selection, not election (see 'The "Indirect Election" That Wasn't Called an Election'). The word "election" was deliberately omitted from the text of the Act. The legal mechanism was "nomination on the basis of recommendation". Governors nominated to the PLCs on recommendations from District Boards, Municipalities, Universities, Trade Associations & Zamindars; the Viceroy nominated to the ILC on recommendations from the non-official members of the PLCs & the Bengal Chamber of Commerce. The recommending bodies only sent names — the final pick was the Viceroy's or the Governor's.

3. The arithmetic of the official majority (see 'Size of the Councils'). The VEC plus the official additional members always outnumbered the non-official Indians. That majority was guaranteed by the structure of the Act itself, not by political preference. Add 'The Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC) — No Change' — the executive was left untouched, so no Indian came near real administrative power.

4. Rights with the teeth removed (see 'What Members Could Do'). Questions were allowed, but with 6 days' prior notice, no discussion of the answers & no supplementary questions. Opposition members could not bring a resolution, nor demand a vote on a government resolution. The Budget could be discussed for the first time, but not voted on or amended. On bills the non-officials were simply outvoted — the legislative function was recommendatory, not mandatory.

5. The scorecard (see 'Scorecard — What the Moderates Won'). Indianisation of civil services & military — no. Non-official majority — no. Elected majority — no. Proper indirect election — no. Powerful legislatures — no. Constitutionalism — no. Only expansion of the ILC & PLCs was granted, & even that was dissatisfactory. One small gain sits beside it in 'Federalism — One Small Step': the Governor no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate Non-Officers to the PLC.

6. The verdict on the method (see 'Legacy — Catalyst for Extremism'). Six demands, one partially met. The Moderates had used every permissible channel & got a hollow Act in return. Belief in British benevolence began to crack. Link to 'What the Moderates Did Next' — they raised their ceiling of demand to Self-Government on the lines of Australia & Canada, adopted as Swaraj at the 1906 Calcutta session, & pressed the Drain Theory alongside it.
Closing verdict: ICA 1892 was the achievement of the Moderates in form only. Its hollowness proved their method had failed & seeded Extremism.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: To what extent did the Indian Councils Act of 1892 concede the principle of election in the Imperial & Provincial Legislative Councils?
body: Demand of the question: "To what extent" wants a graded answer, not a yes or no. Test the claim against the exact legal mechanism the 1892 Act used. Then measure the distance between that mechanism & a real election. Keep the two council tiers separate — the Act treated them differently.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Indian Councils Act of 1892 brought non-official Indians into the Imperial & Provincial Legislative Councils. But it conceded the principle of election in appearance only.
Body guidance — 4 themes:
