1. The wording of the Act (see 'The "Indirect Election" That Wasn't Called an Election'). Members were nominated, not elected. The word "election" was deliberately omitted from the text of the Act. The mechanism was strictly "nomination on the basis of recommendation" — selection, not election.

2. Two separate tiers (see 'The "Indirect Election" That Wasn't Called an Election'). For the PLCs, Governors nominated non-officials on recommendations from District Boards, Municipalities, Universities, Trade Associations & Zamindars. For the ILC, the Viceroy nominated on recommendations from the non-official members of the PLCs & the Bengal Chamber of Commerce. Municipalities fed the PLCs; the PLCs fed the ILC. Do not merge the two tiers.

3. Why this was not a proper indirect election (see 'The "Indirect Election" That Wasn't Called an Election'). In a proper election the choice of the voters is final. Here the recommending bodies only sent names, & the final pick belonged to the Viceroy or the Governor. The "election" was really a shortlist.

4. What was conceded in practice (see 'Size of the Councils'). The ILC grew to 10 to 16 additional members, at least half of them non-officials, & men like Gokhale & Pherozeshah Mehta came in. But the official majority survived. 'Scorecard — What the Moderates Won' records the limit plainly: no elected majority & no proper indirect election. The one genuine loosening lay elsewhere — 'Federalism — One Small Step': the Governor no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate Non-Officers to the PLC.
Closing verdict: ICA 1892 conceded the principle of election only in appearance. The recommending bodies sent a shortlist; the final choice stayed with the Viceroy & Governors.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: Which one of the following defines extremist ideology during the early phase of Indian freedom movement?

options.text: Stimulating the production of indigenous articles by giving them preference over imported commodities
Obtaining self government by aggressive means in place of petitions and constitutional ways
Providing national education according the requirements of the country
Organising coups against the British empire through military revolt

explanation: (B) ✓ — The Extremists' break with Moderate method is the record opening theme: where the Moderates' method was "petition, prayer, and press," the Extremists sought Swaraj through aggressive agitation — boycott, Swadeshi, passive resistance. +.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Preferring indigenous goods defines SWADESHI — one method the movement used, not the defining ideology of Extremism, which was about HOW self-government should be won.
(C) ✗ — National education was likewise one of the four Calcutta-1906 methods, not the ideology itself.

(D) ✗ — Military coups belong to the REVOLUTIONARY stream, not to the Extremists, whose framework was passive resistance — non-cooperation, boycott, civil disobedience — with violence only as an implied last resort.
(Note: The extremist groups of the early phase of Indian freedom movement had believed in obtaining self government by aggressive means in place of petitions and constitutional ways.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: Assertion [A] Partition of Bengal in 1905 brought to an end the moderates role in the Indian freedom movement. Reason [R] The Surat session of Indian National Congress separated the extremists from the moderates.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

explanation: (D) ✓ — A is false: the Partition did not end the Moderates' role — they themselves passed the Boycott Resolution at Calcutta Town Hall (7 August 1905) and stayed in the movement; the INC stayed divided only from Surat 1907 to the 1916 reunion. R is true: the Surat Session (1907) did separate the Extremists from the Moderates. +.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Requires A to be true — but the Moderates led the movement's first phase themselves (Boycott Resolution, Calcutta Town Hall, 7 August 1905); their role did not end in 1905.
(B) ✗ — Same defect: any both-true reading fails because A is false — Moderate politics continued after 1905, inside and beyond the Swadeshi phase.
(C) ✗ — Exactly inverted: it is R that is true (Surat separated the factions) and A that is false.
(Note: Moderates continued to participate in the struggle for freedom even after 1905, Bengal Partition. Later in 1916 both the groups re-united in 1916 at Lahore session.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: The Indian Muslims in general, were not attracted to the Extremist movement because of the

options.text: influence of the Sir Sayyid Ahmed Khan
anti - Muslim attitude of Extremist leaders
Extremists' policy of harping on Hindu past.

explanation: (D) ✓ — The high use of Hindu religious symbolism in the movement's methods — from Bande Mataram to Kali worship — alienated Muslims.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Sir Syed's influence shaped an earlier generation's distance from the INC; the record explanation for low Muslim attraction to EXTREMISM is the movement's own Hindu idiom — Bande Mataram, Kali worship.
(B) ✗ — The record does not describe the Extremist leaders as anti-Muslim in personal attitude; the alienation came from the SYMBOLISM they used — a Hindu-past idiom — not hostility.
(C) ✗ — Indifference understates the record point: it was the ACTIVE use of Hindu religious symbolism — "from Bande Mataram to Kali worship" — that alienated Muslims, i.e., harping on the Hindu past.

(Note: In general, the Indian Muslims were not attracted to the extremist movement because of the religious policy of harping on Hindu past like celebrating Shivaji Jayanti and Ganesh Utsav by Tilak.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: The Congress policy of pray and petition ultimately came to an end under the guidance of
explanation: (B) ✓ — Tilak is the era's symbol of the break with "pray and petition": he built the Extremist/Nationalist party inside the INC with the explicit goal of converting it from within, and carried boycott, Swadeshi, and passive resistance to the country. +.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Aurobindo was the movement's radical intellectual — 'New Lamps for Old', principal of the Bengal National College — but the leadership credited with ENDING petition-politics is Tilak's.
(C) ✗ — Lala Lajpat Rai led the movement's Punjab wing — a lieutenant of the new politics, not the guide under whom pray-and-petition ended.
(D) ✗ — Gandhi's mass politics came a decade later — he united the factions only in 1920; petition-politics had already been ended by Tilak's generation.

(Note: The partition of Bengal and Swadeshi movement marked in the beginning of new era in the history of Indian nationalism. Under the guidance of Bal Gangadhar Tilak the, polity of pray and petition came to an end.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: With reference to the period of extremist nationalist movement in India with its spirit of Swadeshi, which one of the following statements is not correct?

options.text: Liakat Hussain led the Muslim peasants of Barisal in their agitations
In 1889, the scheme of national education was formulated by Satish Chandra Mukherjee
The Bengal National College was founded in 1906 with Aurobindo as the Principal
Tagore preached the cult of Atmasakti, the main plank of which was social and economic regeneration of the villages

explanation: (A) ✓ — Its association with Bharat Mata, and the visible use of Hindu religious symbols, would later become a source of tension with Muslim participation.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Statement (b) is CORRECT as history — Satish Chandra Mukherjee did formulate the national-education scheme in 1889 — so it cannot be the "not correct" pick the stem demands.
(C) ✗ — Statement (c) is CORRECT — The Bengal National College was set up with Aurobindo as principal (1906) — so it is not the odd one out.
(D) ✗ — Statement (d) is CORRECT — Tagore's Atmasakti plank of village social and economic regeneration belongs to the movement's constructive programme — leaving (a) as the only false statement.
(Note: Liakat Hussain did not lead the Barisal movement of peasant. Barisal movement was for salt breaking during Civil Disobedience Movement.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: Consider the following Viceroys of India during the British rule
items: 1. Lord Curzon
2. Lord Chelmsford
3. Lord Hardinge
4. Lord Irwin
questions.stemTail: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of their tenure?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Tenure order: Curzon99-05 → Hardinge10-16 → Chelmsford16-21 → Irwin26-31, i.e. 1, 3, 2, 4. anchors Curzon99-05 as the era's opening Viceroy; the others follow in the standard viceregal sequence.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Opens with Chelmsford (1916–21), third of the four in time — Curzon99-05 heads the sequence.
(C) ✗ — Places Irwin (1926–31) second — but Irwin is the LATEST of the four; Hardinge10-16 and Chelmsford16-21 both precede him.
(D) ✗ — Again opens with Chelmsford and buries Curzon99-05 in third place — the reverse of the actual order.
(Note: The correct chronological order is Lord Curzon from 1899 to 1905, Lord Hardinge from 1910 to 1916, Lord Chelmsford from 1916 to 1921 and Lord Irwin from 1926 to 1931.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.stem: Who among the following gave a systematic critique of the moderate politics of the Indian National Congress in a series of articles entitled 'New Lamps for Old'?
explanation: (A) ✓ — At the Barisal Conference, SNB and Aurobindo Ghosh distributed badges of Bande Mataram.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — R.C. Dutt's critique was ECONOMIC — the drain-theory school; the 'New Lamps for Old' attack on Moderate politics is Aurobindo's.
(C) ✗ — Syed Ahmad Khan stood outside and against Congress politics altogether; he wrote no insider critique of Moderate methods.
(D) ✗ — Viraraghavachari belonged to the Madras journalism world of The Hindu; the 'New Lamps for Old' series came from Aurobindo's radical Bengal.

(Note: Aurobindo Ghosh gave a systematic critique of the moderate politics of the Indian National Congress in a series of articles entitled 'New Lamps for Old.' Aurobindo Ghosh (1872-1950) was an ardent nationalist.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.stem: In the context of the Indian Freedom Struggle, 16th October, 1905 is well-known for which one of the following reasons?

options.text: The formal proclamation of Swadeshi Movement was made in Calcutta town hall
Dadabhai Naoroji declared that the goal of Indian National Congress was Swaraj
Lokmanya Tilak started Swadeshi Movement in Poona

explanation: (B) ✓ — 16 October 1905 is the day the Partition of Bengal took effect — announced July 1905, effected 16 October 1905, splitting the old province into Bengal and the new East Bengal & Assam.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The formal boycott resolution at Calcutta Town Hall came earlier — 7 August 1905, in response to the July announcement.
(C) ✗ — Naoroji's Swaraj declaration belongs to the Calcutta INC SESSION of December 1906, not to 16 October 1905.
(D) ✗ — The launch was a Bengal affair built around the Partition; Tilak's role was carrying the movement to Bombay, not starting it in Poona on that date.

(Note: On 30th December, 1898 Lord Curzon took over as the new Viceroy of India. The Partition of Bengal came into effect on 16th October, 1905, through a Queen proclamation, reducing the old province of Bengal.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.stem: Four resolutions were passed at the famous Calcutta Session of Indian National Congress in 1906. The question of either retention or of rejection of these four resolutions became the cause of a split in Congress at the next Congress Session held in Surat in 1907. Which one of the following was not one of those resolutions?
explanation: (A) ✓ — The four Calcutta-1906 resolutions were Swaraj (goal), Boycott, Swadeshi, and National Education (methods); the Bengal Partition was condemned SEPARATELY — so annulment of Partition was not among the four whose retention split Surat.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Boycott WAS one of the four — listed as method 7.2's account of the 1906 session.
(C) ✗ — National Education WAS one of the four (7.4).
(D) ✗ — Swadeshi WAS one of the four (7.3).
(Note: There was a great deal of public debate and disagreement among Moderates and Extremists in the years 1905-1907, even when they were working together against the partitioning of Bengal.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.10
questions.stem: What was the immediate cause for the launch of the Swadeshi Movement?

options.text: The Partition of Bengal done by Lord Curzon
A sentence of 18 months imprisonment imposed on Lokmanya Tilak
The arrest and deportation of Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh; and passing of the Punjab Colonisation Bill
Death sentence pronounced on the Chapekar brothers

explanation: (A) ✓ — The immediate cause was Curzon99-05's Partition of Bengal — announced July 1905, effected 16 October 1905; the movement grew out of the anti-Partition agitation, opening with the Boycott Resolution of 7 August 1905. +.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Tilak's imprisonment was not the trigger — the movement rose out of Bengal's Partition; Tilak's part was to carry it to Bombay.
(C) ✗ — The deportation of Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh (1907) came two years INTO the movement — a later escalation in Punjab, not its immediate cause.
(D) ✗ — The Chapekar brothers' death sentences belong to the 1897 Poona episode of revolutionary violence — an earlier, separate affair, not the spark of Swadeshi.
(Note: The Swadeshi Movement had its genesis in the Anti-Partition Movement, which was started to oppose the British decision to partition Bengal.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.11
questions.stem: The Partition of Bengal made by Lord Curzon in 1905 lasted until

options.text: the I World War when Indian troops were needed by the British and the partition was ended
King George V abrogated Curzon's Act at the Royal Durbar in Delhi, in 1911
Gandhiji launched his Civil Disobedience Movement
the Partition of India, in 1947 when East Bengal became East Pakistan

explanation: (B) ✓ — (not 'Extremist control of INC' in 1905 — only INM shifted; INC control passed to Gandhi in 1920 Nagpur Session) However, the Swadeshi period also set in motion some negative consequences: 8.7) 1911 — Capital shifted to Delhi, reducing Bengal's dominance in the INM.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The annulment came in December 1911 at the Delhi Durbar — BEFORE the First World War (1914); wartime troop needs played no part.
(C) ✗ — Gandhi's Civil Disobedience began in 1930 — the Partition had been undone two decades earlier (1911).
(D) ✗ — Confuses 1905 with 1947: Curzon's Partition was annulled in 1911 ("Bengal = WB + EB; Assam and 'Bihar & Orissa' became separate"); the 1947 division was a different, permanent event.

(Note: The Partition of Bengal was announced in July, 1905 by the Viceroy of India Lord Curzon, as a concealed attack on Indian nationalism. Lord Curzon wanted to split Bengal to weaken a solid body of opposition.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.12
questions.stem: Which one of the following movements has contributed to a split in the Indian National Congress resulting in the emergence of 'moderates' and 'extremists'?
explanation: (A) ✓ — The Administration of Curzon9905 (1899–1905) Before the Swadeshi Movement erupted, it was Curzon9905's own measures that set the stage.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Quit India (1942) came 35 years after the moderate-extremist rupture; by then those labels were history.
(C) ✗ — Non-Cooperation (1920–22) is when Gandhi UNITED the factions — the opposite pole of the 1907 split.
(D) ✗ — Civil Disobedience (1930–34) belongs to the united Gandhian INC; the moderate-extremist rupture came at Surat 1907, during Swadeshi.
(Note: Surat Split is mainly known for separation of Congress partymen into moderates and extremists at the Surat Session of Congress on 26th December, 1907. This was the time of Swadeshi Movement.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.13
questions.stem: What was the main reason for the split in the Indian National Congress at Surat in 1907?

options.text: Introduction of communalism into Indian politics by Lord Minto
Extremists' lack of faith in the capacity of the moderates to negotiate with the British Government
Aurobindo Ghosh's inability to be elected as the President of the Indian National Congress

explanation: (B) ✓ — The tension between Moderates and Extremists within the INC had been building since the Swadeshi Movement gave the Extremists a platform.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Minto's communal lever — separate electorates — came with the 1909 reforms, AFTER Surat; the 1907 split was an internal INC rupture over method and pace.
(C) ✗ — The Muslim League's founding (December 1906, Dacca) ran on a separate track; the Surat story is about the four resolutions and factional control of the INC.
(D) ✗ — No Aurobindo presidency bid features's Surat account; the split turned on retention of the four 1906 resolutions and the Extremists' lost faith in Moderate negotiation.
(Note: Moderates believed in the policy of settlement of minor issue with the government by deliberations. But the extremists believed in agitation, strikes and boycotts to force their demands.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.14
questions.stem: The 'Swadeshi' and 'Boycott' were adopted as methods of struggle for the first time during the

options.text: agitation against the Partition of Bengal
visit of the Simon Commission to India

explanation: (A) ✓ — "The movement did not begin on the day of Partition."
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — The Home Rule Movement (1916–18) borrowed the energy of an earlier generation — Swadeshi and Boycott had been forged a decade before, in the anti-Partition agitation.
(C) ✗ — Non-Cooperation (1920–22) REUSED boycott on a mass scale; the method's first deployment was 1905–11.
(D) ✗ — The Simon boycott (1928) is two decades too late — "boycott" was first adopted at Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905.
(Note: The Swadeshi and Boycott movements were started to oppose the partition of Bengal. The idea of boycott was started after the failure of peaceful campaigns and petitions.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.15
questions.stem: He wrote biographies of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji and Shrikrishna, stayed in America for sometime and was elected to the Central Assembly. He was
explanation: (C) ✓ — The biography matches Lala Lajpat Rai: biographer of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji and Shrikrishna, a sojourner in America, later elected to the Central Assembly — the leader of the movement's Punjab wing.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Aurobindo's writings in this era are the 'New Lamps for Old' critique and his national-education leadership — not these biographies; no American stay or Central Assembly seat attaches to him.
(B) ✗ — Bipin Chandra Pal was the Bengal voice of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio; the Mazzini-Garibaldi biographies and the American sojourn belong to his Punjab counterpart.
(D) ✗ — Motilal Nehru's prominence came later and as a lawyer-politician of the 1920s, not as the biographer of Mazzini and Shivaji.

(Note: Lala Lajpat Rai regularly contributed to several major Hindi, Punjabi, English, and Urdu newspapers and magazines. He also authored many books like Unhappy India, Young India: An Interpretation.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.16
questions.stem: With reference to Swadeshi Movement, consider the following statements.
items: 1. It contributed to the revival of the indigenous artisan crafts and industries.
2. The National Council of Education was established as a part of Swadeshi Movement.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Both statements hold: the movement revived indigenous crafts and enterprise — Swadeshi textile mills, soap and match factories, tanneries — and the National Council of Education (1906) was created under the movement's national-education plank, the same drive that produced the Bengal National College with Aurobindo as principal.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "Only 1" undercounts: the National Council of Education (1906) was a Swadeshi-era creation.
(B) ✗ — "Only 2" undercounts: craft-and-industry revival was the movement's economic core — Swadeshi mills, factories and tanneries rose to replace boycotted British goods.
(D) ✗ — "Neither" fails on both counts — the movement produced both the industrial revival and the national-education institutions.

(Note: Swadeshi Movement was launched in the year 1905 to protest the Partition of Bengal. During the Swadeshi Movement, Swadeshi textile mills, soap, match factories, tanneries etc., were established.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.17
questions.stem: With reference to the book 'Desher Katha' written by Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar during the freedom struggle, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It warned against the colonial state's hypnotic conquest of the mind and body of the subjugated.
2. It inspired the performance of Swadeshi street plays and folk songs.
3. The use of 'desh' by Deuskar was in the specific context of the region of Bengal.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct ?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Desher Katha (1904) documented British economic exploitation as a warning, and it fed the Swadeshi imagination, street plays and folk songs included. Statement 3 is wrong: Deuskar used 'Desh' for the ENTIRE Indian subcontinent — a conscious attempt to build a pan-Indian economic consciousness — not just Bengal.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Includes the false statement 3: the record is explicit that Deuskar's 'Desh' meant all of India, not the Bengal region.
(C) ✗ — Pairs the true statement 1 with the false statement 3 — the pan-India meaning of 'Desh' is the question's trap.
(D) ✗ — Overcounts: statement 3 fails on the record own words — 'Desh' = the whole subcontinent.

(Note: Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar's (1869-1912) book entitled 'Desher Katha' describes in exhaustive detail the British commercial and industrial exploitation of India. It summarised the work of MG Ranade and Dadabhai Naoroji.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.19
questions.stem: Statement-I: 7th Aug is National Handloom day.Statement-II: Swadeshi movement launched on same day in 1905.

options.text: Both Correct, II doesn't explain I

explanation: (A) ✓ — Both statements are correct and LINKED: the Boycott Resolution at Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905 launched the movement, and National Handloom Day (7 August) commemorates that launch — the Swadeshi embrace of Indian cloth.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — The explanation IS the link: Handloom Day sits on 7 August precisely because the Swadeshi movement began that day in 1905.
(C) ✗ — Statement II is also correct — 7 August 1905, Calcutta Town Hall, the Boycott Resolution.
(D) ✗ — Statement I is also correct — 7 August is National Handloom Day, chosen for the Swadeshi anniversary.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Which one of the following Curzonian measures placed Indian universities under direct government control?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The Indian Universities Act, 1904 brought universities under direct government control; Curzon's stated reasoning was that universities were becoming "factories of sedition."

Why others wrong: (a) reduced elected members in municipalities — attacked local self-governance, not universities; (c) curbed press freedom by allowing censorship of publications hurting British interests; (d) was Curzon's Minute on Territorial Re-distribution leaking the Partition plan, not an education measure.
Memory hook: Universities-1904 → "factories of sedition" muzzled.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: With reference to the Partition of Bengal (October 1905), consider the following statements:
items: 1. East Bengal & Assam was designed as a new Muslim-majority province.
2. The Indian argument was that reorganisation on linguistic lines would have been more logical if administration were the real goal.
3. Nawab Salimullah of Dacca welcomed the Partition.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — All three statements are correct. EBA was deliberately designed as a Muslim-majority province; Indians argued linguistic reorganisation would have served administration without communalising; Nawab Salimullah of Dacca and elite Muslim leadership welcomed the Partition.
Why others wrong: (a), (b), (c) each drop one true statement; the record makes all three explicit, so any subset is incomplete.
Memory hook: EBA = MMP by design; Salimullah's welcome; linguistic was the road not taken.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Who among the following founded the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (1906) at Tuticorin to challenge British monopoly over coastal shipping?
explanation: (C) ✓ — V.O. Chidambaram Pillai founded the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company in 1906 at Tuticorin, applying Swadeshi to maritime trade and directly competing with the British India Steam Navigation Company.
Why others wrong: (a) conceived TISCO, executed by son Dorabji Tata in 1907; (b) set up Bengal Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals; (d) co-founded Punjab National Bank along with Lala Harkishen Lal in 1894.
Memory hook: VOC at Tuticorin — Swadeshi sailed against British steam.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: With reference to the Surat Split (1907), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The immediate flashpoint was the contest over the presidency between Lala Lajpat Rai and Dadabhai Naoroji.
2. The Extremists demanded re-adoption of the four Calcutta (1906) resolutions as a pre-condition.
3. The Allahabad Convention of 1908 declared loyalty to the Raj.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statements 2 and 3 hold. The Extremists refused any settlement unless the four resolutions carried at Calcutta in 1906 — Swaraj, Boycott, Swadeshi and National Education — were re-adopted, and it was on that refusal that the session collapsed; the Allahabad Convention of 1908 then declared the Congress loyal to the Raj. Statement 1 names the wrong contender: at Surat the presidency was fought between Lala Lajpat Rai and Rash Behari Ghosh, the Moderate who went on to preside at Madras in 1908. Dadabhai Naoroji had chaired the Calcutta session of 1906, the one both factions accepted.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — accepts Naoroji as the Moderate contender at Surat. He presided over Calcutta in 1906 precisely because both wings respected him; the man the Extremists fought in 1907 was Rash Behari Ghosh. (c) 1 and 3 only — carries the same misnaming of the presidency contest, and it sets aside the condition that actually broke the session: the Extremists would settle only if the four Calcutta resolutions were re-adopted. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — cannot stand, because statement 1 transplants the president of the 1906 Calcutta session into the 1907 Surat contest.
Memory hook: Naoroji chaired Calcutta 1906; at Surat it was Rai against Rash Behari Ghosh — four resolutions refused, then 'loyal to the Raj' in 1908.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Who was the principal of the Bengal National College, established in 1906 as part of the Extremists' National Education programme?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The Bengal National College was set up with Aurobindo Ghosh as principal, in response to the tightening of British university control under the Indian Universities Act, 1904.

Why others wrong: (a) led the Moderate-phase press campaign and the August 1905 Boycott Resolution, not the College; (c) formulated an earlier scheme of national education but did not head the Bengal National College; (d) founded ShantiNiketan Ashram (1901) and composed Amar Sonar Bangla, but was not principal here.
Memory hook: Aurobindo at the helm — College born from the Universities Act backlash.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Arrange the following events in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Publication of the Risley Papers
2. Calcutta Town Hall Boycott Resolution
3. Annulment of the Partition of Bengal
4. Surat Split
explanation: (A) ✓ — Risley Papers published in 1903; the Calcutta Town Hall Boycott Resolution was passed in August 1905; the Surat Split occurred in 1907; the Partition was annulled in December 1911 at the Delhi Durbar. Sequence: 1 → 2 → 4 → 3. and.
Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) misplace Risley (1903) and/or invert Surat (1907) and the Annulment (1911); only 1-2-4-3 fits the record timeline.
Memory hook: Risley → Town Hall → Surat → Durbar — publish, resolve, split, undo.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: With reference to the Extremists' methods during Swadeshi05-11, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Samitis filled an organisational gap left by the Moderate-led INC's absence at the ground level.
2. Picketing took the form of strikes inside foreign-owned enterprises led by C.R. Das.
3. Jatras were used to mobilise audiences who would not read newspapers.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 hold. Samitis such as the Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (1905) of Ashwini Kumar Dutt in Barisal supplied the ground-level organisation the Moderate-led Congress had never built, and jatras carried the nationalist message to audiences who would never read a newspaper. Statement 2 describes the wrong method: picketing meant physically preventing the sale of British goods at shops and liquor outlets, and its distinctive social weight came from drawing women into direct action. The strikes inside foreign-owned enterprises were a separate front, led by C.R. Das, Liaqat Hussain and B.C. Pal, aimed at the supply side rather than the shop counter.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — takes the strike description of picketing at face value. Picketing blocked sales at shops and liquor outlets and pulled women into the movement; strikes in foreign-owned firms were the separate supply-side method of C.R. Das, Liaqat Hussain and B.C. Pal. (b) 2 and 3 only — repeats that confusion of picketing with workers' strikes, and it discards the organisational point that mattered most: the Samitis existed because the Congress under the Moderates had no machinery below the level of annual sessions and newspapers. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — fails on the picketing description alone, since the shop-gate method and the factory strike were distinct tools with distinct leaders.
Memory hook: Samitis on the ground, jatras on the stage, women at the shop gate — the strikes inside foreign firms were C.R. Das's separate front.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (Leader)
items: 1. C.R. Das and B.C. Pal
2. Bal Gangadhar Tilak
3. Syed Haidar Raza

4. V.O. Chidambaram Pillai
List II (Region of Swadeshi Leadership)
A. Bombay
B. Madras
C. Delhi
D. Bengal
explanation: (A) ✓ — Per the record leader-region pairing: Bengal → C.R. Das & B.C. Pal; Bombay → Tilak; Delhi → Syed Haidar Raza; Madras → V.O. Chidambaram Pillai. Hence 1-D, 2-A, 3-C, 4-B.
Why others wrong: (b) swaps Bombay and Bengal; (c) swaps Bombay and Delhi; (d) places Das-Pal in Madras and VOC in Bengal — contradicting the record regional listing.
Memory hook: Das-Pal Bengal, Tilak Bombay, Raza Delhi, VOC Madras — four cardinals of Swadeshi.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: The Indian Universities Act, 1904 strengthened the Extremists' demand for national education because it

options.text: brought universities under direct government control
introduced English as the sole medium of instruction
imposed a fee structure favouring British students

explanation: (B) ✓ — The Indian Universities Act, 1904 brought universities under direct government control, motivated by Curzon's view that they were "factories of sedition." The Extremists responded by founding parallel institutions like the Bengal National College and the National Council of Education. and.
Why others wrong: (a) the Act did not abolish private universities; (c), (d) are not features the record attributes to the Act — these are distractor details not supported by.
Memory hook: 1904 collared the campus → Extremists built their own.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (Swadeshi-Era Enterprise / Institution)
items: 1. Tata Iron & Steel Company
2. Bengal Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals
3. Bombay Swadeshi Stores

4. Punjab National Bank
List II (Founder)
A. Bal Gangadhar Tilak and others
B. Dorabji Tata
C. Dyal Singh Majithia and Lala Harkishen Lal
D. P.C. Ray
matchTable: A. Bal Gangadhar Tilak and others
C. Dyal Singh Majithia and Lala Harkishen Lal
explanation: (A) ✓ — TISCO was conceived by Jamsetji Tata and established by Dorabji Tata in 1907; Bengal Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals was set up by P.C. Ray; Bombay Swadeshi Stores by Tilak and others; Punjab National Bank (1894) by Dyal Singh Majithia and Lala Harkishen Lal. Hence 1-B, 2-D, 3-A, 4-C.
Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) misalign at least one of the four founder-enterprise pairs explicitly listed's enterprise inventory.
Memory hook: Dorabji steel, Ray chemicals, Tilak stores, Majithia bank — four pillars of Swadeshi capital.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to the Swadeshi Movement's failure to become a proper mass movement, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Swadeshi goods were more expensive than imported British goods.
2. Some Extremists used force and social boycott against Lower Castes and Muslims who did not participate.
3. The Muslim League, dominated by elite Muslims like Syed Haidar Raza, supported the Partition.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 hold. Too few Swadeshi enterprises existed to meet demand, so Swadeshi goods stayed dearer than imported ones and the poor — Muslim ryots, Lower Castes and blue-collar workers — largely stayed out; where they stayed out, some student leaders and volunteers resorted to force and social boycott, which deepened alienation instead of building solidarity. Statement 3 attaches the wrong name to the League: its elite face was Nawab Salimullah of Dacca, whose circle welcomed the Partition and worked with the Ulamas. Syed Haidar Raza stood on the other side of the argument, leading the Swadeshi movement in Delhi.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 only — right on price but silent on coercion. When the poor did not join voluntarily, force and social boycott were used against Lower Castes and Muslims, which cost the movement the very participation it was trying to compel. (c) 1, 2 and 3 — accepts Syed Haidar Raza as a League notable. He was the Swadeshi movement's leader in Delhi; the League's elite leadership ran through Nawab Salimullah of Dacca and its allied Ulamas. (d) 2 and 3 only — carries that same misnaming and also sets aside the economic obstacle: with Swadeshi industry too thin to supply cheap goods, boycott asked the poorest to pay the most.
Memory hook: Costly cloth and coerced participation drove the masses off; the League's elite face was Salimullah of Dacca — Syed Haidar Raza was Swadeshi's man in Delhi.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Curzon's Partition of Bengal weakened the INM in Bengal primarily because

options.text: it shifted the capital from Calcutta to Delhi in 1905
it created two provinces on religious lines, leaving the Bengali Bhadralok a minority in both
it banned the Indian National Congress from holding sessions in Bengal
it imposed direct Crown rule on East Bengal

explanation: (B) ✓ — The Partition's communal design ensured Bengalis became a minority in Bengal (diluted by Bihar & Orissa) and Hindus became a minority in EBA, thereby shrinking the upper-caste Hindu Bhadralok base — the backbone of organised political activity in Bengal — in both new provinces simultaneously.
Why others wrong: (a) the capital shifted in 1911, not 1905, and was a later consequence; (c), (d) are not actions on record for this Partition.
Memory hook: Bhadralok diluted twice → INM base halved in one map-stroke.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Which one of the following is correctly described in the Chapter as the immediate cause for the launch of the Swadeshi Movement?

options.text: The Partition of Bengal by Curzon
The arrest of Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh

explanation: (A) ✓ — The Partition of Bengal (October 1905) by Curzon was the immediate trigger; Moderates had already passed a Boycott Resolution at Calcutta Town Hall in August 1905 in anticipation, and the Partition's formal effect on 16 October 1905 launched the movement. and.

Why others wrong: (b) Tilak's Mandalay deportation occurred in 1908, after the movement had already begun; (c) L.L. Rai-Ajit Singh's arrest was a separate Punjab episode and not the launch trigger; (d) the Universities Act was an underlying driver of Extremist rise, not the immediate launch cause for Swadeshi.
Memory hook: October 1905 — Partition lit the fuse the Town Hall had already laid.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: With reference to the impact of the Swadeshi Movement, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Rabindranath Tagore's "Amar Sonar Bangla" was written in protest against the Partition.
2. The capital of British India was shifted to Delhi in
3. Bande Mataram, composed by Rabindranath Tagore, became the anthem of the Indian National Movement.
questions.stemTail: 1911 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 hold. Tagore wrote 'Amar Sonar Bangla' in protest against the Partition, and it later became the national anthem of Bangladesh; the transfer of the capital to Delhi came in 1911, announced at the Delhi Durbar of December that year during the coronation of King George V, and it duly reduced Bengal's dominance in the national movement. Statement 3 credits the wrong author: Bande Mataram was composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in his novel Anandamath (1882), the same work that gave the idea of Bharat Mata, and it was that song — not Tagore's — which became the anthem of the movement.

Why others wrong: (b) 2 only — accepts the capital transfer but denies Tagore the song that is actually his. 'Amar Sonar Bangla' was written against the Partition and went on to become the national anthem of Bangladesh. (c) 1, 2 and 3 — hands Bande Mataram to Tagore. It came from Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's Anandamath (1882), the novel that also gave the concept of Bharat Mata. (d) 1 and 3 only — repeats that misattribution and additionally sets aside the political consequence the British extracted from the crisis: shifting the capital to Delhi in 1911 pulled the centre of power away from Bengal.
Memory hook: Tagore wrote Amar Sonar Bangla; Bankim wrote Bande Mataram in Anandamath — and the Durbar of 1911 moved the capital to Delhi.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar's book Desher Katha (1904) was significant because it

options.text: provided a constitutional blueprint for Indian self-government
advocated armed revolution against the British
used "Desh" to refer to the entire Indian subcontinent, not just Bengal
recorded the proceedings of the Surat Split

explanation: (C) ✓ — Desher Katha (1904) documented economic exploitation under British rule, and its key significance — flagged — is that Deuskar used "Desh" to mean the entire Indian subcontinent, not just Bengal, building a pan-Indian economic consciousness against colonial drain at a time when political organisation was still largely provincial.
Why others wrong: (a) it offered no constitutional blueprint; (b) the book was an economic critique, not a call for armed revolution; (d) it preceded the Surat Split (1907) by three years.
Memory hook: "Desh" stretched from Bengal to all of India — Deuskar's pan-Indian word.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The Partition of Bengal (1905) was not an administrative necessity but an act of communal engineering." Critically examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" asks you to argue both sides & then judge. The anchor is Bengal — announced July 1905, effected 16 October 1905, under Curzon99-05. The framing phrase "not an administrative necessity" bars a one-sided answer: state the British case fairly first, then weigh the evidence for communal engineering.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Partition of Bengal was announced in July 1905 & effected on 16 October 1905. The British called it administrative necessity. Indians read it as communal engineering.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. The official British case (see 'Bengal Partition (Announced July 1905 / Effected 16 October 1905)'). Undivided Bengal was the most populous province in India & covered a massive area — too large, the British argued, for one administration. Three specific gains were offered: Assam would grow & finally get its own civil services cadre inside a proper Lieutenant-Governor province; Assam-Bengal Railways would come under the unified administration of the new EBA; Assam's tea gardens would gain a cheaper maritime outlet via Chittagong port.

2. Redrawing Bengal was not new (same section). 1765 — Diwani of Bengal Suba. 1801 — half of Awadh ceded under the Treaty of Lucknow 1801 became the Ceded Provinces. 1803 — Orissa after the Bhonsle of Nagpur was defeated in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War. 1826 — Assam annexed under the Treaty of Yandobo. 1836 — NWP1836 carved out. 1874 — Assam made a separate CC Province. From 1874 to 1905 the Bengal Presidency was Bengal + Orissa + Bihar. Precedent is the strongest plank of the administrative case.

3. The line they chose to draw (same section). If better administration was the goal, the logical solution was to reorganise Bengal on linguistic lines — not religious ones. Instead 1905 created Bengal (WB + Bihar + Orissa) & East Bengal & Assam (EB + Assam), split along the Hindu-Muslim demographic fault line. This is where the administrative logic breaks.

4. The target was the Bhadralok (same section). The INM in Bengal was led by the Bengali Bhadralok — upper-caste Hindu educated professionals who were the backbone of organised politics there. After Partition, Bengalis became a minority in Bengal & Hindus a minority in EBA. The INM's support base shrank in both provinces at once.

5. Appeasing elite Muslims (same section). EBA was designed as a new Muslim Majority Province. Nawab Salimullah of Dacca & the elite Muslim leadership welcomed it. ML1906, formed a year later in 1906, supported the Partition & worked with the Ulamas who controlled the Muslim masses — closing off joint Hindu-Muslim resistance. The backdrop was rising Hindu cultural nationalism since the 1880s — Anandamath (1882), the Ganapati Festival (1893), the Shivaji Festival (1896).

6. Judge the claim by its outcome (see 'Impact of the Swadeshi Movement and the Curzonian Administration'). The Partition was annulled in 1911, yet the capital was shifted to Delhi — announced at the Delhi Durbar, December 1911 — reducing Bengal's dominance in the INM. Curzon99-05 got his strategic outcome anyway. The birth of ML1906 marked the formal & organised beginning of communal politics in India.
Closing verdict: The administrative necessity was real but secondary. The line was drawn on religion, not language — so the Partition of Bengal was communal engineering.

Impact of the Swadeshi Movement and the Curzonian Administration

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: How far did the legislation of Lord Curzon between 1899 and 1905 make the rise of Extremism in Indian politics unavoidable?
body: Demand of the question: "How far" wants a graded answer, not a yes or no. Take the three laws one by one & show what each attacked. Then test the word "unavoidable" against the other drivers of Extremist rise. The window is fixed at 1899 to 1905, so treat later events as consequence, not cause.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Between 1899 and 1905 three laws of Lord Curzon struck local self-government, education & the press. They made the rise of Extremism likely, though not yet unavoidable.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. Local self-governance (see 'The Swadeshi Movement (Swadeshi05-11) — Context and Causes'). The Calcutta Municipal Corporation Amendment Act, 1899 reduced the number of elected members in municipalities. In one move it rolled back the limited representative participation Indians had managed to win in local governance.

2. Education (same section). The Indian Universities Act, 1904 brought universities under direct government control. Curzon99-05's stated reasoning was that Indian universities were becoming factories of sedition — centres producing graduates who questioned British authority. His answer was to clamp down rather than engage. The Extremist reply was National Education: see 'iii) National Education' for the Bengal National College with Aurobindo as principal, the National Council of Education & the Bengal Technical Institute.

3. The press (same section). The Indian Official Secrets Amendment Act, 1904 gave the government power to censor & confiscate any publication that hurt the interests of the British Empire. It made communicating any official secret a criminal offence & defined 'official secret' broadly. It stayed in force until the Indian Official Secrets Act, 1923.

4. Why the three together mattered (see 'Drivers of Extremist Rise'). Each law attacked a different pillar of Indian public life — local self-governance, education & the press. Together they formed a chain of failures in British governance & proved to politically aware Indians that the colonial administration would not reform itself voluntarily. The message mattered more than any single clause.

5. The limits of the claim (see 'Reason 1: The Moderates had failed.'). Extremism had older roots. The Moderates had led the INC since 1885 on petition, prayer & press, & by the early 1900s had won nothing concrete — no self-governance, no economic relief, no political power. Tilak's Ganapati Festival (1893) & Shivaji Festival (1896) had already built a mass-mobilisation method the Moderates never had. The final trigger also sat outside the statute book — the Partition announced July 1905 & effected 16 October 1905 (see 'Bengal Partition (Announced July 1905 / Effected 16 October 1905)').
Closing verdict: The legislation of Lord Curzon between 1899 and 1905 fixed the timing of the rise of Extremism. The failure of the Moderates made it unavoidable.
revise: The Swadeshi Movement (Swadeshi05-11) — Context and Causes

questions.label: FYQ_M.3
questions.stem: The Swadeshi Movement (1905-11) was the first attempt at mass politics in the history of the Indian National Congress. Examine why that attempt fell short of becoming a proper mass movement.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine why" demands a causes analysis, not a narrative of events. The anchor runs from the Partition of 1905 to the annulment of 1911. The phrase "fell short" means you must first grant the scale of what was attempted, then account for the shortfall — economic, social & organisational.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Swadeshi Movement (1905-11) was the first attempt at mass politics by the INC. It reached past the WEMC, yet fell short of a proper mass movement.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. The scale of the attempt (see 'Events During the Swadeshi Movement'). Moderates like SNB & C.R. Das ran the early press campaign through Bengalee, Sanjibani & Hitabadi, & passed the Boycott resolution at Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905. The Extremists then widened the goal to Swaraj & the method to Passive Resistance, & took the movement out of Bengal — Tilak in Bombay, Syed Haidar Raza in Delhi, L.L. Rai & Ajit Singh in Punjab, V.O. Chidambaram Pillai in Madras.

2. The organisational base was thin (see 'Methods of the Extremists During Swadeshi05-11'). The INC under the Moderates had no ground-level structure. Samitis filled the gap — the Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (1905) of Ashwini Kumar Dutt in Barisal did Constructive Work among Muslim ryots & organised the Barisal Conference 1906. Alongside came picketing that drew in women, Jatras, Prabhat Pheris & workers' strikes in foreign-owned enterprises led by C.R. Das, Liaqat Hussain & B.C. Pal. But such bodies were few relative to the ambition.

3. Boycott without a supply base (see 'Why the Swadeshi Movement Did Not Become a Proper Mass Movement'). Not enough Swadeshi enterprises existed to meet demand at affordable prices, so Swadeshi goods were costlier. Participation by the poor stayed low — Muslim ryots, Lower Castes & blue-collar workers. Arbitration courts, schools & enterprises all remained thin. Check the real scale in 'iv) Swadeshi Enterprises': TISCO established by Dorabji Tata in 1907, the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (1906) of V.O. Chidambaram Pillai at Tuticorin, PNB (1894) & the Lakshmi Insurance Company (1906).

4. Coercion in place of persuasion (same section). When Lower Castes & Muslims did not join voluntarily, some student leaders & volunteers used force & social boycott to compel them. That deepened alienation instead of building solidarity — the recurring pattern of UC leadership producing low LC participation.

5. Low Muslim participation (same section). Jatras sometimes depicted Muslims & the British as collaborators. ML1906, dominated by elite Muslims like Nawab Salimullah of Dacca, supported the Partition & partnered with the Ulamas who controlled the Muslim masses. Heavy Hindu symbolism — from Bande Mataram to Kali worship — completed the distance.

6. Leadership priorities & repression (same section). The Extremists spent more energy capturing the INC than building the movement. After the Surat Split of 1907 the leadership was scattered — Tilak deported to Mandalay (1908-14), Aurobindo retired from active politics, B.C. Pal retired temporarily, L.L. Rai abroad from 1914 to 1920. Imports of British goods were not significantly impacted, & from 1908 to 1911 the Revolutionaries rose in the vacuum.
Closing verdict: The first attempt at mass politics fell short because Boycott had no supply base & the movement's symbols excluded the very masses it needed.
revise: Methods of the Extremists During Swadeshi05-11
Why the Swadeshi Movement Did Not Become a Proper Mass Movement

questions.label: FYQ_M.4
questions.stem: "At Surat in 1907 the Congress split over method, not over goal." Comment.
body: Demand of the question: "Comment" asks for a short, reasoned judgement on one proposition. Test what both factions actually wanted against how they differed. The anchor is the 1907 Surat session, with the 1906 Calcutta session as the necessary background. Do not narrate the whole Swadeshi Movement.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Both wings of the INC wanted Swaraj. At Surat in 1907 they split over method — petition against confrontation — not over goal.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The goal was shared (see 'The Surat Split (1907)'). Both factions wanted Swaraj. Moderates believed in petition, Extremists in confrontation. The Bombay-based Moderates opposed Extremist methods on principle — they feared confrontation would provoke British repression & damage the constitutional progress they believed in.

2. Calcutta 1906 set the terms (same section). The 1906 session at Calcutta, with Dadabhai Naoroji as President, passed four resolutions — Swaraj as the goal, then '7.2) Boycott (as method)', '7.3) Swadeshi (as method)' & '7.4) National Education (as method)'. Three of the four are methods. The Bengal Partition was separately condemned. Tilak also set up an Extremist party inside the INC to convert it from within.

3. The rupture itself (same section). The 1907 session was moved from Poona or Nagpur — both Extremist strongholds — to Surat, where the Moderates had control. The flashpoint was the presidency: L.L. Rai against Rash Behari Ghosh. L.L. Rai withdrew to prevent a split, but the Extremists refused any compromise unless the four Calcutta resolutions were re-adopted. The session collapsed & the Extremists were expelled.

4. What the split cost (same section). Morley's Budget speech of 1906 had hinted at council reforms, giving the British a Divide & Rule opening. In 1908 the Allahabad Convention (Mehta Congress) declared loyalty to the Raj, & the annual session met at Madras with Rash Behari Ghosh as President. The division lasted until 1920. The Extremists re-entered in 1916, but re-entry did not end the disagreement over method.
Closing verdict: The Congress split over method, not over goal. That is why re-entry in 1916 settled nothing & only Gandhi's new method reunited it in 1920.

questions.label: FYQ_M.5
questions.stem: "In the methods of mass politics Mahatma Gandhi inherited a tested toolkit, not a blank slate." Evaluate this statement with reference to the Swadeshi Movement (1905-11).
body: Demand of the question: "Evaluate" asks you to weigh the claim & deliver a judgement. Identify method by method what the Swadeshi years actually tested & handed on. Then ask what they failed to hand on. The time anchor runs from 1905 to Gandhi's arrival at the head of the INC in 1920.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Swadeshi Movement (1905-11) was the laboratory of Indian mass politics. Gandhi inherited a tested toolkit — Boycott, Non Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Constructive Work — not a blank slate.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. The methods handed on (see 'Impact of the Swadeshi Movement and the Curzonian Administration'). The Swadeshi period tested Passive Resistance in the form of Non Cooperation (NC) & Civil Disobedience (CD), Constructive Work (CW), the use of theatre & plays (Jatras) & Prabhat Pheris. All of these were later highly used by Mahatma Gandhi.

2. Institutions & enterprise (see 'iii) National Education' & 'iv) Swadeshi Enterprises'). The Bengal National College with Aurobindo as principal, the National Council of Education & the Bengal Technical Institute; TISCO conceived by Jamsetji Tata & established by Dorabji Tata in 1907; BCPL by P.C. Ray; the Bombay Swadeshi Stores of Tilak; the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (1906) of V.O. Chidambaram Pillai at Tuticorin. Constructive Programme had a working precedent.

3. The idea of the masses (see 'Impact of the Swadeshi Movement and the Curzonian Administration'). For the first time the INM tried to involve not just the WEMC but the Working Class (WC), the masses & ordinary people. The attempt was incomplete, but the Working Class movement & Revolutionary activities both grew from this foundation.

4. The economic argument & the symbols (same section). To convince poor buyers to pay more for Swadeshi goods, the Extremists had to explain Drain of Wealth in simple language — that economic education was itself a lasting contribution, & Boycott became a major tool of the future INM. Bande Mataram became the anthem of the INM; Tagore's 'Amar Sonar Bangla', written against the Partition, later became the national anthem of Bangladesh.

5. What was not handed on (see 'Why the Swadeshi Movement Did Not Become a Proper Mass Movement'). The toolkit arrived with unsolved problems — costlier Swadeshi goods, force & social boycott used against Lower Castes & Muslims, & low Muslim participation. Note also that only the INM shifted to mass action: the INC itself stayed under Moderate control until the 1920 Nagpur Session.
Closing verdict: Gandhi inherited a tested toolkit, not a blank slate. What he added was a method that could hold the masses the Swadeshi Movement had lost.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: The Barrah Dacoity was the first major venture of the revolutionary terrorists of the freedom movement in
explanation: (C) ✓ — Simultaneously, a massive and distinct offshoot was growing in East Bengal: in 1906, the Dacca Anushilan Samiti was founded by Pulin Behari Das, with the backing of P.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Bombay-Karnataka stream of revolution ran through Savarkar's Abhinav Bharat — the Barrah dacoity was not its work; the raid belonged to East Bengal's Dacca Anushilan network.

(B) ✗ — Punjab's revolutionary surge came later (the wartime Ghadar current); the first major dacoity venture was East Bengal's — the Barrah raid, masterminded by Pulin Behari Das of the Dacca Anushilan Samiti.
(D) ✗ — The Madras Presidency was not a centre of the early revolutionary-dacoity phase; the Barrah treasury raid took place in East Bengal, the Dacca Anushilan's home ground.
(Note: Barrah dacoity took place at Barrah in East Bengal region in which state treasury was looted. Pulin Behari Das was the master mind behind this conspiracy.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists.
explanation: (A) ✓ — The correct pairs: Shyamji Krishna Varma → The Indian Sociologist — the journal that laid the foundation of militant Indian nationalist movement in Britain; Madam Bhikaji Cama → The Talwar (her Paris-published revolutionary paper); Annie Besant → Commonwealth (her Home Rule-era journal); Aurobindo Ghosh → Bande Mataram.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Every pair fails: it gives Varma the Talwar and Cama the Indian Sociologist, then hands Besant Bande Mataram and Aurobindo the Commonwealth — all four reassigned wrongly.
(C) ✗ — The first two pairs are right but the last two are swapped: Bande Mataram was Aurobindo's paper, not Besant's; Commonwealth was Besant's, not Aurobindo's.
(D) ✗ — Swaps the Varma-Cama journals (the Indian Sociologist was Varma's London journal) while keeping the Besant-Aurobindo pairs.
(Note: Shyamji Krishna Varma — India House | Madam Bhikaji Cama — The Talwar | Annie Besant — Commonwealth | Aurobindo Ghosh — Bande Mataram)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: Abhinava Bharat a secret society of revolutionaries was organised by
explanation: (B) ✓ — Savarkar saw a direct parallel between Austrian colonialism over Italy and British colonialism over India.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Khudiram Bose was the Muzaffarpur bomb-thrower — arrested, tried, and executed — an operative of the Bengal stream, not the founder of Abhinav Bharat.
(C) ✗ — Prafulla Chaki was Khudiram's partner in the Muzaffarpur action — again Bengal's Anushilan world, not the western-India society Savarkar built.
(D) ✗ — Bhagat Singh belongs to the LATER revolutionary generation of the 1920s — two decades after Abhinav Bharat's founding.
(Note: Abhinav Bharat society also known as Young India Society was founded by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and his brother Ganesh Damodar Savarkar in 1903.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: The native state of Tripura became involved in the Freedom Movement early in the 20th century because

options.text: the kings of Tripura were always anti-British
the Bengal revolutionaries took shelter in Tripura
the tribes of the state were fiercely freedom loving
there were already some groups fighting again the kingship and its protector, the British

explanation: (B) ✓ — The Birth of Organised Militant Nationalism in Bengal (1902 onwards) The roots of organised militant nationalism in Bengal trace back to 1902, when Pramathanath Mitra (P.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Tripura's kings were princely rulers under British paramountcy, not standing rebels; the recorded link is geography — refuge for the Bengal revolutionaries next door.
(C) ✗ — Tribal temperament is not the recorded reason; Tripura entered the story as a SHELTER for the Bengal revolutionaries operating across the border.
(D) ✗ — No anti-kingship insurgency drives the record account; Tripura's early involvement came from hosting the hunted revolutionaries of Bengal's network.
(Note: The native state Tripura became involved in the Freedom Movement early in the 20th century as many of Bengali Revolutionaries who took shelter in Tripura.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Who founded the Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta in 1902?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Pramathanath Mitra (P. Mitra) founded the Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta in 1902 as a body for physical training & character building, whose inner purpose was to cultivate the spirit of armed resistance.

Why others wrong: (a) Pulin Behari Das founded the Dacca Anushilan Samiti in 1906, not the Calcutta Samiti of 1902; (b) Barindra Kumar Ghosh was one of the founders of the Jugantar newspaper, not of the Anushilan Samiti; (d) Bhupendranath Datta was a co-founder of the Jugantar newspaper, not of the Anushilan Samiti.
Memory hook: P. Mitra plants the seed (1902), Pulin Das grows the Dacca tree (1906).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Where did Madame Bhikaji Cama unfurl the first version of the Indian national flag in August 1907?
explanation: (C) ✓ — In August 1907, Madame Bhikaji Cama unfurled the first version of the Indian national flag at the International Socialist Congress in Stuttgart, Germany — a dramatic assertion of Indian sovereignty on a global stage, years before any official tricolour was adopted.

Why others wrong: (a) Paris was Madame Cama's operating base for revolutionary work, but the flag was unfurled at the Stuttgart Congress, not in Paris; (b) London hosted India House under Shyamji Krishna Varma & Savarkar, not the flag-unfurling event; (d) Geneva is unconnected with the 1907 flag event.
Memory hook: Stuttgart 1907 — Cama plants India's first flag on foreign soil.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS) founded in 1905:
items: 1. It was founded in London by Shyamji Krishna Varma.
2. Only Indians could become its members.
3. Its propaganda journal in Britain was the weekly Jugantar.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 hold: Shyamji Krishna Varma founded the society in London in 1905, and membership was open to Indians alone. Statement 3 puts the wrong paper in its hands — the society's organ in Britain was The Indian Sociologist, whose name misleads because it was not socialist in ideology, while Jugantar was the Calcutta weekly built around Barindra Kumar Ghosh, Bhupendranath Datta and Abinash Bhattacharya. The society's real London instrument was India House, the student hostel that actively pushed nationalist views.

Why others wrong: (b) endorses statement 3 while dropping the founding fact, but Jugantar belonged to the Bengal revolutionaries and never served as this London society's mouthpiece; The Indian Sociologist did, and Shyamji Krishna Varma did found the society in London. (c) accepts the same misplaced journal and also throws out statement 2, though the rule that only Indians could become members was one of the society's defining features. (d) sweeps in statement 3 unexamined; the society's propaganda in Britain ran through The Indian Sociologist and India House, not through a Calcutta weekly.
Memory hook: IHRS 1905 — London, Indians only, India House hostel; its paper was The Indian Sociologist, while Jugantar belonged to Bengal.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: With reference to the Alipore Conspiracy Case of 1908, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Aurobindo Ghosh was convicted and transported to the Cellular Jail.
Barindra Kumar Ghosh was acquitted while Aurobindo was sentenced to death.
Aurobindo Ghosh was acquitted, while Barindra Kumar Ghosh was transported to the Cellular Jail.
Both Aurobindo and Barindra were acquitted on grounds of insufficient evidence.

explanation: (C) ✓ — In the Alipore Conspiracy Case (1908), Aurobindo Ghosh was acquitted because B.C. Pal refused to testify; he later escaped to Pondicherry. Barindra Kumar Ghosh & Ullaskar Dutta were found guilty & sentenced to death, later commuted to transportation for life in the Cellular Jail.

Why others wrong: (a) Aurobindo was acquitted, not transported; (b) the positions are reversed — Aurobindo was acquitted, Barindra was sentenced; (d) Barindra was not acquitted — he was transported for life.
Memory hook: Alipore — Aurobindo escapes to Pondicherry, Barindra to Kala Pani.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following pairs of revolutionary organisations and their founders:
items: 1. Abhinav Bharat — Savarkar brothers
2. Dacca Anushilan Samiti — Pulin Behari Das
3. Mitra Mela — Pramathanath Mitra
questions.stemTail: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Pairs 1 and 2 are correct. Abhinav Bharat (1904, Pune) was the renamed Mitra Mela set up by the Savarkar brothers Vinayak & Ganesh. The Dacca Anushilan Samiti was founded in 1906 by Pulin Behari Das. Pair 3 is wrong — Mitra Mela was founded by the Savarkar brothers in Nasik in 1899, not by Pramathanath Mitra.
Why others wrong: (a) undercounts — two pairs are correct; (c) Mitra Mela was a Savarkar creation, not P. Mitra's; (d) at least two pairs are correctly matched.
Memory hook: Mitra Mela = Savarkar brothers' baby; P. Mitra fathered the Calcutta Anushilan, not Mitra Mela.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the 1908 Muzzafarpur Conspiracy Case:
items: 1. The intended target was Magistrate Kingsford.
2. Prafulla Chaki was sentenced to transportation for life.
3. Khudiram Bose was awarded the death sentence.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 stand: the bomb was thrown at Magistrate Kingsford's carriage, though he was not inside and two English women died instead, and Khudiram Bose was arrested, tried and given the death sentence. Statement 2 borrows the Alipore punishment — Chaki never faced a court at all, shooting himself in the mouth with his own revolver to avoid capture. Transportation for life to the Cellular Jail was the fate of Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Ullaskar Dutta after their death sentences were commuted.

Why others wrong: (a) treats statement 2 as sound, but no sentence of any kind was ever passed on Chaki; he killed himself with his own revolver rather than be taken alive. (c) repeats that error about Chaki's end and additionally rejects statement 1, although Kingsford was precisely the intended target — the bomb was aimed at his carriage and missed him only because he was not in it. (d) accepts every statement including the transported-for-life claim, which belongs to the Alipore convicts sent to the Andamans, not to a man who died at Muzzafarpur.
Memory hook: Muzzafarpur — Kingsford targeted, Chaki's own revolver, Khudiram hanged; the Cellular Jail was Alipore's punishment, not this case's.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists:
List I (Revolutionary Action)
A. Killing of Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie
B. Killing of District Magistrate Jackson
C. Attempt on Viceroy Hardinge in Chandni Chowk
D. Bomb thrown at Magistrate Kingsford's carriage
List II (Person/Place)
items: 1. Anant Laxman Kanhere (Nasik)
2. Rash Behari Bose (Delhi)
3. Madan Lal Dhingra (London)
4. Prafulla Chaki & Khudiram Bose (Muzzafarpur)
matchTable: A. Killing of Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie
B. Killing of District Magistrate Jackson
C. Attempt on Viceroy Hardinge in Chandni Chowk
D. Bomb thrown at Magistrate Kingsford's carriage
explanation: (A) ✓ — A-3: Madan Lal Dhingra killed Curzon-Wyllie in London (1909). B-1: Anant Laxman Kanhere killed Magistrate Jackson in the Nasik Conspiracy Case (1909). C-2: Rash Behari Bose threw a bomb at Viceroy Hardinge in Chandni Chowk during the 1911 capital-shift procession (Delhi Conspiracy Case, 1912). D-4: Prafulla Chaki & Khudiram Bose threw the bomb at Kingsford's carriage in Muzzafarpur., 3.6 (Key Revolutionary Actions) &.

Why others wrong: (b) swaps A and B incorrectly — Dhingra targeted Curzon-Wyllie, not Jackson; (c) gets C-4 wrong — Rash Behari Bose targeted Hardinge, not Kingsford; (d) wrongly pairs A with Rash Behari Bose.
Memory hook: D-J-H-K — Dhingra-Jackson-Hardinge-Kingsford fall in 1909-09-11-08.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Why was Bal Gangadhar Tilak charged with sedition and deported to Mandalay in 1908?

options.text: For directly funding the Muzzafarpur bombing through the Kesari trust.
For writing an article titled 'Arrival of Bomb' in Kesari, defending the revolutionaries.
For organising the Alipore conspirators from Pune.
For demanding Swaraj at the 1907 Surat Congress.

explanation: (B) ✓ — In his newspaper Kesari, Tilak condemned the violence of Prafulla Chaki & Khudiram Bose but defended them on the deeper ground that sustained oppression will produce violence; the article was titled 'Arrival of Bomb.' This nuanced position was enough for the colonial government to charge him with sedition — six years' imprisonment, deported to Mandalay.

Why others wrong: (a) Tilak did not fund the Muzzafarpur bombing; the charge was sedition through his Kesari article; (c) Tilak was not an organiser of the Alipore conspirators; (d) the Surat split (1907) was an INC internal split, not the cause of the sedition trial.
Memory hook: 'Arrival of Bomb' — Tilak's pen, not pistol, sent him to Mandalay.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the operational distinction between the Jugantar and the Dacca Anushilan Samiti:
items: 1. Jugantar operated as a loose, decentralized confederation of local revolutionary groups.
2. The Dacca Anushilan Samiti was rigidly hierarchical & highly centralised.
3. The Dacca Anushilan Samiti specialised in immediate spectacular acts of assassination.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Jugantar was a loose, decentralized confederation; the Dacca Anushilan Samiti under Pulin Behari Das was rigidly hierarchical, highly centralised, & strictly disciplined. Statement 3 is wrong — it was Jugantar that practised 'propaganda of the deed' (immediate spectacular assassinations); the Dacca Samiti was built for long-term military preparation & mass action.
Why others wrong: (b) statement 3 is wrong & statement 2 is correct; (c) statement 3 is wrong & statement 1 is correct; (d) statement 3 is wrong.
Memory hook: Jugantar = loud & loose; Dacca = quiet & coiled spring.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists:
List I (Revolutionary)
A. Shyamji Krishna Varma
B. Madame Bhikaji Cama
C. Veer Savarkar
D. Lala Hardayal
List II (Base Abroad)
items: 1. United States
2. London (IHRS founder)
3. Paris
4. London (Abhinav Bharat branch from 1906)
explanation: (A) ✓ — A-2: Shyamji Krishna Varma founded the IHRS in London in 1905. B-3: Madame Bhikaji Cama operated from Paris. C-4: Veer Savarkar opened the Abhinav Bharat branch in London from 1906. D-1: Lala Hardayal eventually reached the United States where he became a key organiser.
Why others wrong: (b) swaps Shyamji & Savarkar's London roles incorrectly; (c) wrongly places Cama in the US and Hardayal in Paris; (d) wrongly places Shyamji in Paris and Cama in London.
Memory hook: Shyamji & Savarkar in London, Cama in Paris, Hardayal sails to USA.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to the formal establishment of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) by the colonial government, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The CID was set up in 1903 on the recommendations of the Fraser Police Commission of 1902.
The CID was set up under the Indian Police Act of 1861 itself.
The CID was established in 1905 in response to the Swadeshi Movement.
The CID was established in 1908 after the Alipore Conspiracy Case.

explanation: (A) ✓ — The colonial government formally established the CID in 1903, following the recommendations of the Fraser Police Commission of 1902 — a specialised intelligence apparatus beyond the foundational Indian Police Act of 1861, designed to track, infiltrate, and dismantle political dissent & secret societies.

Why others wrong: (b) the Indian Police Act of 1861 was foundational policing law — the CID was a separate specialised body set up later; (c) the CID precedes the Swadeshi Movement & was set up in 1903, not 1905; (d) the CID was already operating five years before the Alipore Case (1908).
Memory hook: Fraser Commission 1902 -> CID 1903 — the spy machine before the bombs.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about Veer Savarkar:
items: 1. He renamed Mitra Mela as Abhinav Bharat in 1904 in Pune.
2. He compiled Mazzini Charitra in 1906 in London.
3. He was sentenced to transportation for life in 1910 in connection with the Nasik Conspiracy Case.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — All three statements are correct. The Savarkar brothers set up Mitra Mela in 1899 in Nasik, renamed it Abhinav Bharat in 1904 in Pune. In London, Savarkar compiled Mazzini Charitra (1906). He was sentenced to transportation for life in 1910 in connection with the Nasik Conspiracy Case (1909). &.
Why others wrong: (a) omits statement 3 which is correct; (b) omits statement 1 which is correct; (c) omits statement 2 which is correct.
Memory hook: Mela -> Abhinav Bharat (1904) -> Mazzini (1906) -> Cellular Jail (1910).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Why is any UPSC option linking Barindra Kumar Ghosh to the Ghadar Movement (1913–15) considered an elimination trap?

options.text: Because Barindra Kumar Ghosh died in 1908 in the Muzzafarpur bombing.
Because Barindra Kumar Ghosh had been transported to the Cellular Jail from 1908 onwards.
Because Barindra Kumar Ghosh joined the INC moderates after his acquittal.
Because Barindra Kumar Ghosh moved to Pondicherry with his brother Aurobindo and renounced politics.

explanation: (B) ✓ — Barindra Kumar Ghosh was sentenced & transported to the Cellular Jail from 1908 onwards (after the Alipore Case). This means he could not have been a participant in the Ghadar Movement (1913–15) — any UPSC option linking him to Ghadar is an elimination trap, since once transported he was cut off from all revolutionary activity on the mainland.

Why others wrong: (a) Barindra did not die in the Muzzafarpur bombing — that was a separate event in which Chaki shot himself and Khudiram was hanged; (c) Barindra did not join the INC moderates — he was transported for life; (d) Aurobindo escaped to Pondicherry, not Barindra.
Memory hook: Barindra in Kala Pani from 1908 — cannot be in Ghadar's 1913 ship.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Consider the following statements concerning the aftermath of the Revolutionary phase:
items: 1. In 1911, the Partition of Bengal was annulled and Assam was made a full province.
2. The capital shift was announced at the Delhi Durbar of December 1911 where King George V & Queen Mary were coronated.
3. In 1912, the province of 'Bihar & Orissa' was separated from Bengal Presidency.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statements 2 and 3 stand: the move of the capital was announced at the Delhi Durbar of December 1911, where King George V and Queen Mary were coronated as Emperor and Empress, and 'Bihar & Orissa' was separated from the Bengal Presidency in 1912. Statement 1 pulls a 1912 change back by a year — 1911 brought the annulment of the Partition and the shift of the capital to Delhi, while Assam was raised from the old 'East Bengal & Assam' arrangement into a full province only in 1912, having been a Chief Commissioner's province since 1874.

Why others wrong: (a) keeps statement 1, but the elevation of Assam into a full province came with the 1912 tidying up of Bengal's territory; what 1911 delivered was the annulment and the new capital. (c) carries the same one-year slip in statement 1, dating to 1911 a provincial reorganisation that followed only after the capital had already moved. (d) repeats that error and additionally discards statement 2, which correctly fixes the announcement at the December 1911 Delhi Durbar where George V and Queen Mary were coronated.
Memory hook: 1911 = Partition annulled + Delhi Durbar capital shift; 1912 = Bihar & Orissa split off and Assam raised to full province.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: How is Rash Behari Bose linked to the formation of the first Indian National Army (INA)?

options.text: He personally led the first INA into Imphal-Kohima in 1944.
He convened Tokyo & Bangkok conferences in 1942 to form the Indian Independence League (IIL), which backed Mohan Singh's INA.
He founded the Ghadar Party in San Francisco in 1913 and later transferred its cadres to the first INA.
He handed over the INA directly to Subhas Chandra Bose in 1942 in Singapore.

explanation: (B) ✓ — After the Delhi Conspiracy Case (1912), Rash Behari Bose escaped to Japan in 1915 & later, in 1942, convened conferences in Tokyo & Bangkok to establish the Indian Independence League (IIL). It was under the political backing & guidance of his IIL that Captain Mohan Singh organised Indian POWs (captured by the Japanese) into the first INA.

Why others wrong: (a) Rash Behari Bose did not lead the INA into Imphal-Kohima — by then Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose led the reorganised Azad Hind Fauj; (c) the Ghadar Party in San Francisco was founded by Lala Hardayal, not Rash Behari Bose; (d) he handed over INA leadership to Subhas Chandra Bose in 1943, not directly in 1942, and after taking it over himself following Mohan Singh's arrest.
Memory hook: Rash Behari: Delhi 1912 -> Japan 1915 -> IIL 1942 -> hands INA baton to Netaji 1943.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The revolutionaries of 1907-12 failed in every objective they set themselves, yet they restored to Indians a sense of pride & dignity." Critically examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" wants a two-sided verdict - concede the failure first, then test whether the psychological gain was real. The time anchor 1907-12 runs from the failed attempt on the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal to the Delhi Conspiracy Case, 1912. The phrase "every objective they set themselves" fixes your method: state their own stated goals, then measure the record against those goals, not against ours.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The revolutionaries of 1907-12 wanted to repeat 1857. They failed in every objective they set themselves, yet they restored to Indians a sense of pride & dignity.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. What they set out to do (see 'Rise of Revolutionaries'). By 1908 the Swadeshi Movement was leaderless - Extremist leaders arrested, deported or forced into exile. The long-term goal was to repeat 1857: start a civil rebellion & cause disaffection within the army. The immediate method was individual heroic action - assassinate hated British officials, use the public trial as propaganda, treat a death sentence as supreme sacrifice.

2. The network they built (see 'Organisational Network of the Revolutionaries'). Anushilan Samiti, founded 1902 in Calcutta by Pramathanath Mitra. Jugantar (1906) around the newspaper of Barindra Kumar Ghosh, Bhupendranath Datta & Abinash Bhattacharya. Dacca Anushilan Samiti (1906) under Pulin Behari Das. Abhinav Bharat (1904), renamed from Mitra Mela (1899, Nasik). Note the split - Jugantar was loose & decentralised, Dhaka Anushilan rigidly centralised.

3. The record of failure (see 'Key Revolutionary Actions'). The 1907 attempt on the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal failed.
