At Muzzafarpur (1908) Kingsford was not in the carriage - two English women were killed instead. In 1912 Rash Behari Bose's bomb wounded but did not kill Hardinge10-16. No army disaffection followed. No 1857 followed.

4. Repression worked (see '1908 Alipore Conspiracy Case (also: MurariPukur / ManickTolla Conspiracy Case)'). The CID was established in 1903 on the Fraser Police Commission of 1902 recommendations - machinery, not just law. Alipore decimated the Jugantar leadership: Barindra Kumar Ghosh & Ullaskar Dutta were transported for life to the Cellular Jail. Aurobindo, defended by C.R. Das, escaped to Pondicherry. Tilak got six years & Mandalay (1908); Savarkar transportation for life (1910).

5. The other side of the ledger (see 'Result of the Revolutionary Phase'). Indians were shown to be active agents, not passive subjects. Khudiram Bose was executed at 18 - the deterrent created a martyr instead. Many contemporaries felt the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 were partly British anxiety about revolutionary spread. The 1911 annulment of Bengal Partition came in the same climate.

6. The long tail (see 'Delhi Conspiracy Case, 1912'). Rash Behari Bose later led the Ghadar Movement (1913-15), escaped to Japan in 1915, convened the Tokyo & Bangkok conferences of 1942 & founded the Indian Independence League - the political cover under which Mohan Singh raised the first INA. The generation was repressed, not erased.
Closing verdict: Measured against every objective they set themselves, the revolutionaries of 1907-12 failed. Measured by the sense of pride & dignity they restored, they did not.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Evaluate the role of the Indian Home Rule Society (1905) & India House in laying the foundation of the militant Indian nationalist movement in Britain.
body: Demand of the question: "Evaluate" asks for a judgement on how much these two bodies actually delivered - so weigh the propaganda work against the armed action that followed from it. The place & time anchor is London between 1905 & 1910. The phrase "laying the foundation" tells you to trace what was built on top, not merely list the Society's rules.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Shyamji Krishna Varma founded the Indian Home Rule Society (1905) in London. With India House, it laid the foundation of the militant Indian nationalist movement in Britain.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Founding & purpose (see 'Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS), 1905 — Revolutionary Activity in Britain'). Shyamji Krishna Varma set it up in London in 1905 with Bhikaji Kama, Dadabhai Naoroji (not a revolutionary himself) & S.R. Rana. Goal - secure self-rule in India & do propaganda in Britain. Method - all practicable means. Only Indians could become members.

2. Built as an institution, not a circle (see 'Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS), 1905 — Revolutionary Activity in Britain'). It had a written constitution modelled on British public institutions of the time. It drew strong support from Indian students, kept close contact with revolutionaries in India, & set up India House - a student hostel that actively promoted nationalist views.

3. The press & the ideas (see 'Inside India: The Revolutionary Organisations'). Shyamji's journal The Indian Sociologist (not socialist in ideology - the name misleads). Savarkar reached London in 1906 to study law, opened an Abhinav Bharat branch, compiled Mazzini Charitra 1906, & wrote The Indian War of Independence 1857 (1909) - banned before publication, yet circulated underground.

4. From propaganda to action (see 'Actions Credited to Abhinav Bharat'). After Shyamji shifted to Paris in 1907, India House passed to Savarkar's Abhinav Bharat Mandal. In 1909 Madan Lal Dhingra killed Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie in London. Savarkar sent pistols from London; one was used by Anant Laxman Kanhere to kill District Magistrate Jackson - the Nasik Conspiracy Case, 1909. Savarkar was sentenced to transportation for life in 1910.
Closing verdict: The Indian Home Rule Society (1905) & India House gave the militant Indian nationalist movement in Britain an institution, a press & a supply of recruits.
revise: Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS), 1905 — Revolutionary Activity in Britain

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: The most short lived of all of Britain's constitutional experiments in India was the
explanation: (C) ✓ — ICA1909 had the shortest life of the constitutional experiments: in force only from 1909 until the Government of India Act 1919 replaced it — barely a decade, against ICA 1861's thirty-one years, ICA 1892's seventeen, and GOI 1919's sixteen.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — ICA 1861 was the LONGEST-lived of the series — three decades passed before ICA 1892 replaced it.
(B) ✗ — ICA 1892 ran seventeen years (1892–1909) — longer than its successor; the shortest span belongs to ICA1909.
(D) ✗ — GOI 1919 operated for sixteen years before the Government of India Act 1935 superseded it — well beyond ICA1909's single decade.
(Note: The Indian Councils Act served as the governance structure of India, famously known as 'Minto Morley Reforms' was the most short lived.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: A London branch of the All India Muslim League was established in 1908 under the presidency of
explanation: (B) ✓ — The London branch of the Muslim League (1908) was established under Ameer Ali's presidency — the lobby that,, influenced the Indian Councils Act 1909 (ICA1909) — which laid the foundation of partition politics by introducing Separate Electorates for Muslims in the reformed councils.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Aga Khan's role was at home: he led the Simla Deputation to Minto0510 in 1906 and headed the parent League — the 1908 LONDON branch was Ameer Ali's charge. +.
(C) ✗ — Liaquat Ali Khan belongs to the League's later, 1940s generation — four decades after the 1908 London branch.
(D) ✗ — In 1908 Jinnah was still a Congress constitutional lawyer with nationalist sympathies — not yet a League man at all.
(Note: A London branch of the All India Muslim League was established in 1908 under the presidency of Ameer Ali to put pressure on British Government for Muslim's educational cause.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: With reference to the Indian freedom struggle, which one of the following statements is not correct?

options.text: Hakim Ajmal Khan was one of the leaders to start a nationalist and militant Ahrar movement
When the Indian National Congress was formed, Sayyid Ahmad Khan opposed it
The All-India Muslim League which was formed in 1906 vehemently opposed the partition of Bengal and separate electorates
Maulana Barakatullah and Maulana Obeidullah Sindhi were among those who formed a Provisional Government of India in Kabul

explanation: (C) ✓ — ML1906 was set up in 1906 to preserve Bengal Partition and secure Separate Electorates.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Statement (a) is CORRECT as history — Hakim Ajmal Khan was among the nationalist founders of the militant Ahrar movement — so it cannot be the "not correct" choice the stem demands.
(B) ✗ — Statement (b) is CORRECT — Sayyid Ahmad Khan opposed the INC from its founding and steered Muslims away from Congress politics.

(D) ✗ — Statement (d) is CORRECT — Maulana Barakatullah and Maulana Obeidullah Sindhi were among those who formed the wartime Provisional Government of India at Kabul; a true statement cannot be the answer.

(Note: The All-India Muslim League formed in 1906 supported by the Bengal division because with the partition the Muslims will be in majority. They demanded separate electorate in the leadership of Agha Khan.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Who led the Simla Deputation of 1906 that met Viceroy Lord Minto to place a memorandum of Muslim political demands?
explanation: (B) ✓ — In 1906, the elite Muslim delegation that met Viceroy Minto at Shimla was led by the Aga Khan; this deputation demanded no annulment of the Bengal Partition, population-proportional reservation in councils and jobs, and separate electorates in future council reforms.

Why others wrong: (a) Nawab Salimullah hosted the founding session of the Muslim League at Dacca in December 1906, he did not lead the Shimla delegation; (c) Sir Syed Ahmed Khan had died in 1898, well before the Deputation; (d) Mohsin-ul-Mulk drafted the Muslim League's constitution but did not head the Simla delegation.
Memory hook: Aga at Shimla, Salimullah at Dacca — two stops, one separatist road.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Who was the first Indian to be inducted into the Viceroy's Executive Council under the Indian Councils Act, 1909?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Satyendra Prasanna Sinha (S.P. Sinha) was inducted into the Viceroy's Executive Council as Law Member, becoming the first Indian on the VEC under the 1909 Act.

Why others wrong: (b) K.G. Gupta was appointed to the Secretary of State's India Council in London in August 1907 (a precursor action, not a 1909 Act provision, and not on the VEC); (c) Syed Hussain Bilgrami likewise went to the India Council in London in August 1907, not the VEC; (d) Romesh Chandra Dutt is not mentioned by the record in the 1909 induction.
Memory hook: Sinha sits at the Viceroy's table; Gupta and Bilgrami sit in London.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Which Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims in India for the first time?
explanation: (C) ✓ — The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates for Muslims for the first time, in the Imperial Legislative Council, the Provincial Legislative Councils, and local bodies.

Why others wrong: (a) ICA 1861 dealt with the addition of non-official members and provincial legislative councils, not communal electorates; (b) ICA 1892 used the word 'selection' and allowed discussion of the budget but introduced no separate electorates; (d) GOI Act 1919 extended the principle but did not introduce it for the first time.
Memory hook: 1909 plants the seed, 1947 reaps the partition.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: The All India Muslim League was founded in December 1906 at which city?
explanation: (D) ✓ — The All India Muslim League was set up by elite Muslims at Dacca in December 1906, immediately following the Simla Deputation, with Mohsin-ul-Mulk authoring its constitution.

Why others wrong: (a) Lahore is associated with the League's later 1940 Resolution, not its founding; (b) Lucknow is linked to the 1916 Lucknow Pact, not the League's founding; (c) Aligarh was the seat of the Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College set up in 1875 but not where the League was founded.
Memory hook: Dacca delivered the League; Lahore later demanded Pakistan.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Who founded the Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College in 1875?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817–98) set up the Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College in 1875 (later Aligarh Muslim University) to combine Western education with Islamic values and build a Muslim middle class able to compete for government positions.

Why others wrong: (a) Mohsin-ul-Mulk wrote the Muslim League's 1906 constitution but did not found the MAO College; (c) Nawab Wakar-ul-Mulk is not credited with founding the College; (d) Ameer Ali was associated with the Muslim League's London branch in 1908, not with founding the College.
Memory hook: Sir Syed builds Aligarh's bricks; Mohsin-ul-Mulk later drafts the League's rules.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Who was the Secretary of State for India whose name is attached to the reforms enacted by the Indian Councils Act, 1909?
explanation: (A) ✓ — John Morley was the Secretary of State for India, sitting in London, when the Indian Councils Act, 1909 was enacted; together with Viceroy Lord Minto (1905–1910), his name became attached to what is formally called the Indian Councils Act, 1909.

Why others wrong: (b) Lord Minto was the Viceroy in India, not the Secretary of State in London; (c) Lord Curzon was the Viceroy who carried out the 1905 Bengal Partition, not the Secretary of State of 1909; (d) Lord Hardinge succeeded Minto as Viceroy and is not associated with the 1909 reforms.
Memory hook: Morley in London, Minto in India — Liberal pen, viceregal seal.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Indian Councils Act, 1909:
items: 1. It introduced separate electorates for Muslims in the Imperial Legislative Council.
2. It introduced a non-official majority in the Imperial Legislative Council.
3. The word 'election' was used officially for the first time in this Act.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims in the ILC, PLCs and local bodies; the word 'election' was used officially for the first time in ICA 1909. Statement 2 is wrong because the ILC retained an official majority (37 officials vs 32 non-officials); non-official majority appeared only in the PLCs.
Why others wrong: (a) wrongly includes Statement 2 — official majority continued in the ILC; (b) wrongly includes Statement 2 and drops Statement 1; (d) wrongly accepts Statement 2.
Memory hook: ILC keeps officers in charge; PLCs let non-officials breathe.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to the Indian Councils Act, 1909, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Members could vote on individual items of the Budget but could not vote on the Budget as a whole.
2. Members could ask supplementary questions, with the supplementary restricted to the member who had asked the original question.
3. Resolutions moved by members were binding on the government.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Voting was allowed on individual budget items but not on the budget as a whole (this would have amounted to a No Confidence Motion); supplementary questions were allowed but only by the original questioner. Statement 3 is wrong — resolutions could be initiated and passed but were recommendatory only, not binding on the government.
Why others wrong: (a) wrongly treats resolutions as binding; (b) wrongly treats resolutions as binding and drops the budget point; (c) wrongly treats resolutions as binding.
Memory hook: Vote a line, ask a follow-up, suggest a resolution — but the Executive may yawn.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Simla Deputation of 1906:
items: 1. The delegation demanded that the Partition of Bengal should not be annulled.
2. The delegation demanded separate electorates for Muslims in future council reforms.
3. The delegation demanded full Responsible Government for India.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Shimla Deputation asked for no annulment of the Bengal Partition, reservation proportional to population in the ILC, PLCs and government jobs, and separate electorates in future council reforms. Statement 3 is wrong — the Deputation sought elite Muslim safeguards, not Responsible Government.
Why others wrong: (b) wrongly attributes a Responsible-Government demand to the Deputation; (c) wrongly attributes a Responsible-Government demand; (d) same error as (b) and (c).
Memory hook: Keep the Partition, give us the seats, fence the votes — that was Shimla's ask.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the All India Muslim League founded in 1906:
items: 1. Its constitution was written by Mohsin-ul-Mulk of the Aligarh movement.
2. A London branch of the League was set up in
3. It was established with the goal of promoting Muslim loyalty to the British and securing the promises of the Simla Deputation.
questions.stemTail: 1908 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — All three statements are correct. The League's constitution was drafted by Mohsin-ul-Mulk of the Aligarh movement; a London branch was set up in 1908; and its stated goals were to ensure the British did not retreat from the Simla Deputation promises, to promote Muslim interests, and to promote Muslim loyalty to the British.
Why others wrong: (a) drops the correct loyalty/Simla goal in Statement 3; (c) drops Mohsin-ul-Mulk's authorship; (d) drops the London branch fact.
Memory hook: Mohsin pens it, Dacca launches it, London branches it — loyalty all the way.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about Sir Syed Ahmed Khan:
items: 1. He argued that India was a summation of qaums and that the Hindu and Muslim qaums had separate interests.
2. He founded the Mohammadan Educational Congress in 1886 as a rival to the Indian National Congress.
3. He actively encouraged Muslim participation in the Indian National Congress.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Sir Syed argued that India was a summation of qaums with the Hindu and Muslim qaums forming separate communities with separate interests (the early form of the Two Nation Theory), and he set up the Mohammadan Educational Congress in 1886 as a rival to the INC. Statement 3 is wrong — he actively discouraged Muslim participation in the INC, which he believed was a Hindu organisation.
Why others wrong: (a) wrongly says he encouraged INC participation; (b) wrongly says he encouraged INC participation and drops the qaum framing; (d) wrongly accepts Statement 3.
Memory hook: Two qaums, one rival Congress — Sir Syed's three-line manifesto.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: The Indian Councils Act, 1909 is often described as the shortest-lived among Britain's council reforms in India primarily because:

options.text: it satisfied neither the Moderates nor the Extremists, while planting the seed of communal politics that destabilised it.
it transferred real executive power to elected Indian ministers, which the British soon revoked.
it abolished the Imperial Legislative Council, which had to be quickly restored.
it was overturned by the Lucknow Pact of 1916.

explanation: (A) ✓ — ICA 1909 lasted only 10 years — the shortest of all council reforms — because it satisfied no one. Moderates wanted real legislative power and got a toothless body; the INC's stated goal since 1906 was Swaraj, and the Act fell far short; Extremists had never cared for council reforms; and the grant of separate electorates planted long-term communal trouble.

Why others wrong: (b) factually wrong — the Act did not transfer executive power to elected Indian ministers; the Executive remained non-responsible; (c) factually wrong — the ILC was expanded, not abolished; (d) factually wrong — the Lucknow Pact was a Congress–League agreement, not a constitutional repeal.
Memory hook: Pleased nobody, planted partition — ten years and out.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: The British grant of separate electorates to Muslims under the Indian Councils Act, 1909 is regarded as the legislative seed of Partition because:

options.text: it gave Muslims a numerical majority in the Imperial Legislative Council.
it abolished joint electorates throughout British India.
it created a Muslim-majority province by partitioning Bengal.
it institutionalised Muslim-only constituencies, accepting the Two Nation Theory in law.

explanation: (D) ✓ — Once it was institutionally accepted that Muslims must elect Muslim representatives from Muslim-only constituencies, the Two Nation Theory had been accepted in legislation; the 1909 grant of separate electorates therefore became the legislative seed of 1947 — Minto came to be called the Father of Communal Electorate.

Why others wrong: (a) wrong — 8 of 27 elected ILC seats (about 30%) were reserved for Muslims, not a numerical majority of the ILC; (b) wrong — joint electorates continued for unreserved seats; Muslims could also vote in those; (c) wrong — the partitioning of Bengal happened in 1905 under Curzon, separate from ICA 1909.
Memory hook: Separate seat, separate ballot, separate nation — the chain that broke India.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below: List I (Person) A. Aga Khan B. Mohsin-ul-Mulk C. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan D. Satyendra Prasanna Sinha; List II (Association)
items: 1. First Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council
2. Founder of the Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College, 1875
3. Author of the Muslim League's constitution
4. Leader of the Simla Deputation, 1906
matchTable: 1. First Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council
2. Founder of the Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College, 1875
3. Author of the Muslim League's constitution
explanation: (B) ✓ — Aga Khan led the Simla Deputation of 1906 (A-4); Mohsin-ul-Mulk of the Aligarh movement authored the Muslim League's constitution (B-3); Sir Syed Ahmed Khan set up the Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College in 1875 (C-2); Satyendra Prasanna Sinha became the first Indian in the Viceroy's Executive Council as Law Member under ICA 1909 (D-1).
Why others wrong: (a) swaps Aga Khan and Mohsin-ul-Mulk's roles; (c) swaps Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Sir Syed's associations; (d) wrongly makes Aga Khan the first VEC Indian and S.P. Sinha the Simla leader.
Memory hook: Aga at Shimla, Mohsin at the pen, Sir Syed at Aligarh, Sinha at the Council — four men, four firsts.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below: List I (Provision of ICA 1909) A. Total ILC strength B. Muslim reserved seats among elected ILC seats C. Indian inducted into Viceroy's Executive Council D. Indian Members of Secretary of State's India Council, London (precursor action, August 1907); List II (Number / Person)
items: 1. K.G. Gupta and Syed Hussain Bilgrami
2. 69 members
3. S.P. Sinha
matchTable: 1. K.G. Gupta and Syed Hussain Bilgrami
B. Muslim reserved seats among elected ILC seats
C. Indian inducted into Viceroy's Executive Council
D. Indian Members of Secretary of State's India Council, London (precursor action, August 1907)
explanation: (C) ✓ — The ILC was expanded to 69 members in total (8 ex-officio + 1 rotating Governor + 27 elected + 33 nominated) (A-2); 8 of the 27 elected ILC seats were reserved for Muslims under separate electorates (B-4); S.P. Sinha was inducted into the Viceroy's Executive Council as Law Member (C-3); K.G. Gupta and Syed Hussain Bilgrami were appointed to the Secretary of State's India Council in London in August 1907 as a precursor action (D-1).

Why others wrong: (a) puts 8 of 27 against ILC total and 69 against Muslim seats — sizes swapped; (b) swaps Sinha and the Gupta–Bilgrami pair across the VEC and the London India Council; (d) misplaces Sinha and the number 8 of 27.
Memory hook: 69 total, 8 of 27 Muslim, Sinha in Council, Gupta-Bilgrami in London — the 1909 scoreboard.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The All India Muslim League (1906) was as much a creation of British policy as of Muslim elite anxiety." Examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" asks you to test the claim by weighing both causes named in it. The two sides are British policy & Muslim elite anxiety — the body must carry both, not one. The phrase "as much as" blocks any answer that makes a single cause the whole story. Anchor the sweep between Census 1881 & the Dacca meeting of December 1906.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The All India Muslim League was founded at Dacca in December 1906. It was as much a creation of British policy as of Muslim elite anxiety.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. The Census made a community (see 'Census and Communal Consciousness'). Census 1881 was the first full census of British India — the 1872 attempt was not completed for all of British India. It counted Muslims at roughly 20% overall, with a majority in Punjab & roughly 50% in Bengal. Mass enumeration told a poor Muslim weaver in Bengal & a rich Muslim landlord in Punjab that they were one community with one set of interests. Government reports on education, employment & poverty were published religion-wise, which built a sense of relative deprivation.

2. The education gap behind the anxiety (see 'Why Western Education Uptake Was Low Among Muslims'). The reasons were structural. Western education was expensive & most Bengal Muslims were poor ryots. The Ulamas resisted it because the Western curriculum carried values that cut against Islamic teaching. Persian, the language of Mughal high culture & administration, had to be defended against English & Hindi. Rich Muslim landlords had low utility for middle-class government jobs. Hindus therefore gained more from the new professions.

3. British Divide & Rule supplied the opening (see 'British — Divide & Rule'). W.W. Hunter's Indian Musalmans (1871) argued that Muslim economic decline since the end of Mughal rule had fed the Faraizi movement of the 1830s–70s in Bengal, so the British should appease Muslims for stability. Pair with 'The British deployed several specific DnR measures toward Muslims' — 1897, reservation in government jobs for Muslims; 1905, Bengal Partition creating East Bengal & Assam as a Muslim Majority Province.

4. The elite built its own separate identity (see 'Muslim Western-Educated Elite — Path to Separate Political Identity'). Mohammadan Association (1855) was pro-British & opposed the 1857 revolts. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817–98) argued India was not one nation but a summation of qaums, with the Hindu qaum & the Muslim qaum separate — the early form of the Two Nation Theory. He set up Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College, 1875 & Mohammadan Educational Congress, 1886 as a rival to the INC, & discouraged Muslim participation in the INC.

5. Hindu revivalism pushed from the other side (see 'Hindu Cultural Nationalism Deepens Communal Distance'). Shudhhi & Cow Protection by Arya Samaj (1875) turned aggressive after Swami Dayanand Saraswati died in 1883, ending in the Cow Killing Riots of 1893. The INC did not condemn them, because its 1886 rule was to take up only political issues — Muslim participation in the INC fell sharply. The Hindi-Urdu Controversy succeeded in 1900 & tied Hindi to Hindus, Urdu to Muslims. Swadeshi05-11 symbolism — Bande Mataram, Kali worship, Ganpati & Shivaji Festivals — alienated Muslims further.

6. From deputation to organisation (see 'Simla Deputation: What It Demanded'). In 1906 elite Muslims led by the Aga Khan met Minto05-10 at Shimla & asked for no annulment of Bengal Partition, reservation proportional to population in the ILC, PLCs & government jobs, & Separate Electorates in future council reforms. The League followed at once — see 'Formation of All India Muslim League (ML1906)': set up at Dacca in December 1906, its Green Book constitution written by Mohsin-ul-Mulk & Mohammed Ali Jauhar, its goals to hold the British to the Simla promises & to promote Muslim loyalty to the British.
Closing verdict: The League of 1906 was as much a creation of British policy as of Muslim elite anxiety; each cause deepened the other.
revise: Why Western Education Uptake Was Low Among Muslims
Muslim Western-Educated Elite — Path to Separate Political Identity
Hindu Cultural Nationalism Deepens Communal Distance
Formation of All India Muslim League (ML1906)

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Lord Minto is remembered as the "Father of Communal Electorate". Analyse the provisions of the Indian Councils Act, 1909 that justify this description.
body: Demand of the question: "Analyse" asks you to break the reform into parts & show which parts carry the charge. The title "Father of Communal Electorate" is the framing phrase — stay on the electorate provisions, not on the whole Act. The anchor is 1909, with Morley as Secretary of State in London & Minto05-10 as Viceroy in India. Close by judging how far the description is justified.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Indian Councils Act, 1909 introduced separate electorates for Muslims for the first time. These provisions earned Lord Minto the title "Father of Communal Electorate".
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The demand & the grant (see 'Simla Deputation: What It Demanded'). In 1906 elite Muslims led by the Aga Khan met Minto05-10 at Shimla. They asked not just for reserved seats but for Separate Electorates — only Muslims to have the right to vote in a seat reserved for a Muslim candidate. Minto05-10 obliged, because the demand suited British Divide & Rule.

2. What the Act actually gave (see 'The Muslim Separate Electorate — Communal Appeasement'). Separate electorates came for the first time in the ILC, PLCs & local bodies. 8 of the 27 elected ILC seats were reserved for Muslims — about 30% of elected seats against a Muslim population of about 20%. The INC's own 1889 Minority Clause had asked only for reservation proportional to population, so the extra 10% was pure appeasement. The income criteria for the right to vote were set lower for Muslims. Muslims could also vote in general unreserved seats — a double advantage. Muslim reserved seats saw the first direct elections.

3. The small space this was carved from (see 'The Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) — Composition'). The ILC had 69 members, of whom only 27 were elected & 33 were nominated. The officer majority held at 37 to 32. The word 'election' was used officially for the first time in ICA1909. So the communal seats were cut out of a narrow elected space inside a council the British still controlled.

4. The long shadow (see 'The Long Shadow: Foundation of Partition'). Separate electorates laid the direct foundation for the partition of India in 1947 — when you tell a community to vote separately, you tell them they are separate. Minto05-10 became known as the "Father of Communal Electorate". Pair with 'The Long Thread: From ML1906 to 1947' — ML1906 asked for this in 1906, got it in 1909, & the institutional separation never reversed.
Closing verdict: The description is justified. The Indian Councils Act, 1909 made separate voting the rule, & Minto's name stayed with the communal electorate he fathered.
revise: The Muslim Separate Electorate — Communal Appeasement
The Long Shadow: Foundation of Partition
The Long Thread: From ML1906 to 1947

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: Who was the leader of the Ghadar Party?
explanation: (B) ✓ — It’s headquarters in San Francisco was called Yugantar Ashram (notice same terminology as of secret society of Bengal) 3.4) 1913 — Lala Hardayal, professor of Sanskrit and Indian philosophy in San Francisco, set up the weekly The Ghadr"."
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Bhagat Singh belongs to the LATER revolutionary generation — the record own ⚠ trap note separates the First Lahore Conspiracy Case (1915, Ghadar) from the Second (1929–30, Bhagat Singh and HSRA).
(C) ✗ — Tilak's arena was the Extremist politics of the INC, not the NRI revolutionary party of San Francisco.

(D) ✗ — Savarkar's society was Abhinav Bharat, run from India House, London — a separate stream from the Ghadar Party, whose moving spirit was Lala Hardayal with Sohan Singh Bhakna as first president.

(Note: The original name of Ghadar party was Pacific Coast Hindustani Associacium. The founding president of Ghadar Party was Sohan Singh Bhakana and Lala Hardayal was the co-founder of this party. Headquarters were at San Francisco.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: What was Komagata Maru?

options.text: A political party based in Taiwan
A navalship on voyage to Canada
A Chinese villager where Mao Tse Tung began his long march

explanation: (C) ✓ — Canada rule: only Indians making an unbroken direct journey from India could enter.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — No political party, and no Taiwan connection: Komagata Maru was the Japanese SHIP Baba Gurdit Singh chartered from Hong Kong in 1914 to challenge Canada's racist immigration rules.
(B) ✗ — Not a person at all — it was the chartered vessel carrying 376 mostly Punjabi Sikh passengers to Vancouver.
(D) ✗ — Nothing Chinese about it — the voyage ran Hong Kong → Vancouver and ended at Budge Budge near Calcutta, where police firing killed about 20 passengers.

(Note: Baba Gurdit Singh chartered a Japanese ship called Komagata Maru, early in 1914 to carry large number of voyage to Canada, reaching Vancouver on 23rd May, 1914. The government did not allow the ship to land.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: Where were the Ghadar revolutionaries, who became active during the outbreak of the World War I based?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Thousands of Ghadarite NRIs returned to India from North America to trigger a massive sepoy mutiny in Punjab & ignite civil rebellion.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Central America never figures in the Ghadar geography — the base was the Pacific coast of NORTH America, with the Yugantar Ashram headquarters at San Francisco.
(C) ✗ — "West America" is not a region; the party's home was San Francisco on the US Pacific coast — North America.
(D) ✗ — South America had no Ghadar presence; the returning Ghadarites sailed from NORTH America to trigger the Punjab mutiny plan.
(Note: Ghadar revolutionaries had headquarters at San Francisco in North America.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: The Ghadr (Ghadar) was a

options.text: a revolutionary association of Indians with headquarters at San Francisco
militant organisation with headquarters at Berlin
communist movement for India's freedom with headquarters at Tashkent

explanation: (A) ✓ — Ghadar Movement was a massive global conspiracy spanning across continents — San Francisco, Berlin, Bengal, Punjab.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Singapore was a mutiny SITE in the wartime conspiracies, not the party's base — the organisation was built by NRIs in the US with headquarters at San Francisco.
(C) ✗ — Berlin was one node of the wider wartime conspiracy (the German connection), but the Ghadar Party's own headquarters was the Yugantar Ashram in San Francisco.

(D) ✗ — Tashkent and communism belong to a different story (M.N. Roy's later communist beginnings); the Ghadar was a secular-republican REVOLUTIONARY movement of Punjabi NRIs and Bengal revolutionaries, run from San Francisco.

(Note: Ghadr (Ghadar) means revolt or rebellion. The Ghadar Party was a revolt against the British rule in India organised overseas by the Indian immigrants to Canada and USA, with its headquarters at San Francisco.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: Who were actively associated with the Ghadar Party?
items: 1. Barindra Kumar Ghosh
2. Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee
3. Rash Behari Bose
explanation: (D) ✓ — Only Rash Behari Bose was actively associated with the Ghadar effort: he "operated in Lahore to establish contact with the sepoys" for the planned mutiny of 21 February 1915.. Barindra Kumar Ghosh belonged to Bengal's Anushilan-Jugantar stream, and Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee to the later HRA generation.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Includes both non-Ghadarites: Barindra Kumar Ghosh (Bengal's Anushilan-Jugantar world) and Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee (the 1920s HRA) — while omitting the one genuine Ghadar coordinator, Rash Behari Bose.
(B) ✗ — Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee's organisation was the Hindustan Republican Association of the 1920s, not the Ghadar Party — and this option also drops Rash Behari Bose.
(C) ✗ — Right to include Rash Behari Bose, wrong to add Barindra Kumar Ghosh, whose field was the Bengal samiti network, not the NRI party.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Who was the first President of the Ghadar Party, established by NRIs in the United States in 1913?
explanation: (A) ✓ — When the Ghadar Party was set up by NRIs in the US in 1913, Sohan Singh Bhakna became its first President; its headquarters in San Francisco was called Yugantar Ashram, echoing the Bengal secret society.

Why others wrong: (b) Lala Hardayal was a Sanskrit & Indian philosophy professor in San Francisco who set up the weekly The Ghadr in 1913, but he was not the first President of the party; (c) Baba Gurdit Singh chartered the Komagata Maru in 1914, he had no role in founding the party; (d) Rash Behari Bose contacted sepoys in Lahore in 1915 and later escaped to Japan, he was not the founding President.
Memory hook: Bhakna chairs, Hardayal writes — first seat in San Francisco goes to the Punjabi farmer-ex-soldier.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Ghadar Movement:
items: 1. Its declared goal was a secular Republic of India i.e. Purna Swaraj.
2. Its method had two stages — a press campaign overseas, then a return to India to repeat a 1857-style revolt.
3. It was primarily led by elite Bengali zamindars.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Ghadar Movement aimed at a secular Republic of India i.e. Purna Swaraj, and used a two-stage method — first a press campaign overseas, then a physical return to India to cause disaffection in the army plus a civil rebellion. Statement 3 is wrong — it was a movement of Punjabi NRIs and Bengal revolutionaries, drawing members from farmers, labourers, students and ex-soldiers, not Bengali zamindars.
Why others wrong: (a) wrongly includes Statement 3 and drops the two-stage plan; (c) wrongly includes Statement 3 and drops the secular republic goal; (d) wrongly accepts Statement 3.
Memory hook: Build the fire abroad, light it inside India — secular republic, not zamindar drawing-room.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Which newspaper, published from Vancouver in 1907 by Tarak Nath Das, exposed the irony of Britain sending Indians to Fiji plantations while barring their entry into North America?
explanation: (C) ✓ — In 1907, Tarak Nath Das launched Free Hindustan from Vancouver to highlight the plantation-versus-migration irony — Britain sent Indians as plantation labourers to Fiji yet barred their entry into Canada and the US.

Why others wrong: (a) Swadesh Sevak was G.D. Kumar's Gurmukhi weekly from Canada in 1909, not Tarak Nath Das's 1907 paper; (b) The Ghadr was Lala Hardayal's weekly from San Francisco, launched in 1913; (d) Yugantar was a Bengal secret-society publication, not a Vancouver Indian-NRI paper.
Memory hook: Tarak in Vancouver, paper named Free Hindustan — plantation in Fiji, no land in Canada.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: The Bakunin Institute, described by its founder as a "monastery of anarchism," was set up in California in 1912 by which leader?
explanation: (D) ✓ — In 1912, a year before the Ghadar Party was formally set up, Lala Hardayal established the Bakunin Institute in California and described it as a "monastery of anarchism," marrying European anarchist strategy to Punjabi NRI grievances.

Why others wrong: (a) Sohan Singh Bhakna was the first President of the Ghadar Party but did not set up the Bakunin Institute; (b) Rash Behari Bose worked inside India contacting sepoys in Lahore in 1915, he was not the institute's founder; (c) Bagha Jatin reorganised the Jugantar network in Bengal, he had no role in the California institute.
Memory hook: Hardayal in 1912 builds the anarchist monastery — California gets a Bakunin chapel.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Which Russian thinker, identified as a founding figure of anarchism, supplied the Ghadar Movement with the key concept of "Propaganda of the Deed"?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Michael Bakunin (1814–1876), a Russian thinker and founding figure of anarchism, argued that all States are instruments of oppression and must be destroyed; the key anarchist concept he supplied to the Ghadar Movement was "Propaganda of the Deed" — armed acts ignite the masses more powerfully than any speech.

Why others wrong: (b) Karl Marx supplied the linked idea of a Stateless Society but is not credited by the record with the "Propaganda of the Deed" formulation; (c) Vladimir Lenin is not named by the record in connection with the Ghadar ideological framework; (d) Peter Kropotkin is not mentioned for this movement.
Memory hook: Bakunin says destroy the State — Hardayal turns the slogan into smuggled rifles.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: The Ghadr newspaper carried on its front page an exposé of British imperialism with which exact title?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Every front page of The Ghadr newspaper carried "Angrezi Raj ka kachcha Chithha" — an exposé of British imperialism — and the masthead carried the date of the 1857 revolt to reinforce the inspiration.

Why others wrong: (a) Indian War of Independence (1909) was Veer Savarkar's book, which the paper published in parts — it was not the front-page exposé title; (c) Ghadr Di Goonj was the title of the patriotic poems carried in the paper, not the exposé heading; (d) Amra Morbo, Jagat Jagbe was Bagha Jatin's rallying cry in Bengal, not a front-page headline.
Memory hook: Front page = "kachcha Chithha", masthead = 1857 — every issue puts the Raj on the dock.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Ghadr newspaper:
items: 1. It was published in Urdu, Punjabi, Hindi and sometimes English.
2. It published Veer Savarkar's Indian War of Independence 1909 in parts.
3. It was smuggled into India and distributed among soldiers and peasants in Punjab.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (C) ✓ — All three statements are correct. The Ghadr newspaper was published in Urdu, Punjabi, Hindi and sometimes English; it published Veer Savarkar's Indian War of Independence 1909 in parts; and it was smuggled into India and distributed among soldiers and peasants in Punjab.

Why others wrong: (a) drops the smuggling-and-distribution dimension which the record explicitly states; (b) drops the multi-language fact which is also explicitly stated; (d) drops Savarkar's book serialisation, which the record lists among the paper's contents.
Memory hook: Four tongues in print, Savarkar in parts, sepoys in Punjab as the audience — Ghadr ticks every box.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Komagata Maru incident (1914):
items: 1. The ship was chartered by Baba Gurdit Singh.
2. It sailed from Hong Kong to Vancouver carrying 376 passengers, mostly Punjabi Sikhs.
3. On its forced return, it landed at Balasore in Odisha, where about 20 passengers were killed in police firing.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct; statement 3 is wrong. Baba Gurdit Singh chartered the Japanese ship Komagata Maru from Hong Kong in 1914 to challenge Canada's racist immigration laws, and it sailed to Vancouver carrying 376 passengers, mostly Punjabi Sikhs. But on its forced return the ship arrived at Budge Budge near Calcutta in September 1914, where the British tried to force the passengers onto a special train to Punjab and police firing killed around 20 of them. Balasore in Odisha is a different episode a year later — September 1915, where Bagha Jatin was cornered on the Burhabalanga.

Why others wrong: (b) keeps statement 3, which shifts the landing from Budge Budge to Balasore — two different Septembers and two different events. (c) keeps statement 3 and also drops the 376-passenger Hong Kong-to-Vancouver detail. (d) treats all three as correct, but the Balasore landing is false — the ship came in at Budge Budge near Calcutta.
Memory hook: Charter from Gurdit, 376 Punjabis aboard, firing at Budge Budge — Balasore is Bagha Jatin's ground, one year later.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Which Canadian rule, in force since 1908, did the Komagata Maru voyage specifically seek to challenge?

options.text: The "direct journey" / continuous-journey rule restricting Indian entry to Canada
A blanket ban on all Asian immigration to Canada
A literacy test in English imposed on incoming Indians
A poll-tax payable in gold sovereigns by Indian passengers

explanation: (A) ✓ — Canada had restricted Indian entry since 1908 by allowing only those who made a direct (continuous) journey from India to enter; the Komagata Maru, chartered by Baba Gurdit Singh in 1914 from Hong Kong, was an explicit challenge to this racist "direct journey" rule.
Why others wrong: (b) the record describes a "direct journey" condition, not a blanket Asian-immigration ban; (c) no English literacy test is mentioned; (d) no gold-sovereign poll tax is mentioned.
Memory hook: Only an unbroken voyage from India counted — Hong Kong stop made the ship "illegal."

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Who reorganised the shattered revolutionary network across Bengal during the Ghadar period and is remembered by the rallying cry "Amra morbo, jagat jagbe"?
explanation: (B) ✓ — While Hardayal supplied the ideological framework from abroad, inside Bengal it was Jatindranath Mukherjee — universally known as Bagha Jatin (Jatin the Tiger) — who reorganised the shattered revolutionary network and unified Jugantar factions; his rallying cry was "Amra morbo, jagat jagbe" — "We shall die to awaken the nation".

Why others wrong: (a) Barindra Kumar Ghosh (B.K. Ghosh) had set up the Jugantar Party in 1906 but did not lead its Ghadar-era reorganisation, and the rallying cry is not attributed to him; (c) Aurobindo Ghosh, B.K. Ghosh's elder brother, is not credited by the record with this reorganisation; (d) Rash Behari Bose worked in Lahore on sepoy disaffection — he was not the Bengal organiser.
Memory hook: Tiger of Bengal stitches Jugantar back together — "we die, the nation wakes."

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Rodda & Co. Arms Heist of August 1914:
items: 1. The target was R.B. Rodda & Co., a German-owned gunsmith in Calcutta.
2. The insider was Shrish Chandra Mitra, a trusted Rodda employee.
3. Not a single shot was fired during the heist.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statements 2 and 3 are correct; statement 1 is wrong. R.B. Rodda & Co. of Calcutta was a prestigious BRITISH-owned gunsmith and arms dealer, the primary supplier of firearms to British officials, the military and wealthy elites. What was German was the consignment, not the firm — in August 1914 Rodda received a restricted German firearms shipment at Calcutta Customs House. Shrish Chandra Mitra, a trusted Rodda employee, was the insider, and not a single shot was fired in the whole operation.

Why others wrong: (a) keeps statement 1, which turns a British-owned firm into a German-owned one — it was the crates that were German, not the company. (c) treats all three as correct, though Rodda was British-owned. (d) keeps statement 1 and also drops Shrish Mitra, the named insider.
Memory hook: British firm, German crates, seven bullock carts — the 7th slips into Malanga, and not one bullet is fired.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Arrange the following events of the Ghadar Movement in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Ghadar Party founded in San Francisco
2. Tarak Nath Das publishes Free Hindustan from Vancouver
3. Lala Hardayal sets up the Bakunin Institute in California
4. Komagata Maru forced out of Canadian waters
explanation: (D) ✓ — The record Key Dates table gives 1907 — Tarak Nath Das, Free Hindustan, Vancouver; 1912 — Hardayal sets up Bakunin Institute, Oakland; 1913 — Ghadar Party founded in San Francisco; July 1914 — Komagata Maru forced out of Canada. Hence the correct order is 2-3-1-4.

Why others wrong: (a) puts the 1913 party before the 1907 newspaper and the 1912 institute, reversing the actual sequence; (b) puts the 1912 institute before the 1907 newspaper; (c) puts the 1913 party before the 1912 institute, reversing two years.
Memory hook: 1907 paper, 1912 monastery, 1913 party, 1914 ship — chronology in four heartbeats.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Match List I (Press / publication) with List II (Place of publication):
items: 1. Free Hindustan — A. Vancouver
2. Swadesh Sevak — B. Canada
3. The Ghadr — C. San Francisco
4. Yugantar Ashram (HQ) — D. San Francisco
explanation: (A) ✓ — Tarak Nath Das publishing Free Hindustan from Vancouver in 1907; G.D. Kumar publishing Swadesh Sevak (Gurmukhi weekly) from Canada in 1909; Lala Hardayal launching the weekly The Ghadr from San Francisco in 1913; and the Ghadar Party headquarters in San Francisco itself being named Yugantar Ashram. Hence 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D.

Why others wrong: (b) swaps the Vancouver-Canada pair and swaps the two San Francisco entries, scrambling all four; (c) wrongly relocates The Ghadr to a different listing while keeping Yugantar Ashram at the wrong slot; (d) swaps Free Hindustan and Swadesh Sevak between Vancouver and Canada.
Memory hook: Tarak-Vancouver, Kumar-Canada, Hardayal-San Francisco, Yugantar Ashram-San Francisco — press map in one sweep.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: The Ghadar Party fixed which date in 1915 as the day for a coordinated sepoy mutiny in Punjab, a plan crushed pre-emptively by British intelligence?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Under Plot 1 — The Punjab Mutiny, Rash Behari Bose in Lahore contacted sepoys to cause disaffection, and February 21, 1915 was fixed as the date for the coordinated mutiny; British intelligence infiltrated the movement and the mutiny was crushed pre-emptively before it could start, leading to the First Lahore Conspiracy trials.

Why others wrong: (a) the record specifies February 21, not February 18; (c) March 1, 1915 is not the planned mutiny date; (d) April 21, 1915 is not the planned mutiny date — by April the First Lahore Conspiracy Case had begun.
Memory hook: Twenty-first of February — Rash Behari's date with destiny, leaked before dawn.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Hindu-German Conspiracy (Zimmermann Plan):
items: 1. Germany was keen to destabilise British India from within as part of its WWI strategy.
2. Lala Hardayal masterminded the Indian side.
3. Under the Pacific Arms Plot, the SS Maverick was to ship 30,000 rifles from the United States to the eastern coast of India.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (d) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are correct; statement 2 is wrong. The German Foreign Office sought to destabilise British India from within by funding and arming Indian revolutionaries, and under the Pacific Arms Plot (April–July 1915) the SS Maverick was to carry 30,000 rifles from the United States to India's eastern coast. But Lala Hardayal supplied the ideological framework from abroad; the Indian side was masterminded on the ground in Bengal by Jatindranath Mukherjee — Bagha Jatin.

Why others wrong: (a) keeps statement 2, which hands Bagha Jatin's on-the-ground role to Hardayal, whose work was ideological and overseas. (b) keeps statement 2 and also drops Germany's WWI motive, the spine of the Zimmermann Plan. (c) treats all three as correct, though Hardayal never led the Indian side.
Memory hook: German marks, Maverick on the Pacific, Bagha Jatin's hands inside Bengal — Hardayal's post was abroad.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_16
questions.stem: Arrange the following events of 1914–15 in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Rodda & Co. Arms Heist
2. Budge Budge Riot
3. Battle of Balasore / Buribalam
4. Kartar Singh Sarabha's execution
explanation: (D) ✓ — The Key Dates table records: August 1914 — Rodda & Co. Arms Heist; September 1914 — Budge Budge Riot; September 1915 — Battle of Balasore / Buribalam, Bagha Jatin martyred; November 1915 — Kartar Singh Sarabha executed. Hence the order is 1-2-3-4.

Why others wrong: (a) puts Sarabha's November 1915 execution before the September 1915 Balasore battle, reversing two months; (b) puts Budge Budge before the Rodda heist, reversing August-September 1914; (c) puts Balasore (September 1915) before the August-September 1914 events, an entire year early.
Memory hook: August heist, September riot, September battle, November gallows — clean march from 1914 to 1915.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_17
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Defence of India Act, 1915:
items: 1. It was a wartime emergency law used to suppress the Ghadarites from March
2. Revolutionaries could be detained without trial under this Act.
3. Ordinary criminal courts continued to hear all Ghadar cases under this Act.
questions.stemTail: 1915 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct. From March 1915 the Ghadarites were suppressed under the Defence of India Act, 1915 — a wartime emergency law; under this Act, revolutionaries could be detained without trial. Statement 3 is wrong — special tribunals replaced ordinary courts and there was no right of appeal.

Why others wrong: (b) wrongly accepts Statement 3, which contradicts the special-tribunal provision; (c) wrongly accepts Statement 3 and drops detention without trial; (d) wrongly accepts Statement 3.
Memory hook: No trial, no appeal, no ordinary court — DIA 1915 short-circuits the Raj's own rulebook.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_18
questions.stem: Match List I (Ghadar-era plot) with List II (Defining feature from the Chapter):
items: 1. Plot 1 — Punjab Mutiny — A. Date February 21, 1915 fixed for coordinated mutiny
2. Plot 2 — Pacific Arms Plot — B. SS Maverick to carry 30,000 rifles from the US
3. Plot 3 — Christmas Day Plot — C. Massive uprising planned in Calcutta and surrounding areas
4. Battle of Balasore — D. Five revolutionaries with stolen Mauser C96 pistols
matchTable: A. Date February 21, 1915 fixed for coordinated mutiny
B. SS Maverick to carry 30,000 rifles from the US
C. Massive uprising planned in Calcutta and surrounding areas
D. Five revolutionaries with stolen Mauser C96 pistols
explanation: (B) ✓ — Plot 1 (Punjab Mutiny) fixed February 21, 1915 as the date for coordinated mutiny; Plot 2 (Pacific Arms Plot, April–July 1915) used the SS Maverick to ship 30,000 rifles from the US; Plot 3 (Christmas Day Plot, December 1915) planned a massive uprising in Calcutta and surrounding areas; Battle of Balasore (September 1915) saw five revolutionaries with stolen Mauser C96 pistols pin down a full police force. Hence 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D.
Why others wrong: (a) swaps Plot 1 and Plot 2, also swaps Plot 3 and Balasore; (c) swaps the Pacific Arms Plot and the Christmas Day Plot; (d) swaps the Punjab Mutiny with Balasore.
Memory hook: Feb date, Pacific rifles, Calcutta Christmas, Mauser stand — four plots, four signatures.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_19
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about Kartar Singh Sarabha:
items: 1. He was hanged in November 1915 at the age of
2. Bhagat Singh later said he kept Sarabha's photograph in his pocket.
3. He was the masthead editor of The Ghadr newspaper.
questions.stemTail: 19 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Kartar Singh Sarabha was arrested and hanged in November 1915 at only 19 years of age, becoming a martyr-hero of the revolutionary movement, and Bhagat Singh later said he kept Sarabha's photograph in his pocket. Statement 3 is wrong — the record does not describe Sarabha as the masthead editor of The Ghadr; Lala Hardayal set up the weekly.

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly accepts Statement 3 and drops the Bhagat Singh photograph link; (b) wrongly accepts Statement 3 and drops the November 1915 / age-19 hanging; (d) wrongly accepts Statement 3.
Memory hook: Nineteen at the gallows, photograph in Bhagat's pocket — Sarabha walks into legend.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_20
questions.stem: Arrange the following events of 1915 in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Defence of India Act used to crush the movement
2. First Lahore Conspiracy Case trials begin
3. RB Bose escapes to Japan
4. Christmas Day Plot collapses
explanation: (D) ✓ — The Key Dates table gives: March 1915 — Defence of India Act used to crush the movement; April–September 1915 — First Lahore Conspiracy Case trials; May 1915 — RB Bose escapes to Japan; December 1915 — Christmas Day Plot collapses. Hence the order is 1-2-3-4.

Why others wrong: (a) puts the April Lahore trials before the March DIA crackdown; (b) puts RB Bose's May escape before the April Lahore trials; (c) puts RB Bose's escape before the DIA crackdown of March.
Memory hook: March cuffs, April court, May flight, December collapse — 1915 in four scenes.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: The Ghadar Movement was the first organised attempt to use the Indian diaspora for armed revolution against British rule. Critically examine why it failed despite the opportunity offered by the First World War.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" wants a weighed judgement, not a list of causes. Split the failure into two halves — what the colonial state did, & what Indian society did not do. The time anchor is 1913-15, the wartime years. The framing phrase "Indian diaspora" must be treated as both the movement's strength & its weakness, & a critical answer must also record what survived the defeat.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Ghadar Movement was the first organised attempt to use the Indian diaspora for armed revolution. The First World War gave it an opening it could not use.
Body guidance — 6 themes:

1. The plan & the men (see 'The Ghadar Movement' + 'Drivers of the Ghadar Movement'). Aim: overthrow British rule & set up a secular Republic of India i.e. Purna Swaraj. Two-stage method — a press campaign overseas, then a physical return to India to repeat an 1857-style revolt through army disaffection plus civil rebellion. Ghadar Party 1913, headquarters Yugantar Ashram in San Francisco, Sohan Singh Bhakna 1st President. Members were farmers, labourers, students & ex-soldiers, mostly Punjabis, pushed out by Canada's entry rules & American racism.

2. The war as the opening (see 'WWI 1914–19: The Opportunity Arrives' + 'Rodda & Co. Arms Heist (August 1914)'). World War I began on July 28, 1914. Britain was stretched on multiple fronts & the Ghadarites saw their opportunity. Arms followed: in August 1914 the Rodda & Co. heist in Calcutta took 50 Mauser C96 pistols & 46,000 rounds of 7.63mm ammunition without a shot fired. Opportunity & weapons were both real — show that first, so the failure is not read as inevitable.

3. Three plots, three interceptions (see 'Three Plots: Global Dimensions of the Ghadar Conspiracy'). The Hindu-German Conspiracy (Zimmermann Plan) funded the effort. Plot 1 — Rash Behari Bose in Lahore, sepoy mutiny fixed for February 21, 1915, crushed pre-emptively. Plot 2 — 30,000 rifles shipped from the United States via the Annie Larsen & SS Maverick, intercepted at sea. Plot 3 — the Christmas Day Plot of December 1915 in Calcutta, broken when the codes were cracked. A global design defeated at every node.

4. The state's side of the failure (see 'Failure & Aftermath of the Ghadar Movement'). Strong British intelligence & effective policing of the seas. Pre-emptive strikes from late 1914 to early February 1915 against Ghadarites & regiments suspected of disloyalty. March 1915 — the Defence of India Act, 1915 allowed detention without trial, replaced ordinary courts with special tribunals & removed the right of appeal. April–September 1915 — the First Lahore Conspiracy Case, a mass trial with death sentences, transportation for life & village internments.

5. The society's side of the failure (see 'Failure & Aftermath of the Ghadar Movement'). Rash Behari Bose's appeal to the sepoys in Lahore drew a poor response — the Peel Commission after 1857 had deliberately reduced political consciousness in the army, & low western education left Ghadarite arguments little traction. The Udasi Sikh Mahants, socially influential priests of the Gurudwaras, were pro-British & told the religious masses not to support the Ghadarites. A returning diaspora had no organisation waiting for it inside India.

6. The balance sheet (see 'Failure & Aftermath of the Ghadar Movement' + 'Bagha Jatin — The Call for Sacrifice'). India lost a generation of secular nationalists; Bagha Jatin died after Balasore in September 1915 & Kartar Singh Sarabha was hanged in November 1915 at nineteen — Bhagat Singh kept his photograph. Sikh, Hindu & Muslim revolutionaries had worked together without communal friction. Survivors carried the politics into the Kisan Sabhas, the Communist movement & the Akali movement in Punjab.
Closing verdict: Ghadar failed for want of a base inside India, not of courage. The First World War gave the diaspora an opportunity, never an army.
revise: Three Plots: Global Dimensions of the Ghadar Conspiracy
Failure & Aftermath of the Ghadar Movement

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: "The Komagata Maru incident (1914) did more to radicalise Punjab than the overseas press campaign of the Ghadarites ever did." Comment.
body: Demand of the question: "Comment" asks for your own judgement on a comparison, backed by evidence on both sides. You must handle two things — the voyage of 1914 & the press campaign that ran from 1907 — & then say which moved Punjab more. Do not narrate the voyage alone; the marks lie in the weighing.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Komagata Maru incident (1914) ended in police firing at Budge Budge. One voyage proved what the overseas press campaign of the Ghadarites had argued since 1907.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The rule that the voyage was meant to break (see 'Drivers of the Ghadar Movement'). Canada had restricted Indian entry since 1908 — only those making a direct journey from India could enter. In the USA Indians faced racism & were legally barred from buying land. The same British government was sending Indians as plantation labourers to Fiji, an irony Tarak Nath Das had exposed in Free Hindustan (1907) from Vancouver.

2. The voyage & the standoff (see 'The Komagata Maru Incident (1914)'). Baba Gurdit Singh chartered the Japanese ship Komagata Maru from Hong Kong in 1914 to challenge Canada's racist immigration laws; 376 passengers, mostly Punjabi Sikhs. April 1914 — departure from Hong Kong. May 1914 — arrival at Vancouver, a Shore Committee formed, a two-month standoff. July 1914 — the ship forced out of Canadian waters.

3. Budge Budge — humiliation at home (see 'The Komagata Maru Incident (1914)' + 'WWI 1914–19: The Opportunity Arrives'). September 1914 — the ship reached Budge Budge near Calcutta & the British tried to move the passengers to Punjab by special train. They resisted; police opened fire & killed around 20. Because the war had begun in July, the returning passengers were treated as enemy operatives. The incident proved Indians were humiliated both abroad & at home, & fed Ghadar recruitment directly.

4. What the press had already built (see 'Press Campaign Builds Narrative & Awareness' + 'The Ghadr Newspaper — Propaganda of the Deed in Print'). Free Hindustan (1907), Swadesh Sevak (1909) which asked Indian troops to revolt, & The Ghadr from 1913. Its front page carried "Angrezi Raj ka kachcha Chithha", its Ghadr Di Goonj poems preached unity of all religions, & its final call was for 31 crore Indians to rise against 1.2 lakh British. Printed in Urdu, Punjabi, Hindi & English, it was smuggled in to soldiers & peasants in Punjab — the argument was already in circulation when the ship came home.
Closing verdict: Komagata Maru did most to radicalise Punjab, but only because the overseas press campaign had already named the grievance the voyage then proved.
revise: The Ghadr Newspaper — Propaganda of the Deed in Print

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of the following events?
items: 1. Tilak's Home Rule League.
2. Komagata Maru Incident.
3. Mahatma Gandhi's arrival in India.
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists:
explanation: (D) ✓ — The sequence is 2, 3, 1: Komagata Maru incident (1914 — see) → Gandhi's arrival in India (January 1915) → Tilak's Indian Home Rule League (April 1916).
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Opens with Tilak's Home Rule League (April 1916) — the LAST of the three events, not the first.
(B) ✗ — Puts Gandhi's arrival (January 1915) before the Komagata Maru voyage (1914) — the ship's saga had already ended at Budge Budge before Gandhi landed.
(C) ✗ — Starts correctly with Komagata Maru (1914) but then places Tilak's league (April 1916) before Gandhi's arrival (January 1915).
(Note: Komagata Maru - 1914 Mahatma Gandhi's arrival in India - 1915 Home rule league established by Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant 1916.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: Who among the following was a proponent of Fabianism as a movement?
explanation: (A) ✓ — It was launched independently by two leaders — Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — A.O. Hume was the INC's liberal founder-organiser — not a Fabian; the Fabian Society membership belongs to Annie Besant's British years.
(C) ✗ — Michael Madhusudan Dutt was the Bengali poet of an earlier generation — he died (1873) before the Fabian Society itself was even founded (1884).
(D) ✗ — R. Palme Dutt was a COMMUNIST theoretician — well to the left of Fabian gradualism; the Fabian connection is Besant's.

(Note: As a member of the National Secular Society, Annie Besant preached free thought and as a member of the Fabian Society in India. Annie Besant was a prominent British Socialist, theosophist, and a women's rights activist.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: Annie Besant was
items: 1. responsible for starting the Home Rule Movement.
2. the founder of the Theosophical society.
3. the President of the Indian National Congress.
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below
explanation: (C) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are true: Besant launched the All India Home Rule League (September 1916) and was made INC President at the 1917 Calcutta Session. Statement 2 fails: she was the HEAD of the Theosophical Society in Madras but not its founder — that was Madame Blavatsky and Colonel Olcott.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "Only 1" undercounts: statement 3 is also true — Besant presided over the INC's 1917 Calcutta Session.
(B) ✗ — Keeps the false statement 2 (Besant led, but did not found, the Theosophical Society) and discards the true statement 1 (she launched the Home Rule Movement).
(D) ✗ — Overcounts: statement 2 is the trap — the Theosophical Society's founders were Blavatsky and Olcott; Besant was its later head.

(Note: Even though, Annie Besant was associated with the Theosophical society, she was not its founder. It was founded by Madame Blavatsky and Henry Olcott. Thus, Statement 2 is incorrect. Statement 3 is correct.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: In 1920, which of the following changed its name to Swarajya Sabha?
explanation: (A) ✓ — (Tilak is Indian, hence Indian Home Rule League.) 5.2) September 1916 — Besant set up the All India Home Rule League.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — The Hindu Mahasabha kept its own name and communal-political track; it was never renamed Swarajya Sabha.
(C) ✗ — The South Indian Liberal Federation was the Justice Party of Madras — a non-Brahmin party with no Swarajya Sabha phase.
(D) ✗ — Gokhale's Servants of India Society (1905) retained its name and social-service mission; the 1920 renaming happened to the All India Home Rule League under Gandhi.
(Note: The Indian Home Rule Movement was a movement in British India on the lines of Irish Home Rule Movement and other home rule movements. The movement lasted around two years between 1916-1918.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: In which month and year did Bal Gangadhar Tilak set up the Indian Home Rule League?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Tilak set up the Indian Home Rule League in April 1916; Annie Besant's All India Home Rule League followed in September 1916. The Indian HRL had its headquarters at Poona with 6 branches and operated in Bombay Province/Maharashtra (except Bombay city), Berar, Karnataka and Central Provinces).

Why others wrong: (b) September 1916 is when Besant set up the All India Home Rule League, not Tilak's Indian HRL; (c) December 1916 is the date of the Lucknow Session where Extremists actually re-entered INC, not the founding of Tilak's league; (d) April 1917 is unrelated — Besant's arrest occurred in 1917 but the leagues were already founded by then.
Memory hook: Tilak's Indian league bloomed in April; Besant's All-India league arrived in September.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Where was the headquarters of Annie Besant's All India Home Rule League located?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Besant's All India Home Rule League had its headquarters at Madras and operated 200 branches across the rest of British India outside Tilak's zone; Madras was also the seat of Besant's Theosophical Society).

Why others wrong: (a) Poona was the headquarters of Tilak's Indian Home Rule League, not Besant's; (b) Bombay city was excluded even from Tilak's zone and was not the HQ of either league; (d) Calcutta is the venue of the 1917 INC Session where Besant was made President, not the HQ of her league.
Memory hook: Besant the Theosophist anchored both her Society and her League at Madras.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Annie Besant, the founder of the All India Home Rule League, was inspired by the Home Rule movement of which country?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Annie Besant was an Irish woman inspired by the Home Rule movement in Ireland; she joined INC in 1914 and later headed the Theosophical Society based in Madras).

Why others wrong: (a) Scotland had no Home Rule movement that inspired Besant; (c) Wales is not mentioned as the source of Besant's inspiration; (d) Canada was already a Self-Governing Dominion and not a Home Rule model.
Memory hook: Irish Home Rule fired the Theosophist; Indian Home Rule followed her ship.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Tilak's famous quote on untouchability — "If God tolerates untouchability then I won't recognise him as God" — was delivered at which forum?

options.text: The All India Depressed Classes Conference (1918)

explanation: (C) ✓ — Tilak delivered the specific quote against untouchability at the 1918 All India Depressed Classes Conference. His focus on caste unity went back much earlier — at the Ganpati Festival of 1893, he had made Lord Ganapati, worshipped by both Upper and Lower Castes, the centrepiece).

Why others wrong: (a) The Ganpati Festival of 1893 was where Tilak began his caste-unity outreach using Lord Ganapati as a common deity, but the specific quote came later; (b) The Lucknow Session 1916 saw the Pact and Extremists' re-entry, not this quote; (d) The 1915 Bombay Session permitted Extremists' re-entry but was not the venue for this specific quote.
Memory hook: Ganapati in 1893 opened the temple door; the 1918 Depressed Classes platform delivered the line.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Who held the post of Organising Secretary of Annie Besant's All India Home Rule League?
explanation: (B) ✓ — George Arundale was the Organising Secretary of Besant's All India HRL — the person who did the heavy lifting of building the league's network across India and acted as the right hand to Besant; the Organising Secretary handles correspondence, campaigns and network-building.

Why others wrong: (a) Sir S. Subramania Iyer was the Honorary President of Besant's All India HRL, not its Organising Secretary; (c) Jinnah joined Besant's All India HRL and became President of its Bombay branch, but was not the Organising Secretary of the league as a whole; (d) Nehru joined Besant's League through this movement but did not serve as Organising Secretary.
Memory hook: Iyer the honorary face, Arundale the organising hands.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Who renounced his knighthood in 1917 in protest against the arrest and internment of Annie Besant?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Sir S. Subramania Iyer (the Jurist, 1842–1924) renounced his knighthood in 1917 in protest of Besant's arrest and also wrote an explosive letter to US President Woodrow Wilson; he had been knighted in 1900 (K.C.I.E.) and was the Honorary President of Besant's All India HRL).

Why others wrong: (a) G. Subramania Iyer (the Journalist, 1855–1916) had died in 1916, before Besant's arrest, and was never knighted; (c) George Arundale was Organising Secretary of Besant's league but had no knighthood to renounce; (d) Tilak had no knighthood and is not associated with this protest act.
Memory hook: Knighthood off, letter to Wilson on — Sir S. Iyer for Besant.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: In 1920, the All India Home Rule League changed its name to which of the following?
explanation: (A) ✓ — In 1920, the All India Home Rule League changed its name to Swarajya Sabha; this is explicitly noted's ⚠ Alert (Prelims 2018)).

Why others wrong: (b) The Servants of India Society was founded by G.K. Gokhale in 1905 and is a separate body; (c) Hindu Mahasabha was a distinct communal organisation, not a renaming of the All India HRL; (d) The South Indian Liberal Federation (Justice Party) was a non-Brahmin political body in Madras, unrelated to the HRL.
Memory hook: Home Rule traded its English name in 1920 for the Sanskritic Swarajya Sabha.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Who authored the Commonwealth of India Bill (1925) proposing Dominion Status for India?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Annie Besant authored the Commonwealth of India Bill (1925) proposing Dominion Status for India — a direct extension of her lifelong campaign for self-governance within the Empire; she had earlier popularised the idea of a voluntary 'Commonwealth of Nations', a phrase coined by Lord Rosebery in 1884).

Why others wrong: (a) Motilal Nehru authored the Motilal Nehru Report of 1928, which first formally used the phrase "Dominion Status", but not the 1925 Bill; (b) Tilak had died in 1920 and could not have authored a 1925 Bill; (d) Jinnah did not author the Commonwealth of India Bill 1925.
Memory hook: Rosebery coined Commonwealth, Besant bottled it into a 1925 Indian Bill.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Home Rule League Movement of 1916–18:
items: 1. It was launched as an initiative of the Indian National Congress.
2. Its method was educative propaganda on Home Rule and Swaraj.
3. It was a programme of Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Only Statement 2 is correct. The HRL Movement was launched independently by Tilak and Besant, not as an INC initiative, so Statement 1 is wrong. Its method was educative propaganda about Home Rule and Swaraj within the British Empire. It was explicitly NOT a programme of Non-Cooperation or Civil Disobedience, so Statement 3 is wrong.
Why others wrong: (a) wrongly includes Statement 1 — HRL was independent of INC; (b) wrongly includes Statement 3 — HRL did not adopt NC/CD; (c) wrongly accepts both Statements 1 and 3.
Memory hook: Two leaders, one method (propaganda) — never INC, never CD.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the territorial division between the two Home Rule Leagues:
items: 1. Tilak's Indian Home Rule League operated in Bombay Province/Maharashtra (except Bombay city), Berar, Karnataka and Central Provinces.
2. Tilak's Indian Home Rule League had its headquarters at Poona with 6 branches.
3. Besant's All India Home Rule League had 200 branches with headquarters at Bombay.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Tilak's Indian HRL operated in Bombay Province/Maharashtra (except Bombay city), Berar, Karnataka and Central Provinces, with 6 branches and HQ at Poona. Statement 3 is wrong on the headquarters — Besant's All India HRL did have 200 branches covering the rest of British India, but it was headquartered at Madras (Besant's Theosophical Society base), not Bombay. Bombay was only a branch of her league — the branch whose President was Jinnah.

Why others wrong: (b) wrongly accepts Statement 3, which shifts Besant's headquarters from Madras to Bombay, and also drops the correct Statement 1 on Tilak's operational zone. (c) wrongly accepts the same false Statement 3 and drops the correct Statement 2 on Tilak's 6 branches and Poona HQ. (d) fails because Statement 3 is false — Bombay held only a branch of the All India HRL (Jinnah was its President); the HQ was Madras.
Memory hook: Tilak = Poona, 6 branches; Besant = Madras, 200 branches. Bombay was only Jinnah's branch, never a headquarters.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Lucknow Pact of 1916:
items: 1. It was the first time INC and the Muslim League jointly demanded constitutional reforms from the British.
2. The Muslim League agreed to give up its right to vote in General/Unreserved constituencies in exchange for a fixed quota of seats.
3. INC formally accepted the principle of Separate Electorates in future council reforms.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — All three statements are correct. The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was the first joint INC–ML1906 platform for constitutional reform; in the Hindu-Muslim Electoral Compromise, the Muslim League gave up voting in General/Unreserved seats in exchange for a guaranteed fixed quota of Muslim seats; and INC formally accepted the principle of Separate Electorates in future council reforms.

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly drops the correct Statement 3 on INC's acceptance of Separate Electorates; (b) wrongly drops the correct Statement 1 on the joint demand; (c) wrongly drops the correct Statement 2 on the Muslim League's concession.
Memory hook: Joint platform, fixed quota, accepted separation — Lucknow's triple bargain.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Consider the following demands placed jointly by INC and the Muslim League at the Lucknow Pact of 1916:
items: 1. Continuation of Separate Electorates in future council reforms.
2. An elected majority in the expanded councils.
3. Universal Adult Franchise.
4. At least 50% Indians in the Viceroy's Executive Council.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The Lucknow Pact demanded continuation of Separate Electorates, an elected majority in expanded councils, and at least 50% Indians in the Viceroy's Executive Council. Statement 3 is wrong — they demanded a franchise as broad as possible and direct elections, but did NOT yet demand Universal Adult Franchise; the formal UAF demand came with the Motilal Nehru Report of 1928.
Why others wrong: (b) wrongly includes UAF and drops the elected-majority demand; (c) wrongly includes UAF and drops Separate Electorates; (d) wrongly accepts UAF as a 1916 demand.
Memory hook: 1916 asked broad, 1928 asked Universal — don't merge the two reports.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about G. Subramania Iyer (1855–1916):
items: 1. He co-founded the English newspaper The Hindu in
2. He founded the Tamil nationalist daily Swadesamitran in
3. He moved the very first resolution at the 1885 Bombay Session of the INC.
4. He renounced his knighthood in protest against Annie Besant's arrest.
questions.stemTail: 1878 1882 Which of the statements given above are correct?
