explanation: (C) ✓ — Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. G. Subramania Iyer (the Journalist) co-founded The Hindu in 1878, founded Swadesamitran in 1882 and moved the first resolution at the 1885 INC Bombay Session. Statement 4 is wrong — it was Sir S. Subramania Iyer (the Jurist) who renounced his knighthood in 1917 in protest against Besant's arrest).

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly includes Statement 4 — knighthood renunciation belongs to Sir S. Iyer; (b) wrongly drops Statement 1 and adds Statement 4; (d) wrongly drops Statement 2 and adds Statement 4.
Memory hook: G. for journalist 1885; Sir S. for jurist 1917 — never swap their stories.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Extremists' conception of "Passive Resistance" in 1917:
items: 1. It was drawn from Bal Gangadhar Tilak's articles in the Marathi newspaper Kesari (April 1907).
2. It explicitly included Non-Cooperation — boycott of British goods, schools, courts and administrative roles.
3. It directed nationalists to break oppressive laws deliberately and accept the punishment.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct. To the Extremists, "Passive Resistance" was an umbrella term covering a comprehensive Non-Cooperation programme (boycott of British goods, government schools, courts and administrative roles) and its escalation into Civil Disobedience — deliberately breaking oppressive laws and accepting the punishment. Statement 1 misattributes the source: the doctrine came from Aurobindo Ghosh's seven-article series "The Doctrine of Passive Resistance" in Bande Mataram (April 1907). Kesari (Marathi) and Maharatta (English) were Tilak's papers, and Tilak was not the author of this doctrine.

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly accepts Statement 1, which credits Tilak's Kesari instead of Aurobindo's Bande Mataram, and also drops the correct law-breaking (Civil Disobedience) component. (c) wrongly accepts the same false Statement 1 and drops the correct Non-Cooperation (boycott) component. (d) fails because Statement 1 is false — the Doctrine of Passive Resistance was Aurobindo Ghosh's, published in Bande Mataram in April 1907, not Tilak's in Kesari.
Memory hook: Doctrine of Passive Resistance = Aurobindo, seven articles, Bande Mataram, April 1907. Kesari and Maharatta belong to Tilak.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the impact of the Home Rule League Movement:
items: 1. The HRLs brought Gujarat, Sindh, United Provinces, Bihar and South India more actively into the Indian National Movement.
2. About 60,000 members joined the HRLs.
3. Lower Castes in Madras strongly supported the All India HRL.
4. The HRL period permanently decreased the influence of Moderates in INC.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The HRLs activated Gujarat, Sindh, United Provinces, Bihar and South India in the INM; 60,000 members joined the HRLs; and the period permanently decreased the influence of Moderates in INC. Statement 3 is wrong — in Madras, Lower Castes did NOT support the All India HRL because its leadership was Upper Caste dominated).

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly includes Statement 3 — Lower Castes did not back the Madras HRL; (c) wrongly drops Statement 1 and includes Statement 3; (d) wrongly drops Statement 2 and includes Statement 3.
Memory hook: 60,000 members, four new regions, Moderates eclipsed — but Madras Lower Castes stayed away.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_16
questions.stem: Arrange the following events in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Tilak returns to India from Mandalay
2. Tilak sets up the Indian Home Rule League
3. Besant is arrested and interned
4. Besant is made INC President at Calcutta Session
explanation: (A) ✓ — The correct sequence is 1, 2, 3, 4. Tilak returned to India from Mandalay (Burma) in 1914 after six years of imprisonment; he set up the Indian Home Rule League in April 1916; Besant was arrested and interned in 1917; and Besant was released and made INC President at the 1917 Calcutta Session — Setting Up the Two Leagues; — After Besant's Arrest (1917)).

Why others wrong: (b) wrongly places Tilak's league before his return from Mandalay; (c) wrongly places Besant's arrest before Tilak's league founding; (d) wrongly places Tilak's league before his return and inverts the arrest-Presidency order.
Memory hook: Mandalay return then Poona league then Madras arrest then Calcutta gavel.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_17
questions.stem: Arrange the following events in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Tilak's Home Rule League is founded
2. Komagata Maru Incident
3. Mahatma Gandhi's arrival in India
4. Lucknow Pact between INC and Muslim League
explanation: (C) ✓ — The correct sequence is 2, 3, 1, 4. The Komagata Maru Incident (1914) and Gandhi's return to India (1915) both predate Tilak's Indian Home Rule League (April 1916), which itself slightly predates the Lucknow Pact (December 1916); this aligns with the record ⚠ Alert citing UPSC Prelims 1998 on the first three of these events — After Besant's Arrest (1917); — Lucknow Pact (1916)).

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly places Tilak's league before the Komagata Maru Incident; (b) wrongly places Tilak's league before Gandhi's arrival; (d) wrongly places Gandhi's arrival before the Komagata Maru Incident.
Memory hook: Komagata first, Gandhi sails in, Tilak leagues up, Lucknow signs off.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_18
questions.stem: Arrange the following Phase-1 "Decade of Alienation" events that triggered the Muslim League's shift toward the Lucknow Pact, in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Annulment of Bengal Partition
2. Italy's takeover of Libya from the Ottoman Empire
3. First Balkan War
4. Outbreak of World War 1
explanation: (D) ✓ — The correct sequence is 1, 2, 3, 4. The Annulment of Bengal Partition and Italy's takeover of Libya both occurred in 1911; the First Balkan War broke out in 1912; and the outbreak of World War 1 came in 1914. The record lists these in this exact order as Phase 1 triggers for the Lucknow Pact).

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly inverts the 1911 ordering as given by the record; (b) wrongly places the 1912 Balkan War before the 1911 Libya takeover; (c) wrongly places the 1912 Balkan War before both 1911 events.
Memory hook: Bengal undone, Libya gone, Balkans aflame, World War on — that was 1911-to-1914.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_19
questions.stem:
Match List-I (Newspaper/Journal) with List-II (Founder/Publisher):

List-I: A. Kesari ; B. New India ; C. The Hindu ; D. Swadesamitran

List-II:
items: 1. Annie Besant ;
2. Bal Gangadhar Tilak ;
3. G. Subramania Iyer (with co-founders) ;
4. G. Subramania Iyer
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
explanation: (A) ✓ — Correct matching: Kesari (Marathi) was published by Tilak; New India was published by Besant; The Hindu was co-founded in 1878 by G. Subramania Iyer (along with M. Veeraraghavachariar and P. Anandacharlu); Swadesamitran (1882, Tamil daily) was founded solely by G. Subramania Iyer — The Two Subramania Iyers).

Why others wrong: (b) wrongly swaps Tilak and Besant for Kesari and New India; (c) wrongly swaps the co-founded vs solely-founded labels for The Hindu and Swadesamitran; (d) wrongly swaps both pairs simultaneously.
Memory hook: Tilak roars in Kesari, Besant glows in New India; Iyer co-built The Hindu, Iyer alone built Swadesamitran.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_20
questions.stem:
Match List-I (Event/Treaty) with List-II (Year):

List-I: A. Annulment of Bengal Partition ; B. Italy's takeover of Libya ; C. Balfour Declaration ; D. Treaty of Sevres

List-II:
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
explanation: (B) ✓ — Correct pairing: Annulment of Bengal Partition (1911), Italy's takeover of Libya from the Ottoman Empire (1911), Balfour Declaration (1917) declaring British intent to create a Jewish homeland in Palestine, and Treaty of Sevres (1920) signed with the Ottoman Empire after WW1 — a harsh treaty seen by Indian Muslims as breaching British wartime promises about the dignity of the Khalifa).

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly swaps the Balfour Declaration (1917) and Treaty of Sevres (1920) years; (c) wrongly swaps Balfour and Sevres years; (d) wrongly swaps Balfour and Sevres years; option (B) gets all four pairings to their correct years.
Memory hook: Two 1911 shocks, one 1917 declaration, one 1920 treaty — the road from Lucknow to Khilafat.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) failed as a mass movement but succeeded as a preparation for one." Critically examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" asks you to test both halves of the claim & then judge. The anchor is 1916–18 — Tilak & Besant, working outside INC. The two framing phrases pull opposite ways: "failed as a mass movement" points to the repression of 1917–18, while "succeeded as a preparation for one" points to what the Gandhian era inherited. Judge the movement by what came after it, not only by what it won at the time.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) failed as a mass movement — by 1918 the leagues were defunct. Yet it succeeded as a preparation for one.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. The vacuum the leagues filled (see 'Context: Why the Movement Was Necessary'). Tilak returned from Mandalay (Burma) in 1914 after six years of imprisonment & found the INM at a dull phase. The British had firmly suppressed the Extremists & Revolutionaries. The Moderates had worked within the system in 1892 & again in 1909 with the Indian Councils Act (ICA1909), but no Self-Government came — the goal INC had set for itself since the 1906 Calcutta Session. Pair with 'Tilak's Strategy' — Tilak publicly declared that Swaraj meant self-rule within the British Empire, disowned violence, backed the war effort & professed loyalty to the Crown, so that the British could not easily repress the Extremists again.

2. A method that ruled out mass action (see 'Home Rule League Movement (1916–18)'). This was not an INC initiative. Tilak & Besant launched it independently. The method was educative propaganda on Home Rule & Swaraj — not Non-Cooperation, not Civil Disobedience. Add 'Demands & Spread of the Movement' — the slogan "Swaraj is my birthright & I shall have it", demands for education in vernacular languages, linguistic reorganisation of Provinces & an end to untouchability, & heavy use of the press: Kesari & Maharatta by Tilak, New India & Commonweal by Besant.

3. The organisation actually built (see 'Setting Up the Two Leagues'). April 1916 — Tilak set up the Indian Home Rule League: Bombay Province/Maharashtra (except Bombay city), Berar, Karnataka, Central Provinces, 6 branches, HQ at Poona. September 1916 — Besant set up the All India Home Rule League: the rest of British India, 200 branches, HQ at Madras. The two leagues cooperated but chose not to merge, to prevent friction among their followers.

4. The failure side — repression & the split of 1917 (see 'Overall Impact — Positives & Negatives'). By 1917–18 the British had repressed the HRLs & they became defunct. Educative propaganda could not convert itself into a mass movement. In Madras, Lower Castes did not support the All India HRL because its leadership was Upper Caste dominated. Extremists failed a second time to take over INC. Pair with 'Understanding "Passive Resistance": Extremists, Besant, and Gandhi' — the Extremists proposed a programme of Passive Resistance in 1917, the Moderates opposed it, & Besant sided with the Moderates. No common programme emerged.

5. The preparation side — what Besant's arrest handed on (see 'After Besant's Arrest (1917)'). Her arrest & internment in 1917 energised the movement instead of killing it. Now even Moderates joined the HRLs. Sir S. Subramania Iyer, Honorary President of her All India HRL, gave up his knighthood. Gandhi began a signature campaign; Besant was released & made INC President at the 1917 Calcutta Session (see 'The Two Subramania Iyers'). Return to 'Overall Impact — Positives & Negatives' for the balance sheet — 60,000 members joined the HRLs; Gujarat, Sindh, United Provinces, Bihar & South India came more actively into the INM; Nehru joined Besant's League; the organisational network survived for later phases; the movement was secular in its methods & helped Hindu-Muslim unity; & Moderate influence in INC fell permanently.
Closing verdict: It failed as a mass movement because propaganda alone cannot become action. It succeeded as a preparation for one — Gandhi inherited its network & leaders.
revise: Context: Why the Movement Was Necessary

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Evaluate the Lucknow Pact (1916) as both a landmark of Hindu-Muslim political cooperation & a concession that hardened communal division.
body: Demand of the question: "Evaluate" asks for a judgement on both sides, not a list of clauses. The anchor is 1916 — INC & ML1906 at Lucknow, in the middle of the Home Rule years. The word "both" bars a one-sided answer. Show the same electoral bargain working as unity & as division, then judge it.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Lucknow Pact (1916) was a landmark of Hindu-Muslim political cooperation. The same electoral bargain was also a concession that hardened communal division.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Why ML1906 came to the table (see 'Why ML1906 Turned Against the British — World Context'). ML1906 was founded largely with British support & began with a loyal, deferential tone. Four shocks changed that: 1911 — the annulment of the Bengal Partition, which ML1906 had supported; 1911 — Italy took Libya from the Ottoman Empire & Britain did nothing; 1912 — the 1st Balkan War dismembered Ottoman territory; 1914 — World War 1, with the Ottoman Empire fighting as part of the Central Powers against Britain.

2. Who built it & what it asked for (see 'Lucknow Pact (1916)'). It was the first time INC (founded 1885) & ML1906 gave joint demands to the British, & ML1906 also supported the HRLs. It came from the combined efforts of Tilak, Jinnah & Annie Besant; Jinnah had joined Besant's All India HRL & became President of its Bombay branch (see 'Demands & Spread of the Movement'). The common platform asked for expanded councils with an elected majority, at least 50% Indians in the Viceroy's Executive Council, a franchise as broad as possible with direct elections, & self-government at an early date with equal status with other Self-Governing Dominions.

3. The price paid — the Hindu-Muslim Electoral Compromise (see 'Lucknow Pact (1916)'). ML1906 gave up its right to vote in General/Unreserved constituencies. In exchange INC formally accepted the principle of Separate Electorates & a guaranteed, fixed quota of Muslim seats. The British later adopted the mechanics of this compromise into the Government of India Act 1919, which created strictly segregated, "watertight" electoral rolls.

4. The two-sided verdict (see 'Lucknow Pact (1916)'). Negative — a major landmark in the Two Nation Theory, because INC formally conceded that Hindus & Muslims were separate political communities needing separate electoral representation. Positive — the INC-ML1906 unity that MG later used in the Khilafat Movement (1919–24) & the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22); it created pressure on the British, contributed directly to the Montague Statement of 1917 & the GOI Act 1919, & defeated the British strategy of Divide & Rule for the time being.
Closing verdict: The Lucknow Pact (1916) bought unity at a price. It was a landmark of Hindu-Muslim political cooperation & a concession that hardened communal division.
revise: Why ML1906 Turned Against the British — World Context

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem:
What is the correct sequence of the following events?
1. The Lucknow Pact
2. The Introduction of Dyarchy
3. The Rowlatt Act
4. The partition of Bengal
explanation: (B) ✓ — The chain runs 4, 1, 3, 2: Partition of Bengal (effected 16 October 1905 — see) → Lucknow Pact (December 1916 — see) → Rowlatt Act (March 1919) → introduction of Dyarchy under GOI 1919.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Opens with the Lucknow Pact (1916) and parks the Partition of Bengal (1905) LAST — the Partition is the earliest of the four events.
(C) ✗ — Same defect as (a): the Partition of Bengal (1905) cannot come after Rowlatt (1919) and Dyarchy — it precedes them all.
(D) ✗ — Starts rightly with the Partition but then reverses the rest: the Lucknow Pact (1916) preceded the Rowlatt Act (1919) and Dyarchy, not the other way round.

(Note: 16th October, 1905 — Partition of Bengal | 29th December, 1916 — Lucknow Pact | 19th March, 1919 — Rowlatt Act | 23rd December, 1919 — Introduction of Dyarchy (through Montagu Chelmsford Reforms.))

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: When Congress leaders condemned the Montague-Chelmsford report, many moderates left the party to form the
explanation: (D) ✓ — When the INC's 1918 special session condemned the Montford scheme, the Moderates walked out and formed the All India National Liberal Federation (1918) under leaders like Surendranath Banerjea and Tej Bahadur Sapru — the "Indian liberal federation" of the option.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Swarajya Party (1923) was C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru's Council-entry party born of the Non-Cooperation aftermath — not the Moderates' 1918 walkout vehicle.
(B) ✗ — No "Indian freedom party" exists in the era's record — the seceding Moderates took the LIBERAL name (All India National Liberal Federation, 1918).
(C) ✗ — "Independence federation of India" is a distractor coinage; the real body the Moderates founded in 1918 was the All India National Liberal Federation.
(Note: When Montague-Chelmsford report was announced on 20th August, 1917 then moderates welcomed and extremists in the leadership of Tilak condemned it.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: The Montague-Chelmsford Report formed the basis of
explanation: (B) ✓ — It is known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918), and it directly led to the Government of India Act, 1919 — which is why the Act is also called the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms or simply the Montford Reforms.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Indian Councils Act 1909 PRE-dates the Report — its basis was the Morley-Minto scheme, not the 1918 Montford Report.
(C) ✗ — GOI 1935 grew out of the Simon Commission-Round Table-Communal Award lineage; the Montford Report's direct product was the 1919 Act.
(D) ✗ — The Indian Independence Act 1947 implemented the Mountbatten Plan three decades later; the Report of 1918 "directly led to the Government of India Act, 1919."

(Note: The Montague-Chelmsford Report which was announced in August, 1917 formed the basis of the Government of India Act, 1919. The Government of India Act was passed to expand participation of Indians in the government.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: Which of the following is/are the principal feature(s) of the Government of India Act, 1919?
items: 1. Introduction of dyarchy in the executive government of the provinces.
2. Introduction of separate communal electorates for Muslims.
3. Devolution of legislative authority by the centre to the provinces.
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below
explanation: (C) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are 1919 features: Dyarchy in the provincial executive and the first division of subjects between Centre and Provinces — devolution of legislative authority. Statement 2 fails: separate communal electorates for Muslims came with ICA 1909 — GOI 1919 only EXTENDED the principle to other communities.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "Only 1" undercounts: the division of subjects between Centre and Provinces (statement 3) is equally a principal 1919 feature.
(B) ✗ — Keeps the 1909 item (Muslim separate electorates — a Morley-Minto creation) while dropping Dyarchy, the Act's most debated feature.
(D) ✗ — Overcounts: Muslim communal electorates predate the Act by a decade (ICA 1909 — see).

(Note: Government of India Act, 1919, also known as Montague-Chelmsford reforms introduced dyarchy in the executive government of the provinces and delivered the legislative authority by the centre to the provinces.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: The Government of India Act of 1919 clearly defined

options.text: the separation of power between the Judiciary and the Legislature
the jurisdiction of the Central and Provincial Governments
the power of the Secretary of State for India and the Viceroy

explanation: (B) ✓ — Subjects were divided between Centre and Provinces for the first time — the Act's clearly defined contribution was the jurisdiction of the Central and Provincial Governments.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Act drew no judiciary-legislature separation; its separations were subject-lists — Centre vs Province, and Reserved vs Transferred within provinces. +.
(C) ✗ — The Secretary of State-Viceroy power equation was inherited machinery, not something the 1919 Act newly defined; the Act's defined line was the Centre-Province division of subjects.
(D) ✗ — "None" fails because the Act DID clearly define one thing: the first formal division of subjects between Centre and Provinces.

(Note: Montague-Chelmsford Reform and Government of India Act, 1919, in 1918, Edwin Montague, the Secretary of State, and Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy, produced their scheme of constitutional reforms.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals were related to
explanation: (D) ✓ — The Montague-Chelmsford proposals led to initiation of Government of India Act, 1919. They proposed constitutional reforms with following salient features 1. Diarchy was introduced in provinces. The provinces subjects were divided into two groups. One was reserved and another transferred. 2. It proposed bicameral in Central Legislature. 3. The Act provided for establishment of a Public Service Com
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The proposals carried no social-reform agenda — their whole substance was the redesign of councils, executive and franchise.
(B) ✗ — Education figures only as a transferred SUBJECT under Dyarchy, not as the proposals' theme.
(C) ✗ — Police was a RESERVED subject kept with the Governor — a subject allocation inside the scheme, not the scheme's purpose, which was constitutional reform.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.stem: In the context of Indian history, the principle of 'Dyarchy (diarchy)' refers to

options.text: Division of the central legislature into two houses.
Introduction of double government i.e., Central and State governments.
Having two sets of rulers; one in London and another in Delhi.
Division of the subjects delegated to the provinces into two categories.

explanation: (D) ✓ — Dyarchy means dividing provincial subjects into Reserved (governed by Governor) and Transferred (governed by Ministers responsible to PLA). Option (D) — Division of the subjects delegated to the provinces into two categories — precisely captures this definition.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Splitting the central legislature into two houses is BICAMERALISM — a separate 1919 feature; 'Dyarchy' names the provincial executive's split into Reserved and Transferred halves.
(B) ✗ — Centre-State double government describes a FEDERAL division, not Dyarchy — the dual rule sat INSIDE each province, between the Governor's Reserved half and the Ministers' Transferred half.
(C) ✗ — London-Delhi dual control describes the Secretary of State-Viceroy axis, the old machinery — not the provincial Reserved/Transferred split that 'Dyarchy' denotes.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.stem: In GOI Act 1919, which were “Reserved” subjects?
items: 1. Justice
2. Local Self-Govt
3. Land Revenue
4. Police
explanation: (C) ✓ — Reserved subjects stayed with the Governor: Justice, Land Revenue, and Police (statements 1, 3, 4) — while Local Self-Government (statement 2) was a TRANSFERRED subject under Indian ministers.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Includes Local Self-Government — a TRANSFERRED subject under Indian ministers — and drops Police, which the Governor kept.
(B) ✗ — Again counts Local Self-Government among the Reserved list and omits Justice — but Justice stayed on the Governor's side.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: The Montagu Statement of August 1917 declared that British policy in India would henceforth aim at which of the following?

options.text: The progressive realisation of responsible government in India within the British Empire
The immediate grant of Dominion Status to India after the conclusion of World War I
The full establishment of responsible government at the Centre within ten years
The conferment of universal adult franchise across British India

explanation: (A) ✓ — The August Declaration of 1917, issued by Edwin Montagu as Secretary of State for India, set the goal as the "gradual development of self-governing institutions" with a view to the progressive realisation of responsible government in India within the British Empire. The key words 'gradual' and 'progressive' kept the timeline in British hands; GOI 1919 was conceived as the 1st step toward this goal.

Why others wrong: (b) Dominion Status was not part of the 1917 Statement; the promise was only "progressive realisation" within the Empire, not Dominion Status. (c) The Statement set no time-bound commitment for responsible government at the Centre; the timeline was firmly British-controlled, and GOI 1919 itself did NOT make the Centre responsible. (d) Universal adult franchise was never promised in 1917; the Lucknow Pact 1916 demand for broad franchise was not conceded even in the 1919 Act.
Memory hook: Montagu's two magic words — 'gradual' and 'progressive' — meant: yes Swaraj, but on British clock.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: The Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) was authored jointly by Edwin Montagu and:
explanation: (B) ✓ — Secretary of State Edwin Montagu personally visited India in 1917-18 — an unusual step for someone in his position — and toured various provinces. The joint report he co-authored with Viceroy Chelmsford16-21 became the foundational document for the Government of India Act, 1919, which is why the Act is also called the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms or Montford Reforms.

Why others wrong: (a) Hardinge's viceroyalty ended before the Report; he was not its co-author. (c) Reading succeeded Chelmsford and his tenure began in 1921 — after the Report (1918) and the Act (1919). (d) Irwin came still later in the late 1920s; he had no role in drafting the 1918 Report.
Memory hook: Mont-ford = Mont-agu + Chelms-ford — Report 1918, Act 1919.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Which of the following was introduced for the first time at the Centre by the Government of India Act, 1919?

options.text: Non-official majority in the Central legislature
Indirect election of Indian members to the Central legislature
Bicameral legislature of the Central Legislative Assembly and the Council of States
Universal adult franchise for the Council of States

explanation: (C) ✓ — The GOI Act 1919 introduced a Bicameral Legislature at the Centre for British India for the first time, consisting of the Central Legislative Assembly (CLA, ~145 members, lower house) and the Council of States (CoS, ~60 members, upper house). It also introduced an elected majority and direct elections in CLA, CoS, and Provincial Legislative Assemblies for the 1st time.

Why others wrong: (a) Non-official majority at the Centre was NOT new in 1919 — under ICA1909 a non-official majority already existed in Provincial Legislative Councils (though not at the Centre); the genuine first in 1919 was an ELECTED majority at the Centre, which is not what option (a) states. (b) GOI 1919 introduced DIRECT, not indirect, elections in CLA, CoS, and PLAs for the 1st time. (d) Right to vote remained linked to strict income/property criteria as under ICA1909; no universal adult franchise was granted, and certainly not for the CoS, which actually carried HIGHER income criteria than the lower house.
Memory hook: 1919 = first time British India sees two Houses at the Centre — CLA (lower) + CoS (upper).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Under the Government of India Act, 1919, the Narendra Mandal (Chamber of Princes) was:

options.text: A legislative body for the Princely States with the power to make binding laws
An elected body of Princes with representation proportional to State revenue
Constituted directly by the GOI Act, 1919 itself in the year 1919
An advisory body for the Princely States, formally constituted by Royal Proclamation in 1921

explanation: (D) ✓ — The Narendra Mandal — Chamber of Princes — was a key recommendation of the Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) and was formally constituted by Royal Proclamation in 1921, not by the GOI Act 1919 itself. The Act provided the framework; the Proclamation brought it to life. It was created as an advisory body for the Princely States and carried NO legislative power — purely advisory. It was a reward to the Princes for their support during WWI.

Why others wrong: (a) The Mandal had no legislative power — it was purely advisory; the British only promised to consult the Princes on policy matters affecting the Princely States. (b) Membership was nominated/representational, not elected, and was certainly not tied to State revenue. (c) The Act provided the framework but did NOT itself constitute the body in 1919; the formal constitution came by Royal Proclamation in 1921.
Memory hook: MC Report recommended → Royal Proclamation 1921 inaugurated → Mountbatten 1947 finally addressed it.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: With reference to the Government of India Act, 1919, what was the position regarding women's right to vote?

options.text: The Act did not directly grant women the vote; it empowered Provincial Legislative Assemblies to remove the sex disqualification
The Act granted universal adult suffrage to women in all British Indian provinces
The Act enfranchised women on the basis of their husband's property and a lower income threshold for women
The Act explicitly barred all women from voting in any provincial election

explanation: (A) ✓ — The Act did not directly grant women the right to vote. Instead, it empowered Provincial Legislative Assemblies to pass resolutions removing the sex disqualification. When women were admitted to vote, they had to meet the exact same strict property qualifications as men, meaning less than 1% of women actually qualified.

Why others wrong: (b) Universal adult suffrage was never granted by GOI 1919; the Lucknow Pact 1916 demand for broad franchise was explicitly not conceded. (c) The husband's-property + lower-income criterion for women came only with the Government of India Act, 1935 — NOT 1919; this is a UPSC-tested 1919 vs 1935 trap. (d) The Act did not bar women — it left the matter to PLAs, which gradually removed the sex disqualification.
Memory hook: 1919 = PLAs may lift the bar, same male yardstick. 1935 = husband's property + lower threshold.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Under the Government of India Act, 1919, separate electorates were extended to which of the following communities for the first time (over and above the existing Muslim separate electorate)?

options.text: Only Depressed Classes through reserved elected seats

explanation: (B) ✓ — Separate electorates for Muslims continued from ICA1909 but were made watertight under GOI 1919, and were now extended to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, and Christians as well — all with watertight rolls. Members of these communities could vote only in their respective reserved constituencies, not in unreserved seats.

Why others wrong: (a) Depressed Classes did NOT get a separate electorate under GOI 1919; they got reservation of nominated seats — not elected seats — in all legislatures. (c) Parsis and Buddhists were not added to the separate electorate list under the 1919 Act. (d) Depressed Classes received nominated seats, not elected reserved seats, and nothing more; this option excludes Sikhs, Anglo-Indians and Christians who were the actual additions.
Memory hook: SAC = Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, Christians — added to the 1919 watertight rolls.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: With reference to the Government of India Act, 1919, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Direct elections were introduced for the first time in the Central Legislative Assembly, the Council of States, and the Provincial Legislative Assemblies.
2. The Council of States had direct elections with a higher income criterion for the right to vote than the Central Legislative Assembly.
3. The life of the Central Legislative Assembly was 5 years and that of the Council of States was 3 years.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Statement 1 is correct: Direct elections were introduced for the first time in CLA, CoS, and PLAs. Statement 2 is correct: The CoS also had direct elections with higher income criteria for the right to vote — an unusual feature for an upper house. Statement 3 is INCORRECT — the life of the CLA was 3 years and the life of the CoS was 5 years (the option reverses these). Hence only 1 and 2 are correct.

Why others wrong: (a) Includes statement 3 which reverses the CLA/CoS terms. (b) Drops statement 1 — direct elections in all three bodies were indeed introduced for the 1st time — and retains the reversed statement 3. (d) Includes the reversed statement 3.
Memory hook: Lower CLA = 3 yr, Upper CoS = 5 yr; CoS = 'upper house' but still direct elections — higher income gate.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to the Viceroy's Executive Council under the Government of India Act, 1919, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Act removed the old statutory maximum limit on the number of ordinary members of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
2. The Act statutorily mandated that exactly three of the six ordinary members must be Indians.
3. The Lucknow Pact of 1916 had demanded that half the total Viceroy's Executive Council be Indians.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Statement 1 is correct: The GOI Act 1919 removed the old statutory maximum limit on the number of ordinary members of the VEC (under ICA1861 it was 5, under the 1874 amendment 6; GOI 1919 lifted the cap). Statement 2 is INCORRECT — the 3-Indians-of-6 was a CONVENTION (political/administrative practice), NOT a statutory mandate of the Act. Statement 3 is correct: The Lucknow Pact 1916 had demanded that HALF the total VEC be Indians; 3 of 8 left this demand unmet.
Why others wrong: (a) Treats the 3-Indians figure as a statutory mandate, which it was not. (b) Same error on statement 2 plus drops the correct statement 1. (c) Includes the false statement 2.
Memory hook: Cap lifted by statute; 3 Indians by convention — Lucknow asked half, got three of eight.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: With reference to Dyarchy at the provincial level under the Government of India Act, 1919, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Reserved subjects included Law and Order i.e. Police, Administration of Justice, Finance, Land Revenue, and Control over Officials.
2. Ministers handling Reserved subjects were responsible to the Provincial Legislative Assembly.
3. In case of a failure of constitutional machinery, the Governor could take over executive and legislative powers over Transferred subjects.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statement 1 is correct: Reserved subjects were politically important — namely Law & Order i.e. Police, Administration of Justice, Finance, Land Revenue, and Control over Officials. Statement 2 is INCORRECT — Ministers handling Reserved subjects were NOT responsible to the PLA; legislative & executive powers on reserved subjects were with the Governor & his officials; only the Ministers handling TRANSFERRED subjects were responsible to the PLA. Statement 3 is correct: In case of failure of constitutional machinery, the Governor could take over executive & legislative powers over transferred subjects as well.
Why others wrong: (b) Includes the wrong statement 2. (c) Includes the wrong statement 2 and drops the correct statement 1. (d) Includes the wrong statement 2.
Memory hook: Reserved = Governor's politically important basket; Transferred Ministers answer to PLA, but Governor can swallow Transferred subjects too if machinery fails.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: With reference to the powers of the Viceroy under the Government of India Act, 1919, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Viceroy had veto power over all bills.
2. The Viceroy could pass bills that had been rejected by the Central Legislative Assembly or the Council of States.
3. The Viceroy's ordinances were valid for 12 months.
4. 75% of the budget items were non-votable.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statement 1 is correct (veto power over all bills). Statement 2 is correct (the Viceroy could pass bills rejected by CLA/CoS — "power to approve rejected bills"). Statement 3 is INCORRECT — the Viceroy's ordinances were valid for 6 months, not 12. Statement 4 is correct — 75% of the budget items were non-votable; the legislature could discuss but real financial control stayed with the executive.

Why others wrong: (a) Includes the wrong 12-month ordinance figure and drops the correct 75% non-votable statement. (c) Same 12-month ordinance error and drops the correct veto power statement. (d) Includes the wrong 12-month ordinance figure.
Memory hook: Veto, override CLA/CoS, 6-month ordinance, 75% budget locked — 'Taxation Without Representation' continued past 1919.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: With reference to the civil services reforms under the Government of India Act, 1919, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Act mandated that the ICS examination be held simultaneously in India alongside England.
2. Section 96C of the Act mandated the setting up of a Public Service Commission for India.
3. The Public Service Commission under the Act was established in 1919 itself with Sir Ross Barker as its first Chairman.
4. The Act also mandated a gradual increase to 33% Indians in senior civil service positions.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Statement 1 is correct: The GOI Act 1919 mandated simultaneous holding of the ICS exam in India alongside England (the first such examination in India was held in 1922). Statement 2 is correct: Section 96C mandated the setting up of a Public Service Commission for India. Statement 3 is INCORRECT — the Commission was established in 1926 (NOT 1919), with Ross Barker as its first Chairman. Statement 4 is correct: The Act mandated a gradual increase to 33% Indians in senior civil service positions.

Why others wrong: (a) Includes the wrong 1919 establishment date for the PSC; the correct year is 1926. (b) Includes the wrong 1919 PSC date. (d) Drops the correct Section 96C statement and retains the wrong 1919 PSC date.
Memory hook: 1919 mandated, 1922 first Indian ICS exam, 1926 PSC under Ross Barker — institutional ancestor of UPSC.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order:
items: 1. Lucknow Pact between INC and the Muslim League
2. Montagu Statement / August Declaration
3. Montagu-Chelmsford Report
4. Government of India Act, 1919
questions.stemTail: Choose the correct sequence from the options below:
explanation: (D) ✓ — The correct sequence is: Lucknow Pact (1916) → Montagu Statement / August Declaration (1917) → Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) → Government of India Act (1919). The Lucknow Pact of 1916 preceded the Montagu Statement of August 1917; Montagu's India visit in 1917-18 produced the joint Report of 1918; the Report directly led to the Act of 1919.

Why others wrong: (a) Places the August Declaration (1917) before the Lucknow Pact (1916). (b) Places the Report (1918) before the August Declaration (1917). (c) Places the Report (1918) before the Lucknow Pact (1916).
Memory hook: Pact 16 → Promise 17 → Plan 18 → Pass 19.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Consider the following institutional firsts associated with the Government of India Act, 1919, and arrange them in the correct chronological order of occurrence after the passing of the Act:
items: 1. First ICS examination held in India
2. Formal constitution of the Narendra Mandal by Royal Proclamation
3. Establishment of the Public Service Commission for India
questions.stemTail: Choose the correct sequence:
explanation: (A) ✓ — The correct sequence after the GOI Act 1919 is: Formal constitution of the Narendra Mandal by Royal Proclamation in 1921 → First ICS examination in India in 1922 → Establishment of the Public Service Commission in 1926 with Ross Barker as first Chairman. Hence the chronological order is 2 - 1 - 3.

Why others wrong: (b) Places the ICS exam (1922) before the Narendra Mandal Proclamation (1921). (c) Inverts the entire sequence — PSC came LAST, not first. (d) Places the PSC (1926) before the ICS exam (1922).
Memory hook: 21 Mandal → 22 ICS-in-India → 26 PSC under Ross Barker.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Provision under GOI 1919) — List II (Authority / Body responsible)
A. Reserved subjects at the provincial level —
items:
1. Governor & his officials
B. Transferred subjects at the provincial level —

2. Ministers responsible to PLA
C. Ordinance-making at the Centre —

3. Viceroy
D. Advisory consultation on Princely States affairs —
4. Narendra Mandal
questions.stemTail: Choose the correct matching:
matchTable: A. Reserved subjects at the provincial level
B. Transferred subjects at the provincial level
D. Advisory consultation on Princely States affairs
explanation: (B) ✓ — A-1: Reserved subjects (Law & Order i.e. Police, Administration of Justice, Finance, Land Revenue, Control over Officials) were under the Governor & his officials. B-2: Transferred subjects (e.g., health, education, local government, agriculture) were administered by Ministers responsible to the PLA. C-3: Ordinance power — the Viceroy could make law by executive order, valid for 6 months. D-4: The Narendra Mandal was an advisory body for the Princely States, with the British promising to consult the Princes on policy matters affecting them.

Why others wrong: (a) Reverses A and B — Reserved was with the Governor (not Ministers/PLA), and Transferred was with Ministers/PLA (not the Governor). (c) Swaps the Viceroy's ordinance power with the Narendra Mandal — the Viceroy held the ordinance power, not the Mandal, which was purely advisory. (d) Puts the Viceroy on Reserved subjects (the Governor's domain, not the Viceroy's) and the Governor on ordinance-making (which was the Viceroy's power at the Centre).
Memory hook: Reserved-Governor / Transferred-Minister / Ordinance-Viceroy / Princes-Mandal.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Year) — List II (Event linked to GOI Act, 1919)
A. 1917 —
items:
1. Montagu Statement / August Declaration
B. 1918 —

2. Montagu-Chelmsford Report
C. 1921 —

3. Royal Proclamation constituting the Narendra Mandal
D. 1926 —
4. Public Service Commission established under Section 96C
questions.stemTail: Choose the correct matching:
matchTable: List II (List II (Event linked to GOI Act, 1919))
3. Royal Proclamation constituting the Narendra Mandal
4. Public Service Commission established under Section 96C
explanation: (C) ✓ — A-1: The Montagu Statement / August Declaration was issued in 1917 by Edwin Montagu, Secretary of State for India. B-2: The Montagu-Chelmsford Report was the joint document by Montagu and Viceroy Chelmsford16-21 in 1918. C-3: The Narendra Mandal was formally constituted by Royal Proclamation in 1921. D-4: The Public Service Commission for India, mandated under Section 96C of the Act, was established in 1926 with Ross Barker as its first Chairman.

Why others wrong: (a) Swaps the 1917 Statement with the 1918 Report. (b) Swaps the 1921 Narendra Mandal Proclamation with the 1926 PSC establishment. (d) Swaps both pairs — Statement-Report and Mandal-PSC.
Memory hook: 17 Statement, 18 Report, 19 Act, 21 Mandal, 22 ICS-exam, 26 PSC — the GOI 1919 timeline.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The Dyarchy introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919 was designed not to share power but to discredit Indian self-government." Examine.
body: Demand of the question: The prompt is a strong critical claim — that Dyarchy's purpose was sabotage, not power-sharing. The directive verb "Examine" asks for evidence-based scrutiny: take the claim seriously, test it against the Act's structural features, & decide whether the structural features support the claim. The phrase "designed not to share but to discredit" is the load-bearing assertion — you must show how the design did the discrediting.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Dyarchy split provincial subjects into Reserved and Transferred — but the split was so loaded against Indian Ministers that failure was structurally guaranteed before any minister took office.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The Reserved/Transferred split itself (see 'Dyarchy at the Provincial Level — The Most Debated Feature'). Reserved subjects (Law and Order, Police, Administration of Justice, Finance, Land Revenue, Control over Officials) stayed with the Governor and his officials — no accountability to PLA. Transferred subjects (health, education, local government, agriculture) went to Indian Ministers responsible to PLA. Verdict: Indians received the politically soft subjects with no control over the levers of governance.

2. The money problem (see 'Dyarchy at the Provincial Level — The Most Debated Feature'). Finance was Reserved. Indian Ministers running Transferred subjects had no budget of their own; they had to negotiate funds from a Governor's purse over which they had no claim. Without money, education/health/agriculture could not be staffed, run, or reformed.

3. The bureaucracy problem (see 'Dyarchy at the Provincial Level — The Most Debated Feature'). Control over Officials was Reserved. Indian Ministers could not appoint, transfer, discipline, or override their own staff. A Minister of Education could not move a District Inspector. The Governor could overrule Ministers on any matter (vi).

4. The fallback clause (see 'Dyarchy at the Provincial Level — The Most Debated Feature'). "In case of failure of constitutional machinery", the Governor could take over executive and legislative powers over Transferred subjects too — the safety net for the British, not for the Indian Minister. Verdict: the architecture predicted failure and built in the response in advance.

Closing verdict: Dyarchy's specific design — soft subjects without money, soft subjects without staff, soft subjects with an overruling Governor, & a safety clause for British takeover — was not the awkward result of a transitional compromise. It was a deliberate construction in which Indian Ministers were set up to fail, & the failure was meant to demonstrate that Indians could not govern. The chapter's anchor sentence captures it: "The title was real. The power was not."
revise: Why Dyarchy Was a Problem in Practice

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: The Government of India Act, 1919 went further than ICA 1909 but fell short of Swaraj. Discuss the principal sources of INM dissatisfaction with the Act.
body: Demand of the question: "Discuss" + "principal sources" = enumerate and explain the specific gaps the INM saw. The prompt frames the Act as a transitional step — better than ICA 1909 (acknowledged) but short of Swaraj (the actual goal). The body must list and briefly explain each gap.

Suggested intro (~25 words): GOI 1919 introduced elected majorities at Centre and Provinces — a real advance over ICA 1909 — but the INM judged it against the Lucknow Pact (1916) & the post-1906 Swaraj benchmark, & found it wanting on six counts.
Body guidance — 6 sources of dissatisfaction (see 'Why Were INM Leaders Dissatisfied?'):
1. No true federalism (5.1). Subject division between Centre and Provinces was not federal — Centre kept overriding power; no constitutional list-system like the future 7th Schedule (COI 1950).
2. Dyarchy mockery (5.2). At Provincial level, Governor as Centre's agent kept control over Reserved subjects — federalism subverted from within.
3. Limited franchise (5.3). Income-linked right to vote, far short of the Lucknow Pact 1916 demand for franchise "as broad as possible". No universal adult franchise.
4. No responsible government at Centre (5.4). VEC was not accountable to legislature. Provinces had only partial responsibility (for Transferred subjects).
5. Seat allocation by importance, not population (5.5). Punjab weighted for military importance, Bombay for commercial importance — population principle subordinated.
6. No effective self-government (5.6). An improvement over ICA 1909's "limited self-government" but still far from Swaraj — the INC's stated goal since the 1906 Calcutta Session.

Closing verdict: Six specific gaps — federalism, provincial dyarchy, franchise, responsibility, seat allocation, & the self-government ceiling — made the Act a milestone the INM walked past, not one it celebrated.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: With reference to the British colonial rule in India, consider the following statements.
items: 1. Mahatma Gandhi was instrumental in the abolition of the system of 'Indentured Labour'.
2. In Lord Chelmsford's 'War Conference', Mahatma Gandhi did not support the resolution on recruiting Indians for World War.
3. Consequent upon the breaking of Salt Law by Indian people, the Indian National Congress was declared illegal by the colonial rulers.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are correct; statement 2 is wrong. Statement 1: Gandhi was instrumental in abolishing indentured labour — he led the campaign against the indenture system that culminated in its abolition in 1917; the record alert marks this as the examiner-tested anchor. Statement 2 fails: at the April 1918 Delhi War Conference Gandhi DID support recruitment of Indians for the war — so the claim that he did not support it is false. Statement 3 is correct: after the Salt Law was broken in 1930, the colonial government declared the INC illegal.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "1 and 2" keeps the false statement 2: Gandhi did NOT oppose recruitment at the 1918 War Conference — he supported it, hoping wartime loyalty would earn post-war reform.
(C) ✗ — "2 and 3" rests on the same false statement 2 and throws away the true statement 1 — the indenture-abolition campaign.
(D) ✗ — "1, 2 and 3" overcounts: statement 2 inverts Gandhi's actual War-Conference position.

(Note: The first agitation that Mahatma Gandhi launched during his days in South Africa was against the system of 'Indentured Labour'. It was a system based on contract, in which the labours from India were sent to work in distant British colonies.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: At Pietermaritzburg railway station in 1893, Gandhiji was ejected from a first-class compartment despite holding a valid ticket. What was the immediate consequence of this incident for him?

options.text: He immediately returned to India to file a legal complaint
It became his political catalyst to fight racial discrimination
He launched the Natal Indian Congress the same week
He renounced his profession as a barrister

explanation: (B) ✓ — The humiliation at the cold station platform became his political catalyst — the moment he resolved to fight racial discrimination rather than quietly endure it.
Why others wrong: (a) He stayed on for twenty-two years, not returned. (c) Natal Indian Congress was founded in 1894, not the same week. (d) He continued legal work; no renunciation mentioned.
Memory hook: Pietermaritzburg platform — cold night, hot resolve.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Franchise Amendment Bill, 1894 (Natal):
items: 1. It sought to disenfranchise Indians by stripping them of the right to vote.
2. Some Indians had earlier qualified to vote on a wealth/property criterion.
3. The Bill was confined to the Transvaal province.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Stmt 1 correct: Bill sought to disenfranchise Indians — to strip them of the Right to Vote. Stmt 2 correct: Some Indians had earlier qualified for the vote based on a wealth criterion. Stmt 3 wrong: it was Natal, not Transvaal.
Why others wrong: Any option including Stmt 3 fails — Bill was Natal-specific.
Memory hook: Natal '94 — vote stripped on race, not on coin.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: The Immigration Law Amendment Bill, 1895 (Natal) gave Indian indentured labourers, on completion of their contract, which of the following choices?

options.text: Acquire South African citizenship, or return to India free of cost
Move freely between provinces, or pay a registration fee
Settle on Crown land, or carry a registration certificate
Leave South Africa, or re-indenture for two more years, or pay a poll tax of £3 per year

explanation: (D) ✓ — Chapter: Indians had to leave South Africa, or re-indenture for two more years. If they chose neither, they had to pay a poll tax of £3 per year.
Why others wrong: (a) No citizenship offer in Chapter. (b) Inter-provincial movement is the 1907 Transvaal law, not this. (c) Registration Certificate belongs to the 1906 Black Act.
Memory hook: Three doors, all closing — leave, re-bond, or pay £3.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes Gandhiji's Phase 1 — the Constitutional Struggle (1896–1906) in South Africa?

options.text: Mass civil disobedience and bonfires of identity cards
Armed self-defence by Indian indentured labourers
Petitions, prayers, founding of the Natal Indian Congress and Indian Opinion
Boycott of British goods coordinated with the INC in India

explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: He organised petitions, prayers, and public meetings. He founded the Natal Indian Congress. He also launched a newspaper, Indian Opinion.

Why others wrong: (a) Bonfires & mass disobedience belong to Phase 2 (post-1906). (b) No armed self-defence; approach was non-violent and constitutional. (d) No INC-coordinated boycott mentioned in this phase.
Memory hook: Phase 1 — three Ps: petitions, prayers, press.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the personal code of a Satyagrahi as laid down by Gandhiji in South Africa:
items: 1. Truthful — in word, action & intention
2. Non-violent — absolutely, even under provocation
3. Fearless — willing to face arrest and imprisonment
4. Vengeful toward the wrongdoer
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Stmts 1, 2, 3 correctly listed in Chapter. Stmt 4 is the opposite of Gandhiji's code: a Satyagrahi had to be "Loving toward the wrongdoer — hate was to have no place."
Why others wrong: Any option including Stmt 4 contradicts the loving-toward-wrongdoer requirement.
Memory hook: Satyagrahi — truth, ahimsa, fearless, love (never hate).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Phoenix Settlement, established by Gandhiji in 1904 near Durban, was inspired by which of the following works?

options.text: Leo Tolstoy's *The Kingdom of God Is Within You*

explanation: (B) ✓ — Chapter: In 1904, inspired by John Ruskin's Unto This Last, he established the Phoenix Settlement near Durban.

Why others wrong: (a) Tolstoy's writings inspired Tolstoy Farm (1910), not Phoenix Settlement. (c) Thoreau not mentioned in Chapter. (d) Tilak's Gita commentary not mentioned in Chapter in this connection.
Memory hook: Phoenix '04 — Ruskin's "Unto This Last".

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: The Asiatic Law Amendment Act 1906 — bitterly called the 'Black Act' — was passed by which government and what did it require?

options.text: Natal government; required Indians to pay an annual £3 poll tax
Cape government; barred Indians from owning property
Transvaal government; required every Indian to carry a Registration Certificate (RC)
Orange Free State government; disenfranchised Indians

explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: The Asiatic Law Amendment Act 1906…was passed by the Transvaal government. It required every Indian to carry a Registration Certificate (RC) at all times.
Why others wrong: (a) Poll tax belongs to the 1895 Natal Immigration Law, not the 1906 Black Act. (b) Property bar not in Chapter. (d) Disenfranchisement was the 1894 Franchise Bill (Natal).
Memory hook: Black Act '06 — Transvaal, carry your card.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Transvaal Immigration Restriction Act, 1907 and Gandhiji's response:
items: 1. It barred Indians from moving freely between provinces — from Cape Province, Natal, or Orange Free State into Transvaal.
2. Gandhiji's response was to encourage Indians to apply for new licences and stay within their province.
3. Indians deliberately crossed provincial boundaries illegally, courted arrest, and refused bail.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Stmts 1 and 3 are verbatim from Chapter. Stmt 2 is the opposite: Indians engaged in hawking without a licence — a minor illegal act, deliberately committed to fill the jails.
Why others wrong: Any option including Stmt 2 contradicts the deliberate illegality strategy.
Memory hook: 1907 — cross the line, fill the jail.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Tolstoy Farm, established by Gandhiji in 1910 near Johannesburg, served primarily as:

options.text: A printing press for the Indian Opinion newspaper
A military training camp for Indian volunteers
A residential base for Satyagrahis & their families during the passive phases
A school exclusively for indentured labourers' children

explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: Tolstoy Farm was established as a residential base for Satyagrahis & their families during the passive phases of the struggle.

Why others wrong: (a) Indian Opinion was printed at Phoenix Settlement, not Tolstoy Farm. (b) No military training — movement was strictly non-violent. (d) Not an exclusive school; it was a communal settlement teaching self-reliance to Satyagrahis.
Memory hook: Tolstoy Farm '10 — home for the Satyagrahi family.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Gopal Krishna Gokhale's strategic advice to Gandhiji in 1912 was to focus the South African movement on which two specific demands?

options.text: Repeal of indentured labour and recognition of Indian Christian marriages
Right to inter-provincial movement and right to own land
Restoration of the franchise and abolition of indentured labour
Abolition of the Poll Tax and abolition of the Registration Certificate requirement

explanation: (D) ✓ — Chapter: Gokhale advised Gandhiji to focus on abolition of the Poll Tax (under the Immigration Law) and abolition of the Registration Certificate requirement (under the Black Act).

Why others wrong: (a) Indentured-labour abolition is a separate Prelims 2019 anchor, not Gokhale's 1912 advice. (b) Inter-provincial movement was an issue but not one of Gokhale's two named focuses. (c) Franchise was the 1894 issue; not on Gokhale's 1912 short-list.
Memory hook: Gokhale 1912 — two arrows: poll tax + RC.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "Gandhiji did not bring Satyagraha to India — he brought it back from South Africa." Examine.
body: Demand of the question: The prompt rejects the popular framing that Gandhi was the architect of Satyagraha as an Indian innovation. "Examine" requires you to test the claim against the evidence — was the method actually built in South Africa, & what makes that location pedagogically necessary?

Suggested intro (~25 words): Satyagraha was forged not in India's freedom struggle but in 22 years of South African experiment (1893–1915) — the method, the personnel and the conviction all preceded Gandhiji's 1915 return.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The personal code came before the political programme (see 'Phase 2 — The Extra-Constitutional Struggle (1906–1915)'). Gandhiji's 5-point Satyagrahi standard — truthfulness, non-violence, fearlessness, willingness to suffer, love for the wrongdoer — was distilled from a decade of personal experiment in South Africa, not theorised from a desk.

2. The training infrastructure was built in SA, not India (see 'Phase 2 — The Extra-Constitutional Struggle (1906–1915)'). Phoenix Settlement (1904, Ruskin-inspired) & Tolstoy Farm (1910) were physical training grounds for Satyagrahis and their families. India had no equivalent until Sabarmati Ashram (1917), built on the SA template.

3. The repertoire was tested live on real laws (see 'Phase 2 — The Extra-Constitutional Struggle (1906–1915)'). Bonfire of Registration Certificates, Jail Bharo, deliberate boundary-crossing arrests, hawking without licence — every tactic later used in India was rehearsed against the Black Act 1906 & the Transvaal Immigration Restriction Act 1907.

4. The mass character came from the 1913 turning point (see 'The Poll Tax Campaign and the Final Countdown (1913)'). The Poll Tax Campaign drew in women, miners and plantation workers — Satyagraha was no longer a middle-class lawyers' protest but a multi-class movement. The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) inherited this pattern directly.

Closing verdict: Gandhiji's 22 South African years were Satyagraha's R&D phase — code, training, repertoire and mass-character all developed in the Transvaal and Natal before any of it touched Indian soil. India received the finished method, not the prototype.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: The year 1913 marked the decisive turn in Gandhiji's South African struggle. Identify the three developments that converged that year, & explain why they together pushed the movement to its peak.
body: Demand of the question: "Identify... and explain" = enumerate + give the mechanism for each. The prompt frames 1913 as a convergence point, not a single-cause turning point.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Until 1913 the struggle had been confined to the educated Indian middle class fighting specific laws. Three converging developments in that one year transformed it into a mass movement with imperial-level backing.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'The Poll Tax Campaign and the Final Countdown (1913)'):

1. The Christian-marriage judgement. The South African Supreme Court ruled in 1913 that only Christian marriages were legally valid — automatically de-recognising Hindu, Muslim and Parsi marriages of Indians in SA. The ruling hit every Indian family, including those who had not previously joined the struggle. Mechanism: turned a legal grievance into a personal-family insult, drawing women into the movement for the first time.

2. The Poll Tax Campaign acquires mass character. Gokhale's 1912 strategic advice had narrowed the demand to two emotionally resonant items — the £3 Poll Tax and the RC. By 1913, miners and plantation workers (the population actually paying the tax) joined the campaign in large numbers. Mechanism: the demand finally aligned with the grievance of the worst-affected class.

3. Viceroy Hardinge10-16's public condemnation. An unprecedented diplomatic intervention — a British Viceroy in India publicly condemned a British dominion government for treating Indians as inferior subjects. Mechanism: the SA government could no longer treat the issue as a local Indian-community matter; it was now an imperial embarrassment.

Closing verdict: Marriage-validity (family front), Poll Tax mass mobilisation (class front), Hardinge's pressure (imperial front) — three simultaneous fronts forced the Smuts-Gandhi compromise of 1914.
revise: The Poll Tax Campaign and the Final Countdown

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: Mahatma Gandhi said that some of his deepest convictions were reflected in a book titled, 'Unto This Last' and the book transformed his life. What was the message from the book that transformed Mahatma Gandhi?

options.text: Uplifting the oppressed and poor is the moral responsibility of an educated man
The good of individual is contained in the good of all
The life of celibacy and spiritual pursuit are essential for a noble life
All the statements (a), (b) and (c) are correct in this context

explanation: (B) ✓ — The record pins Ruskin's Unto This Last to one transformative message for Gandhi: the good of the individual is contained in the good of all — the seed of Sarvodaya.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — A noble sentiment, but not THE message Gandhi attributed to Ruskin's book — the record record is the Sarvodaya line: individual good contained in the good of all.
(C) ✗ — Celibacy and spiritual pursuit belong to Gandhi's personal vows, not to Ruskin's economics of the common good.

(D) ✗ — Per of the record, "Unto This Last" had one specific transformative message for Gandhi (the good of individual lies in the good of all = Sarvodaya). Options (a) and (c) are valid Gandhian values but are NOT the specific message Gandhi attributed to this particular book in his autobiography.

(Note: John Ruskin, the English thinker was the most powerful source of inspiration when Gandhiji himself described Ruskin's book. 'Unto This Last' as 'The Magic Spell'. The book gripped Mahatma Gandhi so much.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: One common agreement between Gandhism and Marxism is:
explanation: (A) ✓ — Per of the record, both Gandhism and Marxism converge on a "final goal of a stateless society". Marx: classless-stateless society emerges after Dictatorship of the Proletariat withers away. Gandhi: Ram Rajya / Sarvodaya where individuals govern themselves through moral self-rule (Sarva Seva Sangh / Gram Swaraj), needing no coercive State. The means and the path differ sharply, but the ultimate end-state both envision is one without organised state coercion.
Wrong options:

(B) ✗ — Per of the record, "Class struggle" is the Marxist engine of history but Gandhi explicitly rejected it. Gandhi promoted the Trusteeship theory — asking the rich and poor to cooperate peacefully like one family — directly opposing the Marxist call for the oppressed to violently overthrow capitalists. Hence "class struggle" is NOT a Gandhism-Marxism common point.
(C) ✗ — Abolition of private property is the Marxist plank Gandhi REFUSED: his Trusteeship asked owners to hold wealth for society — property preserved but moralised.
(D) ✗ — Economic determinism is Marx's engine of history; Gandhi's springs were moral — self-rule of the soul. The one convergence is the FINAL goal of a stateless society.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: Who among the following is associated with 'Songs from Prison', a translation of ancient Indian religious lyrics in English?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Songs from Prison (1934) belongs to Gandhi: an English rendering of ancient Indian religious lyrics from his prison years, prepared with his secretary Mahadev Desai — listed among Gandhi's publications in.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Per and the Alert anchor on Prelims 2021, "Songs from Prison" is the English translation by Mahadev Desai (Gandhi's secretary) of selected hymns from the Tirukkural — NOT a Bal Gangadhar Tilak work. Tilak's prison-period writing was "Gita Rahasya" (1915), an entirely separate work.
(B) ✗ — Nehru's prison books are An Autobiography and The Discovery of India — works of history and memoir, not translations of religious lyrics.
(D) ✗ — Sarojini Naidu wrote original English poetry; the prison translation of ancient lyrics belongs to Gandhi's jail years.

(Note: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (Mahatma Gandhi) was associated with 'Songs from Prison', a translation of ancient Indian religious lyrics in English, in 1934. Songs from Prison was a translation from Sanskrit.)

questions.label: PYQ_M.1
questions.stem: What was the difference between Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore in their approach towards education and nationalism?
body: Demand of the question: "What was the difference" asks for a two-sided comparison, not two separate profiles. Two fields are named - education & nationalism - so both must get space. Open with the common ground: both men loved Indian civilisation. The difference is about sequence & method, not about loyalty to India.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore both loved Indian civilisation. Their approach towards education and nationalism differed on sequence - mobilise the masses first, or raise consciousness first.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The shared ground (see 'What Kind of Nationalist Was Gandhi?'). Both stood inside the cultural nationalist tradition that answered British contempt for Indian civilisation - the tradition of Dayanand's Arya Samaj (1875) & Vivekananda's Ramakrishna Mission (1897). Tagore shared Gandhi's love of Indian civilisation. Say this first, or the contrast turns into a caricature.

2. Nationalism - Gandhi's method (see 'What Kind of Nationalist Was Gandhi?' + 'The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined'). Gandhi mobilised through religion & shared symbols - Ram Rajya, Sita & Draupadi - because in India religion is a stronger social bond than class. He also left Swaraj undefined, so that a peasant, a worker, a woman & an intellectual could each read their own hope into it.

3. Nationalism - Tagore's fear (see 'What Kind of Nationalist Was Gandhi?' + 'The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined'). Tagore feared that mass religious nationalism could slide into dangerous intolerance, & that undefined mass emotion could turn narrow. Gandhi's answer never changed: mobilise first, refine after - you cannot teach philosophy to an empty stomach.

4. Education (see 'Summary: The Core of Gandhian Ideology' + 'The Strategic Method — Rising Tempo, Controlled Movement, and S-CW-S'). Gandhi's new education, Nai Talim, is one of the 18 points of his Constructive Programme (1941, revised 1945). It was work-centred, resting on Ruskin's argument in Unto This Last (1862) that manual labour carries the same dignity as intellectual labour - the idea behind Phoenix Settlement (1904), Tolstoy Farm (1910) & Sabarmati Ashram (1917). Tagore's Shantiniketan (1901) belongs to the same constructive-work lineage, but its accent was creative rather than vocational.

Closing verdict: The difference between Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore was never about the worth of Indian civilisation. It was about sequence - mobilise the nation first, or educate it first.
revise: What Kind of Nationalist Was Gandhi?
The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined
The Strategic Method — Rising Tempo, Controlled Movement, and S-CW-S
Summary: The Core of Gandhian Ideology

questions.label: PYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Throw light on the significance of thoughts of Mahatma Gandhi in the present times.
body: Demand of the question: "Throw light on the significance" asks you to show why the ideas still matter; it does not ask for a life story. "In the present times" is the anchor - every theme must end in today's India. Pick a few thoughts & carry each one forward. Breadth without a present-day landing point earns nothing.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The thoughts of Mahatma Gandhi were not only about ending British rule. Their significance in the present times lies in how India runs its democracy, its economy & its protests.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Democracy from below (see 'Stateless Society and Enlightened Anarchism'). Gandhi wanted Village Republics built on direct democracy & mutual cooperation. Article 243, which makes the Gram Sabha the base of the Panchayati Raj system, is his most concrete institutional legacy in India's Constitution. His warning - that multi-party democracy delivers the will of parties, not the will of the people - is alive today in debates on the anti-defection law, party whips overriding individual conscience & the weakening of Parliament as a deliberative institution.

2. Morality inside the economy (see 'Trusteeship and Arbitration — Reforming Capitalism Without Destroying'). Trusteeship asked the capitalist to hold his enterprise for the welfare of his workers & the wider community: the ownership stays, the purpose of ownership changes. For disputes Gandhi preferred Arbitration - open the capitalist's balance sheet & the worker's cost of living, then find a just middle path, instead of strikes & lockouts. On land he backed voluntary donation, which later produced Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan Movement in Telangana, 1951 (see 'The Economic Vision — Village Self-Sufficiency').

3. A method of protest anyone can use (see 'Why Was Satyagraha So Strategically Effective?'). Satyagraha needs no weapons & no military training - only courage & conviction. That is why peasants, women & workers could join. Non-violence also makes repression expensive for the ruler, because a crackdown on peaceful protesters becomes a propaganda disaster. Gandhi drew on Ruskin, Tolstoy, Thoreau, the Bhagavad Gita & the Sermon on the Mount (see 'Key Intellectual Influences on Gandhi'), which is why the method travels as a universal moral one.

4. Communal peace & the ethics of means (see 'Table — Major Fasts of Mahatma Gandhi'). The Calcutta fast of September 1947 stopped the rioting within days - Lord Mountbatten called him a one-man boundary force; the Delhi fast of January 1948 won a seven-point pledge guaranteeing Muslim safety. Add his two personal rules - never benefit from the weakness of the evil doer, never break a promise (see 'Two Principles That Defined Gandhi's Character'). Both are standing tests for public life today.
Closing verdict: The significance of the thoughts of Mahatma Gandhi in the present times is not nostalgia. Each idea still names a problem India has not yet solved.
revise: Trusteeship and Arbitration — Reforming Capitalism Without Destroying
Why Was Satyagraha So Strategically Effective?
Table — Major Fasts of Mahatma Gandhi

questions.label: PYQ_M.3
questions.stem: Highlight the difference in the approach of Subhash Chandra Bose and Mahatma Gandhi in the struggle for freedom.
body: Demand of the question: "Highlight the difference" wants a point-by-point contrast, not two biographies. Both men wanted the same freedom, so the contrast sits in means, in wartime choices, in the State & in the economy. Keep the pair side by side inside every theme. One line of common ground keeps the answer balanced.
Suggested intro (~25 words): Subhash Chandra Bose and Mahatma Gandhi shared one goal. The difference in the approach lay in means, in wartime choices, & in the India each wanted after freedom.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. Means - the central split (see 'The Method of Satyagraha'). Satyagraha = Non-Cooperation + Civil Disobedience + Constructive Work + Non-Violence + Spirituality/Morality. Gandhi's logic was strategic as well as moral: if a Satyagrahi turns violent, the British gain a justification for their own repression. Bose's reply was "Give me blood, and I shall give you freedom" - a nation still in chains has no luxury of clean methods. Gandhi's implicit answer: a nation born of violence will remain violent.

2. The war years (see 'Two Principles That Defined Gandhi's Character'). Gandhi's first rule was never to benefit from the weakness of the evil doer, so he supported Britain in both World War I & World War II although India was still under colonial rule. Tilak took the opposite pragmatic line & was willing to use World War I as leverage. Bose went further still & allied with the Axis powers to fight Britain.

3. The State after freedom (see 'Stateless Society and Enlightened Anarchism'). Gandhi's ideal was a stateless society through Enlightened Anarchism, with Village Republics as direct democracy & a weak State only as a transitional arrangement. Bose wanted temporary authoritarian rule to eliminate poverty fast. Gandhi was the only major leader who feared State power itself, not merely British State power.

4. The economy (see 'The Economic Vision — Village Self-Sufficiency' + 'Summary: The Core of Gandhian Ideology'). Gandhi rejected the Industrial Revolution because it uproots rural masses into urban factories where they are dependent & exploited. His programme was village self-sufficiency, Trusteeship instead of expropriation & voluntary land donation instead of forced redistribution. Bose's route out of poverty ran through heavy industrialisation. The contrast is village republics against heavy industry.

5. Discipline of the movement (see 'The Strategic Method — Rising Tempo, Controlled Movement, and S-CW-S'). Gandhi raised the tempo in stages & insisted on strict adherence by the masses to the agreed programme. After Chauri Chaura in February 1922 - where a mob burned a police station killing 22 policemen - he withdrew Non-Cooperation even at its peak. To critics that was betrayal at the movement's most powerful moment; to Gandhi it was keeping a promise of non-violence. Bose's path allowed no such brake, because it was armed struggle with foreign allies.
Closing verdict: The difference in the approach of Subhash Chandra Bose and Mahatma Gandhi was about means, not about the goal - & means shape the nation that follows freedom.

questions.label: PYQ_M.4
questions.stem: How different would have been the achievement of Indian independence without Mahatma Gandhi? Discuss.
body: Demand of the question: This is a counterfactual, so "How different" + "Discuss" means weigh, do not assert. Show first what was already moving before him, then isolate what only he supplied, then judge the gap. Freedom would probably still have come; your answer is about its timing, its breadth & its character. Avoid hero-worship & avoid dismissal.

Suggested intro (~25 words): A national movement existed before Mahatma Gandhi arrived on the scene. Without Mahatma Gandhi, Indian independence would probably still have come - but slower, narrower & more violent.
Body guidance — 5 themes:

1. What was already moving (see 'What Kind of Nationalist Was Gandhi?'). Cultural nationalism was built before Gandhi arrived on the scene - Dayanand's Arya Samaj (1875), Vivekananda's Ramakrishna Mission (1897) & Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. Constructive work had its own lineage: Ramakrishna Mission (1897), the Arya Samaj's DAV schools, Tagore's Shantiniketan (1901) & Tilak's Constructive Swadeshi (see 'The Strategic Method — Rising Tempo, Controlled Movement, and S-CW-S'). A freedom struggle of some form was certain without him.

2. He closed a split no one else could close (see 'Why Was Satyagraha So Strategically Effective?'). Satyagraha attracted Moderates by its non-violence & Extremists by its mass struggle, so it healed the split of Surat (1907).
