In 1920 Gandhi used Arbitration in political form - Moderates accepted Non-Cooperation & Civil Disobedience, Extremists gave up violence (see 'Trusteeship and Arbitration — Reforming Capitalism Without Destroying'). A Congress still split would have faced the Raj far weaker.

3. He made the struggle a mass one (see 'Why Was Satyagraha So Strategically Effective?'). Armed struggle needs weapons & military training; Satyagraha needs only courage & conviction. Peasants, women & workers who had been spectators became participants - the democratic revolution inside the freedom struggle. His simple attire, his use of Hindi, Ram Rajya & icons like Sita & Draupadi let people who would never attend a constitutional conference feel the movement was theirs (see 'The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined').

4. He changed the cost of repression (see 'Why Was Satyagraha So Strategically Effective?'). A violent crackdown on non-violent Satyagrahis became a propaganda disaster in Britain's Parliament, in British public opinion & in international opinion. At Dharasana in 1930, Webb Miller's press report of unarmed resisters being beaten shocked the world (see 'Table — Arrests and Imprisonments of Mahatma Gandhi'). An armed movement would have handed the British the justification that non-violence denied them.

5. The other side of the ledger. Chauri Chaura (February 1922) forced him to withdraw Non-Cooperation at its peak, which critics called betrayal (see 'The Strategic Method — Rising Tempo, Controlled Movement, and S-CW-S'). Jinnah held that an undefined Swaraj was a Hindu cultural concept dressed as a national one (see 'The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined'). Ambedkar held that only a strong State with constitutional law protected the oppressed (see 'Stateless Society and Enlightened Anarchism'). Without Gandhi the struggle would have been narrower in participation & more violent in method - & the State that followed would have carried those means into its own character.
Closing verdict: Indian independence would probably have arrived without Mahatma Gandhi. What would have been different is who took part, how long it took, & at what moral cost.
revise: Why Was Satyagraha So Strategically Effective?
The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined
The Strategic Method — Rising Tempo, Controlled Movement, and S-CW-S
What Kind of Nationalist Was Gandhi?

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: With reference to Gandhi's Hind Swaraj (1909), which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: It was written during a ten-day sea voyage and is structured as a dialogue between a "Reader" and an "Editor."
It was written during Gandhi's imprisonment in Yerwada Jail and is structured as an autobiography.
It was first published in English in 1909 and later translated into Gujarati.
It was written as a direct reply to Bal Gangadhar Tilak's Gita Rahasya.

explanation: (A) ✓ — Hind Swaraj was written in 1909 during a ten-day sea voyage, structured as a dialogue between a 'Reader' and an 'Editor.'.

Why others wrong: (b) it is a sea-voyage work, not a Yerwada Jail work, and it is a dialogue, not an autobiography; (c) Hind Swaraj was published in 1909 in Gujarati with the English translation in 1910 — the reverse of option (c); (d) Hind Swaraj has no link to Tilak's Gita Rahasya — it is Gandhi's own critique of Western civilisation.
Memory hook: Ten days at sea, two voices in dialogue — Reader asks, Editor answers, India listens.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Which book, read by Gandhi on a train journey in South Africa, did he himself say "transformed my life" and inspired him to found the Phoenix Settlement in 1904?

options.text: Leo Tolstoy's The Kingdom of God is Within You

explanation: (B) ✓ — Chapter: Gandhi himself said this book 'transformed my life.'... Gandhi read it on a train journey in South Africa & was so moved that he immediately founded the Phoenix Settlement (1904) near Durban.

Why others wrong: (a) Tolstoy's The Kingdom of God is Within You (1894) inspired the Tolstoy Farm (1910) near Johannesburg, not the Phoenix Settlement; (c) Thoreau's Civil Disobedience (1849) gave Gandhi the term "civil disobedience" — Chapter does not link it to Phoenix Settlement; (d) Chapter never names Anandamath as an influence on Gandhi.
Memory hook: Ruskin on a moving train — Phoenix rises near Durban, labour with dignity, life rebuilt.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the intellectual influences on Mahatma Gandhi:
items: 1. Leo Tolstoy's The Kingdom of God is Within You inspired Gandhi to set up Tolstoy Farm near Johannesburg in
2. The term "civil disobedience" entered Gandhi's political vocabulary through Henry David Thoreau.
3. Gandhi called the Bhagavad Gita his "spiritual dictionary" and read from it every day.
questions.stemTail: 1910 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Chapter verifies all three: Tolstoy Farm (1910) "named the Tolstoy Farm (1910) near Johannesburg after him"; Thoreau — The very term 'civil disobedience' entered Gandhi's political vocabulary through Thoreau; Gita — He called the Gita his 'spiritual dictionary' and read from it every day.
Why others wrong: (a) omits the verified Gita statement; (b) omits the verified Tolstoy Farm statement; (c) omits the verified Thoreau statement.
Memory hook: Tolstoy gave him the Farm, Thoreau gave him the term, Gita gave him the daily compass.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: With reference to Gandhi's Epic Fast of 1932, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: It was undertaken at Aga Khan Palace, Pune, against the Rowlatt Act.
It was undertaken to pressure caste Hindus to open temples and wells to Dalits.
It was undertaken at Yerwada Jail against Ramsay MacDonald's Communal Award and resulted in the Poona Pact.
It was undertaken to protest Gandhi's detention without trial during the Quit India Movement.

explanation: (C) ✓ — The Epic Fast 1932 took place at Yerwada Jail, Pune; the trigger was Ramsay MacDonald's Communal Award, which granted separate electorates to Depressed Classes; the outcome was the Poona Pact (September 1932) — Ambedkar agreed to joint electorates with reserved seats.

Why others wrong: (a) The Aga Khan Palace fast was the 21-Day Fast of 1943 during Quit India detention, not the 1932 Epic Fast; (b) the temple-and-well opening campaign was the 1933 21-Day Fast for Self-Purification, not the 1932 Epic Fast — Chapter explicitly warns: Do not confuse the 1932 Epic Fast (against separate electorates for Dalits) with the 1933 fast (for temple entry); (d) the Quit India detention fast was 1943 at Aga Khan Palace, not the 1932 Epic Fast.
Memory hook: 1932 = Communal Award + Yerwada + Poona Pact — three letters, three Ps, one fast.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about Gandhi's Great Trial of 1922:
items: 1. He was charged for three seditious articles published in Young India.
2. The trial was conducted by Judge C.N. Broomfield at the Ahmedabad Sessions Court.
3. Gandhi pleaded not guilty and contested every charge framed against him.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Chapter: Charged for three seditious articles published in Young India — 'Tampering with Loyalty,' 'The Puzzle & Its Solution,' and 'Shaking the Mane'; Tried before Judge C.N. Broomfield at the Ahmedabad Sessions Court; Gandhi pleaded guilty & delivered his famous courtroom speech asking the judge to impose the maximum penalty.
Why others wrong: (a) includes statement 3 which contradicts the record "pleaded guilty"; (c) includes statement 3 which contradicts Chapter; (d) includes statement 3 which contradicts Chapter.
Memory hook: Three articles, one guilty plea, one judge calling him "high ideals and noble life" — Gandhi turned the dock into a pulpit.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about Gandhi's political method:
items: 1. Gandhi believed in a stateless society achieved through Enlightened Anarchism.
2. Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri Chaura incident of February 1922 in which a mob burned a police station killing 22 policemen.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Chapter: Gandhi believed in a stateless society... This is what Gandhi called Enlightened Anarchism — true self-rule. Chapter: Chauri Chaura in February 1922 — where a mob burned a police station killing 22 policemen — led Gandhi to withdraw the entire Non-Cooperation Movement.
Why others wrong: (b) wrongly drops statement 2 which Chapter verifies verbatim; (c) wrongly drops statement 1 which Chapter verifies verbatim; (d) wrongly drops both, although Chapter verifies both.
Memory hook: Stateless dream above, Chauri Chaura discipline below — moral ideal plus movement control.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Match List I (Influence / Work) with List II (Linked outcome in Gandhi's life):
items: 1. John Ruskin — Unto This Last — A. Tolstoy Farm (1910) near Johannesburg;
2. Leo Tolstoy — The Kingdom of God is Within You — B. Civil disobedience entered Gandhi's vocabulary;
3. Henry David Thoreau — Civil Disobedience — C. Phoenix Settlement (1904) near Durban. Select the correct match
matchTable: 2. Leo Tolstoy — The Kingdom of God is Within You
B. Civil disobedience entered Gandhi's vocabulary
explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: Ruskin's Unto This Last → "founded the Phoenix Settlement (1904) near Durban" (1—C); Tolstoy's The Kingdom of God is Within You → "named the Tolstoy Farm (1910) near Johannesburg after him" (2—A); Thoreau's Civil Disobedience → the very term 'civil disobedience' entered Gandhi's political vocabulary through Thoreau (3—B).

Why others wrong: (a) swaps Ruskin with Tolstoy Farm and Tolstoy with the term civil disobedience — both reversed against Chapter; (b) puts Ruskin against the term civil disobedience, which Chapter attributes to Thoreau; (d) puts Tolstoy against the term civil disobedience, again contradicting Chapter's attribution to Thoreau.
Memory hook: Ruskin→Phoenix, Tolstoy→Tolstoy Farm, Thoreau→the word itself — match the man to the legacy.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Which one of the following best explains why Gandhi demanded universal disarmament rather than abstract pacifism?

options.text: Because Tolstoy had argued for non-resistance to evil by force in The Kingdom of God is Within You.
Because the Bhagavad Gita's doctrine of Nishkama Karma prohibited the carrying of any weapon.
Because the Sermon on the Mount taught loving the enemy and turning the other cheek.
Because the Arms Act of 1878 under Viceroy Lytton disarmed Indian civilians while exempting Anglo-Indians and Eurasians.

explanation: (D) ✓ — Chapter: Gandhi favoured universal disarmament — but this was not naive idealism. It had a precise Indian context. The Arms Act of 1878 under Viceroy Lytton76-80 had disarmed Indian civilians while exempting Anglo-Indians & Eurasians... disarmament is just only when it is universal, not when it is a colonial tool to keep one side defenceless.

Why others wrong: (a) Chapter links Tolstoy to non-resistance and the Tolstoy Farm under, but the universal-disarmament demand is grounded by the record in the Arms Act 1878 asymmetry, not in Tolstoy; (b) Chapter links Nishkama Karma to inner detachment from results, not to weapons policy; (c) Chapter links the Sermon on the Mount to Ahimsa as moral courage, not to the universal-disarmament demand.
Memory hook: Arms Act 1878 disarmed one side — Gandhi's reply: disarm both, or no one.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "Gandhi stood almost alone in 20th-century Indian thought in rejecting the Industrial Revolution." Discuss.
body: Demand of the question: "Discuss" + "almost alone" demands both (a) the substance of Gandhi's rejection and (b) its uniqueness against the consensus position. The body must establish the contrast — name the Indian thinkers who were pro-IR, then explain Gandhi's reasons for the opposite view.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Across the 20th-century Indian intellectual spectrum — Moderates, Extremists, Nehru, Ambedkar — the Industrial Revolution was the path to modernity and national strength. Gandhi was the sole significant dissenter.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The consensus around IR (see 'Was Gandhi Anti-Modern?'). Naoroji, Tilak, Aurobindo, Nehru, Ambedkar — all backed industrialisation, differing only on tactics (state-led vs free-market). Even Marx held IR was the necessary precursor to socialist transformation.

2. Gandhi's substantive rejection (see 'Was Gandhi Anti-Modern?' and 'The Economic Vision — Village Self-Sufficiency'). IR centralised production, destroyed village handicrafts, created urban concentrations that uprooted moral self-sufficiency. Gandhi's village economy preserved the conditions for individual moral responsibility — which industrial wage-labour systematically erodes.

3. The deeper reasoning — moral, not just economic (see 'Stateless Society and Enlightened Anarchism' and 'The Economic Vision — Village Self-Sufficiency'). Gandhi's anti-IR position was downstream of his vision of the human person as fundamentally moral. Industrial society makes morality optional; village society makes it structural. Sarvodaya — welfare of all — required the village.

4. The unique uniqueness — even Mao broke ranks ('Was Gandhi Anti-Modern?' ◆). Mao's Great Leap Forward (1958-62) eventually turned anti-IR — but in Gandhi's lifetime, no major political thinker held this position. Gandhi was first; Mao followed two decades later.

Closing verdict: Gandhi's anti-IR position was not Luddite nostalgia. It was a coherent moral-political analysis — village = moral autonomy; industry = wage-labour dependency. The position cost him allies within the INM, but it shaped Khadi, Trusteeship, & Sarvodaya — the trio that defined the Gandhian alternative to both capitalism and socialism.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Examine why Mahatma Gandhi deliberately kept "Swaraj" undefined as a political goal, & the strategic effect of that choice.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" + "deliberately undefined" = explain the choice as a strategic decision, not a vagueness. The body must show what the strategic effect was — & the cost.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Gandhi never precisely defined "Swaraj" — not because he didn't know what it meant, but because the strategic value of leaving it open exceeded the cost of leaving it ambiguous.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined'):

1. The choice was deliberate (see 'The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined'). Gandhi was fully aware of India's caste, religious, linguistic and class divisions. A precise political definition of Swaraj would have alienated at least one major bloc — depending on whether it was "Hindu Raj", "republican democracy", "village federation" or "stateless society".

2. The strategic effect. The ambiguity allowed every community to read its own aspirations into "Swaraj" — Hindus saw cultural revival; Muslims initially saw constitutional protection; peasants saw zamindari abolition; workers saw labour rights. Inclusive mobilisation depended on this openness.

3. The cost — Jinnah's critique (see 'The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined'). Jinnah's sharpest criticism was that "Swaraj" was a Hindu cultural concept dressed as a national one, & that Muslims could never be safe inside its undefined borders. Gandhi's counter was that the openness was the source of inclusivity — but Jinnah's critique drove the 1940 Pakistan demand. The ambiguity that enabled inclusive mobilisation in the 1920s-30s could not bear the weight of partition negotiation in the 1940s.
Closing verdict: Deliberate ambiguity built the mass movement; the same ambiguity could not carry the constitutional moment. Both effects came from the same choice.
revise: The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: Consider the following statements: The Non-cooperation movement led to the
items: 1. Congress becoming a mass movement for the first time.
2. Growth of Hindu-Muslim unity.
3. Removal of fear of the British might from the minds of the people
4. British Government's willingness to grant political concessions to Indians.
questions.stemTail: Of these statements
explanation: (C) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the NCM made the Congress a MASS movement for the first time, and ordinary people shed their fear of British might — the movement's lasting psychological gain. Statement 2 fails the test of results: the Khilafat-built Hindu-Muslim unity proved temporary and collapsed after the movement. Statement 4 fails outright: Britain offered no political concessions — it answered the NCM with repression.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Overcounts: statements 2 and 4 do not survive — the unity was transient and no concessions came; only the mass-movement gain (1) and the loss of fear (3) endured.
(B) ✗ — Keeps the failed unity claim (2) while discarding the movement's central achievement — the Congress becoming a mass movement for the first time (1).
(D) ✗ — Statement 4 sinks it: the British government conceded nothing — the NCM ended in suppression and Gandhi's arrest, not in political concessions.

(Note: It aimed to resist British rule in India through non-violent means. The ideas of Ahimsa and non-violence and Gandhiji's ability to rally hundreds of thousands of common citizens towards the cause of Independence.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: The Anarchical and Revolutionary Crime Act (1919) was popularly known as
explanation: (A) ✓ — The Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919 is the formal name of the ROWLATT ACT — drafted on the Sedition (Rowlatt) Committee's recommendations, extending wartime emergency powers of the Defence of India Act into peacetime.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Pitt's India Act belongs to 1784 — the EIC-era statute creating the Board of Control, 135 years before this 1919 law.
(C) ✗ — The Indian Arms Act is Lytton's 1878 licensing law, not the 1919 anti-sedition act.
(D) ✗ — The Ilbert Bill (1883) was about which judges could try Europeans — a judicial controversy, not a criminal-law statute of 1919.
(Note: The Anarchical and Revolutionary Crime Act, 1919 was passed by a committee under the Chairmanship of Justice Sydney Rowlatt. That's why this Act was popularly known as Rowlatt Act.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: Assertion [A] Gandhi stopped the Non-cooperation Movement in 1922. Reason [R] Violence at Chauri Chaura led him to stop the movement.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

explanation: (A) ✓ — Both true, and R is exactly why: at Chauri Chaura (5 February 1922) the mob burned the police station, killing 22 policemen — Gandhi, reading it as proof that mass non-violent discipline had failed, withdrew the mass movement and suspended the planned Bardoli CDM.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — R is not incidental — it IS the explanation: the record ties the withdrawal directly to the Chauri Chaura violence breaking the movement's non-violent foundation.
(C) ✗ — R is true: the Chauri Chaura killings of February 1922 are precisely what as the trigger.
(D) ✗ — A is true: Gandhi did stop the mass movement in February 1922 — only institutional non-cooperation continued.

(Note: The Chauri Chaura incident occurred at Chauri Chaura in the Gorakhpur district on 5th February, 1922 when a large group of protesters was participating in the Non-Cooperation Movement clashed with police.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: Which one of the following events, was criticised by Montague as preventive Murder?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The massacre of Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsaar was severely criticised by Edwin Montague, and called it as 'Preventive Murder'.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The killing of INA men belongs to 1945–46 — two decades after Montagu's career; his "preventive murder" verdict was on Jallianwala Bagh (April 1919).
(C) ✗ — The Mahatma's assassination came in 1948 — after independence and long after Montagu (Secretary of State till 1922) had left the scene.
(D) ✗ — Curzon Wyllie was shot in London in 1909 by Madan Lal Dhingra (the India House world — see); Montagu's phrase belonged to the 1919 Amritsar massacre.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Gandhi stopped the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922.
Reason (R): Violence at Chauri-Chaura led him to stop the movement.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

explanation: (A) ✓ — Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Gandhi suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 directly because of the Chauri-Chaura incident (5 Feb 1922) where a mob set fire to a police station killing 22 policemen — per Chapter.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — R is the very explanation of A: the Chauri Chaura violence (5 February 1922) is what convinced Gandhi the movement must stop.
(C) ✗ — R is true — the burning of the Chauri Chaura police station with 22 policemen inside is the record recorded trigger.
(D) ✗ — A is true — the mass movement was withdrawn in February 1922; only institutional non-cooperation continued.
(Note: The anti-imperial movement were the reasons because of urban Muslims came into the fold of National movement.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: The first venture of Gandhi in all India politics was the
explanation: (B) ✓ — (He feared the movement spiralling as Rowlatt Satyagraha had — mass energy without adequate non-violent discipline.) 9.4) Chauri Chaura — February 1922, United Provinces (Agra and Oudh, 1902) At Chauri Chaura in UP, police fired on a procession of satyagrahis, killing 3 of them.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Non-Cooperation Movement came LATER (1920–22) — Gandhi's first ALL-INDIA venture was the Rowlatt Satyagraha of April 1919; the 1917–18 projects were local pilots. +.
(C) ✗ — Champaran (1917) was Gandhi's first satyagraha IN INDIA but a LOCAL one — a single Bihar district; the stem asks for his first venture in ALL-INDIA politics, which was Rowlatt 1919. +.
(D) ✗ — The Dandi March belongs to 1930 and the Civil Disobedience Movement — a decade after the first all-India venture.
(Note: Gandhiji began his experiment with Satyagraha in Champaran - Bihar (in 1917), Ahemdabad (1918) Kheda - Gujarat (in 1918). These were localised and confined to that regions only.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.stem: After returning from South Africa, Gandhi launched his first successful Satyagraha in
explanation: (C) ✓ — Champaran (1917) was Gandhi's first satyagraha on Indian soil — and a successful one: the Tinkathia system was abolished after his inquiry forced the planters' hand.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Chauri Chaura is the site of the 1922 VIOLENCE that ended the NCM — not a satyagraha Gandhi launched.
(B) ✗ — Dandi is the 1930 Salt March of the Civil Disobedience era — thirteen years after Gandhi's first Indian satyagraha.
(D) ✗ — Bardoli is Patel's no-revenue triumph of 1928; Gandhi's first success after returning was Champaran, 1917.
(Note: Gandhiji returned from South Africa in 1915 and 1917, he launched his first successful Satyagraha in Champaran against the indigo planters at the insistence of Rajkumar Shukla.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.stem: Who among the following leaders proposed to adopt complete independence as the goal of the Congress in the Ahmedabad Session of 1920?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Within the Muslim League (ML 1906), radical figures rose — Muhammad Ali Jauhar, Shaukat Ali (the Ali Brothers), Abul Kalam Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Hasrat Mohani — and became prominent.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Azad was among the Khilafat-era radicals but the Ahmedabad complete-independence resolution was moved by Hasrat Mohani.
(C) ✗ — Nehru's 1920s role was the Pratapgarh village awakening that radicalised him; the complete-independence motion at Ahmedabad was Mohani's.
(D) ✗ — Gandhi resisted defining Swaraj as complete independence at this stage — he kept the goal deliberately open; the proposal came from Mohani, not from him.
(Note: It was Hasrat Mohani who proposed to adopt complete independence as the goal of the Congress in the Ahmedabad Session of 1920.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.stem: The Hunter Commission was appointed after the
explanation: (B) ✓ — The British Government appointed Hunter Commission to investigating Jalianwala Bagh massacre which occurred on 13th April, 1919.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Black Hole episode belongs to 1756 Calcutta — Siraj-ud-Daula's era, one hundred and sixty years earlier; no Hunter Commission followed it.
(C) ✗ — The 1857 uprising's inquiries were a different affair altogether; the Hunter Commission of 1919–20 was constituted for the Punjab disturbances — Jallianwala Bagh.
(D) ✗ — No Hunter inquiry followed the 1905 Partition; the classic trap is the OTHER Hunter — the 1882 Hunter EDUCATION Commission. The 1919 Hunter Commission investigated Jallianwala.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.10
questions.stem: Assertion (A) In 1916, Maulana Mohammad Ali and Abul Kalam Azad resigned from the Legislative Council. Reason (R) The Rowlatt Act was passed by the Government in spite of being opposed by all Indian members of the Legislative Council.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

explanation: (D) ✓ — A is FALSE (the resignations against the Rowlatt Act came in 1919, not 1916; the actual resignees were Mohammed Ali Jinnah, Madan Mohan Malaviya and Mazhar-ul-Haq — NOT Maulana Mohammad Ali or Abul Kalam Azad). R is TRUE (the Rowlatt Bill 1919 was passed despite unanimous opposition of every elected Indian member of the Imperial Legislative Council).
(Note: Maulana Muhammed Ali and Abul Kalam Azad resigned from the Legislative Council in 1916 during Khilafat Movement not in 1916. The Rowlatt Act was passed in 1919.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.11
questions.stem: During the Indian Freedom Struggle, who among the following proposed that Swaraj should be defined as complete independence free from all foreign control?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Maulana Hasrat Mohani — the radical who had already moved the complete-independence resolution at Ahmedabad (1921) — proposed that Swaraj be defined as complete independence free from all foreign control. lists him among the era's radical voices.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Mazharul Haque was a Bihar nationalist of the Champaran milieu — not the mover of the complete-independence definition; that was Hasrat Mohani.
(C) ✗ — Hakim Ajmal Khan was a Khilafat-era radical and unity man, but the Swaraj-as-complete-independence proposal is Mohani's.
(D) ✗ — Abul Kalam Azad shared the radical Khilafat platform yet the recorded mover of the definition was Hasrat Mohani.

(Note: Maulana Hasrat Mohani proposed that Swaraj should be defined as complete independence free from all foreign control in 1921 when he was presiding the session of all Indian Muslim League in Lucknow.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.12
questions.stem: The name of the famous person of India who returned the knighthood conferred on him by the British Government as a token of protest against the atrocities in Punjab in 1919 was
explanation: (C) ✓ — Rabindranath Tagore returned his knighthood in protest against the Punjab atrocities of 1919 — Jallianwala Bagh; the record alert marks it as the examiner-tested anchor.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Tej Bahadur Sapru was a Liberal constitutionalist (of the 1918 Liberal Federation walkout — see Ch 34 context); he made no knighthood renunciation over Punjab.
(B) ✗ — Ashutosh Mukherjee, the educationist-judge of Calcutta, kept his honours; the 1919 renunciation was Tagore's gesture.
(D) ✗ — Syed Ahmed Khan had died in 1898 — two decades before Jallianwala; he could not have returned anything in 1919.
(Note: Rabindranath Tagore returned his Knighthood to British Government as a token of protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in 1919.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.13
questions.stem:
Consider the following events during India's freedom struggle
1. Chauri-Chaura Outrage
2. Minto-Morley Reforms
3. Dandi March
4. Montague-Chelmsford Reforms
Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the events above?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The chain runs 2, 4, 1, 3: Minto-Morley Reforms (1909 — see) → Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919 — see) → Chauri-Chaura outrage (February 1922) → Dandi March (1930).
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Opens with Chauri-Chaura (1922) — but two whole reform eras (1909, 1919) precede it.
(C) ✗ — Again leads with Chauri-Chaura (1922) and buries Minto-Morley (1909) in third place — the reverse of time.
(D) ✗ — Slots the Dandi March (1930) second — before Chauri-Chaura (1922) and even before Montford (1919); Dandi is the LAST event of the four.
(Note: The correct chronology is Minto-Morley reforms in 1909, Montague Chelmsford reforms in 1917, Chauri- Chaura Outrage in 1922 and Dandi March in 1930)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.14
questions.stem: Which of the following pairs are correctly matched?
items: 1. Champaran — Rajendra Prasad
2. Ahmedabad Mill Workers — Morarji Desai
3. Kheda — Vallabhbhai Patel
questions.stemTail: Codes
explanation: (C) ✓ — 1 and 3 are correct. Champaran Satyagraha 1917 — Rajendra Prasad collaborated; Kheda Satyagraha 1918 — Vallabhbhai Patel led. Statement 2 wrong — Ahmedabad Mill Workers Strike 1918 was led by Gandhi/Anasuya Sarabhai, NOT Morarji Desai.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "1 and 2" keeps the false pair 2: the Ahmedabad strike's leadership was Gandhi with Anasuya Sarabhai — Morarji Desai has no place in it.
(B) ✗ — "2 and 3" carries the same false Morarji pair and discards the true Champaran-Rajendra Prasad pair.
(D) ✗ — Overcounts: pair 2 is the trap — the 1918 mill strike was led by Gandhi (with Anasuya Sarabhai), not Morarji Desai.
(The single trap in this question is pair 2 — Ahmedabad Mill Strike belongs to Gandhi and Anasuya Sarabhai; Morarji Desai is a much later Gujarat figure.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.15
questions.stem: Which one of the following aroused a wave of popular indignation that led to the massacre by the British at Jallianwala Bagh?
explanation: (C) ✓ — The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh had shattered whatever goodwill towards British governance remained.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Arms Act is Lytton's 1878 law — four decades before the 1919 Amritsar protests.
(B) ✗ — The Public Safety legislation belongs to the late 1920s (the Simon-era crackdown) — not to the spring of 1919.
(D) ✗ — The Vernacular Press Act was Lytton's 1878 press gag, repealed by Ripon; the 1919 indignation rose against the ROWLATT Act.

(Note: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre took place on 13th April, 1919. People had gathered in Jallianwala Bagh to protest against the arrest of Dr Satya Paul and Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew, during Anti Rowlatt Act agitation.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.16
questions.stem: At which one of the following places did Mahatma Gandhi first start his Satyagraha in India?
explanation: (C) ✓ — "Champaran tested passive resistance and civil disobedience."
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Ahmedabad came SECOND (1918) and tested the mill strike, hunger strike and arbitration; the FIRST Indian satyagraha site was Champaran (1917).
(B) ✗ — Bardoli is the 1928 no-revenue campaign — a decade after Gandhi's first satyagraha at Champaran.
(D) ✗ — Kheda was the THIRD pilot (1918, the first no-revenue movement); Champaran preceded it.

(Note: At Champaran, Mahatma Gandhi first started his Satyagraha in India. Rajkumar Shukla invited Gandhi from Lucknow and mobilisation of peasantry was done by Rajkumar Shukla and other local leaders.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.17
questions.stem: Who was the Viceroy of India when the Rowlatt Act was passed?
explanation: (C) ✓ — The Rowlatt Act was passed in March 1919 under Viceroy Chelmsford16-21 — the same Viceroy of the Montford reform years; the record alert pins this as the examiner-tested anchor.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Irwin's viceroyalty (1926–31) belongs to the Simon-CDM era, seven years after the Rowlatt Act.
(B) ✗ — Reading (1921–26) presided over the NCM's end and Gandhi's 1922 arrest — he arrived two years AFTER the Rowlatt Act.
(D) ✗ — Wavell (1943–47) is the WWII-era Viceroy of the Simla Conference years — a quarter-century too late.

(Note: During the Viceroyalty of Lord Chelmsford, a Sedition Committee was appointed by the government in 1918, with Justice Rowlatt, which made certain recommendations to curb seditious activities in India.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.18
questions.stem: Who among the following Gandhian followers was a teacher by profession?
explanation: (C) ✓ — J.B. Kripalani was the teacher: professor of English and History at Muzaffarpur College, Bihar (1912–17), who joined Gandhi's Champaran investigation — the record alert marks the teacher-by-profession Gandhian.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — A.N. Sinha belonged to the Bihar lawyer-politician circle around the Champaran inquiry, not to the teaching profession.
(B) ✗ — Braj Kishore Prasad was one of the LAWYERS who assisted Gandhi at Champaran — the teacher among the colleagues was Kripalani.
(D) ✗ — Rajendra Prasad too came to Champaran as a LAWYER (and rose to be India's first President); the teacher of the group was Kripalani.

(Note: Acharya Kripalani was a Gandhian all his life. He had his education in Karachi. J B Kripalani was professor of English and History at Muzaffarpur College in Bihar for 5 years from 1912 to 1917.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.19
questions.stem: Who of the following founded the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association?
explanation: (A) ✓ — The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (1918) grew out of the mill strike — founded by Mahatma Gandhi, with Anasuya Sarabhai as his collaborator in organising the workers.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Patel's organising triumphs were Kheda (1918) and later Bardoli (1928); the textile workers' association was Gandhi's creation.
(C) ✗ — N.M. Joshi's field was the AITUC trade-union movement (1920) — not the Ahmedabad association of 1918.
(D) ✗ — Kripalani was the teacher-Gandhian of the Champaran circle; the ATLA was founded by Gandhi himself.

(Note: The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association was formed by Mahatma Gandhi in 1918. The 'Mahatma' or 'Great Soul' hailed as the 'Father of the Nation' was born at Porbandar (Gujarat) on 2nd October, 1869.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.20
questions.stem: During the Indian Freedom Struggle, why did Rowlatt Act arouse popular indignation?

options.text: It curtailed the freedom of religion
It suppressed the Indian traditional education
It authorised the government to imprison people without trial
It curbed the trade union activities

explanation: (C) ✓ — The Rowlatt Act "authorised the government to imprison people without trial" — it extended the Defence of India Act's emergency powers into peacetime, with detention without trial and summary procedures; passed over the unanimous opposition of every Indian ILC member.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Religion was untouched by the Act — its target was civil liberty: detention without trial.
(B) ✗ — Education was nowhere in the Act's text; the indignation rose because Indians could now be jailed without trial.
(D) ✗ — Trade unions were not its object either — the Act was an anti-'sedition' detention law, not labour legislation.
(Note: During the period of Lord Chelmsford, a Sedition Committee was appointed by the government in 1918 with Justice Rowlatt, which made certain recommendations to curb sedition activity in India.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.21
questions.stem: Consider the following statements
items: 1. Dr Rajendra Prasad persuaded Mahatma Gandhi to come to Champaran to investigate the problem of peasants.
2. Acharya JB Kripalani was one of Mahatma Gandhi's colleagues in his Champaran investigation.
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statement 2 is true: J.B. Kripalani was among Gandhi's Champaran colleagues. Statement 1 is false: it was RAJKUMAR SHUKLA, the peasant leader who met Gandhi at the 1916 Lucknow Session, who persuaded him to come to Champaran — not Rajendra Prasad (who joined as a lawyer-colleague).
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "Only 1" picks the false statement: the man who brought Gandhi to Champaran was Rajkumar Shukla.
(C) ✗ — "Both" fails on statement 1 — Rajendra Prasad was a colleague in the inquiry, not the persuader; Shukla was.
(D) ✗ — "Neither" fails on statement 2 — Kripalani genuinely served in the Champaran investigation.

(Note: The story of Champaran begins in the early 19th century when European planters had involved the cultivators in agreement that forced them to cultivate indigo on 3/20th of their holdings (known as the Tinkathia system).)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.23
questions.stem: The Rowlatt Act aimed at

options.text: compulsory economic support to war efforts
imprisonment without trial and summary procedures for trial
imposition of restrictions on freedom of the press

explanation: (B) ✓ — The Rowlatt Act aimed at imprisonment without trial and summary procedures — extending the Defence of India Act's wartime powers into peacetime against 'anarchical and revolutionary' crime.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Compulsory war support was the stuff of wartime loans and recruitment drives — not this 1919 peacetime detention law.
(C) ✗ — The Khilafat Movement was formally launched only in June 1920 at Allahabad — the Act of March 1919 could not have aimed at a movement that did not yet exist.
(D) ✗ — Press restriction was the Vernacular Press Act's territory (1878 — see); Rowlatt struck at personal liberty — jail without trial.

(Note: A Sedition Committee was constituted under Justice Rowlatt in 1918. On its recommendations Rowlatt Act, 1919, was passed, which gave unlimited powers to the government to arrest and imprison the suspects.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.24
questions.stem: With reference to Rowlatt Satyagraha, which of the following statements is/are correct?
items: 1. The Rowlatt Act was based on the recommendations of the 'Sedition Committee'.
2. In Rowlatt Satyagraha, Gandhiji tried to utilise the Home Rule League.
3. Demonstrations against the arrival of Simon Commission coincided with Rowlatt Satyagraha.
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Act was built on the Sedition (Rowlatt) Committee's recommendations, and Gandhi tried to use the Home Rule League machinery for the Satyagraha. Statement 3 fails: the Simon Commission demonstrations came in 1928, nine years after the Rowlatt Satyagraha.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "Only 1" undercounts: Gandhi did harness the Home Rule League network for the Rowlatt agitation.
(C) ✗ — Keeps the false statement 3 — the Simon protests belong to 1928, not 1919 — and drops the true Sedition-Committee statement.
(D) ✗ — Overcounts: statement 3 is nine years out of place — Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) and the Simon boycott (1928) never coincided.
(Note: The Rowlatt Committee was a Sedition Committee appointed in 1918 by the British Indian Government with Justice Rowlatt, an English Judge, as its President.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.25
questions.stem: Which one of the following is a very significant aspect of the Champaran Satyagraha ?

options.text: Active all-India participation of lawyers, students and women in the National Movement
Active involvement of Dalit and Tribal communities of India in the National Movement
Joining of peasants unrest to India's National Movement
Drastic decrease in the cultivation of plantation crops and commercial crops.

explanation: (C) ✓ — "Gandhi (MG) arrived in India in January 1915."
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Champaran's helpers were LOCAL Bihar lawyers and teachers, not an all-India wave of lawyers, students and women — that scale came with later movements. The significance UPSC wants is the peasant link.
(B) ✗ — Dalit and tribal mass entry belongs to the NCM's results — not to Champaran 1917.
(D) ✗ — Indigo cultivation did shrink after Tinkathia's abolition, but that is a sectoral outcome — the era-defining significance was peasant unrest joining the national movement.

(Note: The centenary of Mahatma Gandhi's first Satyagraha in India was marked in April 2017. It was undertaken in the erstwhile undivided Champaran district in Northern Bihar. He went there in April 1917 on the request of Rajkumar Shukla.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.26
questions.stem: Consider the following statements in respect of Non-Cooperation Movement:I. Congress declared ‘Swaraj’ as objective.II. To be implemented in stages.
explanation: (C) ✓ — Both statements hold: the Congress adopted Swaraj as the objective (Nagpur Session, December 1920), and the non-cooperation programme was implemented in STAGES — the graded boycott ladder approved at the Special Calcutta Session.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — "I only" undercounts: the staged, escalating design — titles first, then institutions, then taxes — is exactly how the Calcutta programme was built.
(B) ✗ — "II only" undercounts: Swaraj WAS declared the objective at Nagpur (December 1920).
(D) ✗ — "Neither" fails on both: Swaraj objective (Nagpur) + staged implementation (Calcutta programme). +.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.27
questions.stem: Who provided legal defence to the people arrested in the aftermath of Chauri Chaura incident?

options.text: Madan Mohan Malaviya and Krishna Kant
Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Khwaja Hasan Nizami

explanation: (B) ✓ — "Madan Mohan Malaviya fought their cases in court."
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — C.R. Das's preference was fighting from WITHIN the councils and his celebrated defences lay elsewhere; the Chauri Chaura accused were defended by Malaviya.
(C) ✗ — Kitchlew's name belongs to the AMRITSAR story — already arrested in the Rowlatt-era crackdown; the Gorakhpur trials' defender was Malaviya.
(D) ✗ — Jinnah, the Lucknow-Pact constitutionalist, had already parted ways with mass politics by 1920; he was no Chauri Chaura defence counsel. The record names Malaviya.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.28
questions.stem: Consider the following subjects with regard to Non-Cooperation Programme: I. Boycott of law-courts II. Strict non-violence III. Retention of titles IV. Establishment of Panchayats
explanation: (C) ✓ — I, II and IV belong to the programme: boycott of law courts (with panchayats as the Swadeshi alternative for dispute resolution), strict non-violence as the movement's foundation, and panchayat-building itself. III is the trap: titles were to be SURRENDERED and boycotted, not retained.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Includes III — but the programme demanded the surrender/boycott of titles, never their retention. +.
(B) ✗ — Doubly wrong: keeps the false title-retention item AND drops the boycott of law courts, which headed the programme.
(D) ✗ — "All four" founders on III: title-surrender, not retention, was the first step of the boycott ladder.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: With reference to Mahatma Gandhi's choice of the three pilot projects (1917-1918), which one of the following correctly identifies the method tested at each site?

options.text: Champaran tested civil disobedience; Ahmedabad tested hunger strike and arbitration; Kheda tested non-cooperation.
Champaran tested arbitration; Ahmedabad tested civil disobedience; Kheda tested hunger strike.
Champaran tested hunger strike; Ahmedabad tested no-revenue; Kheda tested civil disobedience.
Champaran tested no-revenue movement; Ahmedabad tested non-cooperation; Kheda tested civil disobedience.

explanation: (A) ✓ — Chapter: Champaran tested passive resistance & civil disobedience. Ahmedabad tested a mill strike, hunger strike, and arbitration. Kheda tested non-cooperation through a no-revenue movement.

Why others wrong: (b) swaps Champaran and Ahmedabad — Chapter fixes civil disobedience at Champaran and arbitration at Ahmedabad; (c) misassigns hunger strike to Champaran — Chapter places the hunger strike at Ahmedabad; (d) flips no-revenue to Champaran — Chapter places the no-revenue movement at Kheda.
Memory hook: Bihar 1917 disobeys, Ahmedabad fasts and arbitrates, Kheda withholds — one lab, three methods.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917:
items: 1. Rajkumar Shukla, a peasant leader from Bihar, met Gandhi at the Lucknow Session of the INC in 1916 and persuaded him to visit Champaran.
2. The Tinkathia System forced ryots to cultivate indigo on three-twentieths of their land as plantation rent payable to British planters.
3. The British passed the Champaran Agricultural Act, 1918, after which planter oppression ended completely.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Chapter: Rajkumar Shukla, a peasant leader from Bihar, met MG at the Lucknow Session of the INC in 1916 & requested him to visit Champaran; ryots... were forced to cultivate indigo on 3/20th of their land as plantation rent payable to British planters; Statement 3 contradicts Chapter which states the British passed the Champaran Agricultural Act, 1918 — though planter oppression did not fully stop even after it.
Why others wrong: (b) includes statement 3 which Chapter explicitly contradicts; (c) includes statement 3 (false) and omits statement 2 (correct); (d) includes statement 3 which Chapter contradicts.
Memory hook: Shukla at Lucknow, three of twenty under indigo, 1918 Act passed but planters lingered.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: With reference to the Ahmedabad Mill Strike of 1918, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Workers demanded a 50% wage increase, Gandhi pressed for 35%, and the Arbitration Board settled on 27.5%.
Workers demanded a 35% wage increase and the Arbitration Board granted the full demand.
Workers demanded a 27.5% wage increase and mill owners conceded without arbitration.
Workers demanded a 50% wage increase and Gandhi himself fixed the final award at 50%.

explanation: (A) ✓ — Chapter: The demand of workers was a 50% wage increase... MG stepped in & demanded a 35% wage increase... An Arbitration Board was set up & settled on a 27.5% wage increase.

Why others wrong: (b) wrongly fixes the initial demand at 35% and the award at 35% — the figures were 50%, 35%, 27.5%; (c) wrongly drops arbitration entirely — arbitration was the very hallmark of Ahmedabad; (d) fabricates a 50% final award — the settled figure is 27.5%.
Memory hook: Fifty asked, thirty-five urged, twenty-seven-and-a-half awarded — the midpath through arbitration.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Ahmedabad Mill Strike of 1918:
items: 1. Gandhi was invited to Ahmedabad by Anasuya Sarabhai, a social worker.
2. Her brother Ambalal Sarabhai headed the Ahmedabad Mill Owners' Association.
3. The strike laid the foundation of the working-class movement in Ahmedabad and led directly to the formation of the Textile Labour Association in 1920.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Chapter: MG was invited to Ahmedabad by Anasuya Sarabhai, a social worker. Her brother Ambalal Sarabhai headed the Ahmedabad Mill Owners' Association; This strike laid the foundation of the working-class movement in Ahmedabad, leading directly to the formation of the Textile Labour Association in 1920.
Why others wrong: (a) drops verified statement 3; (b) drops verified statement 1; (c) drops verified statement 2.
Memory hook: Anasuya invites, Ambalal resists, 1920 Textile Labour Association is born.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Which one of the following best explains why the Kheda Satyagraha of 1918 is classified as Non-Cooperation rather than Civil Disobedience?

options.text: Because the ryots demanded Swaraj and refused to pay tax permanently to the British government.
Because crop failure legally entitled the ryots to remission, and the government was violating its own law.
Because Sardar Patel, not Gandhi, led the movement and chose the label.
Because the ryots refused to pay any revenue ever again, challenging colonial sovereignty itself.

explanation: (B) ✓ — Chapter: the law supported the ryots. Hence, Non-Cooperation: withholding cooperation with an unjust action, without challenging colonial sovereignty as such; The ryots were not refusing to pay tax permanently. They were temporarily withholding payment because the law was on their side.

Why others wrong: (a) the goal at Kheda was NOT Swaraj — that is precisely what would have made it Civil Disobedience; (c) Patel did follow Gandhi through Kheda but he was not the one who classified the method; (d) the ryots were not refusing tax permanently — they were withholding only because the law backed them.
Memory hook: Law on the ryot's side, tax merely deferred — withholding cooperation, not challenging the State.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Under the Ryotwari settlement system applicable in Kheda district of Gujarat in 1918, farmers were entitled by law to a remission of Land Revenue if their crop yield fell below what proportion of normal output?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: Under the Ryotwari settlement system, farmers in Kheda district of Gujarat were entitled by law to a remission — a reduction — of Land Revenue (LR) if their crop yield fell below one-quarter of normal output.
Why others wrong: (a) one-half is not the record threshold; (b) one-third is not the record threshold; (d) one-fifth is not the record threshold — Chapter's exact figure is one-quarter.
Memory hook: Crop below a quarter — remission was the legal right Kheda asked the British to honour.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Rowlatt Act of 1919:
items: 1. It was formally titled the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act and was based on the recommendations of a sedition committee chaired by Justice S.A.T. Rowlatt.
2. It was passed by the Central Legislative Assembly (CLA) created under the Government of India Act
3. It extended the emergency powers of the Defence of India Act 1915 into peacetime.
questions.stemTail: 1919 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Chapter: the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) passed what became known as the Rowlatt Act — the Anarchical & Revolutionary Crimes Act. It was based on recommendations of a sedition committee chaired by Justice S.A.T. Rowlatt; this was passed by the ILC, not the Central Legislative Assembly (CLA). The CLA came into existence only in December 1919 under the GOI Act 1919; The Act extended the emergency powers of the Defence of India Act 1915 into peacetime.
Why others wrong: (a) Statement 2 is false — Chapter explicitly warns the CLA did not yet exist; (c) includes false statement 2 and drops verified statement 1; (d) includes false statement 2.
Memory hook: ILC passed it in Feb 1919 — CLA had not even been born; sedition committee under Rowlatt drafted, peacetime kept wartime powers.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to the passage of the Rowlatt Act in the Imperial Legislative Council, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: It was passed with the support of a majority of Indian members of the ILC.
It was passed despite unanimous opposition from every single Indian member of the ILC.
It was passed with abstention by all Indian members of the ILC.
It was withdrawn after Indian members of the ILC opposed it.

explanation: (B) ✓ — Chapter: the Act was passed despite unanimous opposition from every single Indian member of the ILC. Every Indian member voted against it. It passed anyway.
Why others wrong: (a) every Indian member voted against — not in support; (c) they voted against, they did not abstain; (d) it passed anyway; it was never withdrawn at this stage.
Memory hook: Every Indian vote a No — every British vote a Yes — the Act passed against unanimous Indian dissent.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919:
items: 1. People had gathered peacefully in the enclosed garden of Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar to celebrate Baisakhi and to protest the arrest of their leaders.
2. General Dyer ordered firing without any warning, and the firing continued for ten minutes.
3. The Hunter Committee, set up in October 1919 with its report in 1920, awarded General Dyer a lifetime imprisonment sentence.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Chapter: People had gathered peacefully in the enclosed garden of Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar — to celebrate Baisakhi & to protest the arrest of their leaders; Without any warning, General Dyer ordered his troops to open fire. The firing continued for 10 minutes; Statement 3 contradicts Chapter — The Hunter Committee found him guilty — but only of being overly zealous in the Empire's service. No meaningful punishment followed.

Why others wrong: (b) includes false statement 3 — Hunter Committee gave no meaningful punishment, let alone life imprisonment; (c) includes false statement 3 and drops verified statement 2; (d) includes false statement 3.
Memory hook: Baisakhi gathering, ten silent minutes of fire, Hunter Committee whitewash — two wounds in one season.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the official British count and the INC's count of deaths in the Jallianwala Bagh massacre?

options.text: British count: 200 dead; INC count: 1,000 dead
British count: 500 dead; INC count: 2,000 dead
British count: 379 dead; INC count: 1,500 dead
British count: 1,000 dead; INC count: 379 dead

explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: Official British records counted 379 dead. The INC's count was 1,500 dead.

Why others wrong: (a) Chapter's exact figures are 379 (British) and 1,500 (INC), not 200/1,000; (b) Chapter nowhere lists 500/2,000; (d) reverses the relationship — INC's count was higher than the British count, not lower.
Memory hook: Three-seventy-nine on Britain's page, fifteen hundred on INC's page — same garden, two numbers.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following events associated with Mahatma Gandhi in 1917-1919. Arrange them in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Relocation of the Satyagraha Ashram from Kochrab to Sabarmati
2. Champaran Satyagraha
3. Ahmedabad Mill Strike
4. Rowlatt Satyagraha
explanation: (B) ✓ — Chapter: Satyagraha Ashram founded... at Kochrab (1915), later relocated to Sabarmati (1917) — the Ashram was already at Sabarmati when Gandhi went to Champaran later in 1917; Champaran Satyagraha 1917; Ahmedabad Mill Strike 1918; Rowlatt Satyagraha April 1919.

Why others wrong: (a) places Champaran before the Sabarmati relocation — Chapter's sequence sets the Ashram move first; (c) places Ahmedabad 1918 before the 1917 Sabarmati move — chronologically impossible; (d) places Ahmedabad 1918 before Champaran 1917 — reverses Chapter's year order.
Memory hook: Kochrab to Sabarmati first, then Bihar's indigo, then Ahmedabad's mills, then Rowlatt's storm.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Consider the following events of 1919. Arrange them in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Passage of the Rowlatt Act by the Imperial Legislative Council
2. Jallianwala Bagh massacre
3. Establishment of the Hunter Committee
4. Coming into existence of the Central Legislative Assembly under the GOI Act 1919
explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: Rowlatt Act passed "In February 1919" by the ILC; Jallianwala Bagh "13 April 1919"; Hunter Committee "set up in October 1919"; CLA came into existence only in December 1919 under the GOI Act 1919.

Why others wrong: (a) places CLA (December) before Hunter Committee (October); (b) starts with Jallianwala Bagh before the Rowlatt Act — Chapter sets the Act in February, the massacre in April; (d) starts with Hunter Committee (October) before the Rowlatt Act (February).
Memory hook: Feb Act, April fire, October inquiry, December CLA — 1919 told in four steps.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Match List I (Pilot Project, 1917-1918) with List II (Hallmark recorded in Chapter):
items: 1. Champaran Satyagraha — A. First Hunger Strike and arbitration
2. Ahmedabad Mill Strike — B. First Non-Cooperation through No-Revenue movement
3. Kheda Satyagraha — C. First Civil Disobedience through passive resistance
questions.stemTail: Select the correct match:
matchTable: List II (List II (Hallmark recorded in Chapter))
A. First Hunger Strike and arbitration
B. First Non-Cooperation through No-Revenue movement
C. First Civil Disobedience through passive resistance
explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: Champaran — The hallmark of Champaran: Passive Resistance & Civil Disobedience; Ahmedabad — "Hallmark: New technique of arbitration + 1st hunger strike"; Kheda — "Hallmark: 1st Non-Cooperation / No Revenue Movement."

Why others wrong: (a) ties Champaran to hunger strike — Chapter places hunger strike at Ahmedabad; (b) ties Ahmedabad to no-revenue — Chapter places no-revenue at Kheda; (d) ties Champaran to no-revenue — Chapter places civil disobedience at Champaran.
Memory hook: Champaran — disobey; Ahmedabad — fast and arbitrate; Kheda — withhold revenue.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Match List I (Personality) with List II (Role in pilot-project / Rowlatt years):
items: 1. Rajkumar Shukla — A. Social worker who invited Gandhi to mediate the mill strike
2. Anasuya Sarabhai — B. Lieutenant Governor under whom martial law was applied in Punjab
3. Ambalal Sarabhai — C. Bihar peasant leader who persuaded Gandhi to visit Champaran
4. O'Dwyer — D. Head of the Ahmedabad Mill Owners' Association
questions.stemTail: Select the correct match:
matchTable: A. Social worker who invited Gandhi to mediate the mill strike
B. Lieutenant Governor under whom martial law was applied in Punjab
C. Bihar peasant leader who persuaded Gandhi to visit Champaran
explanation: (A) ✓ — Chapter: "Rajkumar Shukla, a peasant leader from Bihar"; MG was invited to Ahmedabad by Anasuya Sarabhai, a social worker; Her brother Ambalal Sarabhai headed the Ahmedabad Mill Owners' Association; Under Lieutenant Governor O'Dwyer, General Dyer... applied martial law in Punjab with O'Dwyer's approval.

Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) all break at least one Chapter-anchored pairing — Shukla is the Bihar peasant, Anasuya is the inviting social worker, Ambalal heads the Mill Owners' body, O'Dwyer is the Lt. Governor of Punjab.
Memory hook: Shukla calls Gandhi to Bihar, Anasuya calls him to Ahmedabad, Ambalal owns the mills, O'Dwyer governs the lathi.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: With reference to the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917, which one of the following statements regarding Gandhi's response to the British order to leave the district is correct?

options.text: Gandhi complied with the order and left the district, returning later with a Congress delegation.
Gandhi appealed against the order in the Patna High Court before deciding his next step.
Gandhi negotiated with the planters first and then accepted to leave the district peacefully.
Gandhi defied the order and courted arrest, and that refusal itself constituted Civil Disobedience.

explanation: (D) ✓ — Chapter: British authorities ordered him to leave the district. He refused. This refusal — to comply with a direct official order — was the act of Civil Disobedience. He courted arrest.
Why others wrong: (a) he refused, he did not comply; (b) there was no Patna High Court appeal; (c) what followed was refusal and arrest, not a negotiated departure.
Memory hook: Order to leave, refusal to go, arrest accepted — three steps that made it Civil Disobedience.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_16
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Rowlatt Satyagraha of April 1919:
items: 1. The call for a nationwide non-violent strike was given by Gandhi alone, not by the INC.
2. It was the first Satyagraha launched by Gandhi on Indian soil.
3. Gandhi withdrew the movement after the violence it generated, recognising that mass action without training and discipline was dangerous.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Rowlatt Satyagraha was called by MG alone — not by the INC. Overwhelmed by the violence the movement had generated, MG withdrew it. He recognised that mass action without training & discipline was dangerous. Statement 2 is incorrect — Rowlatt 1919 was Gandhi's first all-India venture and India's first mass strike, but the first Satyagraha on Indian soil was Champaran (Bihar) in 1917; the answer to Prelims 2000 is "Post-SA 1st successful Satyagraha = Champaran" and to Prelims 2007 "first Indian Satyagraha site = Champaran".

Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — retains the incorrect statement 2; Gandhi's first Satyagraha on Indian soil was Champaran 1917, two years before Rowlatt, and it also drops the correct statement 3. (b) 2 and 3 only — retains the incorrect statement 2 and drops the correct statement 1, which fixes the crucial point that Rowlatt was called by Gandhi personally and not by the INC. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — statement 2 is incorrect, so all three cannot be correct together.
Memory hook: Champaran 1917 was the first Satyagraha; Rowlatt 1919 was the first all-India strike — MG called it alone and called it off alone.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_17
questions.stem: Which one of the following correctly identifies the two lessons Gandhi drew from the Rowlatt Satyagraha?

options.text: He needed alliance with the Muslim League and the abandonment of non-violence.
He needed to enter the Imperial Legislative Council and to expand the Home Rule Leagues.
He needed control over the INC for a mass movement, and Indians needed training in non-violent Satyagraha.
He needed to leave India and continue the struggle from abroad as Lajpat Rai had done.

explanation: (C) ✓ — Chapter: MG drew two lessons: he needed control over the INC for a controlled mass movement, and Indians needed training in non-violent Satyagraha before the next round.

Why others wrong: (a) Chapter nowhere mentions abandoning non-violence — quite the opposite; (b) Council entry and Home Rule expansion are not the Rowlatt lessons in Chapter; (d) Chapter never records a plan to leave India after Rowlatt.
Memory hook: Take charge of INC + train the people in non-violence — Rowlatt's twin lessons.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_18
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the Rowlatt Act:
items: 1. The Act extended the emergency powers of the Defence of India Act 1915 into peacetime.
2. Those powers included detention without trial, suppression of press freedom, and trial of cases without juries.
3. The Rowlatt Act was passed by the Central Legislative Assembly, a body created under the Government of India Act 1919.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Chapter: "The Act extended the emergency powers of the Defence of India Act 1915 into peacetime. That Act had been enacted specifically for the duration of WWI (1914–19) — the powers to detain without trial, suppress press freedom, try cases without juries." Statement 3 is incorrect — the Rowlatt Act was passed in February 1919 by the Imperial Legislative Council. Chapter warns explicitly: "this was passed by the ILC, not the Central Legislative Assembly (CLA). The CLA came into existence only in December 1919 under the GOI Act 1919."

Why others wrong: (b) 2 and 3 only — retains the incorrect statement 3 and drops the correct statement 1, which is the core point that wartime powers were carried into peacetime. (c) 1 and 3 only — retains the incorrect statement 3; the Rowlatt Act of February 1919 predates the CLA, which came into existence only in December 1919, and it also drops the correct statement 2. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — statement 3 is incorrect, so all three cannot be correct together.
Memory hook: The old ILC passed Rowlatt in February 1919; the CLA was only born in December 1919 — wartime DOI 1915 powers smuggled into peacetime: detain, gag, jury-less.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_19
questions.stem: Which one of the following statements about the Kheda Satyagraha of 1918 and its impact is correct?

options.text: Gandhi persuaded all peasants to pay full Land Revenue while petitioning the government.
Gandhi asked peasants to withhold Land Revenue, the government agreed not to confiscate the property of those who could not pay, and Sardar Patel became his follower.
The government granted a full and unconditional remission of Land Revenue to all Kheda peasants after the 1918 harvest failed and plague struck.
Subhas Chandra Bose became a follower of Gandhi through the Kheda movement, his first experience of organised mass action.

explanation: (B) ✓ — Chapter: MG asked peasants to withhold payment of LR. The government eventually agreed not to confiscate the property of those who could not pay — effectively conceding the principle that only those who could pay would be required to do so; Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel became a follower of MG through this movement. Kheda was Patel's first experience of organised mass action.

Why others wrong: (a) peasants withheld payment, they did not pay in full; (c) there was a no-confiscation concession for those who could not pay — not a blanket remission; (d) Patel, not Bose, was the leader who joined Gandhi through Kheda.
Memory hook: Withhold revenue, win a no-confiscation pledge, gain Sardar Patel — Kheda's three returns.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_20
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the political and administrative context of the Rowlatt Act and the Punjab events of 1919:
items: 1. The Rowlatt Act was passed despite the joint resignation of Imperial Legislative Council members such as Jinnah, Lala Lajpat Rai and Mazharul Haq in protest.
2. In Punjab, INC leaders Dr. Satya Pal and Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew had been arrested before the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
3. Martial law in Punjab was applied by General Dyer with the approval of Lieutenant Governor O'Dwyer.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Widespread violence followed, especially in Punjab, where INC leaders Dr. Satya Pal & Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew had already been arrested. Under Lieutenant Governor O'Dwyer, General Dyer (Colonel Reginald Dyer) applied martial law in Punjab with O'Dwyer's approval. Statement 1 is incorrect — the ILC members who jointly resigned in 1919 were Jinnah, Madan Mohan Malaviya and Mazharul Haq. Lala Lajpat Rai could not have been among them: he was in voluntary exile in the United States and returned to India in February 1920.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — retains the incorrect statement 1; Lajpat Rai was in the United States, not in the Imperial Legislative Council, in 1919, and it also drops the correct statement 3. (c) 1 and 3 only — retains the incorrect statement 1 and drops the correct statement 2 on the pre-massacre arrests of Satya Pal and Kitchlew. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — statement 1 is incorrect, so all three cannot be correct together.
Memory hook: Malaviya resigned in Delhi while Lajpat Rai was lobbying in Washington until February 1920 — the real pair here is two Punjab arrests plus O'Dwyer's martial-law nod.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: The three Pilot Projects of 1917-18 — Champaran, Ahmedabad, & Kheda — converted South African Satyagraha into a working Indian method. Examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" + "converted" demands a process-oriented answer. The body must show what each Pilot Project added to the method that South Africa hadn't already developed.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 with Satyagraha as a personal method; the three Pilot Projects of 1917-18 tested whether the Indian context could carry the same architecture.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Champaran (1917) — 'Champaran Satyagraha, 1917 — The First Civil Disobedience'. First Civil Disobedience on Indian soil. Tested whether Indian peasants — under the Tinkathia indigo system in Bihar — would follow a non-violent, local-issue-led campaign. Result: yes. Rajendra Prasad joined here. Champaran proved Indian rural communities could be mobilised without violence.

2. Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918) — 'Ahmedabad Mill Strike, 1918 — The First Hunger Strike'. First Hunger Strike (fast unto death). Tested the labour-capital arbitration model — Gandhi's Trusteeship doctrine in live action. Anasuya Sarabhai linked Gandhi to the millworkers. Outcome: 35% wage increase via moral negotiation, not class war.

3. Kheda Satyagraha (1918) — 'Kheda Satyagraha, 1918 — The First Non-Cooperation Movement'. First Non-Cooperation movement. Tested whether peasants would refuse revenue payment to the colonial state. Famine + plague + revenue-collection-as-usual = unjust burden. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel emerged here as a Gandhi lieutenant.

4. The composite outcome. Each Pilot Project proved one repertoire-element worked on Indian soil. Champaran = civil disobedience; Ahmedabad = fast; Kheda = non-cooperation. By 1919, all three were available simultaneously — & Gandhi deployed them at full scale in the Rowlatt Satyagraha.

Closing verdict: The Pilot Projects were not just early campaigns — they were the laboratory in which South African Satyagraha was indigenised. Without the three successful tests of 1917-18, the Rowlatt Satyagraha of 1919 could not have been organised at the all-India scale it took.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Examine the reasons and consequences of Mahatma Gandhi's withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" + "reasons and consequences" = both halves required. Body must explain (a) why Gandhi withdrew despite the movement's momentum, & (b) what it cost — both within the INC and in broader nationalist politics.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Gandhi's withdrawal of the NCM after Chauri Chaura (5 February 1922) was the moment that fixed non-violence as the absolute condition of his political method — & created a permanent rift with sections of the INC.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'Events of the NCM (1920–22)'):

1. The Reason — non-violence as absolute (see 'Events of the NCM (1920–22)'). Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur) saw 22 policemen burnt to death by a mob during the NCM. Gandhi held that violence — even by Indians, even by anti-colonial protesters — voided the moral basis of the movement. Means matter as much as ends; Gandhi's two defining principles allowed no compromise.

2. The Internal Cost (see 'Results of the NCM'). Tilak's wing and C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru, & others held the withdrawal as a strategic blunder — the movement was at peak momentum; pausing for one incident in one district threw away national-scale leverage. C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru went on to form the Swaraj Party (December 1922) — Council Entry strategy = Gandhi's withdrawal forced a tactical split within Congress.

3. The Larger Consequence (see 'Results of the NCM'). The Passive Phase (1922-27) followed — no mass movement against the British. But Constructive Work (see 'The Importance of Constructive Work During the Passive Phase') used these years to build Khadi, national schools, & panchayats — when the next mass round came (Civil Disobedience 1930), the INC had a far stronger institutional machine.

Closing verdict: The Chauri Chaura withdrawal cost the immediate momentum but established non-violence as the structural — not tactical — anchor of Indian nationalism. It also forced the Swaraj Party experiment, which itself produced the Council-Entry skill-set the INM would need in 1937 & after.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: The Sarabandi (no tax) campaign of 1922 was led by
explanation: (D) ✓ — After NCM was withdrawn in 1922, Gujarat saw a unique form of peasant mobilisation under Vallabhbhai Patel.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Bhagat Singh belongs to the revolutionary stream of the late 1920s — the Sarabandi no-tax campaign was Gujarat peasant politics under Patel.
(B) ✗ — Chittaranjan Das's arena in 1922 was the Council-entry debate after the NCM's withdrawal — not Gujarat's village no-tax campaign.
(C) ✗ — Rajaguru was Bhagat Singh's HSRA comrade of the Lahore Conspiracy era — no connection to the 1922 Gujarat campaign.
(Note: In Gujarat, Sardar Vallabhai Patel led the Sarabandi (no tax) campaign. Patel emphasised the principal hardships and the need for complete unity and non-violence.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists:
explanation: (A) ✓ — The correct pairing is A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2: the Mapilla Revolt belongs to Malabar, Kerala; the Pabna Revolt to Bengal; the Eka Movement to Awadh; and Birsa Munda's Ulgulan to Chhota Nagpur in Bihar.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Scrambles every pair: Moplah sent to Bengal, Pabna to Bihar, Birsa to Kerala — none survives the record geography.
(C) ✗ — Keeps Moplah-Kerala but then pairs Pabna with Bihar and Eka with Bengal — Pabna was Bengal's agrarian league country and Eka was Awadh's. +.
(D) ✗ — Sends Moplah to Bengal and Eka to Kerala — both displaced; the Mapilla Revolt is Malabar's and the Eka Movement Awadh's. +.
(Note: Moplah Revolt — Occurred in Malabar in 1921 led by Ali Musliyar and Varian Kunnath Haji. Pabna Revolt — The Revolt occurred in Bengal from 1873-76 was a resistance movement by the peasants.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: The leader of the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) was
explanation: (A) ✓ — Bardoli (1928) was Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's campaign — the no-revenue fight against the enhanced assessment in Surat district, from which Patel emerged with the title 'Sardar'.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Gandhi blessed the campaign but the field general at Bardoli was Patel; Gandhi's own no-revenue pilot had been Kheda a decade earlier.
(C) ✗ — Vithalbhai J. Patel was the OTHER Patel — the legislator brother who presided over the Central Legislative Assembly; Bardoli's leader was Vallabhbhai.
(D) ✗ — Mahadev Desai was Gandhi's secretary-chronicler, not the Bardoli commander; the campaign was Vallabhbhai Patel's.
(Note: The leader of the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) was Sardar Vallabhbai Patel, who was conferred the title of Sardar by the women of Bardoli.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: Who among the following was not associated with the formation of UP Kisan Sabha in February, 1918?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Jawaharlal Nehru was NOT among the founders: the UP Kisan Sabha (February 1918) was set up by Gauri Shankar Mishra and Indra Narayan Dwivedi with Madan Mohan Malaviya's support; Nehru's village engagement came later, from June 1920.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Indra Narayan Dwivedi WAS a founder of the 1918 UP Kisan Sabha — the question asks for the one who was NOT associated.
(B) ✗ — Gauri Shankar Mishra likewise co-founded the Sabha in February 1918.
(D) ✗ — Madan Mohan Malaviya supported the founders' efforts — associated, though not the answer the stem seeks.

(Note: The UP Kisan Sabha was set-up in February 1918 by Gauri Shankar Mishra and Indra Narayan Dwivedi. Madan Mohan Malaviya supported their efforts. By June 1919, the UP Kisan Sabha had 450 branches.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Which of the following were grievances of peasants in Awadh that fuelled the Kisan Sabha Movement around 1918–20?
items: 1. Illegal abwabs and nazrana
2. Bedakhli i.e. eviction at the will of landlords
3. Forced labour (hari and begar)
4. Permanent Settlement of Bengal
explanation: (a) ✓ — Awadh peasants' specific grievances were illegal abwabs and nazrana (extra cesses beyond legal rent), bedakhli (eviction at the landlord's will), and forced labour i.e. hari and begar. Permanent Settlement applied to Bengal, not Awadh, and finds no place in the Awadh peasants' charter — see.

Why others wrong: (b) wrongly includes Permanent Settlement and omits illegal abwabs/nazrana; (c) wrongly includes Permanent Settlement and omits bedakhli; (d) wrongly includes Permanent Settlement, which was a Bengal-specific land-revenue arrangement, not an Awadh grievance.
Memory hook: Awadh's three A-B-H pains — Abwabs, Bedakhli, Hari-begar. Permanent Settlement stayed back in Bengal.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: With reference to the UP Kisan Sabha (UPKS) set up in February 1918, who among the following was NOT among its co-founders?
explanation: (b) ✓ — UPKS February 1918 was co-founded by Gauri Shankar Mishra, Indra Narayan Dwivedi and Madan Mohan Malaviya. Jawaharlal Nehru was NOT associated with UPKS 1918; he engaged with the Kisan Sabha movement only from June 1920 onwards, when he visited Pratapgarh with Baba Ramchandra — see.

Why others wrong: (a) Mishra was an operational organiser and co-founder; (c) Dwivedi was the other operational organiser and co-founder; (d) Malaviya was the senior political patron lending his weight as co-founder.
Memory hook: UPKS 1918 = Mishra-Dwivedi-Malaviya trio. Nehru joined only in 1920 — two years late to the party.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Which one of the following events is identified as the immediate trigger that ignited the Akali Movement (1920–25) for wresting control of Gurudwaras from the Mahants?

options.text: Annexation of Punjab by the British in 1849
Honouring of General Dyer by the Mahants after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919
Formation of the Shiromani Gurudwara Prabandhak Committee in 1920

explanation: (c) ✓ — The trigger for the Akali Movement was the Mahants honouring General Dyer after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919. When the Mahants felicitated the very man who had ordered the massacre of Sikhs at Amritsar, ordinary devotees decided they could no longer tolerate Mahant control over their religious institutions — see.

Why others wrong: (a) the 1849 annexation only worsened the British–Mahant collusion but was not the immediate trigger; (b) the Singh Sabha Movement of the 1880s laid the long-term reformist foundation, not the immediate trigger; (d) the SGPC's formation in 1920 was a consequence of the movement having already begun, not its trigger.
Memory hook: Mahants garlanded Dyer — Sikhs replied with the Akali Movement.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Match List-I (Peasant Movement) with List-II (Leader):
items: 1. Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920)
2. Eka Movement (1921)
3. Borsad Satyagraha (1922–24)
4. Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) A. Madari Pasi B. Vallabhbhai Patel C. Baba Ramchandra D. Vallabhbhai Patel
