explanation: (d) ✓ — Awadh Kisan Sabha 1920 was led by Baba Ramchandra; Eka Movement 1921 by Madari Pasi (a leader from the lower castes); Borsad Satyagraha 1922–24 by Vallabhbhai Patel in Gujarat; Bardoli Satyagraha 1928 again by Vallabhbhai Patel (who received the title "Sardar" from the women of Bardoli) — see.

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly assigns Awadh Kisan Sabha to Madari Pasi and Eka to Baba Ramchandra — the two are swapped; (b) wrongly assigns Awadh Kisan Sabha to Patel and Eka to Madari Pasi while pushing Patel to Bardoli only; (c) wrongly assigns Eka to Patel and Borsad to Madari Pasi.
Memory hook: Awadh = Ramchandra, Eka = Madari Pasi (LC voice), Borsad + Bardoli = Patel (×2).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: As a result of the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928, an independent tribunal was eventually appointed. To what figure did the tribunal revise the original 30% increase in land revenue assessment?
explanation: (a) ✓ — After the truce reached at Bardoli, an independent tribunal was appointed and it revised the land revenue increase down to 6.03% — a far cry from the original 30%. This is offered as a classic example of Gandhian arbitration revealing economic truth through a middle path based on facts — see.

Why others wrong: (b) 12.5% finds no place's outcome of Bardoli; (c) 15% finds no place's outcome of Bardoli; (d) the 30% increase was NOT retained — the very point of the truce was to bring it down sharply to 6.03%.
Memory hook: 30% balloon → 6.03% pin-prick. Bardoli tribunal cut land revenue to one-fifth.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: With reference to the Eka Movement (1921) in Awadh, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It was led by Madari Pasi, a leader from the lower castes.
2. Apart from zamindars, peasants resented the additional tyranny of thikedars (rent collectors).
3. It strictly adhered to the Gandhian principle of non-violence.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (b) ✓ — Statement 1 is correct: Madari Pasi, a leader from the lower castes, emerged at the head of the Eka Movement. Statement 2 is correct: peasants resented zamindars and the added tyranny of thikedars (rent collectors who squeezed peasants even harder than zamindars themselves). Statement 3 is wrong: unlike the Gandhian movements that insisted on non-violence as a non-negotiable principle, the Eka Movement did NOT adhere to non-violence — which is why the British could repress it on law-and-order grounds and crush it by 1922 — see.

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly retains statement 3 (non-violence) and drops statement 2 (thikedars); (c) wrongly retains statement 3 and drops statement 1 (Madari Pasi); (d) wrongly retains statement 3 — Eka was not a non-violent movement.
Memory hook: Eka = Madari Pasi + thikedars rage. Non-violence? Not signed up for it.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: With reference to the Mapilla Revolt of 1921 in Malabar, against which class of landlords was the original agrarian grievance directed?
explanation: (c) ✓ — The Mapilla (Moplah) tenants were predominantly Muslim and their primary grievance was oppression by landlords. These landlords were predominantly Hindu Jenmies (hereditary landowners) who controlled vast tracts of land, and the Mapilla tenants suffered under heavy rents and arbitrary eviction. The revolt later took a communal colour only after INC leaders were arrested and organised political guidance collapsed — see read with.

Why others wrong: (a) Muslim Jagirdars find no place in Malabar's land structure as described; (b) Indigo planters belong to a different agrarian movement and find no place in; (d) Christian missionary estate-holders find no place in the Mapilla grievance described by the record.
Memory hook: Mapilla tenants Muslim, Jenmies Hindu — agrarian fight at the start, communal turn only after leaders were jailed.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: With reference to the Akali Movement and its outcome, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The British conceded Akali demands chiefly because they feared disaffection among Sikh soldiers in the British Indian Army.
2. The Gurudwara Reform Act, 1925 placed all Gurudwaras under the SGPC, an elected body of Sikhs.
3. Post-movement, the Akali ranks split into the Kirti Kisan Party, the Akali Dal and the Unionist Party.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (d) ✓ — All three statements are correct. Statement 1 — the British were anxious about disaffection in the Army since Sikhs formed a significant part of the British Indian Army). Statement 2 — to prevent that very disaffection, the British passed the Gurudwara Reform Act, 1925, and the SGPC, an elected body of Sikhs, got control over all Gurudwaras (What was the Final Outcome?)). Statement 3 — post-movement, the Akalis split into three factions: Gandhians & Leftists forming the Kirti Kisan Party, Communalists continuing as Akali Dal, and Loyalists forming the Unionist Party (How did the Akali Movement strengthen INM?)).

Why others wrong: (a) wrongly omits statement 3 on the three-way Akali split; (b) wrongly omits statement 1 on the British Army-disaffection motive; (c) wrongly omits statement 2 on the Gurudwara Reform Act, 1925 and SGPC.
Memory hook: Army-fear → Act 1925 → SGPC + three-way split (Kirti, Akali, Unionist).

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: "The peasant movements of the 1920s were nationalist in their political vocabulary but agrarian in their motivating grievances." Critically examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Critically examine" + dual claim demands a balanced analysis. The body must (a) accept the dual character — political vocabulary vs material grievance — & (b) trace how each pulled the movements in different directions.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Each peasant movement of the 1920s adopted INM political language (Swaraj, Satyagraha) but was triggered by specific agrarian distress — high revenue, eviction, indebtedness — which is what actually brought peasants to the streets.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Political vocabulary, agrarian core (see 'How did Peasant Movements connect with INM?' and 'Kisan Sabha Movement (1918) and Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920)' and 'Eka Movement (1921) — Awadh' and 'Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) — Surat, Gujarat'). Bardoli was called a "Satyagraha"; Eka Movement adopted oath-bound discipline like NCM; Awadh Kisan Sabha borrowed nationalist vocabulary via Nehru. But the trigger in each case was a specific revenue or rent grievance — not a constitutional question.

2. The INC's tactical relationship (see 'How did Peasant Movements connect with INM?' and 'A Note on Peasant Movements and INC'). INC absorbed peasant energy when convenient (Bardoli, Champaran earlier) but withdrew from peasant struggles when they threatened the multi-class coalition — especially when peasants attacked landlords (Moplah 1921) or threatened zamindari interests (Awadh radicalism 1921-22).

3. The class-coalition problem (see 'A Note on Peasant Movements and INC'). Peasant movements forced the INC to choose between deepening rural mobilisation (which alienated zamindars in the INC's coalition) & containing it (which limited mass-base growth). The 1920s show INC choosing containment — Gandhi suspended NCM partly fearing peasant violence.

4. The deep legacy (see 'A Note on Peasant Movements and INC'). Despite the INC's caution, the peasant movements built infrastructure — Kisan Sabhas in UP, Bihar, Bengal — that would re-emerge in the 1930s All-India Kisan Sabha (1936) & beyond. Tebhaga (1946) & Telangana (1946-51) grew on this base.

Closing verdict: The 1920s peasant movements were not subordinated to the INM nor wholly autonomous from it. They were a partial overlap zone — where nationalist political language met agrarian material struggle. The unresolved tension was the INC's central post-1947 problem.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: What made the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) the most successful peasant movement of the 1920s? Examine its method & outcome.
body: Demand of the question: "What made it the most successful" + "examine method & outcome" — body must identify the structural reasons for Bardoli's success that other peasant movements lacked.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Bardoli succeeded where Mapilla, Eka & Awadh Kisan Sabha had failed — it married disciplined Gandhian Satyagraha to a focused, technical revenue grievance under uncompromised leadership.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) — Surat, Gujarat'):

1. The focused grievance. A 22% revenue increase in a single taluka was a specific, technical issue — not a generalised anti-feudal demand. Easy to document; easy to defend; easy to negotiate. By contrast, Moplah carried communal & landlord-tenant complications; Eka faced fragmented opposition.

2. The disciplined leadership. Sardar Patel had organisational experience from Kheda 1918. Bardoli's tax-refusal was prepared with meticulous record-keeping — every peasant's compliance with non-payment was tracked. The British faced a unified front, not a fragmented agitation.

3. The outcome — the technical win. The Maxwell-Broomfield Inquiry Committee reduced the increase from 30% to 6.03% — a clear quantitative victory that legitimised both Patel's leadership & the Satyagraha method. The women of Bardoli conferred the title "Sardar" on Patel. K.M. Munshi & Lalji Nayak resigned from the Bombay Legislative Council in solidarity.

Closing verdict: Bardoli succeeded because the grievance was technically clean, the leadership was disciplined, the demand was specific, & the negotiation channel stayed open. The pattern became a template — same model used in the 1930-32 Civil Disobedience peasant mobilisations.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: Who among the following organised the famous Chittagong armoury raid?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Context While Gandhiji was leading the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM 1930–34), revolutionaries in East Bengal began their own armed struggle under Surya Sen, a school teacher.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Laxmi Sehgal commanded the INA's Rani of Jhansi Regiment in the 1940s — a different decade and theatre from the 1930 Chittagong raid.
(C) ✗ — Batukeshwar Datta was Bhagat Singh's partner in the 1929 Central Legislative Assembly bomb — not the Chittagong organiser.
(D) ✗ — J.M. Sengupta was a Bengal Congress leader of the constitutional stream; the raid was organised by Surya Sen, the schoolteacher chief of the Chittagong group.
(Note: Surya Sen who was the chief of Chittagong Republican Army organised an armoury raid in Chittagong on 18th April, 1930.)

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Which Act had been used by the British during World War I to crack down on revolutionaries, with mass releases of those jailed under it taking place only after the amnesty of 1920?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) Rowlatt Act came in 1919, not the wartime crackdown instrument named in. (c) Indian Press Act 1910 targeted publications, not the wartime detention of revolutionaries cited here. (d) Criminal Law Amendment Act 1908 pre-dated the war and is not the Act named in.
Memory hook: DIA 1915 jailed them; 1920 amnesty freed them; NCM 1920–22 absorbed them.

explanation: Why others wrong: (a) Ram Prasad Bismil was hanged in the Kakori case but does not link him to the 1912 Delhi Conspiracy or to Bandi Jeevan. (b) Ashfaqullah Khan was hanged in Kakori but is not linked to Bandi Jeevan. (d) Jogesh Chatterjee was an HRA founder but the Bandi Jeevan authorship is attributed only to Sachin Sanyal.

questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) Omits the correct renaming-with-"Socialist" point in. (b) Omits the explicit goal in. (c) Omits Azad's founding-member status listed in.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Bhagwati Charan Vohra, a key member of HSRA 1928, died on 28 May 1930 in which of the following ways?

options.text: Hanged after the Lahore Conspiracy trial
Shot himself to avoid capture at Alfred Park, Allahabad
Killed while testing a bomb near the River Ravi, Lahore
Died of forced feeding during a jail hunger strike

explanation: Why others wrong: (a) The Lahore trial hangings on 23 March 1931 were of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, and Rajguru, not Vohra. (b) The Alfred Park self-shooting on 27 February 1931 was Chandrashekhar Azad. (d) Death by forced feeding during a hunger strike was Jatin Das on the 64th day.
Memory hook: Vohra at Ravi — bomb test, May 1930; "Philosophy of Bomb" outlived him.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Which one of the following events directly motivated Bhagat Singh to plan the action that culminated in the killing of John Saunders, DSP, in the Lahore Conspiracy Case?

options.text: The withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement after Chauri Chaura
The lathi-charge that killed Lala Lajpat Rai at anti-Simon Commission protests in November 1928
The execution of Ram Prasad Bismil and Ashfaqullah Khan in the Kakori case
The discussion of the Public Safety Bill in the Central Legislative Assembly

explanation: Why others wrong: (a) The 1922 withdrawal is the backdrop to the revival of revolutionary activity, not the Saunders trigger. (c) Kakori hangings ended HRA but the Saunders action was specifically to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai. (d) The Public Safety Bill triggered the CLA bomb of 1929, not the Saunders killing.
Memory hook: Sher-e-Punjab fell to lathi → Saunders fell to bullet (mistaken for Scott).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the 1929 bomb thrown in the Central Legislative Assembly by Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt:
items: 1. The bills under discussion that day were the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Disputes Bill.
2. The bomb was intended to kill assembly members opposed to the working-class cause.
3. Bhagat Singh deliberately courted arrest in order to use the trial as a platform for nationalist propaganda.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) states the bomb was harmless and "the intention was not to kill anyone but to draw attention" — Statement 2 is false. (b) Omits the correctly-named bills in Statement 1. (c) Includes the false Statement 2.
Memory hook: Harmless bomb + leaflets "to make the deaf hear" — courtroom became the stage.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Arrange the following events of the revolutionary movement in correct chronological order:

explanation: Why others wrong: (b) Reverses the order of Azad's death (27 February 1931) and the Lahore trial hangings (23 March 1931). (c) Places the 1929 CLA bomb before the 1925 Kakori Robbery, which inverts and. (d) Places Azad's 1931 death before the 1929 CLA bomb, which inverts and.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: The revolutionaries of 1924-31 were not simply continuators of the 1907-15 wave but represented a distinct ideological generation. Examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" + "distinct ideological generation" demands a process-oriented contrast. The body must show what was new in the 1920s wave that the 1907-15 wave lacked.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The 1907-15 wave (Aurobindo, Anushilan, Yugantar) was rooted in religious-spiritual nationalism. The 1924-31 wave (HRA → HSRA) replaced that anchor with socialist analysis of class & State.
Body guidance — 4 themes (see 'Why Did Revolutionary Activities Revive after 1922?' and 'Hindustan Socialist Republican Army / Association (HSRA 1928)' and 'Ideology of Bhagat Singh and HSRA1928'):

1. Generational shift. The 1924-31 wave was younger, educated post-1917 (post-Russian-Revolution era), & disillusioned by Gandhi's withdrawal of NCM after Chauri Chaura. The 1907-15 wave had pre-Russian-Revolution intellectual tools only.

2. Ideological substitution. The 1907-15 wave used religious-cultural nationalism (Aurobindo's Bhawani Mandir, Anushilan's worship-and-violence model). The 1924-31 wave replaced religion with class analysis — Bhagat Singh's Why I Am An Atheist is the formal statement.

3. HRA → HSRA — the structural rename. Adding 'Socialist' was not cosmetic. 'Hindustan Socialist Republican Army / Association (HSRA 1928)' anchors the September 1928 Feroz Shah Kotla meeting where Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev & Azad explicitly tied independence to anti-class-exploitation goals.

4. The CLA Bomb as theatre, not assassination. '1929 Bomb in CLA by Bhagat Singh & B.K. Dutt' anchors the deliberate choice — empty assembly zone, court arrest, use the trial as platform. The 1907-15 wave assassinated to remove individuals; the 1928-29 wave used arrest to broadcast ideology.

Closing verdict: The post-1922 wave shared the older wave's commitment to armed struggle but rebuilt its ideological foundation. Religion-anchored individual heroism became class-anchored systematic struggle. Bhagat Singh's hanging in 1931 made this synthesis a permanent feature of Indian political memory.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Examine the significance of the Chittagong Armory Raid (1930-33) for the revolutionary tradition in India.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine the significance" demands more than a narrative — show what Chittagong added to the revolutionary repertoire that earlier episodes had not.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Chittagong Armory Raid was the most ambitious revolutionary action in Indian colonial history — an attempt not just to assassinate but to capture territory & declare a republic.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'Chittagong Armory Raid 1930–33'):

1. The scale of ambition. Unlike Kakori (a robbery) or the CLA bomb (a courtroom-theatre device), Chittagong attempted to seize the British armory, cut telegraph & rail lines, & declare a temporary Indian Republic. This was a republican insurrection model, not a sabotage operation.

2. Women in the revolutionary front. Pritilata Waddedar led the Pahartali European Club raid in 1932 & died by cyanide rather than be captured. Kalpana Datta was also part of the inner group. The Chittagong wave normalised women in armed revolutionary leadership.

3. The leadership profile. Surya Sen was a schoolteacher; his group included students & teenagers. The action proved that organised revolutionary insurrection could be planned by ordinary local cadres without national-level political networks. Sen was hanged in January 1934.

Closing verdict: Chittagong extended the revolutionary repertoire from sabotage to insurrection, from male-only to mixed-gender, & from elite networks to local cadres. The model remained unique in Indian history — no other revolutionary attempt approached its territorial ambition.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: The radical wing of the Congress Party with Jawaharlal Nehru as its one of its main leaders, founded the Independence for India League in opposition to
explanation: (C) ✓ — The result was the Nehru Report of August 1928 — the first Indian attempt at a constitutional blueprint.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — A timeline check rules this out: the League was formed in 1928 against the Nehru Report's Dominion Status goal, while the Gandhi-Irwin Pact came only in March 1931. A body founded in 1928 could not be opposing a pact that did not yet exist.
(B) ✗ — The Home Rule Movement belongs to 1916–18 — it had ended a decade before the League was formed in 1928. The radicals' target was the Nehru Report's Dominion Status demand, not Home Rule.

(D) ✗ — The Mont-Ford reforms (GOI Act 1919) were what the Simon Commission had come to review. Nehru and Bose formed the League against the Nehru Report's acceptance of Dominion Status — they wanted complete independence — not against the 1919 reforms.
(Note: The Independence of Indian League was formed with Jawahar Lal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose who opposed 1928 Nehru Repot as they wanted complete Independence.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: Simon Commission of 1927 was boycotted because

options.text: there was no Indian member in the Commission
Congress felt that the people of India are entitled to Swaraj
there were differences among the members

explanation: (A) ✓ — Not a single Indian was included among its 7 members. INC opposed the Commission precisely on this ground — that the principle of self-government promised in the Montague Statement of 1917 was being violated, as Indians were not given any say in their own future constitution.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — The Commission had no Muslim League link — all 7 members were British MPs. The boycott ground was the exclusion of Indians as a whole, not a tilt towards any one Indian party.

(C) ✗ — A near-miss option: INC invoked the self-government promise of the Montague Statement as the reason why exclusion was insulting. The boycott trigger was the all-British composition — entitlement to Swaraj by itself was not the stated reason.

(D) ✗ — There were no differences among the members — the 7 British MPs worked as one team under Sir John Simon. The objection came from the Indian side, over Indian exclusion, not from any split inside the Commission.

(Note: Simon Commission was a group of seven British members of Parliament under the chairmanship of Sir John Simon assisted by Clement Atlee. Its objective was to report on India's constitutional progress.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: With reference to Simon Commission's recommendations, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: It recommended the replacement of diarchy with responsible government in the provinces
It proposed the setting up of inter-provincial council under the Home Department
It suggested the abolition of bicameral legislature at the centre
It recommended the creation of Indian Police Service with a provision for increased pay and allowances for British recruits as compared to Indian recruits

explanation: (A) ✓ — Per the ⚠ Alert in Chapter: Prelims 2010 (Simon Commission's key recommendation = abolition of Dyarchy at provincial level). Ending provincial Dyarchy meant replacing it with responsible government in the provinces — exactly what this option states.
Wrong options:

(B) ✗ — No inter-provincial council under the Home Department appears among the Commission's recorded recommendations; the record links the Simon Commission to one key recommendation — ending provincial Dyarchy.

(C) ✗ — Reversed logic: a bicameral legislature at the Centre was what the Indians' own Nehru Report proposed — a 7-year term for the upper house & a 5-year term for the lower house. The Simon Commission's recorded recommendation concerned provincial Dyarchy, not scrapping bicameralism.
(D) ✗ — The Commission's task was reviewing the constitutional reforms of the GOI Act 1919; police service pay scales were not its subject, and no such discriminatory-pay recommendation is on record.

(Note: In March 1944, Mr C Rajagopalachari evolved a formula with the 'Full' approval of Gandhiji for the Congress. The scheme embodying the formula was (i) The league would endorse the demand for independence.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: With reference to the period of Indian freedom struggle, which of the following was/were recommended by the 'Nehru Report'?
items: 1. Complete Independence for India.
2. Joint electorates for reservation of seats for minorities.
3. Provision of Fundamental Rights for the people of India in the Constitution.
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below
explanation: (B) ✓ — The Report asked for Dominion Status — the maximum level of self-government possible without leaving the British Empire — not complete independence, so statement 1 falls. Statements 2 and 3 are both recorded: "No separate electorates" with reservation for Muslims in Muslim minority Provinces & at the Centre (= joint electorates with reserved seats), and "19 Fundamental Rights". Hence 2 and 3 only.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Statement 1 is the one demand the Report did not make: it stopped at Dominion Status, and even Bose's Purna Swaraj resolution against it failed at the Calcutta session.

(C) ✗ — Includes statement 1, which fails because the Report demanded Dominion Status, not complete independence; and it wrongly drops statement 2 — joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities are a recorded communal provision of the Report.
(D) ✗ — Fails on statement 1 alone: complete independence became INC's goal only later as Purna Swaraj; the Nehru Report itself asked for Dominion Status under the British Crown.

(Note: The Nehru Report in August, 1928 was a memorandum outlining a proposed new dominion status Constitution for India. It was prepared by a committee of the all parties conference chaired by Motilal Nehru.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: The people of India agitated against the arrival of Simon Commission because

options.text: Indians never wanted the review of the working of the Act of 1919
Simon Commission recommended the abolition of Dyarchy (Diarchy) in the Provinces
there was no Indian member in the Simon Commission
the Simon Commission suggested the partition of the country

explanation: (C) ✓ — Not a single Indian was included among its 7 members. INC opposed the Commission precisely on this ground — that the principle of self-government promised in the Montague Statement of 1917 was being violated.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — The opposite of the recorded position: the 10-year review was built into the GOI Act 1919 itself, as the path to the gradual Swaraj promise. Indians wanted the review — what they rejected was a review body with no Indian in it.

(B) ✗ — Two-step elimination: ending provincial Dyarchy meant moving toward responsible government — a gain for Indians, so no reason to agitate against it; and the agitation greeted the Commission's arrival, before it had recommended anything.

(D) ✗ — The Commission's object was reviewing the constitutional reforms of the GOI Act 1919; no partition scheme is recorded anywhere — even Jinnah's 14 Points of 1929 contained every divisive demand — except the demand for Pakistan, which came later.

(Note: The Indian Statutory Commission also known as the Simon Commission was sent to India in 1927 to study the Constitutional reforms in India, mainly to study the working of the Government of India Act, 1919.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: The object of the Butler Committee of 1927 was to

options.text: Define the jurisdiction of the Central and Provincial governments.
Define the powers of the Secretary of State for India.
Improve the relationship between the Government of India and the Indian States.

explanation: (D) ✓ — The Butler Committee was appointed in 1927 to examine & clarify the relationship between the British Crown & the Princely States. Clarifying — and thereby improving — the government's relationship with the Indian States was exactly its object.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Centre–Province division of powers was the battlefield of the Nehru Report and ML1906's demands (residuary powers), not the Butler Committee's brief, which ran between the Crown and the Princely States.
(B) ✗ — Defining the Secretary of State's powers was no part of the Committee's recorded mandate; its subject was Paramountcy over the Princely States.

(C) ✗ — Nothing in the Committee's mandate or its 1929 Report touches the press: its two findings were the re-affirmation of British Paramountcy and the consent condition for Princely States joining a Union of India.
(Note: A three-member committee headed by Harcourt Butler, appointed on 16th December, 1927 to examine the relationship between the native states and the paramount power.)

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: The Nehru Report (1928) represented the high-water mark of Hindu-Muslim constitutional consensus before partition. Examine why it ultimately failed.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine why it ultimately failed" demands a structural-causes analysis. Body must trace from initial unanimity to collapse.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Nehru Report (August 1928) was the first all-Indian draft constitution. By March 1929 — when Jinnah issued his 14 Points — the consensus had collapsed entirely.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'Nehru Report (August 1928)'):

1. The Report's promise (see 'Nehru Report (August 1928)'). Drafted by Motilal Nehru with Sapru, Shuaib Qureshi, Ali Imam — included a Bill of Fundamental Rights (first ever in Indian constitutional thought), Dominion Status, joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities. Initial All Parties Conference welcomed it.

2. The Calcutta breakdown (see 'Three Calcutta Amendments (December 1928) by ML1906'). Muslim League's Three Calcutta Amendments (December 1928) demanded: weighted Muslim representation in Punjab & Bengal, 1/3rd Muslim seats in the Central Legislature, residuary powers to provinces. INC rejected these as exceeding what joint electorates could accommodate. The unanimity broke at this December 1928 moment.

3. Jinnah's 14 Points (see 'Jinnah's 14 Points Demand (March 1929)') — the formal rupture. March 1929: Jinnah codified the ML position into 14 demands — every one of them constitutional safeguards that the Nehru Report's framework could not accommodate. From this point, INC & ML moved on separate tracks.

Closing verdict: The Nehru Report failed because it tried to resolve the communal question through one constitutional formula — joint electorates with reserved seats — which the ML viewed as numerically inadequate protection. The unresolved arithmetic of representation drove the 1930s-40s Two-Nation theory & the eventual Pakistan demand.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Examine why the Diwali Declaration (October 1929) — Irwin's promise of Dominion Status as India's natural goal — failed to satisfy the INC despite its apparent generosity.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine why it failed despite generosity" demands tracing the British-side reception & the consequent Indian re-evaluation.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Irwin's October 1929 Diwali Declaration appeared to deliver what the INC had asked for — Dominion Status & a Round Table Conference. By December 1929, the INC had moved past it to Purna Swaraj.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'Diwali Declaration / Irwin Statement (31 October 1929)'):

1. The Declaration's content (see 'Diwali Declaration / Irwin Statement (31 October 1929)'). Viceroy Irwin announced that Dominion Status was the "natural issue" of India's constitutional progress & called a Round Table Conference. Form: a generous Crown commitment.

2. The London reaction (see 'Diwali Declaration / Irwin Statement (31 October 1929)'). The Conservative opposition in London & sections of the British press reacted hostilely. Irwin was forced to clarify that "natural issue" was not "immediate goal" — & that no timeline was being committed. The substance was diluted in days.

3. The Delhi Manifesto + INC re-evaluation (see 'Delhi Manifesto (November 1929)'). INC's Delhi Manifesto conditionally welcomed the Declaration: prisoners released + RTC to draft Dominion Status constitution. Both conditions unmet. The INC concluded that Britain was unable to deliver Dominion Status even when willing — which is why Lahore Session (December 1929) shifted the goal to Purna Swaraj. The Diwali Declaration's failure was the immediate trigger.

Closing verdict: The Diwali Declaration showed that even a sincere British offer was constrained by British domestic politics. The INC's response — moving from Dominion Status to Purna Swaraj — was the rational conclusion that no British government could deliver what they could promise.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: In 1930, Mahatma Gandhi started Civil Disobedience Movement from
explanation: (C) ✓ — The Dandi March began in March 1930 — MG marched from the Sabarmati Ashram (set up in 1917) to the Dandi coast to break the salt law. The starting point of CDM was the Sabarmati Ashram.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The march set out from Sabarmati. Sevagram plays no role in the CDM launch.
(B) ✗ — Dandi was the destination, not the start: MG marched from the Sabarmati Ashram to the Dandi coast, where the salt law was broken. The stem asks where the movement started from.
(D) ✗ — Wardha does not figure in the CDM launch route on record — the march ran from Sabarmati to Dandi.
(Note: Mahatma Gandhi's Dandi March was significant in terms of breaking the salt law and beginning of Civil Disobedience movement in 1930.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: The meeting of Indian and British political leaders during 1930-32 in London has often been referred to as the first, second and third round table conferences. It would be incorrect to refer to them as such because

options.text: the Indian National Congress did not take part in two of them
parties other than the Indian National Congress participating in the conference represented several interests and not the whole of India
the British Labour Party and withdrawn from the conference thereby making the proceeding of the conference partisan
it was an instance of a conference held in three session and not that of three separate conference

explanation: (D) ✓ — The London meetings were, in effect, one continuing exercise. INC rejected the RTC (three RTCs were held — in 1930, 1931, and 1932). It was one conference held in three sessions — not three separate conferences — which is why the 'first/second/third' naming is strictly incorrect.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — A true fact, but the wrong reason: INC did skip the 1st RTC and the 3rd RTC — yet who attended does not change whether the meetings were one conference or three. The naming flaw lies in the session structure, option (d).

(B) ✗ — Also broadly true — the non-INC delegates spoke for sectional interests (the minorities at the 2nd RTC each pressed their own electorate demands) — but representativeness is not what makes the 'three conferences' label incorrect; the session structure is.
(C) ✗ — No Labour withdrawal is recorded — Labour PM Ramsay MacDonald stayed engaged throughout, even announcing the Communal Award in August 1932.
(Note: It was a conference held in three sessions and not of three separate conferences. It was based only on Simon Commission Report and further course of action.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: The Poona Pact which was signed between the British Government and Mahatma Gandhi in 1934 provided for

options.text: the creation of dominion status for India
joint electorate with reservation of Harijans

explanation: (D) ✓ — Separate electorates were removed, but as compensation, the number of reserved seats was more than doubled. The Depressed Classes would contest in joint electorates with reserved seats — exactly what this option states.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — The Poona Pact dealt with how the Depressed Classes would be represented; dominion status was a constitutional-goal question fought over the Nehru Report and at the RTCs, not a Pact provision.

(B) ✗ — Muslims already had separate electorates — Other minorities had already had separate electorates since the GOI Act 1919; the Pact was about the Depressed Classes and did not touch Muslim electorates.

(C) ✗ — The trap option: separate electorates for the Depressed Classes were the Communal Award's method, which the Pact rejected — replacing it with joint electorates plus enlarged reservation (71 to 147 seats). Picking (c) reverses what the Pact did.
(Note: Poona Pact was signed between Dr B.R. Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi in 1934 giving separate electorates to Dalit for electing members of State Legislative Assemblies in British India.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: During the Indian freedom struggle, the Khudai Khidmatgars, also known as Red Shirts called for

options.text: the Union of Pashtun tribal areas in North-West with the Afghanistan
the adoption of terrorist tactics and methods for terrorising and finally ousting the colonial rulers
the adoption of communist revolution ideology for political and social reform
the Pathan regional nationalist unity and a struggle against colonialism

explanation: (D) ✓ — Ghaffar Khan integrated the traditional Pashtun code of honour (Pukhtunwali) with Gandhian non-violence — Pathan regional nationalist unity — and his Khudai Khidmatgars made NWFP "one of the most remarkable chapters of CDM", i.e. a struggle against colonialism.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — No Afghanistan-union demand is recorded: the Khudai Khidmatgars worked within India's CDM; 'Fakhr-e-Afghan' was an honorific title of Ghaffar Khan, not a political programme.
(B) ✗ — The exact opposite: volunteers "took a solemn oath to forgive their oppressors" and faced bullets unarmed at the Qissa Khwani Bazaar — non-violence framed as "the ultimate test of bravery".
(C) ✗ — The recorded ideological fusion was Pukhtunwali plus Gandhian non-violence, not communism — indeed CPI1925 boycotted CDM altogether.

(Note: During freedom struggle, the Khudai Khidmatgar also called Red Shirts movements was organised by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan also called 'Frontier Gandhi'. He called for Pathan regional nationalist unity.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.stem: With reference to colonial period of Indian history, match List I (Person) with List II (Event) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists.
explanation: (A) ✓ — Pair-by-pair: Macdonald → Communal Award; Linlithgow → August Offer; Dalhousie → Doctrine of Lapse; Chelmsford → Dyarchy. That gives A-2 B-3 C-1 D-4.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Fails at C-4: Dalhousie's instrument was the Doctrine of Lapse, not Dyarchy — Dyarchy came with the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms of 1919.
(C) ✗ — Fails at A-3: the August Offer (1940) was Linlithgow's, not Macdonald's; Macdonald's name attaches to the Communal Award.
(D) ✗ — Identical code to option (b) and fails the same way: Dalhousie → Doctrine of Lapse, Chelmsford → Dyarchy — the C and D pairings are swapped.
(Note: The Constituent Assembly of India was elected by the Provincial Assemblies in the year 1946 is correct.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.stem: With reference to Indian freedom struggle, which one of the following statements is not correct?

options.text: The Rowlatt Act aroused a wave of popular indignation and led to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
Subhash Chandra Bose formed the forward Block
Bhagat Singh was one of the founders of Hindustan Republican Socialist Association
In 1931, the Congress Session at Karachi opposed Gandhi-Irwin Pact

explanation: (D) ✓ — Statement (d) is the false one: the Karachi Session did not oppose the Pact — "INC approved the Gandhi-Irwin26-31 Pact." The protest at Karachi was the black flags of Bose's supporters over Bhagat Singh's execution — not a rejection of the Pact.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — A correct statement, so not the answer: the Rowlatt Act provoked the Satyagraha of April 1919, in whose course the Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on 13 April 1919.
(B) ✗ — Also correct: after the Tripuri crisis, Bose resigned and formed the Forward Bloc in 1939. A true statement cannot be the 'not correct' pick.
(C) ✗ — Correct in substance: Bhagat Singh was among the founders of the HSRA in 1928 — the option only jumbles the word order of the organisation's name.

(Note: In 1931, the Congress Session of Karachi which was presided by Vallabhbhai Patel, passed Gandhi-Irwin pact unopposed. The Gandhi-Irwin pact was passed unopposed by the congress in its annual session of Karachi.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.stem: At which Congress Session was the working committee authorised to launch a programme of civil disobedience?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The AICC (set up by the Nagpur Session of 1920) was empowered to launch the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) at an appropriate time. The authorisation to launch civil disobedience came from the Lahore Session.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Bombay's landmark session belongs to 1942 — the Quit India Resolution; the CDM authorisation is recorded at Lahore.
(C) ✗ — Lucknow's recorded landmark is the 1916 INC-ML pact (the Lucknow Pact, LP1916); it had no role in authorising civil disobedience.
(D) ✗ — The Tripuri Session (1939) is remembered for the Bose-Gandhi presidential clash, a decade after the CDM mandate given at Lahore.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.11
questions.stem: Who among the following drafted the resolution on Fundamental Rights for the Karachi Session of Congress in 1931?
explanation: (B) ✓ — The Karachi Session passed resolutions on Fundamental Rights (FRs) and a National Economic Programme the Fundamental Rights resolution was drafted by Jawaharlal Nehru.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Ambedkar's recorded 1931 role was representing the Depressed Classes at the 2nd RTC — he was not drafting INC's Karachi resolutions.
(C) ✗ — Rajendra Prasad has no recorded role at Karachi; the drafting credit recorded for the session is Jawaharlal Nehru's.
(D) ✗ — The classic trap: Sardar Patel presided over the Karachi Session — but presiding is not drafting; the resolution was drafted by Jawaharlal Nehru.
(Note: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel presided, the congress session of 1931 but Jawaharlal Nehru drafted the resolution on Fundamental Rights for the Karachi Session of Congress.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.12
questions.stem: Under whose presidency was the Lahore Session of the Indian Congress held in the year 1929, wherein a resolution was adopted to gain complete independence from the British?
explanation: (C) ✓ — The response came at the INC Lahore Session of December 1929, with Jawaharlal Nehru as President. It was under his presidency that the Purna Swaraj resolution was adopted.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Tilak had died in August 1920 — nine years before the Lahore Session of December 1929.

(B) ✗ — Gokhale belonged to the Moderate generation, whose era closed before Gandhian mass politics — his last recorded appearance in these chapters is the 1912 visit to MG in South Africa. The Lahore chair was Jawaharlal Nehru.
(D) ✗ — The father-son trap: Motilal Nehru chaired the committee that produced the Nehru Report of 1928; the Lahore President of December 1929 was his son Jawaharlal.

(Note: The Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress held in the year 1929, under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru, wherein a resolution was adopted to gain complete independence from the British.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.13
questions.stem: Which one of the following began with the Dandi March?
explanation: (C) ✓ — The Dandi March began in March 1930 — MG marched from the Sabarmati Ashram (set up in 1917) to the Dandi coast to break the salt law. The salt march was the opening act of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The Home Rule Movement (1916–18) was launched through the Leagues of Tilak and Besant — over a decade before Dandi.
(B) ✗ — The Non-Cooperation Movement began in 1920 (NCM 1920–22); its launch had nothing to do with the salt law — Dandi belongs to 1930.
(D) ✗ — The Quit India Movement came twelve years later, in August 1942; the Dandi March of March 1930 opened CDM.
(Note: The refusal of the British Government to accept the Congress plan plunged the nation into countrywide Civil Disobedience Movement.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.14
questions.stem: For the Karachi Session of Indian National Congress in 1931 presided over by Sardar Patel, who drafted the Resolution on Fundamental Rights and Economic Programme?
explanation: (B) ✓ — INC passed resolutions on Fundamental Rights (FRs) and a National Economic Programme influenced by socialist principles. The drafter: Jawaharlal Nehru — with Patel presiding.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — MG's recorded Karachi role was getting the Gandhi-Irwin Pact approved — the Fundamental Rights and Economic Programme resolution is credited to Jawaharlal Nehru.
(C) ✗ — No drafting role at Karachi is recorded for Rajendra Prasad; the record credit goes to Jawaharlal Nehru.
(D) ✗ — Ambedkar in 1931 was pressing the Depressed Classes' case at the 2nd RTC — he was not drafting INC's Karachi resolution.
(Note: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel presided over the Karachi Session of Indian National Congress in 1931. The following resolutions were adopted by the session.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.15
questions.stem: The Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress (1929) is very important in history, because
items: 1. the Congress passed a resolution demanding complete independence.
2. the rift between the extremists and moderates was resolved in that session.
3. a resolution was passed rejecting the Two- Nation Theory in that session.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Statement 1 is exactly the Lahore landmark: The goal of INC was now Purna Swaraj — not dominion status, but complete independence. Statements 2 and 3 appear nowhere among the five recorded Lahore decisions — no moderate-extremist patch-up, no Two-Nation-Theory resolution. Hence only 1.
Wrong options:

(B) ✗ — Selects the two statements with no basis: the five Lahore decisions cover Purna Swaraj, Independence Day, RTC rejection, withdrawal from legislatures, and the CDM mandate — neither a moderate-extremist reconciliation nor a Two-Nation-Theory rejection figures among them.
(C) ✗ — Statement 1 stands, but statement 3 fails — no Two-Nation-Theory resolution appears among the Lahore decisions.
(D) ✗ — Overshoots: statement 1 is precisely the Lahore landmark — Purna Swaraj adopted as INC's goal.

(Note: The Annual Session of INC held at Lahore in December, 1929, under the presidentship of Jawaharlal Nehru, passed a resolution declaring 'Poorna Swaraj' (complete independence) be the goal of the Indian National Congress.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.16
questions.stem: Mahatma Gandhi undertook Fast Unto Death in 1932, mainly because

options.text: Round Table Conference failed to satisfy Indian political aspirations
Congress and Muslim League had differences of opinion
Ramsay MacDonald announced the communal award
None of the statements (a), (b) and (c) given above is correct in this context

explanation: (C) ✓ — The Communal Award was announced by British PM Ramsay MacDonald because Indians could not reach consensus on joint electorates. completes the link: MG undertook a 21-day fast unto death against the Communal Award — fearing separate electorates would permanently divide Hindus.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — The 2nd RTC's failure (deadlock over separate electorates) led to the resumption of CDM — not to the fast. The fast's recorded target was the Communal Award's separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.
(B) ✗ — INC-ML differences belong to the run-up of CDM; the 1932 fast's recorded target was the Communal Award, not League politics.
(D) ✗ — Fails because option (c) is exactly the record account: MacDonald announced the Award and MG fasted unto death against it.

(Note: Ramsay MacDonald announced the communal award on 17th August, 1932, reserving the seats for 'Depressed Classes' i.e similar to separate electorate provided to Muslim. Gandhiji was deeply, grieved by the Communal Award.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.17
questions.stem: The 1929 Session of Indian National Congress is of significance in the history of the Freedom Movement because the

options.text: attainment of self-government was declared as the objective of the Congress
attainment of Poorna Swaraj was adopted as the goal of the Congress
decision to participate in the Round Table Conference in London was taken

explanation: (B) ✓ — The goal of INC was now Purna Swaraj — not dominion status, but complete independence. Adopting Poorna Swaraj as the goal is what makes the 1929 session historic.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Understates 1929: self-government (dominion status) was the earlier position — Lahore's whole point was moving beyond it: "not dominion status, but complete independence".
(C) ✗ — The Non-Cooperation Movement had been launched back in 1920 (NCM 1920–22); what Lahore authorised was the future CDM.
(D) ✗ — The reverse happened: INC rejected the RTC... and therefore did not participate in the 1st RTC of 1930. Participation came only later, under the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.

(Note: The 1929 Lahore Session under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru holds a special significance as in this session 'Poorna Swaraj' (complete independence) was declared as the goal of the Indian National Congress.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.18
questions.stem: Who among the following organised a march on the Tanjore coast to break the Salt Law in April, 1930?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Rajagopalachari marched from Tiruchirappalli to Vedaranniyam with a handpicked group of 98 volunteers — selected from over a thousand applicants and trained to endure police brutality without retaliating.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — V.O. Chidambaram Pillai's fame belongs to the Swadeshi era — the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company, 1906; the 1930 Tanjore-coast march was Rajaji's.
(C) ✗ — The record account of the Tamil salt campaign names C. Rajagopalachari and his 98 hand-picked volunteers; Kamaraj has no recorded role in it.
(D) ✗ — Besant's recorded landmarks are the Home Rule League and the first woman INC Presidency of 1917; she led no salt march.

(Note: Spread of Salt Disobedience once the way was cleared by Gandhi's ritual at Dandi, defiance of the salt laws started all over the country. In Tamil Nadu (Tanjore Coast), C. Rajagopalachari led a march to Vedaranyam.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.19
questions.stem: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact included which of the following?
items: 1. Invitation to Congress to participate in the Round Table Conference.
2. Withdrawal of Ordinances promulgated in connection with the Civil Disobedience Movement.
3. Acceptance of Gandhiji's suggestion for enquiry into police excesses.
4. Release of only those prisoners who were not charged with violence.
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the code given below:
explanation: (B) ✓ — The recorded features include: "INC to participate in the 2nd RTC (1931)" (statement 1), "Withdrawal of emergency ordinances" (statement 2), and "Release of political prisoners not charged with violence" (statement 4). No acceptance of an enquiry into police excesses appears among the features — statement 3 falls. Hence 1, 2 and 4.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Undercounts: release of prisoners not charged with violence is also a recorded feature, so statement 4 must be included.
(C) ✗ — Picks the lone unsupported statement: the Pact's recorded features contain no acceptance of an enquiry into police excesses.
(D) ✗ — Includes statement 3, which is absent from the Pact's recorded features, and drops statement 1 — RTC participation — which is feature 12.2.
(Note: The 'Gandhi - Irwin Pact' was an agreement signed by Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin( Viceroy of India) on 5th March, 1931 before the second Round Table Conference in London.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.20
questions.stem: “Sedition has become my religion” was the famous statement given by Gandhiji at the time of:

options.text: Publicly violating Salt Law at Dandi

explanation: (B) ✓ — "Sedition has become my religion" is Gandhiji's famous CDM-era statement — made in the course of the Salt Satyagraha, when he publicly broke the salt law at Dandi.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Champaran (1917) was MG's first civil disobedience, against the indigo planters — it predates the CDM-era statement by thirteen years.
(C) ✗ — The 2nd RTC was a negotiation in London — no law was being broken there; the statement belongs to the Salt-law defiance.
(D) ✗ — Quit India came in 1942; the Alert ties the statement to the CDM era — the Dandi defiance of 1930.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.21
questions.stem: Subsequent to which event did Gandhiji decided to include the upliftment of ‘Harijans’ in his programme?
explanation: (A) ✓ — after the September 1932 fast and the Poona Pact, MG's primary focus in the 2nd phase shifted decisively to an anti-untouchability campaign — Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932), Harijan Sevak Fund (1932), Harijan Magazine (1933). Gandhiji included upliftment of Harijans after the Poona Pact.
Wrong options:

(B) ✗ — The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) was a truce that sent INC to the 2nd RTC; the Harijan programme's organisational start is dated after the 1932 fast and Poona Pact — all three Harijan bodies were founded 1932–33.
(C) ✗ — Quit India belongs to 1942 — a full decade after the Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932) had already been set up.
(D) ✗ — The GOI Act 1935 post-dates the campaign's start: the Harijan bodies date from 1932–33, while the Act's recorded link in this Chapter is the 1937 elections.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: At the INC Lahore Session of December 1929, INC decided that 26 January 1930 would be celebrated as Independence Day. What was the specific reason for choosing that particular date?

options.text: It was the last Sunday of January 1930, a holiday ensuring maximum public participation
It marked the anniversary of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
It was the date on which the Nehru Report had been submitted
It coincided with the date of the Delhi Manifesto of November 1929

explanation: Why others wrong: (b) — Jallianwala Bagh anniversary is 13 April, the date chosen by Rajaji for the Vedaranniyam March, not Independence Day. (c) — Nehru Report was submitted in August 1928; date not linked. (d) — Delhi Manifesto was rejected by Irwin26-31 in November 1929; not connected to 26 January.
Memory hook: Last Sunday of January 1930 — a holiday-by-design date later inherited by Republic Day 1950.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Which one of the following demands was NOT part of MG's 11-Point Demands of January 1930?

options.text: Lower the exchange rate for the Rupee to 1 Rs = 1s 4d
Grant of Dominion Status within one year
Total prohibition on alcohol & other intoxicants
Abolish the salt tax and the Government salt monopoly

explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Listed under Four Middle-Class / Bourgeoisie Issues (Demand 3.1). (c) — Listed under Five General Issues (Demand 3.9). (d) — Listed under Five General Issues (Demand 3.11) — salt tax was 8.2% of Government revenue.
Memory hook: 11 demands defined what Swaraj would mean for masses — Dominion Status was the 1928 Calcutta deadline, not a 1930 demand.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: The Vedaranniyam Salt March of April 1930 was led from Tiruchirappalli to the Tanjore coast by which leader?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Kelappan led the Malabar Salt March from Calicut to Poyannur on the same day, 13 April 1930. (b) — Konda Venkatappaiah directed operations from a Sibiram in Vijayawada (Andhra). (d) — Pattabhi Sitaramayya played a major organising role in Andhra, not Madras.
Memory hook: Rajaji + 98 volunteers, launched 13 April 1930 — Tamil New Year & Jallianwala anniversary in one stroke.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Who became the first woman in India to pay a penalty for violation of the salt laws during CDM?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Sarojini Naidu led the Dharasana Salt Works raid on 21 May 1930, not the salt-law penalty milestone. (b) — Kamaladevi sold contraband salt outside the Bombay Stock Exchange & Bombay High Court. (c) — Rama Devi led massive women's participation at Inchudi (Odisha), the "Second Dandi."
Memory hook: Rukmini Lakshmipathi — first woman penalised under salt laws, marching with Rajaji to Vedaranniyam.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Which leader led the raid on the Dharasana salt works in May 1930 after the arrests of Abbas Tyabji and Kasturbai Gandhi?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Karnad Sadashiv Rao was a key leader at Ankola, Karnataka. (b) — Jamnalal Bajaj organised Vile Parle as movement headquarters in Bombay city. (c) — Bhashani marched from Sylhet to Noakhali in Bengal (Assam leg).
Memory hook: Sarojini Naidu + Manilal + Imam Saheb — 21 May 1930, 2,500 satyagrahis, steel-tipped lathis.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: In which province did the Khudai Khidmatgars, popularly known as the Red Shirts or Surkh Posh, operate as the main volunteer brigade of CDM?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — In Assam, protests erupted against the Cunningham Circular of 1930–31. (c) — Central Provinces saw violation of forest laws under CDM's 2nd-Stage plan. (d) — Sindh was separated from Bombay & given full province status in 1936; not the Khudai Khidmatgar base.
Memory hook: NWFP + Frontier Gandhi + brick-dust uniforms = Khudai Khidmatgars founded 1929.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem: Who was the President of the INC Lahore Session of December 1929, which adopted Purna Swaraj as the goal?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Patel presided over the Karachi Special Session of March 1931, not Lahore 1929. (b) — Malaviya was the designated 1933 Calcutta President but was arrested. (d) — Nellie Sengupta replaced Malaviya as President at the 1933 Calcutta Session.
Memory hook: Lahore 1929 = Nehru in the chair, Purna Swaraj on the floor.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: The Communal Award of August 1932 was announced by which British Prime Minister?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Stanley Baldwin was not associated with the Communal Award. (b) — Chamberlain not associated with the Award. (c) — Churchill not associated with the Award.
Memory hook: MacDonald Award = Communal Award (August 1932) — extended separate electorates to Depressed Classes.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931:
items: 1. Civil Disobedience Movement was suspended.
2. INC agreed to participate in the 2nd Round Table Conference.
3. The British agreed to commute the death sentence of Bhagat Singh.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) — Statement 3 is wrong: the British rejected commutation of Bhagat Singh's death sentence; he was martyred on 23 March 1931. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.
Memory hook: Pact suspended CDM + invited INC to 2nd RTC — but Bhagat Singh was NOT spared.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Poona Pact of September 1932:
items: 1. It was signed between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr B.R. Ambedkar on behalf of the Lower Castes.
2. Madan Mohan Malviya signed on behalf of the Upper Castes.
3. It reduced the reservation for the Depressed Classes from 147 to 71 seats in the PLAs.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a), (c), (d) — Statement 3 is wrong: the Pact INCREASED reservation from 71 to 147 seats in PLAs, plus 18% in the CLA — it did not reduce it. Statements 1 (Ambedkar signed for LC) and 2 (Malviya for UC) are correct.
Memory hook: Poona Pact: separate electorates OUT, reservation seats DOUBLED (71 to 147).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Karachi Special Session of INC of March 1931:
items: 1. The Session approved the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
2. Resolutions on Fundamental Rights and a National Economic Programme were passed.
3. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was the President of the Session.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a), (b), (d) — All three statements are correct. confirms approval of the Pact (13.1), FR + National Economic Programme resolutions (13.2), and the Topic 27 alert under cites Prelims 2010: Karachi 1931 Session President = Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
Memory hook: Karachi 1931 = Patel chair + Pact-ratified + FRs + Economic Programme; black flags for Bhagat Singh's martyrdom.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the 2nd Round Table Conference of September–December 1931:
items: 1. INC participated in the Conference.
2. The Conference produced a White Paper on the reforms.
3. The Depressed Classes were represented by B.R. Ambedkar.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (c) ✓ — Statements 1 and 3 are correct; statement 2 is incorrect. The White Paper (1933) examined by the Joint Parliamentary Committee was produced by the 3rd RTC of November–December 1932, held without INC. The 2nd RTC ended in deadlock over separate electorates.

Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — includes statement 2. The White Paper → JPC → GOI Act 1935 chain belongs to the 3rd RTC, not the 2nd RTC; it also drops correct statement 3 (Ambedkar represented the Depressed Classes). (b) 2 and 3 only — includes the same wrong statement 2 and drops correct statement 1 (INC did participate in the 2nd RTC, following the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931). (d) 1, 2 and 3 — the everything option, but statement 2 is false: the 2nd RTC produced no White Paper; it collapsed over the separate-electorates deadlock.

Memory hook: 2nd RTC (Sep–Dec 1931) = INC's only RTC; deadlock on separate electorates, Ambedkar for the Depressed Classes. The White Paper (1933) → JPC → GOI Act 1935 belongs to the 3rd RTC, which INC never attended.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding MG's 21-day fast unto death of September 1932:
items: 1. It was directed against the Communal Award's grant of separate electorates to the Depressed Classes.
2. MG opposed greater reservation for the Depressed Classes as a matter of principle.
3. The fast was undertaken while MG was imprisoned in Yeravda prison.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) — Statement 2 is wrong: states He was not against greater reservation — he was against the method of separate electorates. Statements 1 and 3 are correct).
Memory hook: MG's quarrel was with the METHOD (separate electorates), not the QUANTUM (reservation).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the CDM 1st Stage (March 1930 – May 1930):
items: 1. The Dandi March began from the Sabarmati Ashram, which had been set up in
2. Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay sold contraband salt outside the Bombay Stock Exchange & the Bombay High Court.
3. Inchudi in Balasore district of Odisha was called the "Bardoli of Karnataka."
questions.stemTail: 1917 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a), (c), (d) — Statement 3 is wrong: Inchudi was called the "Second Dandi"; Ankola in Uttara Kannada earned the title "Bardoli of Karnataka." Statements 1 and 2 are correct from.
Memory hook: Inchudi = "Second Dandi"; Ankola = "Bardoli of Karnataka" — two different titles, two different states.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Khudai Khidmatgars:
items: 1. The brigade was founded by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan in
2. Their uniforms were dyed with cheap brick-dust, giving them the popular name Red Shirts or Surkh Posh.
3. After the firing, the protesters set up a parallel government in Peshawar, forcing the British to impose martial law there.
questions.stemTail: 1929 Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: (a) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are correct; statement 3 is incorrect. It was Sholapur, after MG's arrest in May 1930, where the crowd established a parallel government and forced the British to impose martial law. At Peshawar the Pashtuns eventually erupted in violence, but no parallel government was set up.

Why others wrong: (b) 2 and 3 only — includes the false statement 3 (parallel government + martial law = Sholapur, 11.3, not Peshawar) and drops correct statement 1 (Ghaffar Khan founded the Khudai Khidmatgars in 1929). (c) 1, 2 and 3 — the everything option, but statement 3 misplaces Sholapur's parallel government and martial law onto the Qissa Khwani Bazaar episode. (d) 1 and 3 only — carries the same wrong statement 3 and drops correct statement 2 (brick-dust-dyed uniforms gave the brigade its Red Shirts / Surkh Posh name).

Memory hook: Khudai Khidmatgars = Ghaffar Khan, 1929, brick-dust Red Shirts / Surkh Posh. Peshawar 23 April 1930 = Chandra Singh Garhwali's Royal Garhwal Rifles refuse to fire and are court-martialled; parallel government + martial law = Sholapur, not Peshawar.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_16
questions.stem: Arrange the following events of the Civil Disobedience Movement in chronological order:
items: 1. Dharasana Satyagraha raid on the salt works
2. Beginning of the Dandi March from Sabarmati Ashram
3. Gandhi-Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact)
4. Communal Award announced
explanation: Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) — Correct order is Dandi March (March 1930) → Dharasana raid (21 May 1930) → Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) → Communal Award (August 1932). Option (c) wrongly places the Pact before Dharasana; (b) and (d) wrongly place Dharasana before Dandi.
Memory hook: Dandi → Dharasana → Delhi (Pact) → Donald (MacDonald Award).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_17
questions.stem: Arrange the following Round Table Conferences and related events in chronological order:
items: 1. 1st Round Table Conference
2. 2nd Round Table Conference
3. 3rd Round Table Conference
4. Karachi Special Session of INC
explanation: Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) — Correct order: 1st RTC (1930) → Karachi Session (March 1931) → 2nd RTC (September–December 1931) → 3rd RTC (November–December 1932). Options (b) and (d) wrongly place Karachi before 1st RTC; (c) wrongly places Karachi after 2nd RTC.
Memory hook: 1930 (1st RTC — no INC) → 1931 (Karachi → 2nd RTC with INC) → 1932 (3rd RTC — no INC).

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_18
questions.stem: Arrange the following events of MG's CDM 2nd Phase in chronological order:
items: 1. INC banned by the Government
2. Communal Award announced by Ramsay MacDonald
3. Poona Pact signed
4. CDM formally ended
explanation: Why others wrong: (a), (c), (d) — Correct order: INC banned (January 1932) → Communal Award (August 1932) → Poona Pact (September 1932) → CDM ended (1934). Option (a) and (d) wrongly start with the Communal Award; (c) wrongly places Poona Pact before the Communal Award (the Pact REJECTED the Award, so Pact must follow).
Memory hook: Ban (Jan '32) → Award (Aug '32) → Pact (Sep '32) → End (1934) — twelve months of high drama, two years of decline.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34) differed structurally from the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) in its goal, method & social base. Examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" + "differed structurally" demands a three-axis comparison (goal/method/social base). Body must show what made CDM a distinct mobilisation, not a repeat.

Suggested intro (~25 words): NCM (1920-22) aimed at "Swaraj within the Empire" through withdrawal of cooperation. CDM (1930-34) aimed at Purna Swaraj through active defiance of unjust laws — a different conception of struggle entirely.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. The goal-shift (see 'The INC Lahore Session, December 1929'). NCM accepted Dominion Status as adequate; CDM was anchored to Purna Swaraj after the 1929 Lahore Resolution. The goal moved from "more autonomy within Empire" to "complete independence from Empire".

2. The method-shift (see 'Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM), 1930–34'). NCM was withdrawal-based — boycott institutions, refuse cooperation. CDM was defiance-based — actively break unjust laws (salt, forest, revenue, customs). The Salt March symbolised this shift.

3. The social base-shift (see 'NWFP: The Khudai Khidmatgars and the Qissa Khwani Bazaar Massacre' and 'Implementation: 2nd Stage (May 1930 – March 1931)'). NCM was middle-class led with peasant participation. CDM mobilised broader rural & gender bases — Khudai Khidmatgars in NWFP, peasant Salt-breaking from Tanjore coast to Vedaranyam, large-scale women's participation (Sarojini Naidu at Dharasana, Kasturba Gandhi, Kamla Devi).

4. The structural conclusion — sustained 4 years (see 'CDM 2nd Phase, September 1932–1934'). NCM lasted 2 years & withdrew after Chauri Chaura. CDM sustained 4 years (1930-34) through two phases, surviving Bhagat Singh's hanging & Gandhi's arrests. CDM's longer endurance built deeper INC institutional infrastructure.

Closing verdict: CDM was not NCM-2.0. The Purna Swaraj goal, the defiance method & the broader social base made it the first truly nationwide mass movement aimed at complete independence — a precursor to Quit India 1942.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) was the first formal political compromise between the INC & the British Crown — but it was attacked from within the INC. Examine why.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine why attacked from within" demands tracing the internal INC objections, not the pact's content.
Suggested intro (~25 words): The Gandhi-Irwin Pact ended CDM's 1st phase. Within the INC, it was seen as a strategic surrender — particularly by the Independence-for-India-League wing.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931 (Delhi Pact, 5 March 1931)'):

1. The substance gap (see 'Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931 (Delhi Pact, 5 March 1931)'). The Pact released CDM prisoners but excluded those convicted of violence — meaning Bhagat Singh & Saunders-murder convicts. This was unacceptable to large parts of the Indian public. Gandhi's failure to extract a commutation of Bhagat Singh's death sentence was held against him.

2. The Bhagat Singh execution & Karachi (see 'Karachi Special Session of INC, March 1931'). Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev & Rajguru were hanged 23 March 1931, just 18 days after the Pact. The INC Karachi Session (held just after) passed a resolution condemning the execution — implicitly criticising the Pact's failure to prevent it. Patel's presidency could not fully contain this.

3. The deeper critique (see 'Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931 (Delhi Pact, 5 March 1931)'). The Pact framed the INC as the British Government's bargaining counterpart — acknowledging the INC's representative status. Critics within (Nehru, Bose) feared this legitimised the British framework rather than dismantling it. The 2nd RTC of September 1931 — to which the Pact obligated Gandhi — produced no progress, confirming the critique.

Closing verdict: The Pact was both a tactical win (release of CDM prisoners, salt-tax relief, INC recognition) & a strategic compromise (no movement on Purna Swaraj, Bhagat Singh's execution). Its mixed legacy made it the most-debated Gandhian negotiation of the 1930s.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: Consider the following statements about Jawaharlal Nehru:
items: 1. He was the President of the Congress Party in
2. He presided over the Constituent Assembly.
3. He formed the first Congress Ministry in United Province before India's Independence. Of these statements
explanation: (D) ✓ — All three statements fail: the INC President in 1947 was J.B. Kripalani (Azad held the post till 1946); the Constituent Assembly was presided over by Dr Rajendra Prasad; and the first Congress Ministry in the United Provinces was formed by Govind Ballabh Pant. Nehru held none of the three roles — hence 'none correct'.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Claims all three statements; each one is contradicted by the record — Kripalani (1947 President), Rajendra Prasad (Constituent Assembly chair), Pant (first UP Congress Ministry).
(B) ✗ — Keeps statements 1 and 3, but the 1947 INC President was J.B. Kripalani and the first UP Congress Ministry was Govind Ballabh Pant's — neither role was Nehru's.
(C) ✗ — Keeps statements 1 and 2, but Kripalani was the 1947 President and Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Constituent Assembly.

(Note: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was the President till 1946 and in 1947 J.B Kripiani was President. Dr. Rajendra Prasad presided over Constituent Assembly. Govind Ballabh Panth formed the first Congress ministry.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: Which one of the following first mooted the idea of a constituent assembly to frame a constitution for India?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Among the given options, the Swaraj Party (1934) is correct — it was the first political party to demand a Constituent Assembly (resolution of May 1934). M.N. Roy floated the idea first in 1934, but in his individual capacity; since no individual is among the options, the Swaraj Party is the keyed answer. INC rejected GOI1935 entirely & demanded a Constituent Assembly elected by Universal Adult Franchise.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — INC pressed the Constituent Assembly demand, but the first party to demand it was the Swaraj Party (1934) — 1936 is too late and the wrong party.

(C) ✗ — The Muslim League's recorded posture toward the GOI1935 framework was fear of a Hindu-majority Centre; no Constituent-Assembly proposal of 1942 is credited to it — among the options, the first party to demand a Constituent Assembly was the Swaraj Party (1934).

(D) ✗ — The All Party Conference’s constitutional document was the Nehru Report of August 1928 — “the wish of the All Party Conference” — not a 1946 Constituent-Assembly proposal; among the options, the first party to demand a Constituent Assembly was the Swaraj Party (1934).

(Note: M.N. Roy first floated the Constituent Assembly idea in 1934 in an individual capacity; the Swaraj Party was the first political party to demand it (May 1934) — the answer keyed by the options.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem: While delivering the presidential address, the Congress President who advocated the introduction of Roman script for Hindi language was
explanation: (D) ✓ — While delivering the Presidential address in 1938. Subhash Chandra Bose advocated the introduction of Roman script for Hindi language.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — The advocate recorded above is Bose, in his 1938 presidential address; MG's 1930s role ran through movements — CDM and the Harijan campaign — not the Congress presidency of 1938.
(B) ✗ — Nehru's landmark presidency was the Lahore Session of December 1929; the 1938 chair — and the Roman-script advocacy — was Bose's (he presided at Haripura, 1938).
(C) ✗ — Azad's presidency belongs to the 1940s — he held the post till 1946; the 1938 presidential address advocating Roman script was Bose's.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: Which one of the following in not a feature of the Government of India Act of 1935?

options.text: Diarchy at the Centre as well as in the provinces

explanation: (A) ✓ — Statement (a) is the non-feature: GOI1935 proposed dyarchy at the Centre but abolished it in the provinces — Dyarchy ended. A Council of Ministers headed by a Premier (Chief Minister) was made responsible to the PLA. Dyarchy 'at the Centre as well as in the provinces' was never the 1935 scheme.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — A bicameral legislature IS a recorded feature — the Federal Assembly plus the Council of States — so it cannot be the 'not a feature' pick.
(C) ✗ — Provincial autonomy is the Act's signature working feature: all subjects in provinces became transferred subjects — under PLAs & popular ministers. A real feature cannot be the answer.
(D) ✗ — An All-India Federation of British India and the Princely States was provided for — it never came into operation, but it was very much a feature of the Act.
(Note: Dyarchy was introduced at centre but not in the provinces. Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces through Govt. of India act, 1919 but it was abolished by Government of India Act, 1935.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: Who among the following was the President of the All India States' Peoples' Conference in 1939?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Jawaharlal Nehru: the AISPC — set up in 1927 as the INC-like organisation of the Princely States' people — had Nehru as its President. The Congress-ministries period saw exactly this States' people's movement surge.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Jayaprakash Narayan's recorded platform is the Congress Socialist Party; the AISPC presidency in question is credited to Nehru.
(B) ✗ — No AISPC presidency is recorded for Sheikh Abdullah in these chapters; the role belongs to Nehru.
(D) ✗ — Patel's recorded chair of this era is the Karachi INC Session of 1931; the States' Peoples' Conference presidency is credited to Nehru.

(Note: The All India States People's Conference was a political organisation of India. The First Session of the organisation was held on December, 1927 in Bombay. Jawaharlal Nehru was the President of this body.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: The real intention of the British to include the princely states in the Federal Union proposed by the India Act of 1935 was to

options.text: exercise more and direct political and administrative
involve the princes actively in the administration of the colony
finally effect the complete political and administrative take-over of all the princely states by the British
use the princes to counter-balance the anti-imperialist doctrines of the nationalist leaders

explanation: (D) ✓ — One-third of FA members were to be Nominees of the Princes — not elected. This practically eliminated the chances of an INC majority in the FA, which was the more powerful lower house. The Princes were brought in precisely to counter-balance the nationalist leaders.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Direct control was not the design: Paramountcy stayed as it was, and a Princely State entered the Federation only by voluntarily signing the Instrument of Accession — a 50% threshold that was never met.
(B) ✗ — The Princes' role in the scheme was to send nominees to the Federal Assembly — a legislative counterweight to INC, not active administrators of the colony.

(C) ✗ — A complete take-over is contradicted by the record: the Butler Committee had promised the British would not change the status of the Princely States without the consent of the Princes — accession was consensual, not confiscatory.

(Note: The princely states remained loyal to the British authorities till independence so Brtish included the princely states in the federal union proposed by the India Act of 1935 to use the princes to counter the nationalists.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.stem: Consider the following statements Some of the main features of the Government of India Act, 1935 were the
items: 1. abolition of diarchy in the Governor's provinces.
2. power of the Governors to veto legislative action and to legislate on their own.
3. abolition of the principle of communal representation.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statements 1 and 2 are both recorded features: Dyarchy ended. A Council of Ministers headed by a Premier (Chief Minister) was made responsible to the PLA, while the Governor kept veto power over bills and ordinance power. Statement 3 fails — separate electorates for all minorities continued as under GOI1919. Hence 1 and 2.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Undercounts: statement 2 is also true — the Governor retained veto power over bills and the power to legislate by ordinance.
(C) ✗ — Includes statement 3, which is false — communal representation was continued and even expanded, not abolished — and wrongly drops statement 1 (dyarchy did end in the provinces).
(D) ✗ — Fails on statement 3: separate electorates for all minorities continued as under GOI1919, with reservation extended to new groups.
(Note: The communal representation persisted in the Government of India Act of 1935. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.stem: In which one of the following provinces was a Congress Ministry not formed under the Act of 1935?
