questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: The Partition of India in 1947 was the outcome of structural failures of Indian constitutional negotiation between 1944 & 1947, not the inevitable consequence of the Two-Nation Theory. Examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" + "structural failures vs inevitable" demands a balanced analysis.

Suggested intro (~25 words): Partition was not pre-determined by the 1940 Lahore Resolution. It was the cumulative outcome of failed negotiations between September 1944 (Gandhi-Jinnah) and June 1947 (Mountbatten Plan).
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Rajaji Formula failure (see 'Proposals'). Gandhi-Jinnah talks Sep 1944. The Formula's sequence (freedom first, then plebiscite) was Gandhi's offer; Jinnah's counter was Two-Nation recognition first. Compromise architecture existed but was rejected.

2. Wavell Plan failure (see 'Wavell Plan, 1945'). Simla 1945. INC + ML structural parity in Executive Council was offered. Jinnah's demand for ML monopoly on Muslim seats — denying Maulana Azad (INC Muslim) any place — was unprecedented & rejected by Wavell. Collapsed.

3. Cabinet Mission Plan + INC ambiguity (see 'Cabinet Mission Plan (CMP1946)'). May-June 1946. The three-tier federation rejected outright Pakistan in favor of grouping. INC initially accepted but later qualified its acceptance on the compulsory grouping interpretation. ML responded with Direct Action Day (16 Aug 1946) → Calcutta Killings → communal violence cascade. INC's interpretive backtracking gave ML the political opening to walk away.

4. Mountbatten Plan as residual outcome (see '3rd June Plan / Mountbatten Plan (1947)'). By June 1947, alternative structures had repeatedly failed. Partition was offered not because it was preferred but because no other arrangement could be made operational. Mountbatten's compressed timeline (15 Aug 1947) made any alternative arrangement impossible.

Closing verdict: Partition reflected institutional inability to design a federal structure both INC & ML could accept. The Two-Nation Theory was ML's framework; INC's competing framework existed too. What failed was the negotiation architecture between them — across Rajaji, Wavell, Cabinet Mission. Partition was not inevitable; it was residual.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Examine how 565 Princely States were integrated into the Indian Union in 1947-49 through the Patel-Menon approach.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine how integrated" requires explaining the framework & tools used.

Suggested intro (~25 words): 565 Princely States had to be integrated quickly between June 1947 (Mountbatten Plan) & October 1948 (Hyderabad). Patel's Department of States + V.P. Menon designed the integration architecture.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'Integration of Princely States'):

1. The Two-Step Architecture. Step 1: Standstill Agreement (continuing existing administrative + economic relations). Step 2: Instrument of Accession (transferring 3 subjects — Defence, External Affairs, Communications — to Indian Union). This was the minimum legal commitment needed.

2. The Stick + Carrot. Patel's stick: implicit threat of public agitation, blockade, military action against holdouts. Carrot: Privy Purses (financial compensation), continued titles & ceremonial dignities, integration into Indian states administrative structure.

3. The Hard Cases. Most States acceded by 15 August 1947. Junagadh (Sept 1947) joined Pakistan but population was Hindu — plebiscite then Indian merger. Hyderabad (Sept 1948) resisted — Operation Polo (police action) forced accession. Kashmir (Oct 1947) — Pakistani tribal raid forced Maharaja Hari Singh's Instrument of Accession in exchange for Indian military intervention.

Closing verdict: The Patel-Menon framework integrated 565 disparate Princely Units within 15 months — an unprecedented administrative achievement. Without the Standstill + Instrument architecture, India would have inherited a fragmented sub-continent.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.1
questions.stem: The word Adivasi was used for the first time to refer to the tribal people by
explanation: (B) ✓ — Thakkar Bappa (Amrit Vithaldas Thakkar): the Servants-of-India-Society social worker who spent his life among remote tribal communities — it was he who gave currency to the word 'Adivasi' for the tribal people.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Gandhi's coinage in this field was 'Harijan', for the Depressed Classes — the name of his post-Poona-Pact campaign and magazine — not 'Adivasi'.
(C) ✗ — No 'Adivasi' coinage is recorded for Jyotiba Phule; the credit belongs to the tribal-welfare worker Thakkar Bappa.
(D) ✗ — Ambedkar's vocabulary and politics centred on the Depressed Classes and Scheduled Castes — AIDCC (1930), AISCF (1942); the word 'Adivasi' is Thakkar Bappa's.

(Note: Amrit Vithaldas Thakkar, popularly known as Thakkar Bappa. He became a member of the Servants of India Society founded by Gopal Krishna Gokhale in 1914. He was an Indian social worker, visited remotest areas.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.2
questions.stem: Which one of the following was an emigree communist journal of M.N. Roy?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Vanguard: M.N. Roy founded the communist journal Vanguard as a major emigre publication carrying the message of the 1917 October Revolution — from the same exile milieu in which he founded the CPI at Tashkent in 1920.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — 'Kisan Sabha' is the name of the peasant-organisation stream — the All India Kisan Sabha of 1936 under Swami Sahajanand Saraswati — not a Roy journal.
(B) ✗ — 'The Worker' is not Roy's recorded emigre journal; note that the first communist journal inside India was Dange's The Socialist — Roy's emigre paper was the Vanguard.
(D) ✗ — 'Anushilan' is the name of the Bengal revolutionary samiti tradition — a different stream altogether from Roy's communist journalism.
(Note: Manabendra Nath Roy (M.N.Roy) founder of communist newspaper Vanguard. It was a major publication for the Indian people about the 1917 October Revolution.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.3
questions.stem:
Which of the following political parties is/are national political parties?
1. Muslim League
2. Revolutionary Socialist Party
3. All India Forward Block
4. Peasants and Workers Party of India
Codes
explanation: (C) ✓ — Only statement 3 (All India Forward Bloc) is correct. AIFB, founded by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1939 after his break from INC, was an ECI-recognised national-level political party at the time of the 1995 UPSC examination. Statement 1 (Muslim League) — by 1995 the surviving Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) was a state-recognised party in Kerala only. Statement 2 (Revolutionary Socialist Party) was a state-recognised party in West Bengal and Kerala. Statement 4 (Peasants & Workers Party) was a state-recognised party in Maharashtra only. Therefore only AIFB qualified as a national party.
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — Includes the Muslim League and the Revolutionary Socialist Party, but by 1995 the IUML survived as a state party in Kerala and the RSP as a state-level party (see the ✓ entry above) — only the Forward Bloc carried national status.
(B) ✗ — The RSP and the Peasants and Workers Party were both state-level parties (✓ entry above) — and this code misses the one genuinely national party, the All India Forward Bloc.
(D) ✗ — Collects the three state-level parties and drops the only national one — the All India Forward Bloc (✓ entry above).

(Note: These all parties were regional level political parties during pre-independence time in India. However only Indian National congress which had least level presence almost entire nation, can be considered a national party.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.4
questions.stem: Who among the following was a prominent leader of the Congress Socialist Party?
explanation: (D) ✓ — In 1934, a group of young left-leaning leaders within the INC — Jayaprakash Narayan, Minoo Masani, and Acharya Narendra Dev — formed the Congress Socialist Party (CSP, 1934).
Wrong options:

(A) ✗ — M.N. Roy's recorded role is founding the CPI at Tashkent in 1920 and at Kanpur in 1925 — the communist stream, not the Congress Socialist Party, whose recorded founders are JP Narayan, Minoo Masani and Acharya Narendra Dev (✓ entry above).
(B) ✗ — Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi is not among the recorded CSP founders — the 1934 trio stands: Narayan, Masani, Narendra Dev (✓ entry above).
(C) ✗ — Pattam Thanu Pillai has no recorded CSP role; the party's recorded leadership is the 1934 trio including Acharya Narendra Dev (✓ entry above).
(Note: Acharya Narendra Dev, Minu Masani and Jai Prakash Narayan were the pioneers of Congress Socialist Party. It was formed in 1934 due to failure of Civil Disobedience Movement.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.5
questions.stem: Assertion (A) The effect of labour participation in the Indian nationalist upsurge of the early 1930s was weak. Reason (R) The labour leaders considered the ideology of Indian National Congress as bourgeois and reactionary. Codes

options.text: A and R are individually true and R is the correct explanation of A
A and R are individually true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

explanation: (A) ✓ — Both true, and R explains A.: the CPI1925 declared the INC a party of the bourgeoisie & described Nehru & Bose as representatives of propertied class interests, went on to oppose the CDM — and worker "participation fell well short of what it could have been". The labour leaders' bourgeois-reactionary reading of INC is exactly why labour's role in the early-1930s upsurge stayed weak.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — The explanation is direct, not incidental: the CPI's bourgeois labelling drove its boycott of the CDM, which is precisely why labour participation stayed weak. R does explain A.
(C) ✗ — R is not false: the bourgeois-and-reactionary characterisation of INC by the communist labour leadership is recorded verbatim.
(D) ✗ — A is not false: outside moments like the Sholapur strikes, working-class participation in the early-1930s upsurge remained limited.

(Note: The labour leaders were influenced by communist ideology and they looked Congress as a party of bourgeois and their ideology as reactionary. So, they did not participate in the Indian nationalist upsurge.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.6
questions.stem: During the colonial period in India, what was the purpose of the Whitley Commission?

options.text: To review the fitness of India for further political reforms
To report on existing conditions of labour and to make recommendations
To draw up a plan for financial reforms for India
To develop a comprehensive scheme for Civil Services in India

explanation: (B) ✓ — The Whitley Commission — formally the Royal Commission on Labour (1929)... was appointed to investigate labour conditions across British India, reporting in 1931 with recommendations on union recognition, collective bargaining, standardised wages and works committees.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Reviewing India's fitness for political reforms was the Simon Commission's brief; Whitley's subject was labour.
(C) ✗ — No financial-reform mandate is recorded; the Commission investigated labour conditions and employer practices.
(D) ✗ — Civil-services design was never its brief; the recorded charge was labour conditions, with recommendations that later shaped the Factories Act (1948) and Minimum Wages Act (1948).

(Note: Whitley Commission (1928) was appointed to report on existing conditions of labour in industrial undertakings and plantations in India on the basis of present working conditions, their health and hygiene.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.7
questions.stem: In October 1920, who of the following headed a group of Indians gathered at Tashkent to set-up communist party of India?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Roy, Abani Mukherji, and others and then set up within India in the Kanpur Conference held in December 1925 to unite scattered communist groups across India into a single legal party.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — H.K. Sarkar is not recorded at Tashkent; the founding names there are M.N. Roy, Abani Mukherji and others.
(B) ✗ — P.C. Joshi's era came later — General Secretary of CPI1925 from 1935 to 1947 — he was not the Tashkent founder of 1920.
(C) ✗ — M.C. Chagla has no recorded Tashkent role; the 1920 founding is credited to M.N. Roy and Abani Mukherji.
(Note: The group was made up of seven men with Avani Mukherjee, Muhammad Ali Shaid at Tashkent.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.8
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements
1. Jawaharlal Nehru was in his fourth term as the Prime Minister of India at the time of his death.
2. Jawaharlal Nehru represented Rae Bareilly constituency as a Member of Parliament.
3. The first non-Congress Prime Minister of India assumed the office in the year 1977.
Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — Statement 1 holds: Nehru's terms began in 1947, 1952, 1957 and 1962 — he was in his fourth term when he died in office in 1964. Statement 3 also holds: the first non-Congress Prime Minister took office only in 1977, long after Nehru's death. Statement 2 fails: Rae Bareilly was not Nehru's seat. Hence 1 and 3.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Includes the false Rae-Bareilly claim (statement 2) and drops statement 3, which holds — no non-Congress Prime Minister came before 1977.
(B) ✗ — Undercounts: the four terms listed (1947, 1952, 1957, 1962) make statement 1 true as well.
(C) ✗ — Drops statement 3, which stands — the first non-Congress Prime Minister belongs to 1977, after Nehru's era.

(Note: Jawaharlal Nehru became Prime Minister in 1947 for Ist term followed by an election in 1952 for 2nd term then election took place in 1957 and he elected for 3rd term and finally after winning 1962 election.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.9
questions.stem: Which one of the following places was associated with Acharya Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan Movement at the beginning of the movement?
explanation: (C) ✓ — Vinoba Bhave organised Sarvodaya Samaj to bring about non-violent social transformation through land reforms with the willing cooperation of landowners. Large landowners were persuaded to gift atleast one sixth of their land.
On 18th April, 1951, the first donation of land took place in a village called Pochampally in Telangana, Andhra Pradesh. But it was most successful mainly in Orissa.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Udaygiri is not the recorded starting point: the first land-gift of the Bhoodan movement took place at Pochampally village in Telangana on 18 April 1951 (✓ entry above).
(B) ✗ — Rapur has no recorded place in the movement's beginning — Pochampally is where Vinoba Bhave received the first donation of land (✓ entry above).
(D) ✗ — Venkatagiri is not the recorded site; the movement began at Pochampally, Telangana, in April 1951 (✓ entry above).

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.11
questions.stem: The demand for the Tebhaga Peasant Movement in Bengal was for

options.text: the reduction of the share of the landlords from one-half of the crop to one-third
the grant of ownership of land to peasants as they were the actual cultivators of the land
the uprooting of zamindari system and the end of serfdom

explanation: (A) ✓ — The Tebhaga ('three shares') demand: cut the landlord's share of the crop from one-half to one-third. records it directly: the famine-devastated peasantry fuelled the CPI-led Tebhaga movement (1946–47), demanding the landlord's share be reduced from half to one-third.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Ownership for the actual cultivator was the All India Kisan Sabha's Kisan-Manifesto demand — Tebhaga's recorded demand was the specific crop-share cut.
(C) ✗ — Uprooting zamindari and ending serfdom goes far beyond the recorded demand — Tebhaga asked for the harvest division to change from one-half to one-third.
(D) ✗ — Debt write-offs are not the recorded demand; Tebhaga was about the division of the crop between sharecropper and landlord.

(Note: The Tebhaga Movement was initiated in Bengal in 1946 by the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha to implement the Flood Commission recommendation, which asked for sharecroppers to give one third of their harvest.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.12
questions.stem: Which of the following parties were established by Dr BR Ambedkar?
items: 1. The Peasants and Workers Party of India.
2. All India Scheduled Castes Federation.
3. The Independent Labour Party.
questions.stemTail: Select the correct answer using the codes given below
explanation: (B) ✓ — Ambedkar formed the Independent Labour Party (1936) and the All India Scheduled Castes Federation (1942). The Peasants and Workers Party was not his — the Workers & Peasants Parties grew up inside the INC under communist leadership. Hence 2 and 3.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Wrongly credits the Peasants and Workers Party to Ambedkar — that formation belongs to the communist stream — and drops his Independent Labour Party of 1936.
(C) ✗ — Keeps the mis-credited Peasants and Workers Party (communist-led); Ambedkar's two recorded parties are the ILP and the AISCF.
(D) ✗ — Fails on statement 1: the Workers & Peasants Party network was built under communist leaders like S.A. Dange — not by Ambedkar.
(Note: Dr Ambedkar founded the Independent Labour Party in 1936. This party won in the 1937 elections to the Constituent Assembly. Further, all India Scheduled Castes Federation was founded by him.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.13
questions.stem: With reference to Congress Socialist Party, consider the following statements :
items: 1. It advocated the boycott of British goods and evasion of taxes.
2. It wanted to establish the dictatorship of proletariat.
3. It advocated separate electorate for minorities and oppressed classes.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: (D) ✓ — None matches the recorded CSP: it was a group of young left-leaning leaders who stayed inside the INC, rejecting the CPI1925's war on the Congress. Proletarian dictatorship belongs to the CPI stream; boycott-and-tax-evasion was the CDM's repertoire; and separate electorates were the divisive instrument the movement fought. Hence none.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Credits the CSP with a boycott-and-tax-evasion programme (the CDM's methods) and with proletarian dictatorship (the CPI stream) — neither is recorded of the CSP.
(B) ✗ — Separate electorates were never a CSP plank — they were the instrument the national movement resisted, settled by joint electorates in the Poona Pact.
(C) ✗ — Sweeps in all three unrecorded claims; the recorded CSP was a democratic-socialist ginger group within the Congress.
(Note: The Congress Socialist Party was founded by radical and young Congressmen who during their long-terms of imprisonment in the Civil Disobedience Movement came into contact with Marxist Ideas.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.14
questions.stem: The Trade Disputes Act of 1929 provided for

options.text: the participation of workers in the management of industries.
arbitrary powers to the management to quell industrial disputes.
an intervention by the British Court in the event of a 'trade dispute.
a system of tribunals and a ban on strikes.

explanation: (D) ✓ — The Trade Disputes Bill (1929) imposed significant restrictions on labour action, limiting the ability of workers to organise & strike effectively. Its machinery was a system of tribunals for disputes coupled with curbs amounting to a ban on strikes.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Worker participation in management is the opposite of the recorded design — the Act was a curbing statute against labour action.
(B) ✗ — The Act armed the state with restrictions on strikes; it did not hand managements arbitrary powers.
(C) ✗ — Court intervention is not the recorded mechanism — statutory tribunals plus strike restrictions were.
(Note: One of the most objectionable features of the original text of Trade Disputes Act of 1929 as follows • Any Union may apply to the Registrar for registration as a recognised Union.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.15
questions.stem: Consider the following statements :
items: 1. The Factories Act, 1881 was passed with a view to fix the wages of industrial workers and to allow the workers to form trade unions.
2. N.M. Lokhande was a pioneer in organising the labour movement in British India.
questions.stemTail: Which of the above statements is/are correct?
explanation: (B) ✓ — Statement 2 is recorded: in 1880, Narayan Lokhande started the Anglo-Marathi weekly Deen Bandhu, and by 1890 had set up the Bombay Mills & Mill Hands Association — the pioneer of labour organising in British India. Statement 1 fails: the Factory Act of 1881 limited working hours and child employment — it neither fixed wages nor allowed trade unions. Hence only 2.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Reversed: the 1881 Act's recorded content is hours and child-labour limits, not wages or union rights; Lokhande's pioneering is the true statement.
(C) ✗ — Statement 1 fails — union recognition came only with the Trade Union Act of 1926, four and a half decades after the 1881 Act — so 'both' overcounts.
(D) ✗ — Statement 2 stands: Lokhande's Deen Bandhu (1880) and Bombay Mills & Mill Hands Association (1890) are recorded — so 'neither' fails.

(Note: To improve the lot of the factory workers in towns, the first Factory Act was passed in 1881. The Act prohibited the employment of children under the age of seven, limited the number of working hours for children.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.16
questions.stem: Who among the following were the founders of the Hind Mazdoor Sabha established in 1948?

options.text: B Krishna Pillai, E.M.S. Namboodiripad and KC George
Jayaprakash Narayan, Deen Dayal Upadhyay and MN Roy
CP Ramaswamy Iyer, K Kamaraj and Veeresalingam Pantulu
Ashok Mehta, TS Ramanujam and GG Mehta

explanation: (D) ✓ — The Hind Mazdoor Sabha was founded at Howrah on 29 December 1948 by socialists, Forward-Bloc followers and independent unionists — with Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam and G.G. Mehta among its founders. The socialist stream here is the CSP lineage.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Krishna Pillai, E.M.S. Namboodiripad and K.C. George belong to the Kerala communist stream (the CPI's peasant build-up in Kerala), not to the socialist Hind Mazdoor Sabha.
(B) ✗ — An impossible trio: JP Narayan was CSP, M.N. Roy the Tashkent communist founder, and Deen Dayal Upadhyay of an entirely different political family — none founded the HMS.
(C) ✗ — C.P. Ramaswamy Iyer, Kamaraj and Veeresalingam have no recorded trade-union founding; the recorded HMS founders are those of option (d).
(Note: The Hind Mazdoor Sabha was founded in Hawrah in West Bengal on 29th December, 1948, by socialists, Forward Bloc followers and independent unionists.
Its founders included Basawon Singh (Sinha), Ashok Mehta and other socialist leaders.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.17
questions.stem: With reference to land reforms in independent India, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The ceiling laws were aimed at family holdings and not individual holdings.
The major aim of land reforms was providing agricultural land to all the landless.
It resulted in cultivation of cash crops as a predominant form of cultivation.
Land reforms permitted not exemptions to the ceiling limits.

explanation: (B) ✓ — Land reforms were enacted in independent India to distribute agriculture land equitably — the driving aim being land for the actual cultivator and the landless, the same impulse the freedom movement had built up (the Kisan Manifesto demanded ownership for those who cultivate).
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Misstates the ceiling design: the maximum size of land which could be owned by an individual was fixed — the family-not-individual claim fails.
(C) ✗ — Cash-crop predominance is no recorded result of land reform — the recorded purpose was equitable distribution of agricultural land.
(D) ✗ — The absolutism fails: ceiling laws did carry exemptions; the recorded essence of the reforms was equitable distribution, not exemption-free ceilings.

(Note: Land reforms were enacted in independent India to distribute agriculture land equitably. The ceiling on land was imposed and maximum size of land which could be owned by an individual was fixed.
The maximum ceiling varied from State to State.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.18
questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs.
    List I (Movement/Organisation) — List II (Leader)
1. All India Anti-Untouchability League — Mahatma Gandhi
2. All India Kisan Sabha — Swami Sahajanand Saraswati
3. Self-Respect Movement — EV Ramaswami Naicker
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
explanation: (a) Only 1
(b) 1 and 2
(c) 2 and 3
(d) 1, 2 and 3

(D) ✓ — All three pairs hold: the All India Anti-Untouchability League (1932) was Gandhi's creation, later the Harijan Sevak Sangh; the All India Kisan Sabha (1936) was founded under Swami Sahajanand Saraswati; and the Self-Respect Movement (1925) was Periyar's — E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker. Hence 1, 2 and 3.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Undercounts: the AIKS-Sahajanand pair and the Self-Respect-Periyar pair are also correctly matched.
(B) ✗ — Drops the Self-Respect-Naicker pair, which is correct — Periyar founded the movement in 1925.
(C) ✗ — Drops the Anti-Untouchability-League-Gandhi pair, which is correct — Gandhi set it up in 1932.
(Note: All India Anti-Untouchability League was established by Mahatma Gandhi in 1932 to better organise the untouchables.
It was later renamed as Harijan Sevak Sangh.
The All India Kisan Sabha was a Peasant organisation.)

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.19
questions.stem: The Vital- Vidhvansak, the first monthly journal to have the untouchable people as its target audience was published by
explanation: (A) ✓ — The Vital-Vidhvansak, the first monthly journal to have the untouchable people as its target audience was published by Gopal Baba Walangkar. He started publishing the monthly journal in 1888.He also wrote articles to Marathi-language newspapers such as Sudharak and Deenbandhu, besides composing couplets in Marathi that were intended to inspire the people. In 1889, he published Vital Viduvansan (An
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Phule's journalism is not the Vital-Vidhvansak; the recorded publisher of that first untouchable-audience monthly (1888) is Gopal Baba Walangkar (✓ entry above).
(C) ✗ — Gandhi's paper in this cause was the Harijan (1933) — four and a half decades after Walangkar's 1888 journal (✓ entry above).
(D) ✗ — Ambedkar's instruments were political — the ILP (1936) and AISCF (1942); the 1888 journal predates him and is Walangkar's (✓ entry above).

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.21
questions.stem: Consider the following regarding Constitution Day:I. Celebrated on 26th Nov.II. Drafting Committee set up on 26 Nov 1949.

options.text: Both Correct, II doesn't explain I

explanation: (C) ✓ — Statement I is correct: Constitution Day is 26 November — because on that day in 1949 the Constitution was adopted, i.e. finalised. Statement II is incorrect: 26 November 1949 marks adoption — the Drafting Committee, chaired by Ambedkar, had been constituted at the start of the constitution-writing process, not on that date. Hence I correct, II incorrect.
Wrong options:
(A) ✗ — Statement II is not correct — 26 November 1949 is the adoption date, not the Drafting Committee's creation date — so 'both correct' fails.
(B) ✗ — Same flaw: statement II is wrong on the record, however the explanation is framed.
(D) ✗ — Statement I is correct — Constitution Day is celebrated on 26 November for the 1949 adoption — so this option fails.

questions.label: PYQ_Pre.22
questions.stem: Who among the following was the founder of the ‘Self-Respect Movement’?
explanation: (A) ✓ — Among them was Periyar — EV Ramaswamy Naicker — who would go on to become the most radical voice of Dravidian anti-caste politics.
Wrong options:
(B) ✗ — Ambedkar's path ran through Mahad, the ILP and the AISCF; the Self-Respect Movement of the Madras Presidency was founded by Periyar in 1925.
(C) ✗ — Bhaskarrao Jadhav is not recorded as its founder; the movement is Periyar's, founded in 1925 in the wake of his Vaikom participation.
(D) ✗ — Dinkarrao Javalkar likewise has no recorded founding role; the Self-Respect Movement was founded by E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker — Periyar.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_1
questions.stem: Who founded the first modern organised trade union in India, the Madras Labour Union (1918)?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Sasipada Bannerjee, a Brahmo Samajist, set up the Working Men's Club in 1870 & launched Bharat Shramjeevi; not a trade union. (b) — Narayan Lokhande started the Anglo-Marathi weekly Deen Bandhu (1880) & the Bombay Mills & Mill Hands Association (1890), a philanthropic body, not a trade union. (d) — N.M. Joshi is associated with AITUC (1920), not the Madras Labour Union.
Memory hook: Madras Labour Union 1918 = B.P. Wadia — India's first modern organised trade union.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_2
questions.stem: Who was the first President of the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), established in 1920?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — N.M. Joshi is recognised as the founder of AITUC per the alert box; he was not its first president. (c) — S.A. Dange led the Bombay Textile Strikes (1928) & built the Girni Kamgar Union; not first AITUC president. (d) — Muzaffar Ahmad commanded the East (Bengal) wing of CPI; not first AITUC president.
Memory hook: AITUC 1920 — Lajpat Rai in the chair, the first all-India workers' platform.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_3
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Communist Party of India:
items: 1. It was first established in Tashkent in 1920 by M.N. Roy & Abani Mukherji.
2. The Kanpur Conference of December 1925 united scattered communist groups inside India into a single legal party.
3. M. Singaravelu Chettiar presided over the Kanpur session.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a), (b), (c) — All three statements are directly affirmed in: Tashkent 1920 founding by M.N. Roy & Abani Mukherji, Kanpur 1925 unification, and Singaravelu Chettiar presiding the Kanpur session.
Memory hook: Tashkent 1920 (Roy + Mukherji) abroad, Kanpur 1925 (Singaravelu chair) inside India.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_4
questions.stem: Who was the first leader to celebrate May Day in India in 1923?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — S.A. Dange led the Bombay Textile Strikes (1928) & founded The Socialist; not the May Day pioneer. (b) — Muzaffar Ahmad built the Workers & Peasants Party (WPP) in Bengal; not the May Day pioneer. (d) — P.C. Joshi served as General Secretary of CPI from 1935 to 1947; he did not introduce May Day in India.
Memory hook: Singaravelu Chettiar — Madras 1923, India's first May Day.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_5
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Trade Union Act, 1926:
items: 1. It gave legal recognition to trade unions for the first time.
2. It protected union funds from arbitrary seizure.
3. It imposed significant restrictions on the right to strike.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (b) 2 and 3 only — carries statement 3, which describes the Trade Disputes Bill (1929); restricting labour action was the opposite of what the 1926 Act did. (c) 1 and 3 only — same error on statement 3: the Trade Union Act, 1926 granted immunity for legitimate strike action, it did not curtail organising and striking. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — statement 3 is false, so the all-inclusive option cannot stand; only the recognition and fund-protection claims belong to the 1926 Act.
Memory hook: 1926 Trade Union Act protects (recognition + funds + strike immunity); 1929 Trade Disputes Bill restricts — similar names, opposite intent.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_6
questions.stem: Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order:
items: 1. Tashkent founding of CPI
2. First May Day in India
3. Kanpur Conference of communist groups
4. Meerut Conspiracy Case begins
explanation: Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) — Per & 1.9 the order is: CPI Tashkent (1920) → First May Day in India by Singaravelu (1923) → Kanpur Conference (December 1925) → Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929). Only option (a) preserves 1920 → 1923 → 1925 → 1929.
Memory hook: Tashkent 1920 → May Day 1923 → Kanpur 1925 → Meerut 1929 — left-movement timeline.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_7
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (CPI Leader) — List II (Defining Role)
items: 1. S.A. Dange
2. Muzaffar Ahmad
3. P.C. Joshi

4. M.N. Roy
A. Tashkent founding of CPI in 1920
B. General Secretary of CPI from 1935 to 1947
C. Bombay Textile Strikes & Girni Kamgar Union
D. Prime accused in the Meerut Conspiracy Case
matchTable: General Secretary of CPI from 1935 to 1947
Bombay Textile Strikes & Girni Kamgar Union
Prime accused in the Meerut Conspiracy Case
explanation: Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) — Per: Dange = Bombay Textile Strikes 1928 + Girni Kamgar Union (C); Muzaffar Ahmad = prime accused, Meerut Conspiracy Case 1929-33 (D); P.C. Joshi = General Secretary 1935-47 (B); M.N. Roy = co-founder at Tashkent 1920 (A).
Memory hook: Dange-Bombay, Muzaffar-Meerut, Joshi-GenSec, Roy-Tashkent.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_8
questions.stem: Which CPI leader spearheaded the creation of the Indian People's Theatre Association (IPTA) and the Progressive Writers' Association (PWA) to take the anti-imperialist message to the rural masses?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Dange founded The Socialist & led the Bombay Textile Strikes (1928); not the IPTA/PWA architect. (c) — Muzaffar Ahmad built the WPP in Bengal & was prime accused in the Meerut Case; not IPTA/PWA. (d) — Singaravelu Chettiar presided the Kanpur session 1925 & celebrated India's first May Day 1923; not IPTA/PWA.
Memory hook: P.C. Joshi — IPTA + PWA, art as anti-imperial propaganda.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_9
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley Commission), 1929:
items: 1. It submitted its report in 1929, the same year in which it was appointed.
2. Its Indian members included GD Birla & N.M. Joshi.
3. Its recommendations on tripartite consultative bodies laid the intellectual foundation for the Indian Labour Conference after independence.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — statement 1 is false: the Commission was appointed in 1929 but submitted its report only in 1931. (c) 1 and 3 only — same error on statement 1; 1929 is the year of appointment, not the year of the report. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — statement 1 is false, so the everything option fails; statements 2 and 3 alone are affirmed.
Memory hook: Whitley — appointed 1929, reported 1931; Birla + N.M. Joshi among six Indian members; tripartite blueprint for the Indian Labour Conference.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_10
questions.stem: Following which directive did the CPI declare the INC a party of the bourgeoisie & sever itself from the largest mass movement in India?
explanation: Why others wrong: (b) — The 7th World Congress (1935) actually reversed course, directing communist parties to unite with all anti-fascist forces; bringing CPI back toward INC. (c) — The October Revolution (1917) inspired the formation of communist parties worldwide; it did not direct opposition to the INC. (d) — The Kanpur Conference (1925) united communist groups inside India; it did not order break with the INC.
Memory hook: 6th Comintern 1928 — "oppose all non-communists" — CPI breaks from INC.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_11
questions.stem: Who founded the Congress Socialist Party (CSP) within the INC in 1934 along with Minoo Masani and Acharya Narendra Dev?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Bose represented the broader left wing inside INC alongside Nehru, but was not a CSP founder. (b) — Nehru represented the INC left wing but did not found the CSP. (d) — M.N. Roy co-founded the CPI at Tashkent in 1920; not the CSP.
Memory hook: CSP 1934 — JP + Masani + Narendra Dev, left-but-inside-Congress.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_12
questions.stem: Which organisation, set up in 1927, became the organised voice of Indian business & refused to negotiate with the British government on constitutional or economic issues without the approval or participation of the INC?

options.text: Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industry

explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — AITUC (1920) was an all-India workers' body, not a business chamber. (c) — The Bombay Mills & Mill Hands Association (1890) was a workers' welfare body set up by Narayan Lokhande. (d) — AIKS (1936) was a peasants' organisation under Swami Sahajanand Saraswati, not a business body.
Memory hook: FICCI 1927 — Indian business voice that spoke only through the INC.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_13
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Bombay Plan (1944):
items: 1. It was drafted by eight leading Indian industrialists & technocrats including JRD Tata, GD Birla, and Purushottamdas Thakurdas.
2. It called for the outright nationalisation of basic industries & workers' control over their management.
3. It called for doubling India's per capita income within 15 years through three five-year plans.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) 1 and 2 only — statement 2 is false: the Plan asked for state *investment* in a mixed economy, not state *ownership*; outright nationalisation or workers' control was precisely what Indian capitalists would not accept. (b) 2 and 3 only — same error on statement 2, and it drops the correctly stated eight-author roll-call. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — statement 2 is false; the left in fact attacked the Bombay Plan for not going far enough and for protecting private property.
Memory hook: Bombay Plan 1944 — eight capitalists ask for state investment, not state ownership; mixed economy, per capita income doubled in 15 years.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_14
questions.stem: Which Satyagraha of 1924-25 was the first major organised temple-entry movement of the modern period, led by the Ezhava community with Narayan Guru & K. Kesava Menon at the forefront?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Mahad Satyagraha (1927) was Ambedkar's water-tank Satyagraha in Maharashtra, not a temple-entry movement. (c) — Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931-33) came later, led by K. Kellapan in Malabar. (d) — Kalaram Temple agitation (Nasik) was the one Ambedkar in 1934 asked Satyagrahis to stop & instead boycott temples.
Memory hook: Vaikom 1924-25 — Ezhavas + Narayan Guru + Kesava Menon, the first big temple-entry push.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_15
questions.stem: At which Satyagraha in 1927 did Dr B.R. Ambedkar lead 15,000 Dalits to draw water from a public tank & publicly burn the Manusmriti?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25) was led by the Ezhava community for road access near the Vaikom temple, not by Ambedkar. (b) — Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931-33) was led by K. Kellapan in Malabar for temple entry, not by Ambedkar. (d) — At the Kalaram Temple (Nasik) in 1934, Ambedkar asked Satyagrahis to stop & boycott temples altogether.
Memory hook: Mahad 1927 — 15,000 Dalits at the tank, Manusmriti burnt in December.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_16
questions.stem: Arrange the following Dalit-rights events in correct chronological order:
items: 1. Mahad Satyagraha
2. Vaikom Satyagraha
3. Communal Award
4. Poona Pact
explanation: Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) — Per, 3.5 & 3.8 the order is Vaikom (1924-25) → Mahad (1927) → Communal Award (August 1932) → Poona Pact (September 1932). Only (a) preserves 1924 → 1927 → Aug 1932 → Sep 1932.
Memory hook: Vaikom → Mahad → Communal Award → Poona Pact — Dalit timeline 1924-1932.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_17
questions.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (Organisation) — List II (Founder/Lead Figure)
items: 1. All India Depressed Classes Association (1926)
2. All India Depressed Classes Congress (1930)
3. Independent Labour Party (1936)

4. All India Scheduled Castes Federation (1942)
A. MC Rajah of Madras
B. Dr B.R. Ambedkar — anti-INC, negotiates with British directly
C. Dr B.R. Ambedkar — merged workers & untouchables
D. Dr B.R. Ambedkar — Dalits distinct from Hindus
matchTable: Dr B.R. Ambedkar — anti-INC, negotiates with British directly
Dr B.R. Ambedkar — merged workers & untouchables
Dr B.R. Ambedkar — Dalits distinct from Hindus
explanation: Why others wrong: (b), (c), (d) — Per: AIDCA (1926) was formed under MC Rajah of Madras (A); AIDCC (1930) was Ambedkar's anti-INC negotiating body (B). Per: ILP (1936) merged poor workers & untouchables (C); AISCF (1942) was founded with the motto that Dalits are distinct from Hindus (D).
Memory hook: AIDCA-Rajah, AIDCC-anti-INC, ILP-class+caste, AISCF-distinct.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_18
questions.stem: Who published Comparison Between Women & Men (1882), arguing that men enjoyed all rights while women were reduced to the stereotype of the pativrata?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Pandita Ramabai married a Sudra man, converted to Christianity & raised funds for a widow's home in Bombay; she did not author the 1882 tract. (c) — Sarala Debi Chaudhrani founded Bharat Stree Mandal (1910) & led the physical-culture movement for Bengal's youth; not the 1882 author. (d) — Sarojini Naidu led the 1917 women's-vote delegation & became INC President in 1925; not the 1882 author.
Memory hook: Tarabai Shinde 1882 — first frontal challenge to the pativrata stereotype.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_19
questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Sarda Act, 1929:
items: 1. Its formal name was the Child Marriage Restraint Act.
2. It set the minimum age of marriage at 14 for girls.
3. It also granted women rights in property, inheritance, and divorce.
questions.stemTail: Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Why others wrong: (b) 2 and 3 only — statement 3 is false: the Sarda Act only restrained child marriage (14 for girls, 18 for males); property, inheritance and divorce were covered by separate bills passed in the 1930s. (c) 1 and 3 only — same error on statement 3, and it drops the correctly stated girls' minimum age of 14. (d) 1, 2 and 3 — statement 3 is false, so the everything option fails; only the formal name and the age of 14 for girls are correct.
Memory hook: Sarda Act 1929 = ages only (14 girls / 18 males); property, inheritance and divorce bills came separately through the 1930s.

questions.label: FYQ_Pre_20
questions.stem: Under whose leadership was the All India Women's Conference (AIWC) founded in 1927?
explanation: Why others wrong: (a) — Annie Besant was central to the Home Rule League Movement (1916-18); she did not found AIWC. (b) — Sarojini Naidu led the 1917 women's-vote delegation & became INC President in 1925; she did not found AIWC. (d) — Sarala Debi Chaudhrani established the Bharat Stree Mandal (1910); she did not found AIWC.
Memory hook: AIWC 1927 — Margaret Cousins, Irish feminist, the most significant women's body.

questions.label: FYQ_M.1
questions.stem: The INM, while presenting itself as a national movement, marginalised the voices of workers, capitalists, Dalits & women in different ways. Examine.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine" + "marginalised in different ways" demands tracing how each group was excluded from INC's core agenda.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The INC's mass strategy was built on coalition-management. To hold the coalition together, it consistently subordinated class, caste & gender questions to the national-political question.
Body guidance — 4 themes:

1. Workers (see 'The Working Class Movement'). Trade unions were tactically supported (AITUC 1920, Lajpat Rai presidency) but never made central to INC's economic platform. Gandhi's Trusteeship framework rejected class struggle. The INC stayed close to capitalists; trade union autonomy under N.M. Joshi & later CPI was tolerated, not integrated.

2. Capitalists (see 'The Role of Indian Capitalists in the INM'). Funded the INC (FICCI 1927, Bombay Plan 1944) but were marginalised in INC's public ideology — Gandhi's anti-modern, anti-industrial framing was uncomfortable for capitalists. Their political voice was muted publicly, even as their financial role grew.

3. Dalits (see 'The Voice of Dalits'). Ambedkar's Mahad Satyagraha 1927, Round Table Conference advocacy, & 1932 Communal Award protest revealed that INC's framework could not accommodate Depressed Classes as autonomous political actors. Poona Pact 1932 ended separate electorates but left reserved-seats-within-Hindu-electorate as second-best compromise. Ambedkar's 1956 conversion to Buddhism expressed his judgment that Hinduism could not be reformed from within.

4. Women (see 'The Voice of Women'). AIWC 1927 led on women's issues. INC mobilised women for civil disobedience (1930 salt march, 1942 QIM) but did not promote them to organisational or parliamentary leadership — Sarala Debi Chaudhrani's "lawbreakers not lawmakers" line captured this.

Closing verdict: The INC's "Many Voices" framing was strategic absorption, not genuine representation. Each constituency — labour, capital, Dalit, women — found INC useful as a vehicle for some demands but had to develop separate organisational forms for autonomous representation. The post-1947 Indian state inherited this incomplete integration as its structural problem.

questions.label: FYQ_M.2
questions.stem: Examine the historical significance of the Ambedkar-Gandhi confrontation over the Communal Award (1932) for the politics of Dalit representation.
body: Demand of the question: "Examine the significance" demands tracing the structural meaning of the conflict.

Suggested intro (~25 words): The Ambedkar-Gandhi confrontation over the Communal Award (1932) was not just about electorates — it was about whether Dalits could be politically autonomous from the Hindu fold.
Body guidance — 3 themes (see 'The Voice of Dalits'):

1. The Award's framing. Communal Award (August 1932) by Ramsay MacDonald provided separate electorates for Depressed Classes — meaning Dalits could elect their own representatives from their own electorate, NOT from a combined Hindu electorate. This was Ambedkar's position: Dalits as an autonomous political community.

2. Gandhi's Fast Unto Death. Gandhi opposed separate electorates because they would split the "Hindu" fold permanently. His fast unto death at Yerwada Jail forced Ambedkar to accept the Poona Pact compromise (24 September 1932) — reserved seats within joint Hindu electorates. Ambedkar agreed under moral pressure, not conviction.

3. The long shadow. The compromise meant Dalits remained politically attached to the Hindu electorate; their representatives needed Hindu votes to win. Ambedkar saw this as second-best; his later trajectory (1936 Independent Labour Party, 1942 Scheduled Castes Federation, 1956 Buddhist conversion) showed his rejection of the assumption that Dalits could be represented through Hindu-mediated structures.

Closing verdict: The 1932 confrontation was the foundational debate of Dalit political autonomy. Gandhi won the immediate constitutional battle; Ambedkar's long-term diagnosis — that Hindu structures cannot represent Dalits — has shaped Indian politics ever since.
revise: Voice of Dalits — Ambedkar + Poona Pact
